Bhagavad Gītā 1:
Now begins the chapter entitled "The Yoga of Arjuna’s Despondency."
First Chapter.
Commentary composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya.
Introduction: Om. Nārāyaṇa is beyond the unmanifest; the cosmic egg originates from the unmanifest.
Within this egg are these worlds and the earth with its seven continents.

Having created this world, that Blessed One, desiring to maintain its stability, first created Marīci and others—the Prajāpatis—and caused them to grasp the dharma characterized by worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*) as declared in the Vedas. Then, having produced others such as Sanaka and Sanandana, he caused them to grasp the dharma characterized by renunciation (*nivṛtti*), which is defined by knowledge and dispassion. For the dharma declared in the Vedas is twofold: that characterized by engagement and that characterized by renunciation; it is the cause for the maintenance of the world.

Dharma is that which is the direct cause of the prosperity and the supreme good for living beings; it is practiced by those belonging to the castes, such as Brahmins, and by those in the stages of life, all seeking their own welfare.

After a long time, when *dharma* was being overwhelmed by *adharma*—caused by the declining discriminative knowledge of practitioners due to the arising of desire—and while *adharma* was increasing, that primordial creator known as Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa, desiring to protect the stability of the world, manifested as Kṛṣṇa through a portion of himself from Vasudeva and Devakī for the sake of protecting Bhauma Brahmā and the status of the *brāhmaṇas*. For by the protection of the *brāhmaṇa* status, Vedic *dharma* would be protected, since the distinctions of the social classes (*varṇas*) and stages of life (*āśramas*) are dependent upon it.

And that Blessed One, ever endowed with knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor, having brought under his control his own Māyā—the Vaiṣṇavī primordial nature consisting of the three guṇas—is unborn, undecaying, the Lord of beings, and by nature eternally pure, awakened, and liberated; yet, through his own Māyā, he appears as if possessing a body and as if born, manifesting grace toward the worlds.

Even in the absence of any personal motive, the Blessed One taught the two-fold Vedic dharma to Arjuna, who was submerged in a great ocean of grief and delusion, out of a desire to favor all beings; for dharma, when adopted and practiced by those superior in virtue, will attain great expansion. The omniscient Lord Vedavyāsa committed that dharma, exactly as it was taught by the Blessed One, to writing in seven hundred verses known as the Gītā.

This Gītā-śāstra is a compendium of the essence of the meaning of all the Vedas, yet its meaning is difficult to comprehend. Although it has been commented upon by many through the analysis of words, word-meanings, sentences, sentence-meanings, and logic, it is observed that worldly people grasp it as having many mutually contradictory meanings. Therefore, for the sake of determining its true meaning through discernment, I shall provide a concise commentary.

The ultimate purpose of this scripture of the Gītā, stated concisely, is supreme liberation (*niḥśreyasa*), characterized by the absolute cessation of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) along with its causes. And that [liberation] arises from the dharma consisting of steadfastness in self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*), preceded by the renunciation of all ritual actions (*sarvakarmasaṃnyāsa*). To this very same dharma, which is the subject matter of the Gītā, the Blessed One himself has said in the *Anugītā*: "For that dharma is fully sufficient for the realization of the state of Brahman" (Mbh 14.16.12).

And it is said in that very same place: "Neither a follower of dharma nor a follower of adharma, and indeed neither virtuous nor non-virtuous; he who is absorbed in the solitary path, silent and not thinking of anything" (Mbh 14.19.7), and "Knowledge has the characteristic of renunciation" (Mbh 14.43.26). And here too, at the conclusion, it was said to Arjuna: "Abandoning all duties, take refuge in Me alone" (Gītā 18.66).

Furthermore, even that dharma characterized by worldly activity (*pravṛtti*) which is prescribed with reference to the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*) for the sake of prosperity (*abhyudaya*), although it is a cause for attaining states such as those of the gods, becomes a means for the purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*) when performed with the intention of dedicating the action to the Lord and free from desire for fruits. And for one whose mind is purified, it also serves as a cause for the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) by way of attaining fitness for steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*) and by being a cause for the arising of knowledge.

And with reference to this very point, he will say: "Having surrendered all actions to Brahman" (Gītā 5.10), and "Yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the purification of the self" (Gītā 5.11).

This scripture of the Gītā possesses a specific purpose, a connection, and a subject matter, as it specifically manifests this twofold doctrine which has the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) as its aim: the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*) known as Vāsudeva, who is the denotable object of the Supreme Brahman. Since the accomplishment of all human goals is achieved through the knowledge of its meaning, I shall therefore make an effort to provide a commentary upon it.
On the field of dharma, at Kurukshetra, gathered together and desiring to fight—
what did my sons and the Pandavas do, O Sanjaya? (BhG 1.1)
Saṃjaya said:
Having seen the Pāṇḍava army drawn up in battle array, King Duryodhana then approached the Teacher and spoke these words.
Behold, O Teacher, this vast army of the sons of Pāṇḍu,
arrayed by the wise son of Drupada, your own disciple.
Here are heroes, great archers equal in battle to Bhīma and Arjuna:
Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada, the great car-warrior.
Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the valiant King of Kashi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Shaibya, that bull among men; BhG 1.5.
And Yudhāmanyu, the valiant, and the heroic Uttamaujas,
as well as the son of Subhadrā and the sons of Draupadī— all of them indeed are great chariot-warriors (mahārathas).
But as for those who are distinguished among us, O best of the twice-born, learn of them;
I shall name to you the leaders of my army for your information.
Yourself, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and Kṛpa, victorious in assembly;
Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, the son of Somadatta, and Jayadratha— BhG 1.8.
And there are many other heroes who have renounced their lives for my sake;
they carry various weapons and missiles, and all are experts in battle.
That army of ours, protected by Bhīṣma, is insufficient;
but this army of theirs, protected by Bhīma, is sufficient.
And in all the divisions, stationed each according to your respective positions,
may you all indeed protect Bhīṣma alone.
Inspiring his joy, the powerful grandfather, the elder of the Kurus,
let out a loud lion’s roar and blew his conch shell.
Then conchs, kettledrums, cymbals, drums, and horns were suddenly sounded; that sound became tumultuous.
Then, stationed upon a great chariot yoked with white horses,
Mādhava and the son of Pāṇḍu blew their divine conch shells.
Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya, Dhanañjaya the Devadatta,
and Vṛkodara, the doer of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra.
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, has the Anantavijaya;
Nakula and Sahadeva have the Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka respectively.
And Kāśya, the supreme archer; Śikhaṇḍin, the great chariot-warrior;
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa, and the unconquered Sātyaki.
Drupada and the sons of Draupadī, O lord of the earth,
as well as the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā, each separately blew their conch shells.
That tumultuous sound, making both heaven and earth resound, rent asunder the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Then, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra arrayed for battle, the son of Pāṇḍu, whose banner bears the emblem of the monkey, raised his bow as the discharge of weapons was about to begin.
Then, O lord of the earth, he spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa:
"O Acyuta, station my chariot between the two armies."
While I am thus observing these who stand here desiring to fight,
with whom must I contend in this exertion for battle?
I behold those who have gathered here,
desiring to do what is pleasing in battle to the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as they prepare for combat.
Thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, having stationed that best of chariots between the two armies, [said: ||BhG_1.24||
In the presence of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and all the rulers of the earth,
he said, "O Pārtha, behold these Kurus assembled here."
There, Pārtha saw standing his fathers and grandfathers,
as well as teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends.
Having beheld all those kinsmen standing there— both fathers-in-law and friends in both armies— that son of Kuntī [was overcome].

Overcome by supreme compassion and despondent at seeing these kinsmen standing here eager for battle, O Kṛṣṇa, he spoke this: 28. Seeing these kinsmen standing here eager for battle, O Kṛṣṇa, [he was overcome].
My limbs fail me and my mouth is parched;
a trembling comes over my body and my hair stands on end. (BhG 1.29)
The Gāṇḍīva bow slips from my hand and my skin is burning all over;
I am unable to remain standing, and my mind seems to be reeling.
And I see adverse omens, O Keśava;
nor do I foresee any good in slaying my own kinsmen in battle.
I do not desire victory, O Kṛṣṇa, nor kingdom, nor pleasures.
What is the use of kingdom to us, O Govinda, or what use are enjoyments or even life itself?
For whose sake we desire kingdom, enjoyments, and pleasures—
those very people stand here in battle, having abandoned their lives and their wealth.
Teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers;
maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives.
I do not wish to kill these men, O Madhusūdana, even though they are killing me,
not even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds, much less for the sake of the earth.
O Janārdana, what joy could there be for us after slaying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?
By killing these aggressors, only sin would take hold of us.
Therefore, O Mādhava, we ought not to slay the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, our own kinsmen; for how, having slain our own people, could we be happy?
Even though these people, their minds overwhelmed by greed, do not perceive the evil in the destruction of a family nor the sin in treachery toward friends.
How is it that we do not understand how to turn back from this sin,
O Janārdana, while clearly perceiving the evil brought about by the destruction of our own kin?
Upon the destruction of the family, the eternal family traditions perish;
when dharma is lost, adharma overcomes the entire family.
O Kṛṣṇa, through the overwhelming of dharma, the women of the family become corrupted;
O Vārṣṇeya, when women are corrupted, a confusion of castes arises.
The confusion of castes leads only to hell for both the destroyers of the family and the family itself;
for their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water.
By these faults of the destroyers of the family, which cause the intermixture of castes, the eternal laws of the classes and the laws of the family are destroyed.
O Janārdana, we have heard from tradition that for those men whose family traditions are destroyed, residence in hell is inevitable.
Alas! We have resolved to commit a great sin, in that, out of greed for the pleasures of sovereignty, we are prepared to slay our own kinsmen.
If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with weapons in hand, should slay me in battle while I am unarmed and unresisting, that would be better for me.
Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna sat down on the seat of his chariot,
casting aside his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed with grief.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Commentary on the Gītā composed by Śaṅkarācārya. ||1||
Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter Two:
The Second Discourse
Saṃjaya said: To him who was thus overcome with pity, whose eyes were clouded and filled with tears,
and who was despondent, Madhusūdana spoke these words.
Whence has this dejection come upon you in this hour of crisis, O Arjuna? It is unworthy of the noble, it leads away from heaven, and it brings infamy.
Do not yield to unmanliness, O Pārtha; it does not befit you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and arise, O scorcher of the foe! (BhG 2.3)
O Madhusūdana, O slayer of enemies, how shall I fight back with arrows in battle against Bhīṣma and Droṇa, who are worthy of worship?
Indeed, it is better to live even on alms in this world than to slay these high-souled gurus;
for by slaying gurus who are motivated by worldly gain and desire, one would only find misery right here.
I would enjoy pleasures stained with blood.
And we do not know which is better for us: whether we should conquer them, or whether they should conquer us;
for having slain whom we do not wish to live.
Those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra stand arrayed before me.
My nature overwhelmed by the defect of pity, and my mind confused about duty, I ask you;
tell me decisively that which would be for my highest good.
I am your disciple; instruct me, who have taken refuge in you.
For I do not perceive what, even having obtained unrivaled prosperity on earth, would dispel this grief of mine that withers the senses.
Even sovereignty over the gods and lordship over the realm.
Saṃjaya said: Having thus spoken to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa, the scorcher of foes,
said to Govinda, "I will not fight," and became silent.
O descendant of Bharata, Hṛṣīkeśa, as if smiling, spoke these words to him who was despondent in the midst of the two armies: BhG 2.10.

And here, the section of the text beginning with "Having seen the army of the Pāṇḍavas" and ending with "Having said to Govinda, 'I will not fight,' he became silent" is to be explained as having the purpose of demonstrating the cause for the arising of defects—such as grief and delusion—which constitute the seed of saṃsāra for living beings.

For instance, Arjuna demonstrated his own grief and delusion—caused by the severance of affection and other such factors rooted in the false notion that "I am theirs" or "these belong to me"—regarding the kingdom, teachers, sons, friends, well-wishers, kinsmen, relatives, and blood-brothers. This was shown through the passage beginning with, "How shall I fight Bhīṣma in battle? and so forth. Indeed, one whose discriminative knowledge is overwhelmed by grief and delusion ceases from that very battle, even though he had previously been engaged in it according to the duty of a Kṣatriya.

And he proceeded to perform the duties of others, such as living on alms and so forth. Likewise, for all living beings whose minds are possessed by defects such as grief and delusion, there would naturally be an abandonment of their own duty (svadharma) and the practice of what is forbidden. Even for those engaged in their own duty, the activity of their speech, mind, body, and so forth, would be preceded solely by the desire for results.

And she (the intellect) becomes possessed of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*). This being the case, because of the accumulation of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*)—characterized by the attainment of birth, pleasure, pain, and so forth, whether desirable or undesirable—continues without ceasing. Therefore, grief and delusion (*śoka-moha*) constitute the seeds of *saṃsāra*. Since their cessation does not occur through any means other than the knowledge of the Self (*ātma-jñāna*) preceded by the renunciation of all actions (*sarva-karma-saṃnyāsa*), the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, desiring to teach that [knowledge] for the sake of favoring the whole world, spoke the words beginning with "those who are not to be grieved for" (*aśocyān*), taking Arjuna as the occasion.

On this point, some say: "Liberation is certainly not attained through mere steadfastness in self-knowledge alone, preceded by the renunciation of all actions. What then? Liberation is attained through knowledge conjoined with the Śrauta and Smārta rites such as the Agnihotra; this is the definitive meaning established throughout the Gītā. And they cite supporting evidence for this position:

Furthermore, regarding the objection that Vedic action leads to unrighteousness (*adharma*) because it involves violence and the like—as expressed in such passages as "If you do not engage in this righteous battle" (Gītā 2.33), "Your right is to action alone" (Gītā 2.47), and "Therefore, perform action itself" (Gītā 4.15)—this suspicion should not be entertained. Why? Because the duty of a Kṣatriya, characterized by battle and involving the killing of teachers, brothers, sons, and others—though exceedingly cruel—is not unrighteous, since it is one's own specific duty (*svadharma*).

And by stating, "By not performing that, you will abandon your own duty and fame and incur sin" (Gītā 2.33), it is clearly established that actions enjoined by Vedic injunctions such as "as long as one lives," as well as those characterized by the injury of animals and so forth, are certainly not unrighteous (*adharma*) from the outset.

That is incorrect. Because of the statement regarding the distinction between the two types of steadfastness—steadfastness in knowledge and steadfastness in action—the portion of the text beginning with "Those who are not to be grieved for" and ending with "and having also considered one's own duty," in which the Lord has provided a determination of the reality of the supreme Self, that is *sāṃkhya*. The intellect (*buddhi*) directed toward that [reality], which arises from the determination of the meaning of the context—that the Self is a non-agent because it is devoid of the six modifications such as birth—is the *sāṃkhya-buddhi*.

Those wise ones for whom this [knowledge] is appropriate are the Sāṃkhyas. Prior to the birth of this intellect, there is *yoga*, characterized by the practice of the means to liberation preceded by the discrimination between dharma and adharma, which depends upon the self’s being distinct from the body and so forth, and its being an agent and an enjoyer. The intellect whose object is that is *yogabuddhi*. Those performers of action (*karmiṇaḥ*) for whom it is appropriate are the Yogins.

And thus, two distinct types of intelligence have been pointed out by the Blessed One as analyzed: "This intelligence has been declared to you according to Sāṃkhya; now hear this [intelligence] regarding Yoga. And he will later declare the distinct steadfastness of the Sāṃkhyas, which rests upon Sāṃkhya-intelligence, as being through the yoga of knowledge, saying: "It was proclaimed by me in the past in the form of the Veda. Likewise, he will declare the distinct steadfastness resting upon Yoga-intelligence as being through the yoga of action, saying: "Of the yogis, [it is] by the yoga of action."

Thus, relying on the Sāṃkhya understanding and the Yoga understanding, the Lord Himself has declared two distinct goals for knowledge and action—which respectively rely on the understandings of agency and non-agency, and unity and multiplicity—having perceived the impossibility of these two residing simultaneously in a single person.

This very statement regarding the distinction has been shown in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*: "Desiring this world alone, the Brahmins go forth as wanderers" (*BAU* 4.4.22). Having thus enjoined the renunciation of all ritual actions (*sarvakarma-saṃnyāsa*), it continues with the remainder: "What shall we do with offspring, for us who have this Self, this world? (*BAU* 4.4.22). And in that same passage, prior to the taking of a wife, a person is a natural self; thereafter, following the desire to know Dharma, he becomes a means for accomplishing the three worlds.

A son, two kinds of wealth, and two kinds of human [wealth]. Among these, human wealth consists of ritual action (*karman*), which is the means for attaining the world of the ancestors, and knowledge (*vidyā*), which is divine wealth, the means for attaining the world of the gods.

In the passage, "He desired" (BAU 1.4.17), all ritual actions, such as those prescribed by the Śruti, are shown to belong specifically to one who possesses ignorance and desire. However, the renunciation expressed in "Having risen above these, they go forth" (BAU 4.4.22) is ordained for one who is free from desire and seeks only the Self as his world. This statement of distinction would be untenable if the Blessed One had intended the combination of ritual action based on the Śruti and knowledge.

Furthermore, Arjuna’s question—beginning with "If, in Your view, wisdom is superior to action" (Gītā 3.1)—would not be appropriate. Since the impossibility of wisdom and action being performed by a single person was not previously stated by the Blessed One, how could Arjuna, having understood what he had not heard, falsely superimpose upon the Blessed One the superiority of wisdom over action by saying, "If, in Your view, wisdom is superior to action"?

Furthermore, if the combination of both intellect (*buddhi*) and action (*karman*) had been taught for everyone, then it would have been taught for Arjuna as well; in that case, how could there be a question regarding only one of the two when both had been instructed? For instance, when a physician instructs a person seeking to pacify bile (*pitta*) that "both sweet and cold food should be eaten," it is not possible for that person to ask, "Tell me which one of these two is the cause for pacifying bile."

Even if it were assumed that Arjuna’s question was prompted by his failure to discern the meaning of the words spoken by the Blessed One, the Blessed One should nevertheless have provided an answer corresponding to that question, saying: "I have taught the conjunction of knowledge and action; for what reason are you thus deluded? It would not, however, be appropriate for him to give an inconsistent reply, stating something entirely different from what was asked, such as: "Two types of steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*) were previously declared by me."

Furthermore, if the intended combination with the intellect (*buddhi*) pertains solely to action prescribed by the Smṛti, then all such statements regarding their distinction and so forth would be untenable. Moreover, for a Kṣatriya who knows that fighting is his own duty (*svadharma*) as a Smārta action, the reproach—"Why do you urge me toward this terrible deed?"—would be unjustified.

Therefore, in the Gītā scripture, it is impossible for anyone to demonstrate the combination of self-knowledge with even the slightest degree of ritual action, whether based on the Vedas (*śrauta*) or the Smṛtis (*smārta*). However, for one who—having been engaged in action due to ignorance or defects such as passion, and whose being (*sattva*) has been purified by sacrifice, charity, or austerity—has attained knowledge concerning the supreme reality of truth, namely that "all this is indeed the one Brahman and is without an agent," then, although his engagement in action and the purpose of action have ceased, [he remains established in that state].

Just as there is an initial engagement preceded by effort for the sake of gathering the world (*lokasaṃgraha*), so too, that which appears as the form of engagement in one who has thus engaged is not "action" (*karman*) by which there could be a combination with knowledge (*jñāna*). This is because, for the sake of accomplishing the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), the activity of the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva in accordance with the duty of a Kṣatriya is not combined with his knowledge; likewise it is for the wise man, since they are equal in the absence of attachment to the fruits and the sense of ego (*ahaṃkāra*).

One who knows the truth thinks, "I do not act," and does not intend for the fruit thereof. Just as in the case of one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and desires heaven and the like, and having commenced the performance of rites such as the *agnihotra*—which are characterized as *dharma* for the sake of that desire—if his desire should perish midway while he is performing that very *agnihotra* and so forth, that *agnihotra* and the rest no longer become acts performed with desire (*kāmya*). Thus the Blessed One shows in various places: "Even while acting, he is not tainted; he does not act, he is not tainted."

As for the statement, "Whatever was done by the ancients in times even more ancient—by action alone indeed did Janaka and others attain perfection"—that must be understood through careful analysis. How so? If those ancients, such as Janaka and others, were knowers of reality (tattvavid) yet remained engaged in action, they attained perfection through knowledge alone, according to the realization that "the qualities act upon the qualities," for the sake of maintaining the world order; thus, although the occasion for renunciation of action had arisen, they attained perfection while still performing action, meaning they did not actually perform the formal renunciation of action.

Alternatively, it should be explained that Janaka and others were not knowers of reality (*tattvavid*); rather, by means of action dedicated to the Lord as an instrument, they attained perfection—either the purification of the mind (*sattvaśuddhi*) or the perfection characterized by the arising of knowledge. The Blessed One will express this very same meaning when He says, "They perform action for the purification of the mind," and after stating, "By worshipping Him with one's own duty, a human being attains perfection," He will further describe the steadfastness in knowledge for one who has attained perfection, beginning with the words, "Having attained perfection, [he realizes] Brahman as it is."

Therefore, the established conclusion in the Gītā scripture is that liberation is attained through the knowledge of reality alone, and not from its combination with action. We shall demonstrate this point by dividing it according to the relevant sections as we proceed.

Seeing no means of extricating Arjuna—who was thus utterly bewildered regarding dharma, possessed of false knowledge, and submerged in a great ocean of grief—except through the knowledge of the Self, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, out of compassion and desiring to lift him up, spoke these words to introduce him to the knowledge of the Self:
"The Blessed Lord said:
You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom."
The wise grieve neither for the dead nor for the living.

The ones beginning with Bhīṣma and Droṇa are not to be grieved for; they are not objects of grief because of their virtuous conduct and because, in their ultimate nature, they are eternal. You have grieved for those who are not to be grieved for, thinking: "They are dying on my account; what shall I do with the pleasures of sovereignty and the like, now that I am deprived of them? Yet you speak words of wisdom—the utterances and sayings of the wise and intelligent.

The intention is this: like a madman, you display in yourself both this folly and this wisdom as contradictory things. For the wise—those who know the Self—do not grieve for those whose life-force has departed, the dead, nor for those whose life-force has not departed, the living. They are called "wise" (paṇḍita) because their intellect (paṇḍā) is directed toward the Self, according to the Vedic text: "Having become disillusioned with wisdom" (BU 3.5.1). But in reality, you grieve for those who are eternal and not to be grieved for; therefore, the intention is that you are deluded.
Why are they not to be grieved for? Because they are eternal. How so?
"Never indeed was there a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these lords of men."
And yet, after this, none of us shall cease to be.

But indeed, never at any time was I not; rather, I certainly was. The intention is that throughout the past births and destructions of bodies, I have existed eternally, just as space exists within jars and other objects. Likewise, you were not non-existent, but certainly were; likewise, these rulers of men were not non-existent, but certainly were. And likewise, we shall not fail to exist, but shall certainly exist—all of us—even after this destruction of the body, in the subsequent time.

The meaning is that they are eternal in all three periods of time by virtue of their own essential nature. The plural number is used because of the persistence of the distinction between bodies, not with the intention of implying a plurality of selves.
In that regard, he provides an illustration as to how the self might be eternal: "Just as in this body of the embodied one there are childhood, youth, and old age..."
Likewise, there is the attainment of another body; the wise man is not deluded by this.

"One who possesses a body" (*dehin*) is so called because he has a body (*deha*); for that embodied self, while this body exists, there are these three states which are mutually distinct: childhood, which is the state of a child or the stage of infancy; youth, which is the state of a young person or the middle stage; and old age, which is the loss of vitality or the stage of decrepitude. Among these, when the first state perishes, there is no perishing of the self, and when the second state arises, there is no arising of the self.

What then? It is observed that for the Self, which is indeed changeless, there is the attainment of second and third states. In the same way, "another body" (dehāntara) means a body different from the current one; the "attainment of another body" (dehāntaraprāpti) refers to the attainment of such a body by the changeless Self itself. Being wise (dhīra)—that is, possessed of intelligence—one does not become deluded, nor does one fall into confusion in this regard.

"Even though delusion caused by the destruction of the self does not occur for one who knows that the self is eternal, nevertheless, worldly delusion is observed to arise from the occurrence of cold, heat, pleasure, and pain; likewise, delusion arises from separation from happiness, and grief from the onset of suffering. Anticipating this objection from Arjuna, the Blessed One said:
"But the contacts with the senses, O son of Kuntī, which give rise to cold, heat, pleasure, and pain..."
They come and go and are impermanent; endure them, O Bhārata.

The sense organs, such as the ear and others, are so called because objects like sound are measured (*mīyante*) by means of these *mātrās*. The "contacts" (*sparśas*) of the *mātrās* are the conjunctions with sound and the other objects; they bestow cold, heat, pleasure, and pain, meaning they provide coldness, heat, happiness, and suffering. Alternatively, "contacts" (*sparśas*) are the objects of contact—sound and the rest—because they are touched (*spṛśyante*). Thus, both the *mātrās* and the "contacts" bestow cold, heat, pleasure, and pain. Cold is sometimes pleasant and sometimes painful; likewise, heat also has an indeterminate nature.

Furthermore, pleasure and pain possess a fixed nature because they do not deviate from it; therefore, cold and heat are mentioned separately from them. Since those contacts with the senses and so forth are subject to coming and going—that is, their very nature is to appear and disappear—they are impermanent. Therefore, endure these things such as cold and heat; the meaning is that you should bear them and not allow joy or dejection to arise toward them.
Listen to what happens to one who endures cold, heat, and so forth:
"For those do not afflict this person, O bull among men."
The steadfast one who is equal in pain and pleasure is fit for immortality.

For that person for whom pleasure and pain are equal—him who is equanimous in pleasure and pain, free from elation and dejection upon encountering happiness or sorrow, steadfast, and wise—the aforementioned pairs such as cold and heat do not afflict nor shake him, because he perceives the eternal Self. Established in the vision of the nature of the eternal Self, he is capable—that is, he becomes competent—for immortality, meaning for the state of being immortal, which is liberation (mokṣa). ||BhG 2.15||
For this reason as well, it is proper to endure cold, heat, and so forth without giving way to grief and delusion, because:
"The non-existent has no being; the existent has no non-being."
But the end of both of these has been seen by those who perceive the truth.
For that which is non-existent and unreal—such as cold, heat, and so forth, along with their causes—there is no existence, no becoming, and no state of being.

Indeed, when examined by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), no entity such as cold or heat exists as having a cause. For that is a modification (*vikāra*), and a modification is subject to deviation. Just as the configuration of a jar or similar object, when examined by the eye, is non-existent because it is not perceived apart from the clay; so too every modification is non-existent because it is not perceived apart from its cause. This is because it is not perceived prior to or after its birth and destruction.
Furthermore, the effect—such as a jar—and its cause—such as clay—are both non-existent apart from their own respective causes.

If it is argued that the non-existence of that [universal] would entail the non-existence of everything, we say no; for in every case two cognitions are perceived: the cognition of "existent" and the cognition of "non-existent. That object regarding which a cognition does not fail is existent; that object regarding which a cognition fails is non-existent. Thus, the distinction between the existent and the non-existent being established as dependent upon cognition, everyone perceives two cognitions in every instance as having a common substratum—not like "blue lotus," but as "the pot is existent," "the cloth is existent," and "the elephant is existent."

The same applies in all cases. Of those two cognitions, the cognition of a jar and so forth is subject to deviation, as has been demonstrated; however, the cognition of "being" (sat) is not. Therefore, the object of the cognition of a jar and so forth is non-existent because it deviates, whereas the object of the cognition of "being" is not non-existent because it does not deviate.

If it is argued that when the jar is destroyed and the cognition of the jar deviates, the cognition of "being" (sat) also deviates, we say no; for the cognition of "being" is observed even in relation to a cloth. That cognition of "being" has only the qualifier as its object.
If it is argued that, like the cognition of "being," the cognition of the jar is also observed in another jar, we say no; because it is not observed in the case of a cloth and so forth.

If it is argued that even the cognition of existence (*sadbuddhi*) is not observed when a jar has perished, we say no; this is because of the absence of the substantive (*viśeṣya*). Since the cognition of existence has the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) as its object, in the absence of the substantive—and consequently the impossibility of the qualifier—what could it have as its object? It is not, however, because of an absence of objects for the cognition of existence itself.

If it is argued that having a single substratum is not tenable in the absence of a qualificandum such as a jar, we say no; for in cases such as a mirage, one observes grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the thought "this is water" even when either [of the two] is absent.

Therefore, for the non-existent body and so forth, as well as for the duality along with its causes, there is no being; likewise, for the existent Self, there is no non-being or non-existence, because it is never absent from anything—this is what we have stated.

Thus, the end—the determination—of both the self and the non-self, whether existent or non-existent, has been seen and perceived by the seers of reality (*tattvadarśibhiḥ*) regarding these two as previously described: that "the existent is indeed existent" and "the non-existent is indeed non-existent. The word *tat* is a pronoun, and everything is Brahman; its name is *tat*, and its state (*tadbhāva*) is *tattva*, which is the true nature of Brahman. Those whose character is to perceive that are the "seers of reality"; by them, the seers of reality.

The intended meaning is: you too, relying on the vision of those who perceive reality, having abandoned grief and delusion, and having resolved in your mind that these dualities such as cold and heat—which are both fixed and unfixed in nature—are merely transformations that are non-existent yet falsely appear like water in a mirage, you must endure them.
What, then, is that which exists as real and is always present? It is said: Know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded.
No one is able to cause the destruction of this imperishable [Self].

"Indestructible" (*avināśi*) means that whose nature is not to perish. The word "but" (*tu*) serves to distinguish it from what is non-existent. Know—that is, understand—this: by what? By that which is called "Being" (*sat*), the Brahman, this entire world is pervaded and encompassed, just as jars and other objects are pervaded by space. "Destruction" (*vināśam*) means disappearance or non-existence. "Of the imperishable" (*avyayasya*): it does not pass away (*na vyeti*); it does not undergo increase or decrease, thus it is "imperishable" (*avyaya*); [the phrase refers to] "of that imperishable one."

This Brahman, which is called "Being," does not perish—that is, it does not deviate—from its own nature, because it is partless, unlike the body and so forth; nor does it perish through anything belonging to itself, because there is nothing that belongs to it. Just as Devadatta perishes through the loss of wealth, Brahman does not perish in such a way. Therefore, no one is able to cause the destruction of this imperishable Brahman; even the Lord cannot destroy the Self, for the Self is Brahman, and action directed toward oneself is a contradiction.
But what is that which is non-existent and thus deviates from its own essential being? It is said:
"These bodies are said to have an end, belonging to the eternal embodied self."
It is indestructible and immeasurable; therefore, fight, O Bhārata.

Those things which possess internal destruction are "finite" (*antavantaḥ*). Just as the persistent cognition of reality regarding a mirage and the like is severed at the conclusion of an investigation into the means of valid knowledge—that is their "end"—so too these bodies are finite, like bodies in dreams or through illusion. The meaning is that they have been described by the discerning as finite in relation to the eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable Self, who possesses a body. The terms "eternal" (*nityasya*) and "indestructible" (*anāśinaḥ*) are not redundant.

Because eternity (*nityatva*) and destruction (*nāśa*) are each of two kinds: [eternity] as when a body that has been reduced to ashes and has vanished from sight is said to be "destroyed"; and [eternity] as when, though still existing, one has undergone a transformation into another state and become afflicted by disease and so forth, one is said to be "destroyed. In this context, the meaning of the phrase "of the eternal, the indestructible" (*nityasyānāśinaḥ*) is that this [Self] is unrelated to both these types of destruction. Otherwise, the Self's eternity would be like that of the earth and other elements; lest that be the case, he says "of the eternal, the indestructible."
The meaning is: of that which is immeasurable, not an object of measurement, and not to be circumscribed by means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth.

Is it not the case that the self is determined by scripture (*āgama*) and by perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means previously? No; because the self is established by itself (*svataḥsiddha*). For the search for means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) occurs in the self, who is the knower (*pramātṛ*), when one desires to know something. Indeed, no one proceeds toward the determination of an object of knowledge (*prameya*) after first failing to cognize the self in the form "I am thus. For there is no one for whom the so-called self is unknown.

The scripture, however, attains the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the Self by merely negating the superimposition of qualities that do not belong to it, and not by making known an unknown object. Thus says the Śruti: "That Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1). Since the Self is thus eternal and immutable, therefore "fight"—the meaning is: do not desist from battle.

For here, the duty to fight is not being enjoined; rather, he who was already engaged in battle remains silent because he is obstructed by grief and delusion. Therefore, the Blessed One merely effects the removal of that obstruction. Consequently, "fight" is a mere restatement (anuvāda), not an injunction (vidhi).

The Blessed One has cited two Vedic verses as witnesses for this point: that the scripture of the Gītā is intended for the cessation of the causes of saṃsāra, such as grief and delusion, and is not an incitement to action. As for what you think—that Bhīṣma and the others are being slain by me in battle, and that I alone am their slayer—this understanding of yours is truly false. How so?
"He who thinks he slays, and he who thinks he is slain..."
Both of them do not understand this: that it neither kills nor is killed.

He who perceives this embodied being under discussion as the slayer—that is, as the agent of the act of killing—and he who thinks of him as slain, thinking "I am killed" due to the destruction of the body, that both do not know; they have failed to understand the Self through a lack of discrimination. The meaning is that those two who perceive the Self—the object of the notion of "I"—as "I am the slayer" or "I am killed" by the destruction of the body, are ignorant of the true nature of the Self.

Because this Self does not kill—that is, it does not become the agent of the act of killing—nor is it killed—that is, it does not become the object of that action—this is the meaning, owing to its changelessness.
How is the Self immutable? This is the second mantra:
"It is never born, nor does it ever die."
Having come into being, this [Self] shall not cease to be hereafter;
it is unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient.
It is not slain when the body is slain.

It is not born, it does not arise; the meaning is that no modification of a thing characterized by birth exists for the Self. Likewise, "it does not die. The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "and" (*ca*); thus, "it does not die" prohibits the final modification characterized by destruction. The word "ever" (*kadācit*) is connected with all the prohibitions of modifications: "it is never born," "it never dies," and so forth.

Since this Self, having come into being—that is, having experienced the act of becoming—is thereafter no longer "to be," meaning it will not go toward non-existence again, therefore it does not die. For that which, having come into being, is not to be, is said by the world to "die. From the word *vā* (or) and from the word *na* (not), it follows that this Self is also not "to be" after having been non-existent, as is the case with the body; therefore, it is not born. For that which, having been non-existent, is to be, is said to "be born. The Self is not thus; hence, it is not born. Because it is so, it is unborn (*aja*); because it does not die, it is eternal (*nitya*).

Although all modifications are effectively prohibited by the denial of the first and last modifications, nevertheless, the modifications occurring in the middle must be denied by their own specific terms, so that there may be a denial of all unmentioned modifications such as youth and so forth. To this end, he says "eternal" (śāśvata) and so on. By "eternal," the modification characterized by decay is prohibited; for "eternal" (śāśvata) means that which exists perpetually (śaśvadbhava).

It does not diminish by way of its own nature, because it is partless; nor is there diminution through the loss of qualities, because it is devoid of qualities. Furthermore, the modification characterized by growth—the opposite of diminution—is also denied by the word "ancient" (*purāṇa*). For that which increases through the addition of parts grows and is called "new. But this Self, being partless, was indeed new even in the past; thus it is "ancient," meaning it does not grow. Likewise, it is not slain.

In this context, the root *han* (to strike) should be understood in the sense of "transformation" (*vipariṇāma*) for the sake of avoiding redundancy; thus, the meaning is "it is not transformed. Even while the bodies are being struck—that is, even while they are being transformed—the Self remains unchanged. In this mantra, the six modifications of being, which are the transformations of worldly objects, are denied of the Self. The meaning of the sentence is that the Self is devoid of all forms of modification. Since this is so, its connection with the preceding mantra is: "therefore, both of them do not know [It]. (BhG 2.20)

Having established by means of the mantra "He who knows him as the slayer" that [the Self] is neither the agent nor the object of the act of killing, and having stated by the mantra "He is not born" the reason for this— namely, its changelessness— he concludes the matter proposed:
"He who knows him as indestructible, eternal, unborn, and immutable..."
How, O Pārtha, does that person cause anyone to be killed, or kill anyone?

The connection is as follows: "He who knows"—that is, he who knows this [Self] which is indestructible, devoid of the final modification (death), eternal, and free from transformation—he knows it. How, by what means, does that learned person, being so qualified, kill—that is, perform the act of killing—or how does he cause to be killed—impel a killer? [For he is unborn, immutable, and undecaying. Thus was the meaning stated in the preceding mantra. How could such a person kill or cause another to kill? He cannot do so. This is the sense. Because he is unborn, immutable, and undecaying, he is incapable of performing the act of killing or causing another to kill. Therefore, the meaning is that one should not entertain the notion that "I am killing" or "I am causing to be killed. This is the intended purport. "He does not kill anyone in any way, nor does he cause anyone to be killed in any way"—in both cases, the meaning is indeed a negation (*ākṣepa*), since the sense of a question is impossible. Furthermore, because the reason—the state of being changeless—is the same for both, the Blessed One intends the prohibition of all action for the wise as the subject matter of this section. As for the negation regarding "killing," it is mentioned merely by way of illustration. Seeing a specific reason for the impossibility of any action on the part of the wise man, the Blessed One negates actions [by asking], "How can that person [be a doer]?"

[Objection: Has it not already been stated that the very immutability of the Self is the specific reason for the impossibility of all action? [Reply: True, it has been stated; yet that is not the specific reason, because the Knower is distinct from the immutable Self. If it be argued that action does not become impossible for one who knows an immutable post, we say no; for the Knower is the Self. Knowledge does not belong to the aggregate of the body and so forth. Therefore, by process of elimination, the Knower is the unconditioned, immutable Self; and since action is impossible for such a Knower, the objection—"How can he be a person?"—is appropriate.

Just as the Self—which remains indeed changeless—is falsely perceived through ignorance by means of the non-discriminative cognition of the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) regarding objects such as sound that have been presented by the intellect, in exactly the same way, the Self, which is in reality changeless, is called "the Knower" (*vidvān*) by means of the mental modification consisting of the knowledge that discriminates the Self from the non-Self, even though that knowledge is unreal in its own nature.

From the statement that action is impossible for the Knower, it is understood to be the Blessed One’s settled conclusion that those actions which are enjoined by the scripture are prescribed only for the non-Knower.

If it is argued: "But surely knowledge (*vidyā*) is also enjoined only for one who is ignorant, since enjoining knowledge for one who has already known it would be as useless as grinding what is already ground; in that case, the distinction that 'rites are enjoined for the ignorant, not for the knower' is untenable"—we say no. For the distinction is tenable based on the presence or absence of something to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*).

Just as after knowing the meaning of injunctions such as the Agnihotra, the ignorant person—who possesses the cognition "I am the agent" and "this is my duty"—must perform the Agnihotra and other rites after collecting their various required materials; however, there is no such thing to be performed after knowing the meaning of the injunction regarding the true nature of the Self, expressed in such passages as "He is not born."

However, from the knowledge whose object is the oneness of the Self and its lack of agency—such as "I am not the doer" and "I am not the enjoyer"—nothing else arises; thus this distinction is logically established. On the other hand, for one who perceives the Self as "I am the doer," the thought "this must be done by me" necessarily arises. With respect to that [thought], such a person is qualified [for action]; therefore, ritual actions are possible for him.

And because of the statement, "That ignorant man does not know both of them," and because there is a statement regarding the specific qualified knower that implies the non-applicability of action to him, how can it be said that "that person" [is the one who acts]? Therefore, only the qualified knower—who perceives the changeless Self—and the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) have the authority for the renunciation of all actions.

For this very reason, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, having distinguished between the Sāṃkhyas who possess knowledge and those who do not, as well as the performers of ritual action, established two distinct disciplines: "for the Sāṃkhyas by means of the yoga of knowledge, and for the Yogins by means of the yoga of action. Likewise, the Blessed Vyāsa said to his son: "Now, these are the two paths," and so forth; similarly: "First the path of action, and afterwards renunciation."

The Blessed One will demonstrate this very distinction again and again: "One whose self is deluded by egoism and who does not know reality thinks, 'I am the doer'; but one who knows reality thinks, 'I do not act. Likewise: 'Having renounced all actions with the mind, he remains,' and so forth."

In this regard, some who consider themselves wise say: "The knowledge that 'I am the one Self, immutable and non-agent, devoid of the six modifications of existence such as birth and so forth' does not arise in anyone; yet it is upon the arising of such knowledge that the renunciation of all actions is taught. This is not so, because it would follow that the scriptural instruction beginning with "He is not born" and so forth would be rendered purposeless.

Just as, through the power of the instruction of the scripture, there arises the knowledge of the existence of dharma and adharma, as well as the knowledge of the agent’s connection with another body, so too it must be asked of them: why does the knowledge of that very Self—its changelessness, non-agency, unity, and so forth—not arise from the scripture? If they say, "Because it is beyond the range of the instruments of cognition," we say no, because of the Vedic revelation: "It is to be perceived by the mind alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19).

The mind, refined by the teachings of the scriptures and teachers, as well as by tranquility, self-control, and other virtues, is the instrument for the vision of the Self. Therefore, to claim that knowledge does not arise despite the existence of inference and scripture for its attainment is mere audacity. Furthermore, it must be admitted that when knowledge arises, it necessarily sublates the ignorance that is its opposite; and that ignorance has been demonstrated in the passage: "I am the slayer, I am slain"—both of these do not understand.

And here, it is shown that the self’s agency, its status as an object, and its causative agency in the act of killing are produced by ignorance. This is the same for all actions; for agency and the rest are produced by ignorance because the self is changeless (*avikriya*). For one who possesses change is an agent who impels another, who has become an object for him, saying, "Do this."

Thus, Lord Vāsudeva, without distinction, negates both the agency and the causative agency of the wise person in all actions, in order to demonstrate that the wise person has no qualification for ritual action, through such passages as "the imperishable" and "how shall that person. But where, then, does the wise person have qualification? This has already been stated previously: "by the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṃkhyas. And likewise, he will speak of the renunciation of all actions with the words "all actions by means of the mind," and so forth.

If it is argued that because of the expression "with the mind," there is no renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of vocal and physical actions, we say no; for [the text] specifies "all actions" (*sarvakarmāṇi*). If it is argued that this refers only to all mental actions, we say no; for vocal and physical activities are preceded by mental activity, and in the absence of mental activity, they cannot occur. If it is argued that one should renounce with the mind all actions other than those mental actions which are the causes of scriptural vocal and physical acts, we say no.

If it is argued that because of the qualification "neither acting nor causing to act," this renunciation of all actions taught by the Blessed One refers to one who is dying and not to one who is living—this is not so; for the qualification "the embodied one dwells in the city of nine gates" would be untenable. Indeed, it is not possible for one who is dead through the renunciation of all actions to dwell in that body.

If it is argued that there is no connection with the body in the sense of "having renounced" for one who neither acts nor causes others to act—on the grounds that he does not "sit in the body"—we say no. This is because the Self is everywhere determined to be changeless, and because the action of sitting requires a locus (an object), whereas renunciation does not require such a locus. Furthermore, the word *nyāsa* preceded by the prefix *sam-* here has the meaning of "abandonment," not "depositing.

Therefore, we shall demonstrate later in the section on the knowledge of the Self that, according to the Gītā scripture, only one who possesses the knowledge of the Self is qualified for renunciation, and not for ritual action. || BhG 2.21 ||
Now we shall speak of the subject at hand. Therein, the indestructibility of the self has been asserted. To the question "What is it like?", it is said:
just as one casts off worn-out garments.
A man takes up other new ones;
even so, the embodied soul, casting off worn-out bodies, enters into others that are new.

Just as a person in this world, having cast off worn-out garments—those that have become weak—takes up others that are new, even so the embodied Self, having cast off worn-out bodies, enters into other new ones; the meaning is that the Self is indeed changeless, like the person. || BhG 2.22 ||
Why is it that he is indeed changeless? He says:
"Weapons do not cut him; fire does not burn him."
Neither do the waters moisten it, nor does the wind dry it up.

Weapons do not cut this embodied being under discussion, because it is partless; they do not effect a division of its parts. "Weapons" refers to swords and the like. Likewise, fire does not burn it; even fire does not reduce it to ashes. Similarly, waters do not moisten it. For water has the power to bring about the disintegration of parts by causing the wetting of an object that possesses parts; that [power] is not possible in the case of the partless Self.
Likewise, the wind destroys a substance possessed of oil by drying up its moisture; but even the wind does not dry up this Self.
Since this is so, therefore it is uncuttable, it is unburnable, it is undissoluble, and indeed it is undrying.
This is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient.

Because swords and other such weapons, though they serve as mutual causes of destruction, are unable to destroy this Self, therefore it is eternal. Because it is eternal, it is all-pervading. Because it is all-pervading, it is like a pillar; that is to say, it is stable. Because it is stable, this Self is immovable. Therefore, it is "sanātana," meaning ancient; it has not been produced from any cause whatsoever, which means it is ever-new.

One should not point out redundancy among these verses, because by means of this single verse alone—beginning with "It is neither born nor does it die"—the eternity and changelessness of the Self have been stated for all worlds. Whatever is said there concerning the Self does not exceed the meaning of this [present] verse; some is repeated verbally, while some is repeated in substance.

Because the reality of the Self is difficult to understand, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, having repeatedly introduced the topic, describes that very same reality through different words, thinking: "How indeed might the unmanifest Reality—which has become the object of the non-transmigrating consciousness of transmigrating beings—lead to the cessation of saṃsāra? (BhG 2.24)
Furthermore,
it is said: "This is unmanifest, this is inconceivable, and this is immutable."
Therefore, having understood this, you ought not to grieve.

This Self is unmanifest (*avyakta*) because it is not an object for any of the instruments of perception; thus, it is not manifested. For this very reason, it is inconceivable (*acintya*). For whatever falls within the range of the senses becomes an object of thought; however, this Self is inconceivable because it does not fall within the range of the senses. For this very reason, it is immutable (*avikārya*); unlike milk, which undergoes transformation through the addition of a ferment such as yogurt, this Self does not change. Furthermore, it is changeless because it is partless (*niravayava*). Indeed, nothing that is partless is ever observed to be subject to modification.

Because it is changeless, this Self is said to be unchangeable; therefore, having known this Self in the manner thus described, you ought not to grieve, thinking, "I am the slayer of these," or "these are being slain by me."
Having accepted the impermanence of the self, this is said:
"And yet you consider him to be eternally born or eternally dead."
Nevertheless, O mighty-armed one, you ought not to grieve in this manner.

And yet—this word "and yet" (atha ca) has the sense of an admission. You regard this very Self under discussion as "constantly born," thinking "born, born" with respect to the production of various bodies according to worldly convention; and likewise, you regard it as "constantly dying," thinking "dead, dead, dead" with respect to each respective destruction. Even so, O mighty-armed one, even though the Self exists in such a manner, you ought not to grieve in this way, for these two—the destruction of that which is subject to birth and the birth of that which is subject to destruction—are inevitable.
And that being so:
for one who is born, death is certain; and for one who has died, birth is certain.
Therefore, you ought not to grieve over that which is unavoidable.

For death is certain and inevitable for one who is born—that is, for one who has attained birth—and birth is certain for one who has died. Therefore, this matter characterized by birth and death is unavoidable; you ought not to grieve over that which is unavoidable.
It is not proper to grieve even for those beings that consist of a collection of causes and effects, because,
O Bhārata, beings have the unmanifest as their beginning and the manifest as their middle.
Their dissolution is indeed unmanifest; what cause for lamentation is there in that?

"Unmanifest in their origin": those beings—consisting of the aggregate of effects such as sons and friends, and instruments such as the body—which have the unmanifest (avyakta), meaning invisibility or non-perception, as their beginning (*ādi*) prior to birth; and which, once born, have the manifest (*vyakta*) as their middle state until death; "unmanifest in their dissolution" (*avyaktanidhanāni*), meaning those whose dissolution or death is again the unmanifest, i.e., invisibility. The meaning is that even after death, they return to the state of being unmanifest.
And so it has been said: "Having emerged from the unseen, he goes again to the unseen."
"He is not yours, nor are you his; why this vain lamentation? (Mahābhārata, Strīparvan 2.13).

In this context, "why this lamentation" means: what is the point of this wailing or delirious speech regarding beings who have become objects of illusion, having perished after being seen or never having been seen at all?

The subject under discussion, the Self, is difficult to understand. Why, then, do you reproach me alone when the cause of error is common to all? To the question "How is this Self difficult to understand? he replies:
"Someone perceives It as a marvel."
One speaks of this as a marvel;
likewise, another hears of it as a marvel;
yet even having heard it, no one at all truly knows it.

As something wonderful—meaning as a marvel never seen before, extraordinary, and appearing suddenly—so does someone perceive this Self as if it were a wonder; likewise another speaks of it as if it were a wonder; and yet another hears of it as if it were a wonder. And even after hearing, seeing, and speaking of it, no one at all truly knows this Self.

Alternatively, he who perceives this Self is like a marvel; he who speaks of it and he who hears of it is someone indeed among many thousands. Therefore, the intention is that the Self is difficult to understand. ||BhGS_2.29||
Now, concluding the meaning of this section, he says:
"O Bhārata, this embodied self in the body of everyone is eternally indestructible."
Therefore, you ought not to grieve for any living beings.

The embodied self (dehin) is always, at all times, and in all conditions, indestructible because it is partless and eternal. In this regard, this embodied self is indestructible within the body of anyone because it is omnipresent; even while situated in stationary objects and so forth, it is not destroyed when the body of any living being is slain. Therefore, with respect to Bhīṣma and all other beings, you ought not to grieve.

It has been stated here that, with respect to the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*), neither sorrow nor delusion is possible. This is not only the case when considering the ultimate reality; rather, having also considered your own duty (*svadharma*), you ought not to waver.
For indeed, there exists nothing better for a Kṣatriya than a righteous war.

"Even your own duty"—the duty of a Kṣatriya is battle; having regard even for that, you ought not to waver or falter. The intention is that this is because of the Kṣatriya’s inherent duty, arising from his very nature. And that battle, by way of conquering the earth, is for the sake of dharma and for the sake of protecting the subjects; thus it is not devoid of dharma, but is supremely righteous (*dharmyam*).
Therefore, there exists nothing better for a Kṣatriya than this righteous battle, for this is the reason why. (BhG 2.31)
And for what reason should that battle be fought? It is said:
"That which has come by chance is the open door to heaven."
O Pārtha, happy are the Kṣatriyas who obtain such a battle as this.
And for those Kṣatriyas, O Pārtha, who obtain such a battle—which has arrived by chance and without being sought, and which is like heaven’s door opened and unbarred—are they not happy?
Even though this duty has presented itself before you, if you nevertheless do not engage in this righteous battle, [then...]
Then, having abandoned your own duty and fame, you will incur sin.

But if you do not engage in this lawful battle—ordained as consistent with dharma—then by its non-performance, having abandoned your own duty and the fame resulting from your encounter with Mahādeva and the other gods, you will incur only sin.
Not only will you abandon your own fame and virtue,
but living beings will also proclaim your undying infamy.
And for one who has been honored, infamy is worse than death.

Furthermore, people will speak of your eternal and long-lasting infamy after the battle. For one who has been esteemed for qualities such as being righteous and heroic, infamy is worse than death; the meaning is that for one so esteemed, death is better than infamy. (BhG 2.34)
Moreover,
the great chariot-warriors will think that you have withdrawn from the battle out of fear.
And having been highly esteemed by those whom you now serve, you will fall into contempt.

Out of fear of Karṇa and others, the great chariot-warriors—Duryodhana and the rest—will think that you have desisted from the battle out of compassion, and not because of [your own prowess]. Having been highly esteemed by them, Duryodhana and the others, as one endowed with many virtues, you will instead incur contempt and insignificance.
Furthermore,
your enemies will utter many unspeakable words against you.
What indeed could be more painful than that—your own capability being censured?

Your enemies, your adversaries, will speak many various kinds of unspeakable and unutterable words, censuring and reviling your prowess on account of the battles with the Nivātakavacas and others. What indeed could be more painful than that? The meaning is that there is no suffering more grievous than that.
Furthermore, if you engage in battle again, you will either attain heaven if slain by Karna and the others, or you will enjoy the earth if victorious.
Therefore, arise, O son of Kuntī, resolved for battle.

"Either slain you shall attain heaven; being slain, you will reach heaven. Or, having conquered Karna and the other heroes, you shall enjoy the earth. The intention is that in either case there is only gain for you. Since this is so, therefore arise, O Kaunteya, for battle—meaning, having made the resolve: 'I shall conquer the enemies' or 'I shall die.'"
In this regard, listen to this instruction for one who fights with the conviction that battle is his own duty:
having made pleasure and pain equal, as well as gain and loss, victory and defeat.
Therefore, engage in battle; in this way, you will not incur sin.

Having made pleasure and pain equal and identical, and having likewise not made attachment and aversion so; and similarly, having made gain and loss, victory and defeat equal—then engage in battle, exert yourself. By fighting in this manner, you shall incur no sin. This is the incidental instruction.

The worldly reasoning for the removal of grief and delusion was stated in the verses beginning with "And having also considered your own duty," but not as the primary intent. Here, the vision of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the subject at hand; that which was taught is now being concluded with the words "This has been declared to you" in order to demonstrate the distinction between the scopes of the scriptures.

For once this division of the subject matter of the scripture has been shown here, the scripture will proceed more easily above with respect to its two-fold goal—namely, "by the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṃkhyas" and "by the yoga of action for the Yogins"—and the listeners, too, will grasp it easily through this division of the subject matter. Therefore, He says: "This wisdom regarding Sāṃkhya has been declared to you; now hear this [wisdom] regarding Yoga, O Pārtha, endowed with which wisdom you shall cast off the bondage of action. (BhG 2.39)

This wisdom—knowledge concerning the discernment of the supreme reality in the context of Sāṃkhya—has been declared and explained to you; it is the direct cause for the cessation of the defects that are the root of saṃsāra, such as grief and delusion. Now, however, hear this wisdom which will be described immediately hereafter regarding Yoga—the means of attaining that [Sāṃkhya]—namely, the performance of action in the yoga of action (karmayoga) for the sake of propitiating the Lord through detachment and the abandonment of dualities, as well as the yoga of meditative absorption (samādhiyoga).

And he praises that intellect for the sake of generating enthusiasm: "O Pārtha, endowed with that intellect which has yoga as its object, you shall cast off the bondage of action—the very bond of action known as merit and demerit—by means of attaining knowledge caused by the grace of the Lord; such is the intended meaning. (BhG 2.39)
Furthermore:
"In this [path], there is no loss of effort, nor does any obstacle exist."
Even a very small amount of this dharma protects one from great fear.

In this yoga of action on the path to liberation, there is no destruction of the "abhikrama"—that is, the "abhikramaṇa," or undertaking; its destruction does not exist, unlike [the results] of agriculture and the like. The meaning is that in the sphere of yoga, the undertaking does not have an uncertain result. Furthermore, there is no adverse consequence (pratyavāya) as in the case of medical treatment. Rather, even a very small portion of this dharma—the dharma of yoga—when practiced, protects and saves one from great fear, namely, the fear of saṃsāra characterized by birth, death, and so forth.

That intellect which has been described in Sāṃkhya and in Yoga, and whose characteristics will be stated hereafter— that intellect, O joy of the Kurus, is here said to be of the nature of resolute determination.
For the intellects of those lacking resolve are indeed many-branched and infinite.

The intellect that is resolute by nature—that is, whose essence is certainty—is indeed one alone; it sublates the various divergent branches of other contrary forms of cognition because it is produced by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) on this path to the highest good. O descendant of Kuru! As for those other contrary cognitions, through the force of the proliferation of their various branches, they are infinite, shoreless, and unceasing.

Samsara becomes perpetually extended and vast; however, when the cognitions of infinite distinctions cease due to the power of the discerning intellect produced by valid means of knowledge, samsara also ceases. Those cognitions have many branches—that is, they possess many branches—and thus they are "many-branched," meaning they have many divisions. For, according to the distinction of each branch, the cognitions are indeed infinite. Of whom? Of the irresolute—meaning those who are devoid of the discerning intellect produced by valid means of knowledge.
Those of little wisdom, who lack an intellect characterized by resolute determination, utter this flowery speech.
O Pārtha, those who delight in the mere recitation of the Vedas argue that there is nothing else.

That speech which they utter—which is about to be described, which is "flowering," like a tree in bloom, appearing beautiful and sounding pleasant—those who speak it are the unwise, meaning those lacking intelligence and discernment. O Pārtha, they are devoted to the talk of the Vedas; that is, they take delight in Vedic statements that illuminate numerous explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) concerning means to results, and they are habitually prone to saying, "There is nothing else [that leads to liberation] than these ritual acts which are the means for attaining results such as heaven. (BhG 2.42)
And those people, devoted to sensual desires and intent upon heaven, [follow the path] which yields the fruits of birth and action.
It abounds in various ritual actions directed toward the attainment of enjoyment and power.

"Those whose nature is desire" means those whose essence is desire; that is, those who are intent upon desire. "Those for whom heaven is the highest goal" means those for whom heaven is the supreme human aim (*puruṣārtha*); they are those for whom heaven is primary. "Bestowing birth as the fruit of action": the fruit of action is *karmaphala*; birth itself is the fruit of action, hence *janmakarmaphala*. That which bestows this is *janmakarmaphalapradā*; [they] speak such speech—this is to be supplied from the context.

"Abounding in various ritual acts": various ritual acts are "kriyāviśeṣas"; that speech in which these are numerous is "kriyāviśeṣabahulā. That speech by which objects such as heaven, cattle, and sons are predominantly proclaimed; with respect to the attainment of enjoyment and power—"bhoga" and "aiśvarya" together are "bhogaiśvarye," and their "gati" is their attainment—those who speak that speech which abounds in the specific ritual acts that serve as the means for that attainment, being deluded, revolve in saṃsāra; this is the intended meaning. (BhG 2.43)
And for them,
who are deeply attached to enjoyments and power, and whose minds have been carried away by that [illusion],
A resolute intellect is not established in meditative concentration.

For those who are deeply attached to enjoyments and power—meaning those for whom enjoyment and power are the sole objects of affection, who have become identified with them, whose minds are carried away by that speech abounding in various activities, and whose discriminative wisdom is obscured—the intellect characterized by resolute determination toward Sāṃkhya or Yoga is not established in *samādhi*. "Samādhi" refers to that in which everything is concentrated for the experience of the Puruṣa; it is the internal organ, the intellect (*buddhi*). The meaning is that such a resolute intellect does not arise or remain steady in that *samādhi*.
To those who are thus devoid of discriminative wisdom—those whose nature is driven by desire—he states their result:
"The Vedas have the three *guṇas* as their domain; be free from the three *guṇas*, O Arjuna."
Free from the pairs of opposites, eternally established in purity, devoid of the desire for acquisition and preservation, and possessed of the Self.

The Vedas have the three *guṇas* as their subject matter; that is, *saṃsāra*, which consists of the three *guṇas*, is the object to be illuminated by them—thus they are "those whose subject matter is the three *guṇas*" (*traiguṇyaviṣayāḥ*). But you, O Arjuna, become free from the three *guṇas*; the meaning is: become desireless. Be free from the pairs of opposites (*nirdvandvaḥ*); the word "pairs" (*dvandva*) refers to pairs of things that are causes of pleasure and pain and exist in mutual opposition. Therefore, become one who has emerged from these, being free from the pairs. Be ever established in purity (*nityasattvasthaḥ*); always take refuge in the quality of *sattva*.

Likewise, be free from the acquisition and preservation of possessions; for "acquisition" (yoga) is the gaining of what has not been gained, and "preservation" (kṣema) is the protection of what has been gained. Since it is difficult for one who is preoccupied with acquisition and preservation to engage in the highest good, therefore, be free from acquisition and preservation. Be self-possessed and vigilant. This is my instruction to you as you fulfill your own duty.

If one does not expect those infinite fruits which are declared for all the rites prescribed in the Vedas, then for what purpose are they performed for the sake of the Lord? Listen: "Whatever purpose there may be from a small reservoir of water when there is a flood of water everywhere..."
Such is the extent of all the Vedas for a discerning Brahmin.

Just as in the world, whatever purpose, result, or utility—such as bathing, drinking, and so forth—exists in various limited-water sources like wells and ponds, all that same purpose is attained in its entirety within a place where water has overflowed; the meaning is that it is contained therein.

Thus, whatever purpose there is in all the Vedas and in the rituals prescribed in the Vedas—namely, the fruit of those rituals—that same purpose is attained by a Brahmin who has renounced the world and understands the supreme reality; that purpose, which is the fruit of such realization, becomes entirely contained within that [knowledge], which is like water flooding everywhere. This is the meaning: it is subsumed therein.

"Just as when one has won a prize in a game of dice, all the lower stakes are gathered together, even so everything that people do well converges upon him who knows what he knows" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1.2); and the Lord will later say, "all action in its entirety. Therefore, prior to attaining the qualification for steadfastness in knowledge, action must be performed by one who is qualified for it, even if that action serves merely as a means to a well or a pond.
And your right is to action alone; let it never be in its fruits.
Let not the fruit of action be your motive, nor let there be attachment to inaction for you.

Your authority lies only in action, not in steadfastness in knowledge. Furthermore, while performing that action, let there be no authority over the fruits; the meaning is that you must never, under any circumstances, have a thirst for the results of action. For when you have a thirst for the fruit of action, you would then become the cause for the attainment of that fruit; thus, do not become the cause of the fruit of action.

For when one engages in action impelled by thirst for the fruit of action, then that very fruit of action becomes the cause of birth. If the fruit of action is not desired, what is the use of action which is of the nature of suffering? Therefore, let there be no attachment of yours to inaction; let there be no delight in non-performance.
If action should not be performed by one impelled by the fruit of action, then how should it be performed? It is said:
"Established in yoga, O Dhanañjaya, perform actions, having abandoned attachment."
Having become the same in success and failure, equanimity is called yoga.

Established in yoga, perform actions solely for the sake of the Lord. Even in that regard, O Dhanañjaya, having abandoned attachment with the thought, "May the Lord be pleased with me," perform actions while being free from thirst for results. When action is performed in this way, there is success characterized by the attainment of knowledge born of the purification of the mind, and there is failure born of its opposite. Having become equanimous—equal toward both success and failure—perform actions. What is this yoga, established in which you are told to act? This very state of equanimity toward success and failure is called yoga.
