Furthermore, regarding the action performed for the sake of worshipping the Lord while endowed with the intellect of equanimity, it has been said: "For action is far inferior to the yoga of the intellect, O Dhanañjaya."
Seek refuge in wisdom; the wretched have fruits as their motive.

By a great distance—that is, by an extremely vast separation—is that inferior, lowest, and base action performed by one seeking fruits [superior] to the action characterized by the yoga of wisdom, because [the former] is the cause of birth, death, and so forth. Therefore, O Dhanañjaya, seek—pray for—the refuge, the support, the cause of attaining fearlessness, in the wisdom concerning yoga, or in the wisdom of Sāṅkhya born from its maturation; the meaning is: "Become one who takes refuge in the knowledge of the supreme reality."

For those who perform inferior action are miserable and wretched, being motivated by the desire for fruits and driven by the thirst for results; as the Śruti declares: "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is miserable" (BAU 3.8.10).

Listen to the fruit that one attains by performing one’s own duty while endowed with the intellect of equanimity: "One who is joined with this wisdom casts off both good and evil deeds in this world."
Therefore, strive for yoga; yoga is skill in actions.

One who is "endowed with intellect" (buddhi-yukta)—meaning one endowed with the intellect whose object is equanimity toward action—casts off and abandons both good and evil deeds, merit and sin, in this world, by means of the purification of the mind and the attainment of knowledge; therefore, strive for and apply yourself to the yoga of the intellect characterized by equanimity.

Yoga is indeed skill in actions—that is, for one engaged in actions known as one's own duty (svadharma), that state of equanimity toward success and failure through a mind surrendered to the Lord is skill; it is a state of proficiency. For that is skill whereby even those actions which are by nature bondage are turned away from their inherent nature through the intellect of equanimity. Therefore, become endowed with the intellect of equanimity.
For,
endowed with wisdom, the wise abandon the fruit born of action.
Freed from the bondage of birth, they go to the state that is free from suffering.

The phrase "having abandoned the fruit born of action" is to be connected with the distant word [pada]. The attainment of desired or undesired bodies is the fruit born of action—that which arises from actions. For, being endowed with wisdom—meaning being endowed with the intellect of equanimity—and having abandoned and relinquished that fruit, the wise ones become knowers; thus, being liberated from the bondage of birth (wherein birth itself is the bondage), they are liberated from the bondage of birth even while still living, and [attain] the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

They go to that which is called liberation, meaning that which is free from affliction and devoid of all calamities. Alternatively, beginning with the words "O Dhanañjaya, through the yoga of the intellect," the very intellect characterized by the vision of the supreme reality—which is comparable to water overflowing everywhere—has been shown to be produced by the purification of the mind born of karma-yoga, since it is heard in scripture to be the direct cause for the abandonment of good and evil deeds and so forth.
It is now stated when that intellect, born from the purification of the mind produced by the practice of yoga, will be attained:
"When your intellect shall transcend the thicket of delusion."
Then you will attain detachment from what is yet to be heard and from what has already been heard.

When—at which time—your "mohakalilam," that turbidity consisting of delusion and characterized by a lack of discrimination, by which the internal organ is directed toward sense objects after having clouded the knowledge that discriminates between the Self and the non-Self; when your intellect shall transcend—that is, pass beyond—that [turbidity], meaning it will attain a state of extreme purity; then, at that time, you shall go to—that is, attain—dispassion (*nirveda*) regarding what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard. The intention is that at that time, both what remains to be heard and what has been heard will appear to you as fruitless.

If you wonder, "When shall I, having attained the wisdom born of self-discrimination through the removal of the thick darkness of delusion, obtain the fruit of Karma-yoga, which is the Yoga of the Supreme Truth?"— then hear this: "When your faith, which has been perplexed by the scriptures, shall stand immovable..."
When your intellect is unshakable in meditation, then you will attain yoga.

When your intellect—having become conflicted, variously opposed, and distracted by the "hearings" (śruti), that is, by those scriptural teachings which reveal the manifold relationships between means and ends characterized by engagement and withdrawal—shall stand firm, having become steady and motionless, free from the movement of distraction, in "samādhi"; [that is to say] in the Self, for it is in this [Self] that the mind is composed (samādhīyate). This is what is meant by "in samādhi."

"Even there, being immovable and free from conceptual construction"—this refers to the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). "Then, at that time, you will attain yoga"—you will obtain discriminative wisdom (*vivekaprajñā*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Having obtained the seed of the question, Arjuna spoke; desiring to know the characteristics of one who has attained meditative absorption and wisdom,
Arjuna said:
Arjuna said:
What, O Keśava, is the description of one whose wisdom is steady and who is established in samādhi?
How does the one of steady intellect speak, how does he sit, and how does he move?

He whose wisdom is established in the realization, "I am the Supreme Brahman," is one of steady wisdom (*sthitaprajña*). What is the description of such a person of steady wisdom? What is his speech—how is he spoken of by others when he is established in *samādhi*, O Keśava? Or what would he himself speak? How does he sit or how does he move; what is his posture or his gait? This verse asks for the characteristics of one whose wisdom is steady.

For one who, from the very beginning, having renounced actions, has set out for steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, and another who [has set out] by means of the yoga of action—for these two, starting from the words "he abandons" (*prajahāti*) and continuing until the end of the chapter, the characteristics of one whose wisdom is established (*sthitaprajña*) and the means thereto are taught. Indeed, in all spiritual treatises (*adhyātma-śāstra*), those very things which are the characteristics of one who has attained his goal are taught as the means, because they are to be accomplished through effort.
Those which are both the means and the characteristics to be accomplished through effort, the Blessed Lord spoke of them:
When one abandons all desires of the mind, O Pārtha,
and is satisfied in the self alone by the self, then one is said to be of steady wisdom.
O Pārtha, when—at which time—one completely abandons, thoroughly relinquishes, and renounces all desires—that is, every variety of longing—whether they have entered the mind or entered the heart.

Since there would be no cause for satisfaction upon the renunciation of all desires, and since the mere necessity of maintaining the body remains, it might follow that one’s activity would be like that of a madman or a drunkard; therefore, it is said: "In the Self alone"—that is, in the very nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*)—"by the Self," by his own self, being satisfied without dependence on external gains, through the attainment of the nectar-essence of the vision of the ultimate truth, possessing the conviction that there is nothing else needed, he is a "steadfast-in-wisdom" (*sthitaprajña*); that is, the wise man whose wisdom (*prajñā*), born from the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self, is "steadfast," meaning firmly established.

To this it is said: one who has renounced the desires for son, wealth, and world is a *saṃnyāsī*; he is one who rejoices in the Self and sports in the Self; such is the meaning of "one whose wisdom is firmly established. (BhG 2.55)
Furthermore:
"One whose mind is undisturbed amidst sufferings, and who is free from longing amidst pleasures,"
One whose passion, fear, and anger have departed, and whose intellect is steady, is called a sage of steadfast wisdom.

When internal and other sufferings have arisen, he whose mind is neither agitated nor disturbed upon encountering suffering is one of undisturbed mind (*anudvignamanas*). Likewise, when pleasures have arisen, he from whom longing (*spṛhā*) or thirst has departed—meaning he does not increase further in accordance with pleasures like a fire fed with fuel—is one who has departed from longing (*vigataspṛha*). One from whom passion (*rāga*), fear (*bhaya*), and anger (*krodha*) have departed—that is, one in whom they have vanished—is one free from passion, fear, and anger (*vītarāgabhayakrodha*).
Such a person is called a sage (*muni*) of steady wisdom (*sthitaprajña*), a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*).
Furthermore:
"And he who is without attachment everywhere, having encountered whatever is auspicious or inauspicious,"
He who neither rejoices nor hates, his wisdom is firmly established.

That sage who is everywhere without attachment—even toward his own body and life—and is free from longing, who, having encountered various things, whether auspicious or inauspicious, neither rejoices nor feels aversion; meaning that upon encountering the auspicious he is not pleased or elated, and upon encountering the inauspicious he does not feel hatred—for him, being thus devoid of joy and dejection, wisdom born of discrimination becomes firmly established.
Furthermore,
when he withdraws these [senses] from all sides, just as a tortoise draws in its limbs;
The wisdom of one whose senses are withdrawn from the objects of the senses is firmly established.

When this ascetic, engaged in the perfection of knowledge, properly withdraws and fully draws back [his senses]—just as a tortoise, out of fear, withdraws its own limbs on all sides from every direction—so too does the one established in knowledge withdraw the senses from the objects of the senses, that is, from all sense-objects. For him, wisdom is firmly established; thus ends the meaning of the statement. (BhG 2.58)

In that regard, even for one who is afflicted and does not take in sense objects, the senses are withdrawn like the limbs of a tortoise; however, the passion for those objects is not withdrawn. How is that passion withdrawn? It is said:
"The sense objects turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food."
Except for taste; even his taste for objects ceases upon seeing the Supreme.

Although objects—and by extension, the sense organs designated by the term "objects"—cease to function for a person who abstains from food, who does not take in sensory objects, and who remains engaged in arduous austerity, even for a fool; this occurs for the embodied being with the exception of *rasa*. Here, *rasa* refers to attachment (*rāga*) toward objects. The word *rasa* is well-known in the sense of attachment, as seen in such expressions as "engaged by one's own *rasa*," "one who possesses *rasa*," and "one who knows *rasa*."

That taste, which consists of attachment, also ceases for this ascetic who, having seen and realized the Supreme Brahman—the ultimate reality—remains with the thought "I am indeed That. The meaning is that his cognition of objects becomes seedless. There is no eradication of taste in the absence of right vision; therefore, the intention is that one must establish the steadiness of wisdom, which is of the nature of right vision.

One who desires to achieve stability in the wisdom characterized by right vision must first bring the senses under one's own control; for He speaks of the fault that arises if they are not so controlled: "For even of a wise man, O son of Kuntī, though he strives..."
The turbulent senses violently carry away the mind.

O Kaunteya, because the senses of even a wise and intelligent man—who is striving, that is, making an effort—are turbulent by nature and prone to agitation, they indeed distract the person by turning him toward sense objects and throwing him into confusion; and having thrown him into confusion, they forcibly carry away the mind, even while it is clearly perceiving and endowed with discriminative knowledge.
Therefore,
having restrained all those [senses], one should sit disciplined, with me as the supreme goal.
For the wisdom of one whose senses are under control is firmly established.

Restraining all those [senses]—having performed their restraint, that is, their subjugation—one should sit disciplined and concentrated, being "devoted to Me," meaning one for whom I, Vāsudeva, the inner Self of all, am the Supreme; the sense is that one should sit thinking, "I am not other than He. For the yogi who sits in this manner, under whose control the senses abide through the power of practice, his wisdom is firmly established.
Now, for one who is about to fall, this root of all calamities is stated:
"For a person dwelling on sense-objects, attachment to them arises."
From attachment arises desire; from desire, anger is born.
From anger arises delusion; from delusion, the confusion of memory;
from the loss of memory, the destruction of intelligence; and from the destruction of intelligence, one perishes.

For a person who meditates, who reflects, and who perceives specific objects such as sound and the rest, attachment—that is, clinging or affection—arises toward those objects. From that attachment, which is affection, desire—that is, craving—is born. From desire, when it is obstructed by some cause, anger is produced.

From anger arises delusion (*saṃmoha*), which is a lack of discrimination regarding what ought and ought not to be done. For one who is angry, being thus deluded, even reviles his teacher. From delusion comes the confusion of memory (*smṛtivibhrama*); that is, the confusion or failure of memory—which is produced by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) instilled by the teachings of the scriptures and teachers—to occur when the conditions for its arising are present; it is the non-arising [of memory]. Then, from that confusion of memory comes the destruction of the intellect (*buddhināśa*). The "destruction of the intellect" refers to the incapacity of the internal organ, the intellect, to discriminate between what ought and ought not to be done.

"He perishes through the destruction of the intellect. For the person exists only so long as his internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is capable of discriminating between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. When it is no longer capable of that, the person is indeed destroyed. Therefore, "through the destruction of the intellect"—that is, of that internal organ—he perishes; the meaning is that he becomes incapable of fulfilling the purpose of the Self (puruṣārtha).
The root of all misfortune has been stated as the longing for sense objects. Now, this cause of liberation is being declared:
"But moving among sense objects with the senses free from attachment and aversion..."
With his senses under his own control, the self-subdued person attains serenity.

"Free from attachment and aversion": attachment and aversion are "rāga-dveṣau"; for the activity of the senses is naturally preceded by those two. In that regard, he who is a seeker of liberation, while moving among unavoidable objects and perceiving them with the senses—such as the ears and others—which are free from those two, [perceives] with those senses that have come under his own control, meaning they have become submissive to him. He whose inner organ (the self) is thus governable at will—that is, one whose mind is subject to his command—attains serenity.
He attains it. Serenity is clarity, a state of well-being.
It is said:
when there is serenity, what happens?
Upon the arising of serenity, the abandonment of all sufferings occurs for him.
For the intellect of one whose mind is serene quickly becomes established.

In serenity, there arises for this ascetic the loss—that is, the destruction—of all sufferings, beginning with those internal. Furthermore, because the intellect of one whose mind is serene, whose inner organ is healthy, quickly—that is, swiftly—becomes fully established; it becomes established all around like the sky, meaning it becomes motionless in the very nature of the Self.

Thus, for one whose mind is serene and whose intellect is established because his task is accomplished, the meaning of the sentence is that he should act with senses free from attachment and aversion, properly engaged in those unavoidable things that are not contrary to the scriptures. ||BhGS_2.65||
This very state of serenity is now praised:
"There is no wisdom for one who is undisciplined, nor is there meditative cultivation for one who is undisciplined."
And for one who does not meditate, there is no peace; for one who lacks peace, how can there be happiness?

The meaning is that it does not exist, is not found, and does not come to be. For one who is unyoked—that is, whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is not composed—the intellect has the nature of the Self as its object; however, for the unyoked, there is no contemplation (*bhāvanā*), which is to say, no intense application toward the knowledge of the Self. Likewise, for one who does not contemplate—that is, who does not apply himself to the knowledge of the Self—there is no peace (*śānti*), which is tranquility. For one who is not at peace, whence can there be happiness? Indeed, happiness is the cessation of the thirst for indulging in sense objects; it is not the thirst directed toward sense objects, for that is nothing but suffering.
The meaning is that as long as craving exists, not even a mere scent of happiness can arise.
It is said: Why does one who is undisciplined lack discernment?
For when the mind follows after the wandering senses, [discernment is lost].
It carries away his wisdom, just as the wind sweeps away a boat upon the waters.

For when the mind follows—that is, conforms to—the senses as they range, that is, as they proceed toward their respective objects, that mind, having become active through the conceptualization of sense-objects, carries away the wisdom of this ascetic; it destroys the wisdom born of the discrimination between the Self and the not-Self.

How? Just as the wind, having diverted a boat from its course upon the water, drives it onto a wrong path, so too does the mind, having stolen the wisdom whose object is the Self, direct it toward the objects of the senses. (BhG 2.67)
Having stated the various arguments for the point introduced by the words "For one who strives," and having established that point, he concludes:
"Therefore, O mighty-armed one, for him by whom [the senses] have been restrained in every way..."
The wisdom of one whose senses are withdrawn from the objects of the senses is firmly established.

Since the defect in the functioning of the senses has been demonstrated, therefore, O mighty-armed one, the wisdom of that ascetic whose senses—whether of the mind or other types—are completely restrained in every way from the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, is firmly established.

This worldly and Vedic conventional practice ceases for one who has attained discriminative knowledge and whose wisdom is established, because it is an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*); and since ignorance ceases through its opposition to knowledge (*vidyā*), he speaks to clarify this point:
"That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man keeps watch."
That in which beings are awake is night for the sage who sees.

That which is night for all beings—that is, the night which, by its nature of darkness, causes the non-discrimination of all objects—what is that? It is the reality of the supreme truth (*paramārthatattva*), the object of the one whose wisdom is steady. Just as it is day for nocturnal creatures while it is night for others, so too the reality of the supreme truth is like night for all ignorant beings, who stand in the place of nocturnal creatures; for it is not within the range of those whose intellects do not perceive it.

In that [state] characterized by the reality of the ultimate truth, the self-controlled one—meaning the yogi who possesses restraint and has conquered the senses—is awake and alert, having awakened from the sleep of ignorance. That night of ignorance, characterized by the distinction between the grasped object and the grasping subject, is said to be when all beings are truly asleep yet are called "awake"; for the sage who perceives the ultimate reality, that night exists because it is of the nature of ignorance, like those who see dreams while asleep.

Therefore, ritual actions are enjoined only in the state of ignorance, not in the state of knowledge. For when knowledge exists, ignorance perishes like the darkness of night upon the rising of the sun. Prior to the arising of knowledge, ignorance—being grasped by the intellect as a valid means of cognition and taking the form of distinctions between action, agent, and fruit—attains the status of being the cause of all ritual acts.

It is not possible for that which is apprehended by a non-authoritative cognition to be established as having action as its cause; for an agent engages in action with the thought, "Action is enjoined for me by the Veda, which is authoritative. For one who possesses self-knowledge—who realizes that this entire world of diversity is mere ignorance—there is qualification only for the renunciation of all actions, not for engagement in them. And so the Lord will show his qualification for steadfastness in knowledge alone through such passages as "with that as their intellect, with that as their self" (Gītā 5.17).

If it is argued that even in that case, activity would be impossible due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that prompts it, we say no; because the cognition of the Self has the Self itself as its object. For the Self does not require a prompting means of valid cognition with respect to itself, precisely because it is the Self. Furthermore, the status of being a means of valid cognition culminates in the Self, since all means of valid cognition have the Self as their ultimate end. Indeed, once the true nature of the Self is realized, the conventional operation of means and objects of cognition is no longer possible; for the final means of valid cognition brings to an end the subjecthood (*pramātṛtva*) of the Self.

And it becomes invalid even while it is turning back, just as the cognition of the time of a dream does upon waking; for in the world, a means of valid knowledge is not observed to be a cause for activity once the object has been apprehended. Therefore, it is established that one who knows the Self has no qualification for ritual action.

The attainment of liberation belongs only to the wise ascetic who has renounced all desires and whose intellect is established in steadiness, and not to the non-renunciant who pursues his desires; wishing to establish this point by means of an illustration, He says:
"Filled [to the brim], with its foundation unshakable..."
Just as the waters enter the ocean,
so do all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires.

Just as the waters flowing from all directions enter the ocean—which is being filled with water, yet remains established immovably, its stability consisting in its lack of motion—and which, though remaining within itself, undergoes no change; even so, that person into whom all particular desires enter from every side—even when objects of sense are present—without causing any agitation, and which, like the ocean, they all dissolve into the Self alone and do not bring under their own control, he is peace.

He attains liberation, and not the other who desires objects of desire; "objects of desire" (kāmāḥ) are those things which are desired, and he whose nature it is to desire them is one who desires objects of desire—the meaning is that such a person does not attain it at all. ||BhGS_2.70||
Therefore, since this is so, that man who, having abandoned all desires, wanders about free from longing—
Free from the sense of "mine" and free from the ego, he attains peace.

Having abandoned—that is, having completely renounced—all desires without exception, that person who is a *saṃnyāsī* "wanders," meaning he roams about with nothing remaining but the mere activity required for physical life; being "free from longing" (*niḥspṛhaḥ*), meaning one from whom desire has departed even regarding the mere maintenance of the body; being "free from the sense of 'mine'" (*nirmamaḥ*), meaning one devoid of the obsession "this is mine" even toward possessions necessitated by the mere maintenance of the body; and being "free from egoism" (*nirahaṃkāraḥ*), meaning one devoid of self-conceit based on causes such as learning and the like—this is what is meant.

Being thus situated, the man of steady wisdom, the knower of Brahman, attains—that is, reaches—peace, characterized by the cessation of all the sufferings of saṃsāra and known as Nirvāṇa; the meaning is that he becomes one with Brahman. ||BhGS_2.71||
This very steadfastness in knowledge is now being praised: "O Pārtha, this is the state of Brahman; having attained it, one is no longer deluded."
Abiding in this even at the time of death, one attains the Brahman-nirvana.

This aforementioned state is "brahmic"—that is, it pertains to Brahman; it consists of remaining in the very form of Brahman after having renounced all action. O Pārtha, having attained and reached this state, one does not become deluded—that is, one does not fall into confusion. Abiding in this aforementioned brahmic state, even at the time of death—even in the final stage of life—one attains, that is, reaches, the bliss of Brahman, which is liberation.
What more need be said? He who, having renounced even from the stage of studenthood (brahmacarya), remains established in Brahman alone for as long as he lives, attains the extinction in Brahman.

Thus ends the second chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya) and disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter Three:
The Third Discourse, with the Commentary of Śaṅkara.

The Blessed One has pointed out two types of intellect, which constitute the objects of engagement and withdrawal in this scripture: the intellect of Sāṅkhya and the intellect of Yoga. Therein, beginning from the verse "When one renounces all desires," up to the end of the chapter, he has taught that those who rely on the intellect of Sāṅkhya must practice renunciation, and that their purpose is fulfilled through steadfastness in that alone, stating, "This is the state of Brahman."

To Arjuna he said, "Your right is to action alone; let there be no attachment to inaction," thus declaring that action itself must be performed by resorting to the intellect of yoga, but he did not say that the attainment of the highest good comes from that alone.

Observing this, Arjuna’s mind became deeply perplexed, and he said: "How is it that, having first taught me—your devotee seeking my highest good—the very means for attaining that goal, namely steadfastness in the wisdom of Sāṅkhya, you now enjoin me to action, which is fraught with many visible evils and whose fruit is the attainment of a highest good that is indirect and uncertain? Thus, Arjuna's state of confusion was entirely justified. His corresponding question begins with the words, "If [action] were superior," and so forth.
And the Lord’s reply to that question was spoken in accordance with the scripture regarding the distinction as previously stated.

However, some, having misconstrued the meaning of Arjuna’s question, describe the Lord’s reply as being contrary to it. Furthermore, they explain the meaning of the question and the reply here in a manner that contradicts how the meaning of the *Gītā* was established by [Madhusūdana Sarasvatī] himself in his own work, the *Sambandha-grantha*. How so? In that *Sambandha-grantha*, he stated that the meaning established in the *Gītā-śāstra* is the combination (*samuccaya*) of knowledge and action for all those belonging to the stages of life (*āśramas*).

Furthermore, it is specifically distinguished that the view that liberation is attained through knowledge alone—having abandoned those rites enjoined by the scriptures for as long as one lives—is categorically prohibited.

But here, by demonstrating the optionality of the stages of life (*āśrama-vikalpa*), the abandonment of those very rites enjoined by the *śruti* for as long as one lives has been stated. How then could the Blessed One speak such a contradictory matter to Arjuna, or how could a listener comprehend such a contradictory meaning? To this, it might be argued that it is only for householders that liberation through knowledge alone—by abandoning the rites of the *śruti*—is prohibited, but not for those in other stages of life.

This too is indeed contradictory to what was stated previously. How so? Having first asserted that the combination of knowledge and action for members of all stages of life (*āśrama*) is the definitive meaning established in the Gītā scripture, how could one here state its opposite—that liberation comes from knowledge alone—for those in other stages of life?

Now, if it is thought that this statement—concerning Vedic rites—prohibits liberation for householders from knowledge alone, that is, from knowledge devoid of Vedic rites, and that in doing so it treats the Smārta rites existing for householders as if they did not exist, thereby declaring that there is no liberation from knowledge alone; even this is contradictory. How? It is impossible for those possessed of discrimination to determine why liberation through knowledge conjoined with Smārta rites is prohibited specifically for the householder, but not for those in other stages of life (āśramas).

Furthermore, if the Smārta rites are combined with those of the *ūrdhvaretas* (celibates) as a means to liberation, then let it be accepted that for the householder (*gṛhastha*) as well, there is combination only with the Smārta rites, not with the Śrauta ones.

Or, if it is argued that for the householder alone there is a combination of both Śrauta and Smārta rites for the sake of liberation, whereas for the *ūrdhvaretas* liberation arises from knowledge combined solely with Smārta rites—this being the case, the householder would be burdened with a great deal of exertion, having placed upon his head the many forms of suffering inherent in both Śrauta and Smārta ritual action.

Now, if it is argued that liberation belongs only to the householder because of the great amount of exertion required, whereas it does not belong to the other stages of life (*āśrama*) due to their lack of obligatory rites prescribed by the Vedas (*śrauta-nityakarman*), that too is incorrect. For in all the Upaniṣads, in the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Yoga-śāstras, the renunciation of all actions is enjoined for one desiring liberation as an auxiliary to knowledge; furthermore, both Śruti and Smṛti enjoin both the option and the combination of the stages of life.

Is it then established that there is a combination of knowledge and action for those in all stages of life (*āśrama*)? No, because for one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*), the renunciation of all actions is enjoined. For instance: "Having withdrawn from worldly life, they then lead the life of a mendicant" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1); "Therefore, they say that among these austerities, renunciation is superior" (Nārada Upaniṣad 2.79); "Renunciation alone would excel" (Nārada Upaniṣad 2.78); and "Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone some have attained immortality" (Nārada Upaniṣad 2.12). Furthermore, there are scriptural texts such as: "One should go forth into the wandering life directly from the stage of studentship" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4).
Abandon both dharma and adharma; abandon both truth and falsehood.
Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, abandon that by which you abandon them.

"Having seen that saṃsāra itself is devoid of essence, and desiring to see the essence, they go forth into homelessness without having performed marriage, relying upon supreme dispassion. Thus spoke Bṛhaspati even to Kaca:
"A living being is bound by action and is liberated by knowledge."

"Therefore, the ascetics who see the further shore do not perform actions" (Mbh 12.241.7). Such is the instruction of Śuka. Here too, it is said, "having renounced all actions with the mind," and so forth. Furthermore, since liberation is not something to be produced by action, action is useless for one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*). If it is argued that obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) must be performed in order to avoid transgression (*pratyavāya*), we say no. For the occurrence of transgression applies only to those who have not renounced; indeed, it cannot be conceived that a transgression accrues to a renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*) from the non-performance of fire-sacrifices and the like, in the same way as it does for students (*brahmacārin*) or for ritualists who have not renounced.

First of all, it is not possible to postulate the arising of a positive entity in the form of transgression (*pratyavāya*) simply from the non-existence of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), because of the scriptural teaching on the impossibility of the birth of the existent from the non-existent: "How could the existent be born from the non-existent? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.2).

If the Veda were to declare that demerit (*pratyavāya*) arises even from the non-performance of what is enjoined—though such a thing is impossible—then the Veda would be said to be unauthoritative (*apramāṇa*) because it causes harm, since both the performance and non-performance of what is enjoined would result solely in suffering. Consequently, the scripture would be imagined to have an untenable meaning, namely that it is prescriptive (*kāraka*) rather than informative (*jñāpaka*). But this is not accepted. Therefore, there are no ritual actions for renunciants; hence, the combination (*samuccaya*) of knowledge and action is untenable. Furthermore, Arjuna’s question—“If you consider wisdom to be superior to action” (*jyāyasī cet karmaṇas te matā buddhiḥ*)—would otherwise be inconsistent.

For if the Blessed One had stated in the second chapter that "knowledge and action must be performed by you in combination," then Arjuna’s question—"If you consider knowledge superior to action, O Janārdana"—would be inappropriate. If it were said to Arjuna that both knowledge and action are to be performed by him, then that knowledge which is superior to action would already have been mentioned; in that case, the question—"Why then do you urge me to this terrible action, O Keśava?"—could not possibly arise in any way.

Nor is it appropriate to assume that the Blessed One previously stated that Arjuna’s superior intellect was not to be practiced—on account of which there would be the question, "If [knowledge] is superior"—for if, however, the Blessed One had previously stated that because knowledge and action are contradictory for a single person, their simultaneous practice is impossible and thus they must be practiced by different persons, then this question beginning with "If [knowledge] is superior" would be appropriate.

Even if one were to assume that the question arises from a lack of discrimination, the Blessed One’s reply would still be untenable, as it prescribes different duties for different types of persons. Nor can the Blessed One’s reply be imagined to be based on ignorance. Since the Blessed One’s reply clearly shows that the steadfastness in knowledge and the steadfastness in action are to be practiced by distinct classes of persons, the combination of knowledge and action is impossible. Therefore, the conclusion that liberation comes from knowledge alone is certain both in the *Gītā* and in all the Upaniṣads.
"Tell me with certainty which one of knowledge and action is superior"—this request for a single object is inappropriate if the combination of both were possible.
Furthermore, by the restrictive phrase "Therefore, you must perform action alone," [the Lord] will demonstrate to Arjuna the impossibility of being established in knowledge.
Arjuna said:
If you consider intelligence to be superior to action, O Janārdana,
then why do you urge me toward this terrible deed, O Keśava?

If *buddhi*—meaning knowledge—is considered by you to be superior (*jyāyasī*) and more beneficial (*śreyasī*) than action, O Janārdana! If both *buddhi* and action were intended to be combined as a single means to the highest good, then Arjuna’s statement that "knowledge is superior to action" would be inconsistent, as it would imply that knowledge is something additional to action; for that very same thing cannot be additional to itself in terms of its result.

Furthermore, the Blessed One has taught that the intellect regarding action leads to the highest good (*śreyas*), yet he now instructs me to perform an action that does not lead to the highest good. What, then, could be the reason for this? Thus, as if censuring the Blessed One, Arjuna asks: "Why, O Keśava, do you urge me toward this terrible, cruel act characterized by violence? This [objection] is also untenable.

Now, if the Blessed One had declared that all [actions] are to be combined with ritual action (smārta-karman), and Arjuna had understood this, then how could such speech as "Why do You urge me toward this terrible action" be appropriate? (BhG 3.1)
Furthermore: "Moreover,
with these seemingly contradictory words, you are, as it were, bewildering my intellect."
Therefore, tell me with certainty that one by which I may attain the highest good.

"As if mixed," even though the Blessed One speaks with distinct clarity, nevertheless, to my dull intellect, the Blessed One's words appear as if mixed. Therefore, it seems You are confusing my intellect; for while You have set out to remove the confusion of my intellect, how is it that You instead cause confusion? Hence I say: "You seem to confuse my intellect."

But if you think it impossible for a single person to perform both knowledge and action—which have different agents—then, this being the case, having determined which one of those two, either wisdom or action, is appropriate for Arjuna according to his capacity, disposition, and state, speak; tell me by which one of these two, whether knowledge or action, I may attain the highest good.

For if knowledge had been taught by the Blessed One as even a subordinate element within the perfection of action, then how could Arjuna’s desire to hear have been directed toward a single subject in the words, "Tell me one of these two"? Indeed, the Blessed One had not previously stated, "I shall speak of only one of these two—either knowledge or action, and not both"—such that Arjuna, considering the impossibility of attaining both, would have requested only one. (BhG 3.2)
The Blessed Lord spoke a reply that was exactly in accordance with the question.
In this world, O sinless one, two kinds of steadfastness were declared by me of old:
that of the Sāṅkhyas through the yoga of knowledge, and that of the Yogis through the yoga of action.

O sinless one, in this world, for the three social orders (traivarṇika) who are entitled to the practice of the meaning of the scriptures, there are two kinds—two types—of steadfastness (niṣṭhā), that is, a state of being or the intent regarding what is to be practiced. This was declared by me, the omniscient Lord, in the past at the beginning of creation, after creating living beings and revealing the traditional transmission of the Vedic meaning as the means for their attainment of worldly prosperity and the supreme good.

Regarding that, as to what those two kinds of steadfastness (niṣṭhā) are, he says: therein, by means of the yoga of knowledge—knowledge itself being the yoga—the steadfastness of the Sāṃkhyas is declared; that is, of those who possess the discriminative discernment regarding the Self and the non-Self, who have performed renunciation from the very stage of the religious student (brahmacarya), whose purpose is well-ascertained through the realization of the Vedānta, who are wandering mendicants of the highest order (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka), and who abide in Brahman alone.
By means of the yoga of action—action itself being the yoga, i.e., karma-yoga—the meaning is that the steadfastness of the Yogis, those engaged in action, is declared.

If it were the Lord’s intention—as expressed, implied, or stated in the Gītā and the Vedas—that knowledge and action should be practiced in combination by a single person for the sake of a single human goal, then why would he here tell Arjuna, who has approached him as a dear disciple, that the two disciplines of knowledge and action have distinct and different agents? Furthermore, [one might argue: "Arjuna will practice both knowledge and action himself upon hearing of them; however, I shall declare that these two are to be practiced by different persons for others."

If it were imagined that this is the Blessed One’s own view, then the Blessed One would have to be imagined as possessing passion and hatred and thus not being an authoritative source; and that is incorrect. Therefore, by no reasoning whatsoever can there be a synthesis of knowledge and action.

That which was stated by Arjuna regarding the superiority of wisdom over action remains established, because it has not been refuted; and that this steadfastness in knowledge is to be practiced only by renunciants follows from the statement that they are to be practiced by different persons. It is understood that the Blessed One himself agrees precisely with this.

Perceiving Arjuna to be dejected in mind—thinking, "You are binding me to action alone"—and observing that he had concluded, "I shall not undertake action," the Blessed One said: "Not by abstaining from actions... [2.46].

Alternatively, since devotion to knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*) and devotion to action (*karman-niṣṭhā*) are mutually contradictory and cannot be practiced simultaneously by a single person, it might follow that they are each independently causes for the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). To show that devotion to action is a cause for the human goal only as a means of attaining devotion to knowledge, and not independently, whereas devotion to knowledge—having acquired its very nature through the means of devotion to action—is an independent cause for the human goal without depending on anything else—the Blessed One speaks as follows:
A person does not attain freedom from action by abstaining from the commencement of actions,
nor does he achieve perfection merely through renunciation.

Knowledge does not arise from ritual actions—such as sacrifices and the like, performed either in this life or in another birth—which, by virtue of being causes for the destruction of accumulated sins, are means for purifying the *sattva*; nor does it arise from those [actions] which, by being the cause of that [purification], serve as causes for the steadfastness in knowledge through the gateway of the arising of knowledge.

For there is a traditional teaching (*smṛti*) stating: "Knowledge arises in men from the destruction of sinful action; one sees the Self within oneself, as if in a surface like a mirror" (Mahābhārata 12.208.8), and so forth.

From non-commencement—that is, from non-performance—one does not attain *naiṣkarmya*, the state of being free from action, the emptiness of action; that is to say, one does not reach the culmination through the yoga of knowledge, which is abiding in the very nature of the inactive Self. The meaning is that the person does not obtain it.

From the statement that "one does not attain freedom from action (*naiṣkarmya*) through the non-commencement of actions," it is understood by its opposite that one attains freedom from action through their commencement. For what reason, then, does one not attain freedom from action through the non-commencement of actions? It is said: because the very commencement of action is the means (*upāya*) to freedom from action; for there is no attainment of the goal (*upeya*) without a means.

Furthermore, the fact that the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) is a means to the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), which is characterized by freedom from action (*naiṣkarmya*), is established both in the Śruti and here [in this text]. In the Śruti, the means of knowing the Self—the object of knowledge under discussion—is set forth as follows: "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice," and so on; thus, the status of the yoga of action as a means to the yoga of knowledge is established.

And here too, He will establish this through such passages as: "But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga" (Gītā 5.6), "The yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the purification of the self" (Gītā 5.11), and "Sacrifice, charity, and austerity are indeed the purifiers of the wise" (Gītā 18.5).

But surely, in such passages as "Having granted fearlessness to all beings, one should practice actionlessness" (*naiṣkarmya*), [the Lord] shows that the attainment of actionlessness occurs even through the renunciation of obligatory duties. Furthermore, in the world, it is more well-known that actionlessness results from the non-commencement of actions. Therefore, the following objection arises: for one who seeks actionlessness, what is the use of commencing action? To this, he says: "Nor indeed by mere renunciation."

Nor does one attain perfection—characterized by freedom from action (naiṣkarmya), which is steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge—merely through renunciation alone, that is, through the mere abandonment of action devoid of knowledge. ||BhG 3.4||

Furthermore, in response to the inquiry as to why a person does not attain perfection characterized by freedom from action (*naiṣkarmya*) through the mere renunciation of action alone, devoid of knowledge, He says: "For no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action."
For everyone is driven to action, even against their will, by the qualities born of material nature.

For indeed, no one ever, at any time, remains even for a moment without performing action. Why? Because every living being is compelled—that is, set in motion—helplessly and without independence by the qualities (*guṇas*) born of *prakṛti*, namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. The ellipsis is "the ignorant person," since the author will later say, "he who is not shaken by the qualities. Because of the Sāṃkhya doctrine of their distinctness, the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) is intended only for the ignorant, not for the knowers.

But for the wise, since they cannot be moved by the qualities (guṇas) and lack any movement of their own, the yoga of action is not applicable; this has been explained in the commentary on the verse beginning, "The Vedas do not lead to the Knower" (Gītā 2.21).
As for the claim that one who does not know the Self does not undertake enjoined action—that is indeed false; thus he says:
"He who sits restraining the organs of action but continues to dwell upon them with the mind..."
He whose self is deluded regarding the objects of the senses is called a hypocrite.

He who sits remaining with the organs of action, such as the hands and so forth, restrained and withdrawn, yet remembers and contemplates the objects of the senses—the sense-objects—with a deluded mind, that is, with a deluded internal organ, is called one of false conduct, one of deceitful conduct, or one of sinful conduct. (BhG 3.6)
But he who, O Arjuna, having restrained the senses by the mind,
engages in the yoga of action through the organs of action without attachment— he is preeminent.

But he who, on the other hand, being ignorant yet qualified for action, O Arjuna, restrains the senses of perception with the mind and undertakes action through the organs of action such as speech and hands—being unattached and free from desire for the fruits—he, performing the yoga of action, excels the other who acts falsely.
Since this is so,
therefore perform your duty with resolve; for action is indeed superior to inaction.
Moreover, even the maintenance of your body would not be possible for you through inaction.

That which is prescribed by the scriptures as constant and obligatory is "niyata" (duty). Whatever action one is qualified for, and for which no specific fruit is heard of in the texts, that is "niyata-karma" (obligatory duty); perform that, O Arjuna! For action is superior—that is, more excellent—than its fruit. Why? Because from "akarma," meaning non-performance or non-undertaking, even the maintenance of the body—the physical subsistence of yourself—would not be accomplished; it would not attain fulfillment through non-action. Therefore, the distinction between action and non-action is evident in the world.
And as for what you think—that action should not be performed because it has the nature of bondage—that too is incorrect. Why?
Because apart from action performed for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by action.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform action for that purpose, free from attachment.

"Viṣṇu is indeed sacrifice," according to the Vedic scripture; thus, the Lord is sacrifice. Whatever is performed for His sake is "action for the sake of sacrifice. Other than that action, this world is occupied with other actions; it is a doer of action, bound by action—this world is "bound by action," meaning its bondage is action—and not [bound] by action for the sake of sacrifice.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform your duty for His sake—that is, for the sake of sacrifice—being free from attachment, that is, devoid of attachment to the fruits of action.
For this reason also, one who is qualified must perform action; having created beings together with sacrifice, Prajāpati spoke to them in the beginning:
By this you shall procreate; let this be the cow of plenty that grants your desired objects.

Having created in the past—at the beginning of creation—the three social orders (varṇas), those subjects accompanied by sacrifice, Prajāpati, the creator of beings, said: "By this sacrifice you shall procreate; 'procreation' means growth or birth, so perform that. Let this sacrifice be for you a cow of plenty (iṣṭakāmadhuk)—that which milks out desired objects, meaning it yields specific fruits according to one's wishes. (BhG 3.10)
How so?
By nourishing the gods with this, may those gods nourish you.
Cultivating one another, you shall attain the supreme good.

Nourish—that is, cause to prosper—the gods, Indra and the others, by means of this sacrifice; may those gods nourish—that is, cause you to swell with abundance—by means of rain and other benefits. Thus, nourishing one another mutually, you shall attain the highest good characterized by liberation through the gradual acquisition of higher knowledge, or you shall attain heaven as the supreme good.
Furthermore,
"The gods, nourished by sacrifice, will indeed grant you the enjoyments you desire."
He who enjoys what has been given by them without giving to them in return is indeed a thief.

For the gods will give—that is, they will bestow—upon you the desired and cherished enjoyments, such as women, cattle, sons, and so forth; the meaning is that these have been nourished, increased, and gratified by sacrifices. He who enjoys those enjoyments given by those gods without giving them back—that is, without discharging his debt—is indeed a thief, a robber who steals the property of the gods and others. (BhG 3.12)
But those who eat the remnants of the sacrifice, being virtuous, are liberated from all sins.
But those wicked ones who cook for their own sake eat only sin.

Those who, having performed the sacrifices to the gods and other rites, have the habit of eating the remnants of those offerings—which are called *amṛta*—are "eaters of the sacrificial remnants" (*yajñaśiṣṭāśinaḥ*). Being such, they are liberated from all sins—that is, from all evils consisting of the five slaughter-houses beginning with the hearth, as well as from others produced by violence committed through negligence. But those who eat for their own sake, being themselves sinful, they indeed consume sin (*agha*); for they cook—that is, they perform the act of preparing food—for their own sake, for the purpose of themselves alone. (BhG 3.13)
For this reason as well, the prescribed action must be performed by one who is qualified. For action is indeed the cause for the continued functioning of the world-cycle. How so? It is said:
"Beings arise from food; the production of food comes from rain."
From sacrifice comes rain; sacrifice originates from action.

From food that has been eaten and transformed into blood and semen, beings are directly seen to be born. From rain comes the production of food; from sacrifice comes rain. As the traditional law (smṛti) states: "The oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun; from the sun rain is produced, from rain comes food, and from that, living creatures" (Manu 3.76).

The sacrifice is the *apūrva* (the unseen potency). And that sacrifice originates from action (*karman*). The activity of both the officiating priests and the sacrificer is "action"; that sacrifice, which is the *apūrva*, has its origin in that [activity], and thus it is called "originating from action."
And as to where such action originates, he says:
"Know that action has its origin in Brahman; Brahman has its origin in the Imperishable."
Therefore, the all-pervading Brahman is eternally established in sacrifice.

"Action has its origin in Brahman. "Brahman" means the Veda; know—that is, understand—that action has that as its origin, its cause, and its illuminator. Furthermore, "Brahman," which is called the Veda, has its origin in the Imperishable (*akṣara*); "originating from the Imperishable" means that whose source is the Imperishable, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). The meaning is that Brahman is the Veda.

Since the Veda has emerged from the Imperishable, which is called the Supreme Self—like the breath of a person—it is all-pervading because it illuminates all objects. And although it is all-pervading, it is eternally established in sacrifice, because it is primarily concerned with the injunctions for sacrifice.
O Pārtha, he who does not follow this wheel thus set in motion lives in vain; he is evil-minded, delighting in the senses.

Thus, having been set in motion by the Lord according to the Vedas and sacrifices, he who does not follow this wheel of the world in this life—being one who is qualified for action but whose life is sinful (aghāyuḥ), meaning his livelihood (āyuḥ) is sin (agham), that is to say, he lives a life of wickedness—and whose delight is in the senses (indriyārāmaḥ), meaning he finds pleasure (ārāmaḥ) and sport (ākrīḍā) in sense-objects—he lives in vain, O Pārtha.

Therefore, the meaning of this section is that action must indeed be performed by one who is unenlightened but qualified. Until one attains fitness for steadfastness in the knowledge of the Self, the performance of *karmayoga* for that purpose must necessarily be carried out by the qualified person who does not yet know the Self. This has been established starting from the verse, "Not by abstaining from actions" (Gītā 3.4), up to the end of the passage, "Even the maintenance of the body would not be possible for you through inaction" (Gītā 3.8). Subsequently, this was further explained in the passage beginning with, "Other than action performed for the sake of sacrifice" (Gītā 3.9).

With the passage ending with "In vain, O Pārtha, does he live," many reasons have been stated incidentally for the performance of action by the person under discussion—the one who does not know the Self—and the proclamation of the fault in its non-performance has also been made. (BhG 3.16)

This being the case, one might ask: must everyone follow this wheel thus set in motion? Or rather, has it not been attained by those who do not know the Self through the yoga of knowledge—which is to be practiced by the Sāṃkhyas who know the Self and which is reached by the means of practicing the previously mentioned yoga of action? Anticipating such a question from Arjuna, or perhaps for the sake of clarifying the meaning of the scripture for himself, [the Lord says: "Having known that very Self, the Brāhmaṇas, their false knowledge having ceased..."

Having renounced the desire for sons and other such duties which must necessarily be performed by those possessed of false knowledge, they then lead the life of a mendicant, motivated solely by the maintenance of the body. "For them, there is no other duty remaining apart from steadfastness in the knowledge of the Self" (BAU 3.5.1). Revealing this intended meaning of the Śruti as it is to be established here in the Gītā-śāstra, the Blessed Lord says: "But that person who rejoices only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self, and who is content in the Self alone—for him, no duty exists. (BhG 3.17)

But he who is a follower of Sāṃkhya, established in the knowledge of the Self, whose delight is in the Self—meaning his delight is in the Self alone and not in sense-objects—he should be one whose delight is indeed in the Self; and he should be satisfied by the Self alone, not by food, flavors, and so forth. That man, that human being, the renunciant, is satisfied in the Self alone. For while satisfaction arises for everyone upon the acquisition of external objects, he is satisfied in the Self alone, regardless of those things, meaning he is free from thirst (craving) toward everything. For such a knower of the Self, no duty remains to be performed; the meaning is that there is none. || BhG 3.17 ||
Furthermore,
he has no purpose whatsoever here through what is done, nor any through what is not done.
And for him, there is no dependence on any object whatsoever among all beings.

For one who delights in the Supreme Self, there is no purpose or need for action performed. Well then, might there be harm known as transgression (*pratyavāya*) resulting from non-performance? No; in this world, there is no such thing as the attainment of transgression, nor even the loss of the self, arising from non-performance. Furthermore, for such a person, there is no dependence upon any object among all beings—from Brahmā down to the stationary entities—for any purpose that must be accomplished through action motivated by a specific goal.

There is no goal to be accomplished by relying upon some particular element of existence as a support, such that an action for its sake would have to be performed. You, however, do not abide in this right vision, which is like a place flooded with water on all sides.
Since this is so, therefore, being unattached, always perform the action that ought to be done.
For by performing action without attachment, a person attains the Supreme.

Therefore, unattached—free from clinging—always, at all times, perform, carry out, and complete the work that must be done, the obligatory duty; for by performing it unattached, acting for the sake of the Lord, a person attains the supreme liberation through the purification of the mind (sattva)—this is the meaning. || BhG 3.19 ||
And because Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone.
Even considering the welfare of the world, you ought to act.

For it is by action alone that the wise Kṣatriyas of old, such as Janaka and others—Janaka being the king of the Vatsas and so forth—set out and attained perfection, which is liberation. If they had already attained right vision (*samyagdarśana*), then, for the sake of maintaining the world (*lokasaṃgraha*) and because their actions were already commenced, the meaning is that they attained perfection through action itself, without renouncing action.

If Janaka and others had not yet attained right vision (*samyagdarśana*), then this verse must be explained as follows: they attained perfection through action that served as a means for the purification of the inner being (*sattvaśuddhi*) in due course. Now, if you think that Janaka and others, while still ignorant, performed their duties, and therefore it is not necessarily required that another person who possesses right vision and has achieved his purpose must likewise perform action; [we reply: The Blessed One says: "Not so, O Arjuna. Even those who have attained right vision must perform action until the end of their bodies. This is stated in the following verse: "Even the men of vision, being embodied, should perform action without attachment, for by performing action one attains the supreme state. (3.20) The meaning is as follows: even those who possess right vision should perform action until the end of their bodies. Why? Because the body is the instrument for the performance of action. Therefore, as long as there is a body, action must be performed. Furthermore, because the body is the instrument for action, it is impossible to remain inactive even for a moment. For one who does not act, the body would fall away, and he would incur sin. Thus, even those who have attained right vision must perform action until the end of their bodies. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the Lord states that even those who have attained right vision must perform action, because action is a means for the purification of the inner being. This is stated in the following verse: "For action is superior to inaction; even the maintenance of the body cannot be accomplished by inaction. He who is attached to the body is bound by action, but he who is free from attachment attains liberation through renunciation of action. (3.8) The meaning is as follows: action is superior to inaction. Why? Because even the maintenance of the body cannot be accomplished by inaction. For one who is attached to the body, action binds him; however, one who is free from attachment attains liberation through the renunciation of action. Nevertheless, being subject to the karma that has already begun to bear fruit, you ought to act even while considering the "gathering of people"—that is, the prevention of the world from following the wrong path—as your very purpose.
To explain for what purpose the maintenance of the world (lokasaṃgraha) must be performed, it is said:
"Whatever a superior person practices, that very same thing other people follow."
Whatever standard he sets, the world follows that.

Whatever action the best person performs—whether he does it or causes it to be done—another person, being his follower, performs that very same action. Furthermore, whatever standard the best person establishes, whether worldly or Vedic, the world follows that; the meaning is that the world accepts that very thing as its authority.
If you have a doubt regarding my duty to gather the world together, then why do you not see me?
O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that must be done by me.
There is nothing further to be attained that has not already been attained, yet one must continue to engage in action.

For me, O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever—nothing at all—that remains to be done in the three worlds. Why? Because there is nothing unattained, nothing not yet reached, and nothing to be attained that must be acquired. Nevertheless, I continue to engage in action.
For if I were not to engage in action tirelessly,
O Pārtha, men would follow my path in every respect.

For if, on the other hand, I were not to engage in action, ever and at any time, being untiring and free from laziness—then men would follow the path, the way of me, who am the best; O Pārtha, in every respect and in all ways. (BhG 3.23)
If I were not to perform action, these worlds would perish;
I would be the author of confusion and would destroy these beings.

All these worlds would perish, they would be destroyed, due to the absence of the karma that is the cause for the maintenance of the world, were I not to perform action. Furthermore, I would be the author of confusion; by that reason, I would destroy these creatures. The meaning is that, being engaged in the favoring of creatures, I would bring about their destruction or ruin; this would result in something inconsistent with my nature as the Lord.

Furthermore, if you, like me, have attained the realization that your purpose is fulfilled—whether you are a knower of the Self or anyone else—even though there is nothing further to be done for that Self, one must still act solely for the sake of favoring others; thus he says:
"O Bhārata, as those who are unlearned act while being attached to action..."
Thus, a wise man, being unattached, should act while desiring the welfare of the world.

O Bhārata, just as some ignorant people act while attached to action, thinking, "The fruit of this action shall be mine," so should the wise man who knows the Self act, remaining unattached. Why does he act in that manner? Listen to that: desiring to effect the welfare of the world (lokasaṃgraha).

Thus, for one who desires to effect the welfare of the world, there is no duty to be performed other than the welfare of the world, whether it be myself or another who knows the Self. Therefore, this is taught to that knower of the Self:
"One should not create a disturbance in the minds of the ignorant who are attached to action."
The wise man, acting with disciplined composure, should encourage all actions.

"Differentiation of the intellect" (buddhibheda) means the breaking or disturbing of the intellect—that is, the intellect in the form of a resolve such as "this must be done by me" or "the fruit of this action must be enjoyed. He should not produce or generate that in the ignorant, the undiscriminating, those who are attached to action, being full of attachment toward action. What indeed should he do? The wise man should cause them to engage; while himself remaining disciplined and intent, he should perform all actions for the sake of those who are ignorant.
How does the ignorant, non-knowing person become attached to actions? To this he says:
"All actions are performed in every way by the qualities of material nature."
One whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer."

Nature (prakṛti) is the primary source (pradhāna), the state of equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas) of sattva, rajas, and tamas. All actions—both worldly and scriptural—that are performed by the modifications (vikāras) of that nature, which consist of the body and the senses, are undertaken by one whose self is deluded by egoism (ahaṃkāra). "Egoism" (ahaṃkāra) is the notion that the aggregate of the body and the senses is the self; one who is "deluded in various ways" (vividhaṃ mūḍha) by that [egoism] is one whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is thus confused. Such a person possesses the attributes of the body and the senses and identifies with the body and the senses.
Through ignorance, imagining actions to belong to the self, one thinks, "I am the doer of those various actions."
But he who is wise, O mighty-armed one, and knows the truth regarding the divisions of the qualities and their functions—
Realizing that "the qualities act upon the qualities," he does not become attached.

But one who knows the truth, O mighty-armed one—of what does he know the truth? The meaning is: one who knows the truth regarding the divisions of the qualities (guṇas) and actions (karma). Having realized that the qualities, which consist of the instruments of perception, abide within the objects consisting of the qualities, and that the Self does not so abide, he does not become attached; he does not form an attachment.
But those who, deluded by the qualities of nature, become attached to the actions of the qualities;
One who knows the whole should not cause those dull-witted ones, who know only a part, to waver from their path.

Being thoroughly deluded and bewildered by the qualities of Prakṛti, they become attached to the actions of the qualities—that is, to the "guṇa-karmas"—thinking, "We perform action for the sake of its fruit. One who knows the Whole (the Knower of the Self), being himself a Knower of the Whole, should not unsettle those who are attached to action, who lack complete knowledge, who see only the results of action, and who are dull-witted. The meaning is that he should not cause a division in their understanding; "unsettling" means precisely the act of creating such a split in the intellect, and he should not do that.
Furthermore, how should one who is unenlightened, yet authorized for action and desirous of liberation, perform action? It is said:
"Having renounced all actions in Me with a mind focused on the inner Self..."
Free from desire and free from the sense of "mine," fight, devoid of feverish anxiety.

Having renounced—that is, having cast off—all actions upon me, Vāsudeva, the Supreme Lord, the Omniscient One, the Self of all, with a mind directed toward the inner self through discriminative intellect; that is, with the understanding: "I am the agent, and I act for the sake of the Lord like a servant. Furthermore, being free from desire—having abandoned all longing—and being free from the sense of "mine"—that is, you who have cast off the notion of possessiveness—fight, meaning while remaining free from fever, free from distress, and free from grief.
That which I have declared as my considered opinion— that action must be performed— is thus: "Those men who always follow this teaching of mine..."
Those who possess faith and are free from malice are also liberated from the bonds of karma.

Those men who constantly follow and abide by this, my teaching—being full of faith, believing, and free from malice, harboring no envy toward me, Vāsudeva, the supreme teacher—they too, being such as these, are liberated from the bonds of action known as dharma and adharma.
But those who, finding fault with this, do not follow my teaching—
know them to be deluded in all knowledge, lost, and devoid of discernment.

But those who, being contrary to this, find fault with my teaching and, censuring it, neither practice nor follow my thought—they are deluded in all matters of knowledge; know them, understand them, to be utterly deluded in all knowledge, ruined, gone to destruction, and devoid of discernment.

But for what reason do they not follow your teaching, yet instead practice the duties of others and do not conform to their own dharma? Being opposed to you, why do they not fear the fault of transgressing your command? To this he replies:
"Even a man of knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature."
All beings follow their own nature; what can restraint accomplish?

One acts—that is, performs an action—in accordance with, that is, conforming to, one's own nature (*prakṛti*). What is this "nature"? It refers to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of previously performed merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth, which have become manifest at the beginning of the present birth. It is in accordance with that very nature that every living being acts—even one possessed of knowledge, let alone a fool. Therefore, all beings—meaning sentient creatures—follow their nature; they go according to it.
What will suppression—consisting of prohibition—do to me or to anyone else? "For nature is difficult to suppress," is the completion of the sentence. (BhG 3.33)

If every living being acts only in accordance with its own nature (*prakṛti*), and there is no one at all devoid of such nature, then, since the scope for human effort (*puruṣakāra*) would be untenable, the scriptures would become useless; to this objection, it is said:
"Lust and hatred are fixed toward the objects of each respective sense-organ."
One should not come under their sway, for they are his adversaries.

Regarding each sense-organ and its object—that is, with respect to the objects of all the senses such as sound and the rest—attachment arises toward what is desired and aversion toward what is undesired. Thus, attachment and aversion necessarily occur in relation to every sense-object; in this regard, the scope of human effort and the purpose of the scripture is stated: one engaged in the purpose of the scripture should not fall under the sway of attachment and aversion from the very beginning. For whatever is the nature of a person, that very nature impels the person toward their own activity, preceded by attachment and aversion.

Then there occurs the abandonment of one’s own duty and the performance of the duty of another. But when one restrains passion and hatred by their opposites, then the person truly possesses the vision of the scriptures and is no longer under the sway of primordial nature (prakṛti). Therefore, one should not fall under the power of those two, passion and hatred; for they are the adversaries of this person, acting as obstacles on the path to the highest good like two robbers on a road—this is the meaning.

In this regard, one impelled by passion and hatred may even misinterpret the meaning of the scriptures, thinking: "Since another's duty is also a duty, it must certainly be performed. That is incorrect;
for one's own duty, though deficient in quality, is better than the duty of another well-performed.
Death in one's own duty is better; the duty of another is fraught with fear.

One's own duty (svadharma), though deficient in qualities (viguṇa)—that is, even if it lacks excellence—is better than the duty of another (paradharma) even when that other is well-performed with all its qualities. Death while established in one's own duty is better than life while established in the duty of another. Why? Because the duty of another brings fear; for it brings about fear characterized by hell and other such states. || BhG 3.35 ||

Although it has been stated that "for a person who meditates on sense-objects, desire and aversion arise, which are the roots of evil" (Gītā 2.62), and that "desire and aversion are indeed his adversaries" (Gītā 3.34)—and although that [evil] was described as being distracted and undetermined—Arjuna, wishing to know it in its condensed and certain form, thinking "once this is known, I shall make an effort to eradicate it," said: "Then, by what impelled does this person commit sin? (Gītā 3.36)
Even though he does not desire it, O Vārṣṇeya, he is as if constrained by force.

Now, by what cause impelled does this person perform—that is, practice—an evil deed, even against his own will, like a servant for a king? O Vārṣṇeya, born of the Vṛṣṇi clan! He acts as if constrained by force, "as if by a king"—this is the illustration mentioned. (BhG 3.36)
"Listen, you must know that enemy who causes all misfortune about whom you ask," the Blessed One said: "This is desire, this is anger, born of the quality of rajas."
He is a great eater and a great sinner; know him here as your enemy.
"Lordship (bhaga) is the designation for the sixfold set consisting of complete sovereignty, virtue, fame, splendor, dispassion, and liberation. Thus,
that Vāsudeva in whom this sixfold set— sovereignty and the rest— exists eternally and in its entirety, without any obstruction, [is called Bhagavān].
"He who knows the origin and dissolution, as well as the coming and going of beings, and who knows both knowledge and ignorance—he is to be called the Blessed One (Bhagavān).
He whose cognition has as its object the origin and so forth is Vāsudeva; he is to be called the Blessed One.

Regarding "desire" (*kāma*): this desire is the enemy of all the worlds, for it is on account of it that all calamities befall living beings. When this very desire is frustrated by someone, it transforms into anger. Therefore, anger too is this same [desire]. It arises from the quality of passion (*rajas*); *rajaḥ* and *guṇaḥ* constitute *rajoguṇaḥ*, and that which has this as its source is "arising from the quality of passion. Alternatively, it is the source of the quality of passion. For desire, once arisen, impels a person by setting the quality of passion into motion.

"Driven by thirst"—this lamentation is heard from those suffering who are engaged in service and other such activities that are effects of *rajas*. One for whom great eating is characteristic is a "great eater"; for this very reason, he is a "great sinner. For a living being impelled by desire commits sin; therefore, know this desire to be the enemy here in this cycle of worldly existence.
How is he an enemy? He makes this understood through examples:
"Just as fire is obscured by smoke, and a mirror by dust."
Just as the embryo is enveloped by the amnion, so is this [world] enveloped by that.

Fire, whose nature is light, is covered by smoke, which is of a non-luminous nature; or as a mirror is covered by dirt; and just as the embryo is covered and concealed by the inner membrane, the outer membrane, and the amnion that envelops it, so too is this [Self] covered by that.
But what, then, is this which is denoted by the word "this" (idam) and said to be covered by desire?
Knowledge is covered by this eternal enemy of the wise.
O son of Kuntī, by means of desire, which is like a fire that is impossible to satiate.

Knowledge is veiled by this eternal enemy of the man of knowledge; for the man of knowledge knows, "By this [desire], I have previously been directed toward what is harmful," and thus he remains constantly miserable. Therefore, it is the eternal enemy of the man of knowledge, but not of the fool. For the fool, perceiving desire as a friend at the time of craving, only realizes when the resulting misery has arrived that "I have been brought to a state of suffering by craving," and not beforehand. Hence, it is the eternal enemy of the man of knowledge alone.

In what form? In the form of desire (*kāmarūpa*); that which has desire—meaning longing—as its very form is "desire-form. By that [fire], which is difficult to fill (*duṣpūra*), meaning that which cannot be filled except with great difficulty; by that [fire], which is insatiable (*anala*), meaning that for which no end or sufficiency (*ala*) exists. And by that [fire]. (BhG 3.39)

In response to the inquiry, "But what is the basis of desire, which acts as an enemy by veiling knowledge for all the world? he says: "The senses, the mind, and the intellect are said to be its basis," for when the basis of an enemy is known, it can be easily destroyed.
By these, it deludes the embodied soul, veiling its knowledge.

The senses, the mind, and the intellect are said to be the seat and support of this desire. By means of these supports—the senses and so forth—this desire deludes, that is, it bewilders in various ways, the embodied being by veiling and obscuring knowledge.
Since this is so,
therefore, O bull among the Bharatas, you must first restrain the senses.
Abandon this evil, which destroys both knowledge and realized wisdom.
