Therefore, O bull among the Bharatas, first of all—meaning at the very outset—having restrained and brought under control your senses, abandon, cast away, this aforementioned enemy, desire, which is sinful in its conduct. "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the understanding of the Self and other principles derived from scripture and the teacher; "realization" (*vijñāna*) is the specific experience thereof. Abandon that which destroys these two—knowledge and realization—which are the causes for attaining the highest good. The meaning is: renounce it from yourself.
It has been stated: "First, having restrained the senses, conquer desire, the enemy. In that regard, it is now explained what the basis is for one who would conquer desire:
"They say the senses are superior; the mind is superior to the senses."
But the intellect is superior to the mind; and he who is beyond the intellect is even superior.

The senses are the five, beginning with hearing. Wise men say they are superior—meaning more excellent—than the gross, external, and limited body, because of their subtlety, internality, and pervasiveness. Likewise, the mind, which consists of volition and doubt, is superior to the senses. And the intellect, which consists of determination, is superior to the mind.

Likewise, he who is internal to all objects of perception ending with the intellect—that embodied being whom desire, joined with its supports such as the senses, deludes by means of the obscuration of knowledge—it has been said that he is beyond the intellect; he is the seer of the intellect, the Supreme Self.
What follows from this?
Having thus realized that which is beyond the intellect, one should steady the self by means of the self.
By which you may slay the enemy, O mighty-armed one, who takes the form of desire and is difficult to overcome.

Thus, having understood—that is, having known—the Self which is beyond the intellect, and having steadied it—meaning having performed a perfect stabilization by properly concentrating the self through the mind itself which has been purified; O mighty-armed one, abandon this enemy in the form of desire, which is difficult to overcome, meaning that its approach or attainment is achieved with great difficulty, and which possesses many insuperable particularities.

Thus ends the third chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya).
Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter Four:
Now begins the fourth chapter.
(Śaṅkara-bhāṣya:

This yoga characterized by steadfastness in knowledge, which has been described in these two chapters, is renunciation (*sannyāsa*) having the means of karma-yoga. In this [yoga], the purpose of the Veda—both that characterized by engagement (*pravṛtti*) and that characterized by withdrawal (*nivṛtti*)—is fully completed; and in all the Gītās, this very yoga is intended by the Blessed Lord. Therefore, considering the purpose of the Veda regarding engagement to be thus completed, the Blessed Lord praises it by recounting its lineage.
The Blessed Lord said:
I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat;
Vivasvat declared it to Manu; and Manu spoke it to Ikṣvāku.

I taught this Yoga, which has been described in these two chapters, to Vivasvat, the son of Aditi, at the beginning of creation, for the sake of bestowing strength upon the Kṣatriyas who are the protectors of the world. Endowed with that power of Yoga, they become capable of protecting the Brahman; and when the Brahman and the Kṣatra are protected, they are able to protect the world. It is "imperishable" (avyaya) because its fruit is imperishable; for the fruit of this [Yoga], characterized by steadfastness in right vision and called liberation, never perishes.
And that Vivasvat told it to Manu; Manu spoke it to his son Ikṣvāku, the first king.
Thus, this yoga, obtained through successive tradition, the royal sages knew.
Over a long period of time, O scorcher of the foe, that yoga has been lost here on earth.

Thus, this yoga—which was obtained through the succession of Kṣatriyas—was known by those royal sages (rājarṣis), who are both kings and seers. That yoga, O scorcher of foes (paraṃtapa), has been lost over a long period of time here, its tradition having become broken. The term "scorcher of foes" means one who, like the sun with its rays of valor and splendor, heats or torments those who are hostile to oneself; that is to say, a destroyer of enemies.
Having encountered those who have failed to conquer their senses— persons rare to find— and having perceived that this world is devoid of the fruits of human endeavor,
I have today declared to you that very same ancient Yoga.
"For you are my devotee and my friend; this indeed is the supreme secret. (BhG 4.3)
This very same ancient yoga has been declared by Me to you today; for you are My devotee and My friend. Indeed, this is a secret, because this yoga is the supreme knowledge—this is the meaning.
Lest anyone should think that what was spoken by the Blessed One is contradictory, Arjuna spoke as if raising an objection for the sake of providing a resolution:
"Your birth was later, while the birth of Vivasvat was earlier."
How may I understand this, that you spoke [this] at the beginning? BhG 4.4.

"Another [birth] was yours recently in the house of Vasudeva; the other, prior [birth], was your birth or origin at the beginning of creation, that of Vivasvat, the Sun. How may I understand this so that its meaning is not contradictory—that you, who yourself first taught this Yoga, are now teaching it to me? (BhG 4.4)

Dispelling the doubt of the foolish who suspect that Vāsudeva is neither the Supreme Lord nor omniscient, the Blessed Lord said: "Indeed, O Arjuna, many births of mine have passed away, as well as yours."
I know all of them, O scorcher of the foe, but you do not know them.

Many births of mine have passed away, and yours as well, O Arjuna; I know them all, but you do not know them, because your power of knowledge is obstructed by merit, demerit, and the like. I, however, know them, for my nature is eternally pure, awakened, and liberated, and thus my power of knowledge is unobstructed—O scorcher of foes!
"How then, for you, the eternal Lord, can there be birth even in the absence of merit and demerit? To this it is said:
"Though being unborn and of imperishable nature, and though being the Lord of all beings..."
Presiding over my own nature, I manifest myself through my own creative power (māyā).

Although He is unborn and free from birth, and likewise possesses an imperishable nature with undiminished power of knowledge, and is the Lord—possessed of sovereign power—over all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass; yet He [descends], having taken hold of His own nature, My Vaiṣṇava *māyā* consisting of the three *guṇas*, under whose control this entire world exists, and by whom the world is deluded so that it does not know its true Self, Vāsudeva.

Presiding over—that is, having brought under control—that very nature of mine, I manifest myself as if possessing a body, as if born, through my own *māyā*—that is, through my own creative power—and not in reality, as is the case with ordinary people.
And as for when and for what purpose that birth occurs, it is said:
"Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bhārata..."
When there is a rise of unrighteousness, then I manifest myself.

Whenever there is a decline and decay of Dharma—characterized by the system of social classes and stages of life (varṇāśrama) and serving as the means for the worldly prosperity and ultimate liberation of living beings—and whenever there is a rise of Adharma, O Bhārata, then I manifest Myself through My creative power (māyā).
For what purpose?
For the protection of the virtuous and for the destruction of the evil-doers.
For the sake of establishing righteousness, I manifest myself age after age.

For the protection and preservation of the virtuous who abide on the true path, and for the destruction of evildoers who commit sins; furthermore, for the sake of establishing righteousness—the perfect establishment of dharma—I manifest myself in every age, in each successive era.
He who thus knows in truth My divine birth and action,
having abandoned the body, does not come to rebirth; he comes to Me, O Arjuna.

He who knows in truth—that is, according to reality—as it has been described, that my birth is of the nature of *māyā* and my action consists of protecting the virtuous and so forth, being divine (*divya*) and non-material (*aprākṛta*), that is, truly sovereign (*aiśvara*), does not, upon leaving this body, undergo rebirth—re-origination—but comes to Me; he is liberated, O Arjuna.
This path to liberation did not begin only now. What then? Even in the past, those who were free from passion, fear, and anger, who were absorbed in Me, took refuge in Me.
Many, purified by the austerity of knowledge, have attained my state of being.

"Free from passion, fear, and anger": passion (*rāga*), fear (*bhaya*), and anger (*krodha*) constitute "passion-fear-anger"; those from whom these have departed—that is, those who are devoid of passion, fear, and anger—are "free from passion, fear, and anger. "Consisting of Me" (*manmaya*) means the knowers of Brahman who perceive their non-difference from the Lord; they have taken refuge in Me alone, the Supreme Lord—the meaning is that they are established in pure knowledge. "Many," meaning numerous, [attain perfection] through "knowledge-austerity" (*jñāna-tapas*); knowledge concerning the Supreme Self is itself the austerity. By that knowledge-austerity.

"Purified" means having attained supreme purity; "having come to my state" means having reached the state of the Lord, which is liberation. The qualification "by the austerity of knowledge" is an indicator that this steadfastness in knowledge is independent of other forms of austerity.
"In that case, you must possess passion and hatred, since you bestow your own self only upon some and not upon all. To this it is said:
"In whatever way people approach me, in that very same way do I reward them."
O Pārtha, human beings follow my path in every respect.

In whatever way, by whatever means, for whatever purpose, and with the desire for whatever fruit people take refuge in me, I honor—that is, I favor—them by granting that very fruit; for they have no desire for liberation. Indeed, it is not possible for a single person to simultaneously possess both the desire for liberation and the desire for fruits. Therefore, those who seek a particular fruit, I favor by granting that fruit; while those who act as prescribed, yet do not seek fruits but desire liberation, I favor by granting knowledge.

The meaning is that I honor those who approach Me—whether they be men of knowledge, renunciants, or seekers of liberation—by granting them liberation, and likewise those who are afflicted by removing their suffering; I do not, however, favor anyone on account of attachment, aversion, or delusion. In every way, human beings follow the path of Me, the Lord, who exists in all states.
O Pārtha, those who, being entitled to a particular action, strive in it because of a desire for its fruit—they are here called "men" in every way, that is, in all respects. (BhG 4.11)

If, because You, the Lord, are free from defects such as passion and possess an equal desire to favor all living beings, and are capable of bestowing all fruits, then why do all those seeking liberation not resort to You alone through the knowledge that "Vāsudeva is everything"? Listen to the reason for this:
"Desiring success in their actions, they worship the deities here."
For in the world of men, success born of action is indeed quickly attained.

Desiring, longing for, and praying for the accomplishment of their actions—the production of results—they worship the deities such as Indra and Agni here in this world. Now, he who worships another deity, thinking, "He is one and I am another," does not know; he is like an animal, according to the Vedic text: "Thus he belongs to the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10). For those who sacrifice to separate deities and long for fruits, it is because in the human world the result comes quickly and swiftly.

For the authority of the scriptures pertains to the world of humans, as indicated by the qualification "quickly indeed in the human world. The Blessed One also shows that the attainment of the fruits of action occurs in other [realms] as well; however, the distinction is that in the human world there is the authority for actions such as those pertaining to the castes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas). And for those performers of action who possess the authority of the castes and stages of life, the attainment of the fruit born of action—that which has arisen from action—occurs quickly.

Is there a restriction that the entitlement to perform duties such as those pertaining to the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*) exists only in the human world and not in other worlds? Or rather, since it has been stated, "Human beings endowed with the distinctions of class, stage of life, and so forth, follow my path in every respect" (Gītā 4.11), for what reason do they follow your path specifically and by rule, and not that of anyone else? It is said in response:
"The fourfold order of society was created by me according to the division of qualities and actions."
Know Me also as the author of that [action], yet the non-agent and immutable.

The fourfold caste system (*cāturvarṇya*)—that is, the four castes themselves—was created and produced by Me, the Lord, according to the Vedic revelation beginning with, "The Brāhmaṇa was His mouth" (*Ṛgveda* 8.4.19.2; *Yajurveda* 32.11). This was done according to the division of qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*). The qualities are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Among these, the duties of the Brāhmaṇa, who is characterized by *sattva* (or for whom *sattva* predominates), consist of tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, and so forth (*Bhagavad Gītā* 18.42).

The duties of the Kṣatriya consist of valor, majesty, and so forth, characterized by Rajas with Sattva as a subordinate quality; the duties of the Vaiśya consist of agriculture and so forth, characterized by Rajas with Tamas as a subordinate quality; and the duty of the Śūdra is service alone, characterized by Tamas with Rajas as a subordinate quality. The meaning is that this fourfold division of qualities and duties was created by Me according to such distinctions. Furthermore, this system of the four castes (cāturvarṇya) does not exist in other worlds; therefore, the qualification "in the world of humans" is specified.

"Well then, since you are the agent of the act of creating the four social orders and so forth, you must be joined with the fruit of that action; therefore, you are neither eternally liberated nor the eternal Lord. It is said in reply:

"Even though, through the conventional usage of *māyā*, I am the agent of that action, know me in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) to be a non-agent; for this very reason, know me to be imperishable and not subject to transmigratory existence (*asaṃsārin*). (BhG 4.13)
But as for those actions of which you consider me to be the agent in the ultimate sense, I am in fact not their agent;
for actions do not taint me, nor do I have any desire for the fruits of action.
He who understands me thus is not bound by actions.

Those actions do not smear me, because of the absence of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) as the initiator of the body and so forth; nor is there any longing or thirst for the fruit of those actions on my part. However, it is logical that actions smear those transmigrating beings who possess the conceit "I am the doer" regarding actions and have a longing for their fruits; since that [conceit] is absent, actions do not smear me.

In the same way, the meaning is that even another who understands Me as the Self—realizing "I am not the doer" and "I have no longing for the fruits of action"—is not bound by actions; for him also, actions that initiate the body and so forth do not come into being.
"Knowing thus— 'I am not the doer, nor is there for me any longing for the fruit of action'— even the seekers of liberation of old performed their work."
Therefore, perform action alone, as it was performed by those of old even before them.

Knowing this—that action was performed even by those seekers of liberation who have passed away in the past—you should perform action accordingly. You must neither remain silent nor undertake renunciation. Therefore, because it was practiced even by those before you: if you are ignorant of the Self, do it for the sake of purifying the self; if you are a knower of reality, do it for the sake of maintaining the world-order. This was performed long ago by Janaka and others of old; it was not something invented or abandoned in the present day.

In that case, if action is to be performed, I shall perform it simply according to your word; what is the use of this qualification, "What was done by the ancients, even more so by those before them" (Gītā 4.15)? It is replied: because there is indeed a great discrepancy regarding action. How so?
Even the wise are deluded in this matter as to what is action and what is inaction.
I shall declare that action to you, by knowing which you will be liberated from evil.

"What is action? And what is inaction?"—even the wise, the highly intelligent, are bewildered and have fallen into delusion regarding this matter of action and so forth. Therefore, I shall declare to you both action and inaction, by knowing which—that is, having understood it—you will be liberated from the evil of saṃsāra.

And you should not think that "action" (karman) is merely the movement of the body and so forth as it is commonly known in the world, while "inaction" (akarman) is simply its non-performance, such as sitting silently. What is there to be understood in that regard? Why? It is said:
"For even in action there is something to be understood, and in wrong action (vikarman) there is likewise something to be understood."
And one must understand the state of non-action; for the course of action is profound.

For there is indeed something to be understood even regarding action prescribed by the scriptures; likewise, there is certainly something to be understood regarding "wrong action" (vikarman), which is prohibited; and similarly, there is something to be understood regarding "inaction," which is the state of silence—thus the word "to be understood" must be supplied in all three cases. Because the "course" (gati)—meaning the true nature or reality—of action and so forth (the mention of "action" being illustrative of action, wrong action, and inaction) is profound, uneven, and difficult to discern. || BhG 4.17 ||
But what, then, is that reality regarding action and the rest which was promised as something to be understood? It is said:
"He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction..."
He is wise among men, he is disciplined, and he is the performer of all actions.

Regarding action (*karman*): "action" (*karman*) is that which is performed; it is mere activity. In that action, he who sees "non-action" (*akarman*), that is, the absence of action—and in non-action, the absence of action—he sees action. Since both engagement and withdrawal depend upon an agent, the entire conventional usage of action, its factors, and so forth, does not reach the ultimate reality but exists only on the plane of ignorance (*avidyā*). He who sees thus, he sees. He is the wise among men, he is the disciplined yogi, and he is the performer of all actions—that is, the performer of every action. Thus, one who perceives action and non-action as mutually related is praised.

Now, is this not a contradiction that is being stated—that one should see "action in inaction" and "inaction in action"? For indeed, action cannot be inaction, nor can inaction be action; how then could a seer perceive such a contradiction? No; for from the perspective of the deluded world, that which is in reality inaction appears as action, and likewise, that which is action appears as inaction. It is for the sake of seeing things as they truly are that the Blessed One said: "He who sees inaction in action," and so forth.

Therefore, there is no contradiction, because the existence of intelligence and so forth is established. Furthermore, "that which is to be known" refers to seeing things as they truly are (*yathābhūtadarśana*). Liberation from the impure cannot result from erroneous knowledge; for it has been said: "Knowing which, you shall be liberated from the impure" (Gītā 4.16). Consequently, since action and inaction are grasped erroneously by living beings, the Lord’s teaching beginning with "He who sees inaction in action," and so forth, is intended to bring about the cessation of that erroneous apprehension.

And here there is no action that has action as its locus, as in the case of jujube fruits in a bowl; nor is there an action that has non-action as its locus, because non-action is the absence of action. Therefore, action and non-action are merely misapprehended by worldly people, just like water in a mirage or silver in mother-of-pearl.

Is it not the case that action is indeed action for everyone, never deviating from its nature? This is not so, because one standing on a boat perceives a contrary motion in the mountains on the bank while they remain stationary even as the boat moves; likewise, when objects far away are brought near by the eye, one perceives the absence of motion in those very things that were moving. Thus, here too, the perception of action in what is non-action, and the perception of non-action in action, constitutes a perverted view. To dispel this, it is said: "He who sees non-action in action," and so forth.

Even though this has been stated in response more than once, people—being utterly deluded by the habitual tendency toward completely contrary views—forget the truth even though it has been heard repeatedly; thus, repeatedly introducing fallacious arguments, they raise objections, and for this reason the Blessed One gives the answer again and again, having observed that the reality of the matter is difficult to comprehend.

The absence of action (*karmābhāva*) in the Self—established by scripture, tradition, and reasoning—is stated in such passages as "This is unmanifest, this is unthinkable" (Gītā 2.25) and "It is neither born nor does it die" (Gītā 2.27), and will be further explained. Regarding that Self which is devoid of action, there exists an extremely deep-seated misconception of action where there is no action. For even the wise are deluded in this matter, asking "What is action? What is inaction? (Gītā 4.16), having superimposed upon the Self the action that actually resides in the body and its adjuncts.

"I am the agent; this is my action; I must enjoy the fruit of this action"—thus [one thinks]. Likewise, "I shall remain silent, so that I may be effortless, free from action, and happy"—having superimposed upon the Self the cessation of activity dependent on the body and organs, as well as the happiness resulting therefrom, the world fancies, "I do nothing at all; I sit silently in happiness.
In this regard, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "He who sees inaction in action," etc., in order to remove such a perverted view of the world.

And here, action—though being merely action—is superimposed by everyone upon the immutable Self, which is devoid of action and serves as the locus for the performance of effects and instruments; for even the wise man thinks, "I am acting. Now, regarding this action, which is well-known to all the world as inherent in the Self, he who perceives non-action—the absence of action—as it truly is, like the absence of motion in trees (despite the appearance of motion in those situated on a riverbank), [perceives correctly].

And regarding "inaction" (*akarma*), which is the cessation of the activity of the body and the organs—when this [cessation] is superimposed upon the Self as if it were action, because of the underlying motive of the ego-sense that "I sit happily doing nothing"—one who sees action in that inaction, he who thus knows the distinction between action and inaction, is wise and learned among men; he is disciplined, a yogi, and a performer of all actions. The meaning is that he is liberated from evil and has accomplished what was to be done.

This verse has been explained otherwise by some. How? It is said that obligatory (*nitya*) rites, when performed for the sake of the Lord, are called "non-actions" (*akarma*) in a figurative sense because they lack [worldly] fruit. Their non-performance is "action" (*karma*), and since that results in demerit (*pratyavāya*), it is called "action" in a figurative sense as well. In this context, one who perceives "non-action" in the obligatory rite—due to its lack of fruit—is meant.

Just as even a cow that is not a milch-cow is called "non-milch" because it does not yield the fruit known as milk, so too, in the case of the non-performance of what is obligatory, the "non-action" (akarma) is regarded as "action" (karma) because it yields the fruit of transgression, such as hell. This interpretation is not tenable, because liberation from evil would be impossible through such knowledge. For the Lord has stated: "Knowing which, you shall be liberated from evil" (Gītā 4.16). This [scriptural] statement would be contradicted.

How so? Liberation might indeed result from the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*), but not from the knowledge that they have no fruit. For neither the knowledge that obligatory rites lack fruit nor the knowledge of obligatory rites has been enjoined as having liberation from evil as its fruit; nor has this been stated by the Blessed One here in this context.

By this, the view that there is action in what is non-action is refuted. For it is not the case that here the perception of action in non-action is enjoined as something to be performed; rather, only the performance of the obligatory (*nitya*) rite is enjoined. Nor would any fruit result from the knowledge that "no transgression occurs through the non-performance of the obligatory. Furthermore, the non-performance of the obligatory is not enjoined as an object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Nor is there liberation from evil through the false perception that "action is non-action."

Intelligence, propriety, and the performance of all duties and so forth result as either a fruit or a praise [of knowledge]. For false cognition alone is directly of an unwholesome nature; how, then, could liberation from other unwholesome things [occur] through it? Indeed, darkness does not become the remover of darkness.

Now, is it not the case that the perception of non-action in action, or the perception of action in non-action, is not a false cognition? What then? Is it not figurative, based on the presence or absence of results? No, because even from such figurative cognitions of action and non-action, no result is heard of in scripture. Nor is any distinction gained by abandoning what is stated in scripture and imagining what is not stated. Indeed, it could have been stated in its own words: "There is no fruit for obligatory rites, and from their non-performance there would be a fall into hell."

In that regard, what is the point of saying "he who would see inaction in action through a pretext" (*vyāja*)—that is, by means of deluding others? By explaining it in that very way, one would clearly be imagining that the statement spoken by the Blessed One was intended for the purpose of deluding the world. Furthermore, it would not be reasonable to say: "This matter need not be protected by a statement in the form of a ruse, nor would it be easily understood even if it were stated again and again using different words."

For the meaning has already been stated very clearly in the passage, "Your right is to action alone" (Gītā 2.47), and thus it need not be stated again. Moreover, in every case, that which is praiseworthy and that which is to be understood must indeed be performed; it is not said that something should be understood merely for its own sake without purpose.

Furthermore, false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) cannot be that which is to be known, nor can it be the appearance of an object presented by such cognition. Nor does the production of demerit (*pratyavāya*) arise from the non-performance of eternal duties due to their non-existence, because of the scriptural statement: "The being of the non-existent is not found" (Gītā 2.16). Moreover, it has been shown [in scripture] that "how could the existent be born from the non-existent? (ChāU 6.2.2). Since the birth of the existent from the non-existent is thus prohibited, one who asserts the production of the existent from the non-existent would effectively be saying that "the non-existent becomes existent" and "the existent becomes non-existent."

And that is illogical, because it contradicts all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, a scripture would not enjoin an action that is fruitless, since [such an action] is of the nature of suffering; and because suffering cannot be a purposeful effect produced through intentional awareness. Moreover, if one were to accept that falling into hell results from its non-performance, it would lead only to misfortune. In either case—whether through performance or non-performance—the scripture would be rendered fruitless.

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with one's own accepted doctrine for one who, having accepted that action is eternally fruitless, then says it is "for the sake of the fruit of liberation. Therefore, the meaning of the passage beginning with "He who sees inaction in action" (BhG 4.18) is exactly as it was heard [in the text]. And thus has this verse been explained by us.
This very vision of action as inaction and so forth is now being praised:
"He whose every undertakings are devoid of desire and purposeful resolve..."
The wise call him a sage whose actions have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge.

For one who has the aforementioned vision, all undertakings—meaning all actions that are commenced—are devoid of desire and devoid of the mental resolves that cause them; they are performed as mere activities, entirely in vain.

Whether engaged in action for the sake of maintaining the world, or withdrawn from it for the sake of mere subsistence, those wise ones who know Brahman call him a true scholar in the ultimate sense—he whose actions, characterized as good or evil, have been burnt by the fire of knowledge. Knowledge is the perception of "non-action" and so forth within action; that itself is the fire, and by that fire of knowledge his actions have been consumed. (BhG 4.19)

But he who perceives the absence of action (*akarma*) and so forth in action and so forth, becomes free from action (*niṣkarmā*) precisely through that perception of non-action; being a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) whose efforts are for the sake of mere subsistence, he does not engage in action, even though he previously engaged in it prior to discrimination. However, one who has begun actions but later attains the correct vision of the Self (*ātma-samyag-darśana*) sees no purpose in any action and thus completely abandons all action along with its means.

When, due to some cause, the abandonment of action is impossible, he—being free from attachment to action and its fruit and having no personal motive—engages in action as before merely for the sake of maintaining the world; yet, because his actions have been burnt by the fire of knowledge, he does nothing at all. Demonstrating this point—that such a person’s action becomes non-action itself—the Lord says:
"Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented and dependent on nothing, even though fully engaged in action, he does nothing at all. (BhG 4.20)

The meaning is that, having abandoned self-conceit regarding actions as well as attachment to their fruits, one is eternally content and free from longing for sense-objects by means of the knowledge previously described. "Without support" (*nirāśraya*) means devoid of a basis; a "basis" is that which one relies upon to desire to accomplish a human goal. Thus, the meaning is being devoid of reliance on any means for achieving seen or unseen results. An action performed by the wise person is, in the ultimate sense, truly no-action (*akarma*), because he is perfected in the vision of the actionless Self.

Since such a person lacks any personal motive, it follows that he should indeed abandon action along with its means; yet, because it is impossible for him to withdraw from it, even though he engages in action as before—either out of a desire to maintain the world order or to avoid the censure of the cultured—he does nothing at all, because he is perfected in the realization of the Self as being beyond all action.

On the other hand, he who is the opposite of those previously mentioned—one who has already developed the vision of the Self within the innermost Brahman, the actionless inward Self even before the ocean of ritual action—being free from longing for desired objects whether seen or unseen, and seeing no purpose whatsoever in actions for the sake of visible or invisible results, renounces action along with its means; such a *yati*, whose activity is limited to the mere maintenance of the body, being established in knowledge, is liberated. To demonstrate this point, He says:
"Free from longing, with mind and self controlled, having renounced all possessions..."
Performing action with the body alone, one incurs no sin.

"Nirāśīḥ" means one from whom desires have departed; he is "nirāśīḥ. "Yatacittātmā": *citta* is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and *ātman* is the external aggregate of the body and its instruments. He whose both of these are restrained—that is, controlled—is "yatacittātmā. "Tyaktasarvaparigrahaḥ": he by whom all possession has been abandoned is "tyaktasarvaparigrahaḥ. Performing "śārīraṃ karma"—action for the sole purpose of maintaining the body, and even therein devoid of egoism—[he attains liberation].

He does not incur, he does not obtain, *kilbiṣa*—that is, undesirable evil (*aniṣṭarūpaṃ pāpam*)—and even *dharma*. For one who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*), even *dharma* is indeed undesirable evil (*kilbiṣa*) because it brings about bondage. Therefore, he becomes free from those two; the meaning is that he becomes liberated from *saṃsāra*.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "bodily action alone," does "bodily" refer to action accomplished by means of the body, or rather does it refer to action whose sole purpose is the maintenance of the body? And what follows from this, whether "bodily" refers to action accomplished by the body or to action whose purpose is merely the maintenance of the body?

It is said: if "bodily action" were intended to mean action accomplished by the body, then for one who says that even while performing with the body an action—whether its purpose be seen or unseen—that is prohibited, one would incur sin, this would result in a contradictory statement. Furthermore, for one who says that even while performing with the body an action prescribed by the scriptures—whether its purpose be seen or unseen—one does not incur sin, there would be the consequence of prohibiting what has not been previously established as forbidden.

Because of the qualification "performing bodily action" and the use of the word "only," it would follow that one incurs sin by performing actions accomplished through speech and mind which are the objects of injunctions and prohibitions and are denoted by the terms "dharma" and "adharma.

Even in that case, if one follows the path of performing what is enjoined by speech and mind, the statement regarding the incurrence of sin would result in a contradiction; and if one follows the path of engaging in what is prohibited, the statement would be a mere restatement of an existing fact and thus useless.

But when bodily action is intended merely for the purpose of maintaining the body, then, while not performing any other action—whether seen or unseen, whether understood through injunctions or prohibitions, and whether accomplished by body, speech, or mind—one who is free from the conceit "I am doing" (due to the use of the word "kevala," meaning "merely") and performs, from the perspective of worldly observation, only the movements of the body and so forth for the sole purpose of maintaining the body, incurs no sin.

Since for one who has become thus there is no possibility of attaining the defilement denoted by the word "sin," he does not attain defilement—that is, saṃsāra. Because all his karmas have been burnt by the fire of knowledge, he is liberated without obstruction; thus, this is merely a restatement of the fruit of the previously mentioned right vision (samyagdarśana). In this way, the interpretation that "the body alone is [the result of] karma" is faultless.

For the ascetic who has renounced all possessions, since there is an absence of any possession such as food that serves as the cause for maintaining the body, the necessity arises of maintaining the body through begging and other means. In this regard, the Lord, revealing the means by which the ascetic obtains food and other necessities for the maintenance of the body—permitted by such scriptural injunctions as "unasked, unprepared, spontaneously offered, and obtained by chance" (Mbh 14.46.19; Baudhāyanadharmasūtra 21.8.12)—says:
"Satisfied with whatever is obtained by chance, transcending the pairs of opposites, and free from envy..."
Being the same in success and failure, even after acting, he is not bound.

Content with what is obtained by chance: "obtained by chance" refers to gain that arrives unbidden; one who is content with that has developed the conviction of sufficiency (*alaṃpratyaya*). Transcending the pairs of opposites: even when struck by dualities such as cold and heat, one whose mind is not dejected is said to have transcended the pairs of opposites. Free from envy: one whose envy has departed possesses a mind devoid of enmity.

He who is equal—meaning the same—in the success or failure of obtaining whatever comes by chance; such a *yati* (ascetic) is equanimous toward the gain or loss of food and other means for the maintenance of the body, being free from joy and dejection. Perceiving inaction within action and so forth, and remaining steadfast in the vision of the Self as it truly is, he regards even those actions necessary for the mere maintenance of the body, such as wandering for alms, as "I do nothing at all" (Gītā 5.8), thinking always: "The qualities (of nature) operate among the qualities" (Gītā 3.28).

While clearly perceiving the absence of agency in himself, he nevertheless performs certain actions such as wandering for alms; yet, because he conforms to worldly conventions, he becomes the agent of actions like begging for alms—though this agency is merely superimposed by worldly people—while according to his own experience, generated through the authority of the scriptures and other means, he is indeed a non-agent.

Thus, even after performing actions such as wandering for alms—whose sole purpose is the maintenance of the body and whose agency is superimposed by others—he is not bound; for action, along with its cause, which is the cause of bondage, has been consumed by the fire of knowledge. This is merely a restatement of what was already said.

By the verse beginning with "Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action" (Gītā 4.20), it is demonstrated that when one who has commenced action becomes endowed with the realization of the Self as the inactive Brahman, then—since for such a person who perceives the absence of agent, action, and purpose, renunciation of action would logically follow—should that renunciation be impossible due to some cause, he remains engaged in that action as before; yet, even so, "he does nothing at all" (Gītā 4.20). Thus, the absence of action is shown.
For one for whom the non-existence of action has been thus shown— for him who is free from attachment, liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge,
and who performs action for the sake of sacrifice— his action dissolves entirely.

For one who is free from attachment, whose interest has ceased in every respect, who is liberated, and whose bonds of dharma and adharma have been removed; for one whose mind is established in knowledge—meaning he is one whose consciousness is fixed solely upon knowledge—for such a person performing action for the sake of sacrifice, that is, for the purpose of accomplishing sacrifice, his entire action—that is, his whole action together with its result—is dissolved; the meaning is that it perishes. (BhG 4.23)

For what reason, then, is it said that an action being performed dissolves entirely without initiating its own effect? Because: "The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman."
By him who is absorbed in the work of Brahman, Brahman alone is to be attained.

The instrument by which the knower of Brahman offers the oblation into the fire is Brahman itself; he perceives that it is Brahman alone, seeing its non-existence apart from the Self. Just as one perceives the absence of silver in mother-of-pearl, so it is said that "the offering is Brahman alone. Just as that which is silver is in fact only mother-of-pearl, so the meaning of the uncompound words "Brahman is the offering" (brahmārpaṇam) is that whatever is grasped in the world with the notion of an offering is, for this knower of Brahman, Brahman alone.

Likewise, that oblation which is perceived by the intellect as the "oblation of Brahman" (brahma-havis) is indeed Brahman itself. Similarly, the compound term is "in the fire of Brahman" (brahmāgnau); the fire, too, is Brahman alone. The meaning is that where it is offered, Brahman is the agent; Brahman alone is the doer. That act of offering which is performed by him is Brahman itself. And even the fruit which is to be attained by him through that is Brahman alone.

By means of the concentration on the work of Brahman—where "work of Brahman" (brahmakarma) refers to that work which is Brahman itself—the one who possesses such concentration is "one whose concentration is on the work of Brahman" (brahmakarmasamādhi); by means of that concentration on the work of Brahman, Brahman alone is to be reached.

Thus, even an action performed by one who desires to gather the world is, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), non-action (*akarma*), because it has been obliterated by the cognition of Brahman. This being so, it is all the more appropriate to represent even the renunciation of all actions by one whose activity has ceased as a sacrifice, for the purpose of praising right vision (*samyagdarśana*). That which is well-known in the context of sacrificial ritual—such as the ladle (*arpana*) and so forth—is, for this person who perceives the ultimate reality, Brahman itself in its spiritual dimension (*adhyātma*).

Otherwise, if everything were Brahman, the specific designation of the offering and so forth as being Brahman would be purposeless. Therefore, for the wise person who realizes that "all this is indeed Brahman," there is an absence of all ritual action.

And because of the absence of the notion of agency (*kāraka-buddhi*). Indeed, no action known as sacrifice is ever observed to be devoid of the notion of agency; every action, such as the *agnihotra* and so forth, is observed to possess the notion of agency regarding the specific recipient deity and other factors presented by the words of the scripture, and to involve the conceit of being an agent and the expectation of a fruit. Nor is it observed to be one that possesses the notion of distinctions between action, its factors, and its fruits, or one that is free from the conceit of agency and the expectation of a fruit. But this [action], in which the notions of distinctions between the action, its factors—such as the offering—and its fruits have been sublated by the cognition of Brahman, is therefore indeed non-action (*akarma*).

And thus it has been shown by such passages as: "He who sees inaction in action" (Gītā 4.18), "Even though engaged in action, he does nothing at all" (Gītā 4.20), "The qualities act upon the qualities" (Gītā 3.28), and "The disciplined knower of reality should think, 'I do nothing at all'" (Gītā 5.8). Demonstrating this in various places, the text effects the destruction of the notion of the distinction between action, its factors, and its results.

It is observed that in the case of the optional *agnihotra* and other such rites, there is a cessation of the optional *agnihotra* and so forth through the suppression of desire. Likewise, it is observed that actions—whether performed intentionally or unintentionally—are the initiators of specific results. Similarly here, for the knower, even ritual action becomes non-action because the cognition of distinctions regarding the agent, the instrument, the action, and the fruit has been suppressed by the realization of Brahman; it remains merely as an external movement. Therefore it is said: "it is entirely dissolved" (Gītā 4.23).

On this point, some say: that which is Brahman is the offering and the other factors. Indeed, it is Brahman itself that, having become established through the fivefold set of causal agents such as the offering, performs that very action. In this regard, the cognition of the offering and so forth is not to be sublated; rather, the cognition of Brahman is to be superimposed upon the offering and the rest, just as the cognition of Viṣṇu and others is superimposed on an image, or as the cognition of Brahman is superimposed on a name and so forth.

This might indeed be so if this section were intended for the purpose of praising the sacrifice of knowledge; however, here, having introduced right vision—designated by the term "sacrifice of knowledge"—alongside many specific ritual acts designated as "sacrifices," the Lord praises knowledge, saying: "The sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects, O scorcher of foes" (Gītā 4.33).

And in this context, this statement beginning with "the offering is Brahman" (*brahmārpaṇam*) is capable of establishing that knowledge itself constitutes a sacrifice; otherwise, if everything were already Brahman, the specific mention of the offering and so forth as being Brahman would be purposeless. As for those who say that the vision of Brahman is superimposed upon the offering and other elements—just as the vision of Viṣṇu is superimposed on an image, or as [names] are [superimposed] on names and so forth—for them, the knowledge of Brahman intended to be taught here would not be what is meant.

Because knowledge has as its object the offering and so forth, the fruit of liberation is not attained through the knowledge that consists in the performance of ritual acts; rather, it is said, "By that [knowledge], Brahman alone is to be reached.

Furthermore, it would be contradictory to say that the fruit of liberation is attained without perfect realization (*samyagdarśana*). Moreover, there is a contradiction with the context: perfect realization is the subject under discussion in the passage, "He who sees inaction in action" (Gītā 4.18), and because perfect realization is what is concluded at the end of that very section.

The chapter concludes by praising right vision (samyagdarśana) through such statements as, "Knowledge-sacrifice is superior to sacrifice performed with material objects, O scorcher of foes" (Gītā 4.33), and "Having attained knowledge, one attains supreme peace" (Gītā 4.39). Therefore, it is untenable to claim that, out of context, the view of Brahman is being enjoined upon the sacrificial implements and so forth—just as the view of Viṣṇu is imposed upon an image. Consequently, this verse has the meaning exactly as it has been explained.
In this context, having now established that right vision (*samyagdarśana*) is itself a sacrifice, other sacrifices are also introduced for the purpose of praising it:
"Other yogis perform the sacrifice to the gods alone."
Others offer the sacrifice by means of the sacrifice itself into the fire of Brahman.

The gods are indeed worshipped by that sacrifice which is divine; that is the divine sacrifice. Other yogis—meaning those engaged in ritual action—devote themselves to that very sacrifice; the meaning is that they perform it. In the fire of Brahman—which is described by such scriptural passages as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" (TaittU 2.1), "Brahman is Consciousness and Bliss" (BAU 3.9.28), and "That Brahman which is immediate and direct, the Self which is within all" (BAU 3.4.1)—there is the Brahman denoted by the word *brahman*, which is devoid of all attributes of transmigratory existence such as hunger and thirst, and from which every distinction has been negated by the statement "not this, not this" (BAU 4.4.22).

That which is Brahman is also Agni; because it is intended to be the locus of the oblation, it is called "Brahma-Agni. In that Brahma-Agni, other knowers of Brahman offer the sacrifice—the self, since the word "sacrifice" (yajña) is listed among the names of the self in the *Nirukta* (14.11)—that self, which is the sacrifice, which in the highest sense is the Supreme Brahman itself, yet is associated with limiting adjuncts such as the intellect and possesses all the attributes superimposed upon those adjuncts, and which takes the form of the oblation; they offer it, they cast it into that very self characterized as above.
The vision of the conditioned self as being of the very nature of the unconditioned Supreme Brahman—that is the oblation in that [fire];

the meaning is that renunciants who are established in the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self perform that [oblation]. This sacrifice characterized by perfect realization is introduced in the verses beginning with "The offering is Brahman" (BhG 4.24) and is included among the sacrifices such as the sacrifice to the gods, for the purpose of praise in the passage beginning with "The sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects, O scorcher of foes" (BhG 4.33).
Others offer the senses, such as hearing and the rest, into the fires of self-restraint;
still others offer the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, into the fires of the senses.

Others, the yogins, offer the senses—beginning with the ear—into the fires of self-restraint; the plural number is used because self-restraint differs for each sense. They offer these very restraints as oblations into those fires; the meaning is that they perform the restraint of the senses itself. Others offer the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, into the fires of the senses; the senses themselves are the fires, and into those fires of the senses they offer, considering the perception of non-prohibited objects by the ear and other senses to be the act of sacrifice.
Furthermore,
others [offer] all the functions of the senses and the functions of the vital breaths.
They offer [all actions] as oblations into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint, which is kindled by knowledge.

"All functions of the senses"—the functions of the senses are "indriyakarmāṇi. Likewise, "functions of the vital breaths"—the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the internal air; its functions are contraction, expansion, and so forth. These others they offer as oblations into the fire of yoga consisting of self-restraint (*ātmasaṃyamayogāgnau*). Self-restraint in the self is "ātmasaṃyama"; that itself is the fire of yoga. Into that fire of yoga consisting of self-restraint, they offer them—they cast them in. The meaning is that they cause them to dissolve into that which has been kindled by knowledge, made to blaze like with oil, brought to a state of brilliance by discriminative wisdom (*vivekavijñāna*). || BhG 4.27 ||
Some perform sacrifices with material substances, others with austerity, and still others with yoga; likewise,
there are ascetics of firm vows who offer sacrifice through self-study and knowledge.

Those who perform the expenditure of wealth at sacred fords with the intention that it constitutes a sacrifice are "sacrificers of wealth" (dravyayajña). Those ascetics for whom austerity is the sacrifice are "sacrificers of austerity" (tapoyajña). Those for whom yoga—characterized by breath control, withdrawal of the senses, and so forth—is the sacrifice are "sacrificers of yoga" (yogayajña). Likewise, others are "sacrificers of self-study and knowledge" (svādhyāyajñānayajña); those for whom the sacrifice consists of the study of the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures according to the prescribed rules are "sacrificers of self-study."

Those for whom knowledge is the sacrifice are "sacrificers of knowledge"—that is, those whose sacrifice is the thorough comprehension of the meaning of the scriptures. The ascetics are those characterized by self-discipline; they are "sacrificers of study" and "sacrificers of knowledge. They are "those of sharpened vows," meaning those whose vows have been properly sharpened, thinned, and made keen.
Furthermore:
"Others offer the prāṇa into the apāna, and likewise the apāna into the prāṇa."
Having restrained the movements of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, they are devoted to the practice of prāṇāyāma.

They offer—that is, they cast—the *prāṇa*, the function of *prāṇa*, into the *apāna*, the function of *apāna*; the meaning is that they perform the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) known as inhalation (*pūraka*). Others likewise offer the *apāna* into the *prāṇa*; this means they perform the breath-control known as exhalation (*recaka*). The "movements of *prāṇa* and *apāna*" refers to the movement of the air through the mouth and nostrils, where the movement of *prāṇa* is its outward departure, and the movement of *apāna* is its downward flow by way of reversal.
The meaning is that these [sages], having restrained and suppressed [the senses] and being devoted to *prāṇāyāma*—that is, intent upon *prāṇāyāma*—perform the *prāṇāyāma* known as *kumbhaka*.
Furthermore,
others, restricted in their food, offer the vital breaths into the vital breaths.
All these, moreover, are knowers of sacrifice, whose taints have been destroyed by sacrifice.

Others, being restricted in food—those for whom food is restricted and measured—offer the vital breaths, which are specific types of air, into the vital breaths themselves. Whichever particular air is being mastered, they offer the other types of air into that very one; thus, those [other airs] become as if they have entered into it. All these are knowers of sacrifice, whose impurities have been destroyed by sacrifice; that is, those whose impurities have been worn away or eliminated by the aforementioned sacrifices.
Thus, having performed the sacrifices as described,
those who eat the nectar of the remnants of sacrifice go to the eternal Brahman.
This world does not exist for one who performs no sacrifice; how much less another, O best of the Kurus?

"Eaters of the nectar of the remnants of sacrifice" (*yajñaśiṣṭāmṛtabhujaḥ*): that which remains of sacrifices is "the remnant of sacrifice" (*yajñaśiṣṭa*); that which is both the remnant of sacrifice and nectar is "the nectar of the remnant of sacrifice" (*yajñaśiṣṭāmṛta*), and they eat that, thus they are "eaters of the nectar of the remnant of sacrifice. Having performed the aforementioned sacrifices, they eat at the time remaining after them food called "nectar," as enjoined by the rules; thus, being "eaters of the nectar of the remnant of sacrifice," they go—that is, they proceed—to the eternal, ancient Brahman, provided they are seekers of liberation. This is understood from the force of the context to mean "in view of the lapse of time."

This world does not belong in common to all living beings; for him who lacks even one of the aforementioned sacrifices, there is no sacrifice—that is, he is a non-sacrificer (ayajña). How much less, O best of the Kurus, can he attain that which is accomplished by superior means?
Thus, various kinds of sacrifices are spread out at the mouth of Brahman;
know them all to be born of action, and by knowing this, you shall be liberated.

Thus, these various and manifold sacrifices described above are spread out and extended at the mouth—the door—of the Brahman, that is, the Veda; they are said to be spread at the mouth of the Brahman because they are understood through the gateway of the Veda. For example: "In speech, indeed, we offer the vital breath," and so forth. Know all those to be born of action—that is, arising from physical, vocal, and mental acts—and not born of the Self, for the Self is devoid of activity. Therefore, knowing this, you shall be liberated from evil.

"Knowing that these are not my activities, and that I am inactive and indifferent—by means of this right vision (samyagdarśana), you will be liberated from the bondage of saṃsāra; this is the meaning. || BhG 4.32 ||

By the verse beginning with "The offering is Brahman" (Gītā 4.24), the nature of perfect realization as a sacrifice has been established. Furthermore, many types of sacrifices have been taught. Knowledge is praised by means of those sacrifices which serve the purpose of accomplishing the goals of human life. How so?
"O scorcher of foes, the sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects."
O Pārtha, every action in its entirety culminates in knowledge.

O scorcher of the foe, the sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects—that which is accomplished by means of material substances. For the sacrifice of material objects initiates a fruit, whereas the sacrifice of knowledge does not initiate a fruit; therefore, it is superior, meaning more praiseworthy. How so? Because, O Pārtha, every action—entirely and without exception—is brought to completion and subsumed within knowledge, the means to liberation, which is like water flooding everywhere. This is the meaning.

"Just as when one has won at dice, the lower stakes are gathered together, even so all that good which creatures do comes together unto him who knows what he knows"—so says the Śruti. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1.4) BhG 4.33.
Now, as to the question of by what means this distinguished knowledge is attained, it is said:
"Know that through prostration, through inquiry, and through service."
The wise who have seen the truth will instruct you in that knowledge.

Know—that is, understand—the method by which that [knowledge] is attained: by approaching the teachers through prostration—prostration being the act of falling down very low with great intensity—and by means of inquiry such as "What is bondage? What is liberation? What is knowledge? And what is ignorance? and by service, that is, by attending upon the guru, and so forth. The teachers, being won over by such humility, will instruct—that is, they will impart—to you that knowledge characterized as previously described, for they are knowers.

Even among those who possess knowledge, some have the habit of perceiving reality as it truly is, while others do not; therefore, [the Lord] specifies "those who see reality. Knowledge taught by those who possess right vision becomes capable of producing its intended effect, whereas that which is taught by others does not—this is the opinion of the Blessed One.
And this being so, this statement is also appropriate:
"O Pāṇḍava, having known this, you shall not again fall into such delusion."
By which you shall see all beings without exception in yourself, and then in me.

Having understood that knowledge which has been taught by them, and having attained it, you shall not again fall into such delusion as you have now fallen into, O Pāṇḍava. Furthermore, by means of that knowledge, you will see all beings—without exception, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—directly within yourself, the inner self, thinking, "These beings abide in Me," and likewise in Me, Vāsudeva, the Supreme Lord, thinking, "And these [beings] are in Me.
The meaning is that you will perceive the identity of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and the Lord, as established in all the Upaniṣads.
Furthermore, what is the majesty of this knowledge?
Even if you are the most sinful among all sinners—
By the boat of knowledge alone, you shall cross over all evil.

Even if you are the most sinful of all sinners, the greatest of all evildoers, you shall cross over all evil—the ocean of sin—by means of the raft of knowledge alone, having made knowledge itself your raft. For in this context, even religious duty is called "evil" for one who seeks liberation.
How does knowledge destroy evil? This is explained with an illustration:
"Just as a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna," so it is said.
In the same way, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes.

Just as a well-kindled, fully ignited, and blazing fire reduces pieces of wood to ashes, O Arjuna, so too does the fire of knowledge—the fire that is knowledge itself—reduce all actions to ashes; the meaning is that it renders them seedless. For the fire of knowledge cannot directly reduce actions to ashes in the same way it burns fuel; therefore, the intention is that right vision (*samyag-darśana*) is the cause for the seedlessness of all actions.

By implication, that karma by which a body was begun has its fruit already set in motion; therefore, it is exhausted only through experience, according to the text: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released, then he shall be merged. Consequently, all those actions whose fruits have not yet begun—which were performed prior to the arising of knowledge, those occurring simultaneously with knowledge, and those performed in various past lives—are reduced to ashes.
Since this is so,
therefore there exists nothing here in this world that purifies as much as knowledge.
One who has attained perfection through yoga finds that within oneself in due course of time.

Indeed, there exists nothing here equal to knowledge as a purifier—that is, a sanctifier or a cause of purification. That knowledge, one who is perfected by yoga—meaning one who has been refined and attained fitness through the yoga of action (karmayoga) and the yoga of meditative absorption (samādhiyoga)—being a seeker of liberation, finds and obtains within himself after a long time; this is the meaning.
The means by which the attainment of knowledge occurs with certainty is taught:
"One who possesses faith, who is devoted to it, and whose senses are restrained, attains knowledge."
Having attained this knowledge, one reaches supreme peace before long.

One who possesses faith (*śraddhāvān*) and is full of faith (*śraddhālu*) attains knowledge. Yet, even among those who possess faith, there may be someone whose progress is sluggish; therefore, he says: "intent upon that" (*tatparaḥ*). This means one who is devoted to the means for attaining knowledge, such as attending upon the teacher and so forth, and who possesses faith. However, even one who is intent upon this might have his senses unsubdued; therefore, he says: "with senses restrained" (*saṃyatendriyaḥ*). One whose senses are restrained—that is, turned away from sense-objects—is "one with senses restrained."

One who is thus endowed with faith, devoted to that [practice], and has his senses restrained, necessarily attains knowledge. However, external acts such as prostration are not invariably effective, as they may arise from deceitful motives and the like; this is not the case with the possession of faith and its attendants, which are therefore the exclusive means for attaining knowledge. What, then, follows from the attainment of knowledge? It is said: having attained knowledge, one very quickly—that is, in no long time—reaches the supreme peace known as liberation, which is cessation.
That liberation occurs very swiftly from right vision is a well-ascertained truth, established by the logic of all the scriptures.
In this matter, no doubt should be entertained, for doubt is most sinful. Why is this so? It is said:
"The ignorant, the faithless, and the doubting soul perish."
Neither this world nor the next exists, nor happiness, for one whose mind is full of doubt.

The ignorant one, the one who does not know the Self, the faithless one—who lacks conviction in the words of the Guru and the scriptures—and the doubting one, whose mind is full of doubt, perish. Although both the ignorant and the faithless perish, they do not perish as much as the doubting one; for the doubting one is the most wretched of all. How so? For such a person, neither this world exists, nor the next world, nor happiness, because doubt arises even there for the doubting one, whose mind is possessed by doubt. Therefore, one should not entertain doubt.
Why?
Because he has renounced actions through yoga and has severed his doubts by means of knowledge.
Actions do not bind one who possesses self-mastery, O Dhanañjaya.

"One who has renounced actions through yoga" means one by whom—through yoga characterized by the vision of the supreme reality—all actions known as dharma and adharma have been renounced, that seer of the supreme reality. How is he "one who has renounced actions through yoga"? To this he says: "one whose doubts are rent asunder by knowledge," meaning one whose doubt has been cut away by knowledge characterized by the vision of the identity of the Self and the Lord; such a person is "one whose doubts are rent asunder by knowledge."

For one who has thus renounced action through yoga, being self-possessed and vigilant, actions—perceived as the movements of the gunas—do not bind him; they do not produce results such as the undesirable and so forth, O Dhanañjaya. (BhG 4.41)

Because one whose doubts have been severed by knowledge— which arises from the cause of the destruction of impurity through the practice of *karmayoga*— is not bound by actions, precisely because his actions have been burnt by the fire of knowledge; and because one who possesses doubt regarding the practice of knowledge and action perishes, therefore [sever] with the sword of knowledge the doubt residing in your heart, which has arisen from ignorance.
Having cut asunder this doubt, take refuge in yoga; arise, O Bhārata!

Therefore, with the sword of knowledge—the knowledge that is right vision (*samyag-darśana*) which removes defects such as grief and delusion—one should cut away this most evil doubt, which has arisen from ignorance—that is, born from lack of discrimination—and which resides in the heart, meaning it is situated in the intellect (*buddhi*). That very knowledge is the sword; with that sword of knowledge, one should cut away the doubt concerning the Self (*ātman*), for doubt has the Self as its object. Indeed, the doubt of another does not require being cut by someone else, such that it would need to be specified as "one's own. Therefore, even though it concerns the Self, it belongs specifically to oneself.

Having cut through this doubt, which has become the cause of your own destruction, "resort to yoga"—meaning, perform the practice of action as the means for right vision; "arise now for battle, O Bhārata."

Thus ends the fourth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka order.
Bhagavad Gītā 5:
Now begins the fifth chapter.
(Śaṅkara-bhāṣya) Arjuna said:
O Kṛṣṇa, you praise the renunciation of actions, and yet again, you praise yoga.
Tell me with certainty that one of these two which is the better.

"You praise—meaning you commend and speak in favor of—renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), which is the abandonment of ritual actions (*karma*) that are specifically enjoined by the scriptures; yet you also praise yoga, which is the necessary performance of those very same actions. Therefore, I have a doubt as to which is better for me: is the performance of action superior, or is its abandonment? For that which is more praiseworthy should be performed."

And therefore, between these two—renunciation of action and the yoga of action—whichsoever is the better, more praiseworthy, by the performance of which I might attain the highest good; tell me that one of the two, since it is impossible for both to be performed by a single person, as your well-ascertained and intended opinion.
Declaring His own intention for the sake of reaching a definitive conclusion, the Blessed Lord said:
"Both renunciation and the yoga of action lead to the supreme good."
But of these two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action.

Renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is the abandonment of actions, and the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) is their performance; both of these lead to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), bringing about liberation by being causes for the arising of knowledge. Although both are causes of the supreme good, he praises the yoga of action by stating that between those two causes of the supreme good, the yoga of action is superior to mere renunciation of action.
To the question "Why?", he says:
He should be known as a perpetual renunciant who neither hates nor desires.
For one who is free from the pairs of opposites, O mighty-armed one, is easily liberated from bondage.

He should be known as a practitioner of action-yoga (karmayogin) and a perpetual renunciant (nityasaṃnyāsī)—he who hates nothing and desires neither pain nor pleasure, nor the means to them. The meaning is that he who is of such a nature, even while engaged in action, should be known as a perpetual renunciant. For, O mighty-armed one, being free from the pairs of opposites (nirdvandva), one is easily liberated from bondage without effort.

(O)(o)(O) Since renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and the yoga of action (karmayoga) are contradictory and are to be practiced by different persons, it would be logical that their fruits are also contradictory; it might thus be concluded that both cannot lead to the supreme good (niḥśreyasa). To this, it is said: "The ignorant, not the wise, speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as distinct."
Even by practicing one of these two correctly, one obtains the fruit of both.

The ignorant, not the wise, declare Sāṃkhya and Yoga to be separate and possessed of contradictory and distinct fruits. The wise, however, who possess knowledge, maintain that their fruit is one and non-contradictory. How so? Even though there is only one [fruit], he who is "well-established" in both Sāṃkhya and Yoga—meaning, he who has practiced them correctly—attains the fruit of both. For the fruit of both is indeed that same supreme good (niḥśreyasa); therefore, there is no contradiction regarding the fruit.

[Objection: But having introduced the subject by means of the terms "renunciation" (saṃnyāsa) and "action-yoga" (karmayoga), why does he here state the identity of the fruits of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, which was not the topic at hand? [Reply: This is not a fault. Although Arjuna posed his question with reference solely to renunciation and action-yoga, the Blessed Lord, without abandoning that very subject, gave his reply using different terminology—namely "Sāṃkhya and Yoga"—while incorporating the specific distinction intended by Himself.

It is the Blessed One’s view that those very two—renunciation and the yoga of action—when conjoined with knowledge, its means, equanimity of intellect, and so forth, are denoted by the terms "Sāṃkhya" and "Yoga. Therefore, there is no introduction of a topic not previously under discussion. ||BhGS_5.4||
[Question: "How does one obtain the fruit of both by the correct practice of even one? [Answer: It is said:
"The state that is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya is also reached by the followers of Yoga."
He truly sees who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one.

The state known as liberation, which is attained by the Sāṃkhyas—those renunciants established in knowledge—is likewise reached by the Yogis. Those who, having surrendered their actions to the Lord as a means for attaining knowledge, perform them without desiring results for themselves, are the Yogis. The intention is that they too go [to that state] by way of attaining renunciation through the knowledge of ultimate reality.
Therefore, he who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one because of the identity of their fruit—he sees truly; this is the meaning. || BhG 5.5 ||

o)O(o If that is so, then renunciation alone is superior because of its union [with knowledge]. How then was it said: "Of these two, however, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action" [Gītā 5.2]? Listen to the reason for that. You asked which of the two is better—referring specifically to the renunciation of action and the yoga of action as distinct from each other. In accordance with that question, I gave the reply: "The yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action," without taking into account [the attainment of] knowledge.

But renunciation based on knowledge is what I intend by "Sāṃkhya," and that alone is the yoga of the ultimate truth. As for the Vedic yoga of action, it is metaphorically called "yoga" and "renunciation" because it has that [knowledge] as its purpose. How is it so? It is said:
"But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga;
the sage disciplined in yoga attains Brahman without long delay. (BhG 5.6)

But renunciation in its ultimate sense is difficult to attain—that is, to reach—without yoga; it cannot be achieved without yoga. One who is "yoked to yoga" is a sage (*muni*) joined with Vedic *karmayoga*—that is, with Vedic action performed as an offering to the Lord, free from expectation of fruit. He is called a "sage" because he meditates (*manana*) upon the true nature of the Lord. "Brahman" refers to the aforementioned renunciation, because it is characterized by steadfastness in the knowledge of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This is supported by the scripture: "Renunciation (*nyāsa*) is Brahman; for Brahman is supreme" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 78).

One attains—that is, reaches—brahman, which is renunciation in the ultimate sense characterized by steadfastness in the knowledge of the ultimate reality, before long, that is, very quickly. Therefore, I have said that the yoga of action is superior.
Furthermore, when this person, being disciplined in yoga as a means for attaining right vision, is pure in soul, self-conquered, and has mastered the senses;
One whose self has become the self of all beings is not tainted, even while acting.

One who is disciplined through yoga, whose self is purified, whose being is pure, who has conquered the self, who has mastered the body, and who has subdued the senses—he is one whose inner consciousness has become the Self of all beings; that is to say, he is one for whom the inward-facing consciousness has become the very Self of all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. The meaning is that he is a seer of reality as it is. Abiding thus, even while performing action for the sake of maintaining the world, he is not tainted; the meaning is that he is not bound by actions.
And since that [agent] does not act from the perspective of ultimate reality, the knower of truth should rightly think, "I do nothing at all."
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, and breathing;
Speaking, releasing, grasping, opening and closing the eyes— even while performing these,
he maintains the conviction that it is the senses alone that operate upon their respective objects.

Being disciplined (*yukta*) and composed (*samāhita*), he should reflect—that is, he should contemplate. "One who knows reality" (*tattvavit*) means one who knows the reality of the self's true nature; the meaning is that he is a seer of the ultimate truth (*paramārthadarśin*). At what time or in what manner does he, ascertaining reality, reflect? This is stated [as follows]: the word "should reflect" (*manyeta*) is to be connected with what precedes.

For that knower of reality who thus perceives non-action alone even in actions—the activities of all the organs and instruments of action—and who possesses right vision, his qualification is indeed for the renunciation of all actions, because he perceives the absence of action. For one who has set out to drink from a mirage with the thought that it is water does not, upon knowing the absence of water, continue to exert himself toward the purpose of drinking at that very spot.
But he who, on the other hand, does not know the Truth, yet engages in the yoga of action and performs deeds by placing them in Brahman, having abandoned attachment—
He is not stained by evil, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.

Having placed all actions in Brahman and the Lord, thinking "I perform this work for their sake," like a servant for the sake of his master—he who performs all actions while abandoning attachment even to the fruit of liberation, he is not smeared by sin; he is not bound, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (BhG 5.10)
o)O(o Only the purification of the being itself would be the fruit of that action,
because [it is performed] by means of the body, the mind, the intellect, and even by the senses alone.
Yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the sake of self-purification.

With the body, the physical frame, the mind, and the intellect—each alone and devoid of the sense of "mine," thinking, "I perform action for the Lord alone, not for my own fruit"—and even with the senses, which are likewise free from the notion of "mine," [one acts]. The word "alone" (kevala) is connected to each term, beginning with the body, in order to exclude the sense of ownership (mamatā) in all activities. The yogis who are performers of action perform their work having abandoned attachment to the results, for the sake of self-purification—that is, for the purification of the *sattva*.
Therefore, since your qualification lies in that very place, perform action alone.
And because one who is disciplined, having abandoned the fruit of action, attains the peace that is final.
One who acts impelled by desire, being attached to the fruit, is bound.

Being thus concentrated, thinking "I perform action for the Lord, not for my own fruit," and having abandoned—having relinquished—the fruit of action, he attains peace called liberation (*mokṣa*), which is final (*naiṣṭhikī*) because it exists in the ultimate state (*niṣṭhā*). The completion of the sentence is that this occurs through the sequence of purification of the mind, attainment of knowledge, renunciation of all actions, and steadfastness in knowledge. On the other hand, however, he who is unsteady and unconcentrated acts according to his own will; "kāra" means the act of doing, and "kāmakāra" is the act of desire.

"By that acting according to desire" means by being impelled by desire. One is bound by being attached to the fruit, thinking, "I perform this action for my own result. Therefore, the meaning is: "Be disciplined (yukta). || BhG 5.12 ||
But he who perceives the ultimate truth,
having mentally renounced all actions, remains happily as a master of himself.
