In the city of nine gates, the embodied self neither acts nor causes action to be done.

Having renounced—that is, completely abandoned—all actions, meaning all obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), optional (*kāmya*), and prohibited (*pratiṣiddha*) deeds; having relinquished all those actions with the mind through the intellect of discrimination, by perceiving the absence of action within action—this is the meaning—he remains, he stays in happiness. Having abandoned the activities of speech, mind, and body, free from exertion, with a serene mind, and with all external purposes ceased apart from the Self, he is said to "remain in happiness."

"Self-controlled" (*vaśī*) means one who has conquered the senses. Where and how does he dwell? To this he says: "In the city with nine gates. There are seven openings on the head which are the gateways for the self's perception; two below are for the discharge of urine and feces. By means of these gates, the body is called the "nine-gated city," for it is like a city. It has the Self as its sole sovereign, and it is presided over by the citizens—namely the senses, mind, intellect, and objects—which produce various results of cognition for the sake of that Self.
In that nine-gated city, the embodied one dwells, having renounced all action.

"What is the purpose of the qualification? For every embodied being—whether a renunciant or a non-renunciant—dwells indeed within the body. Therefore, the qualification is useless. It is replied: An ignorant embodied being, who perceives the mere aggregate of the body and senses as the Self, thinks "I am seated" in a house, on the ground, or on a seat. Indeed, for one who perceives the body alone as the Self, the cognition "I am seated in the body" is not possible in the same way that one might think of being seated in a house.

However, for one who perceives the Self as distinct from the aggregate of the body and so forth, the cognition "I am seated in the body" is logically consistent. Furthermore, the mental renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) by means of discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*)—which is wisdom (*vidyā*)—of the actions of others that have been superimposed upon the supreme Self through ignorance (*avidyā*), is possible. For one who has produced discriminative knowledge and has renounced all actions, even though his seat is the city of the nine gates (the body) just like a house, specific consciousness continues to arise only in the body due to the persistence of the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) of karma whose fruits have already begun to manifest (*prārabdha*).
The qualification "dwells in the body itself" indeed has its purpose, as it depends on the distinction between the perceptions of the knower and the ignorant.

Although it was stated that he dwells having renounced the actions of the body and organs—which have been superimposed upon the Self through ignorance—nevertheless, one might suspect that agency and causality could still be inherent in the Self; therefore, [the Lord] says: "neither acting himself, nor causing the body and organs to act, nor impelling them toward activities."

What is it? Is it that this agency and causality belonging to the embodied soul, which are inherent in its own self, do not exist because of renunciation—just as the motion of one who is walking would not exist upon the cessation of the act of going? Or rather, is it that agency and causality do not belong to the Self by its very nature? To this it is replied: agency and causality do not belong to the Self by its own nature.

For it has been said: "This one is declared to be unchangeable" (Gītā 2.25), and "Though dwelling in the body, O son of Kuntī, he neither acts nor is tainted" (Gītā 3.26); and also from the Śruti: "He meditates, as it were; he moves, as it were" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7).
Furthermore,
the Lord creates neither the agency nor the actions of the world.
But it is nature that operates, not the connection with the fruits of action.

The Lord, the Self, does not Himself create agency, nor does He create or produce for the world the most desired objects of action, such as chariots, jars, or palaces; nor does He bring about the connection with the fruits of action for one who has performed actions such as building a chariot.

If the embodied being (*dehin*) does not itself perform even the slightest action nor cause it to be performed, then who is it that acts and causes action? It is replied: "But its own nature" (*svabhāvas tu svaḥ*); "own nature" (*svabhāva*) means its own state, which is primordial matter (*prakṛti*) characterized by ignorance, or *māyā*, as will be described in such passages as, "For the divine... (Gītā 7.14).
But from the perspective of ultimate truth,
the All-pervading Lord does not take on the sin or even the merit of anyone.
Knowledge is enveloped by ignorance; by that, living beings are deluded.

The All-pervading Lord neither takes nor accepts the sin of anyone, even of His devotee; nor does He accept the merit performed by His devotees. Why, then, do devotees perform such meritorious acts as worship, sacrifice, giving, and oblation? To this He says: Knowledge—that is, discriminative wisdom—is shrouded by ignorance; because of that, undiscriminating beings caught in the cycle of transmigration fall into delusion, thinking, "I act," "I cause to act," "I shall enjoy," and "I cause to enjoy. (BhG 5.15)
But for those whose ignorance regarding the Self has been destroyed by knowledge,
that knowledge reveals the Supreme, like the sun. (BhG 5.16)

But by that knowledge with which [ignorance] has been destroyed by the discriminative knowledge concerning the Self, those beings who were deluded because they were veiled by ignorance—of those beings, that knowledge illuminates all objects of knowledge just as the sun illuminates the entire range of forms; that is the supreme, the reality of the ultimate truth. (BhG 5.16)
Those whose intellect is absorbed in that supreme knowledge which has been revealed, who have that as their self, who are established in that, and for whom that is the ultimate goal— o)O(o.
They go to the state from which there is no return, their impurities shaken off by knowledge.

Those whose intellect has gone into that Brahman are "tad-buddhayaḥ"; those for whom that very Supreme Brahman is the Self are "tad-ātmānaḥ"; those who are "tad-niṣṭhāḥ"—where *niṣṭhā* means firm adherence or intentness—having renounced all actions, they are those whose state of being consists in abiding in that very Brahman; and those who are "tat-parāyaṇāḥ," meaning those for whom that alone is the supreme goal (*param ayanaṃ*) or ultimate resort (*parā gatiḥ*), which is to say, they find delight in the Self alone.

Those whose ignorance regarding the Self has been destroyed by knowledge—such wise ones go to non-return, that is, to the state of no further connection with a body; "those whose impurities have been shaken off by knowledge" means those ascetics (yatayaḥ) whose defects, such as sin and other causes of saṃsāra, have been shaken off—that is, destroyed—by the aforementioned knowledge.
o)O(o It is said that those whose ignorance regarding the Self has been destroyed by knowledge are the wise; how do they perceive reality? [It is said:
"In a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, in a cow, in an elephant..."
The wise see with an equal eye both a dog and an outcaste.

"Vidyāvinayasaṃpanna" means one endowed with knowledge (*vidyā*) and discipline (*vinaya*); *vinaya* is humility. The wise perceive equality in that Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with such knowledge and discipline, as well as in a cow, an elephant, a dog, and even an outcaste.

Those wise ones who possess the habit of seeing that single, immutable Brahman—which is absolutely untouched by the qualities such as *sattva* and the impressions born thereof, as well as by *rājasa* and *tāmasa* impressions—in a *sāttvika* Brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and humility and possessed of the highest refinement, in a *rājasa* cow of middling quality, and even in an elephant or similar being which is utterly devoid of refinement and consists purely of *tamas*, are the "seers of equality. (BhG 5.18)

[Objection: "But surely they are unworthy of food, for they are possessed of faults, according to the Smṛti: 'From the unequal and the equal, the unequal and the equal [are distinguished] by their reception of honor' (Gautama Dharmasūtra 2.8.20). [Reply: They are not possessed of faults. How so?
"Even here, rebirth is conquered by those whose minds are established in equanimity."
For Brahman is indeed faultless and equal; therefore, they are established in Brahman.

Even while still living in this very world, those wise ones who possess equal vision have conquered—that is, brought to an end—the cycle of birth (*sarga*), for their minds (*manas*, the internal organ) are established in equanimity (*sāmya*) toward all beings, remaining steady in Brahman as the state of equality. Although Brahman is "faultless" (*nirdoṣa*)—insofar as it is perceived by the deluded as if possessed of faults due to the defects of those with faults, such as the outcastes and others—it is nevertheless untouched by those defects; thus it is indeed "faultless," being devoid of all blemish.

Nor is [the Self] differentiated by the distinctions of its own qualities (*guṇa*), because consciousness (*caitanya*) is devoid of qualities. And the Blessed One will state that desire and the rest are attributes of the field (*kṣetra*), saying, "because they are beginningless and devoid of qualities. Nor do the ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*) exist as differentiators of the Self, since there is no proof for their existence in every body. Therefore, Brahman is uniform and one. Consequently, they (the senses) are situated in Brahman alone.

Therefore, not even a trace of fault touches them, because they lack the conceit of identifying with the aggregate of the body and so forth. However, that Sūtra—"In unequal and equal [cases], there is [no fault] due to honor"—has as its subject those who possess the conceit of identifying with the aggregate of the body and so forth, since it qualifies [the agent] by way of being an object of honor.

For it is observed that in matters such as honor and gifts, the cause is the connection with specific qualities, as in the cases "one who knows Brahman," "one who knows the six auxiliary sciences," or "one who knows the four Vedas. But Brahman is devoid of connection with any quality or defect; therefore, it is appropriate to say "they are established in Brahman. Furthermore, the rule beginning with "by the equal and the unequal" (Gītā 4.22) concerns the sphere of ritual action (*karma*), whereas this present section, starting from "all actions with the mind" (Gītā 5.13) up to the end of the chapter, concerns the renunciation of all actions (*sarvakarma-saṃnyāsa*).
Since the Brahman-Self is faultless and equanimous, therefore one should not rejoice upon obtaining what is pleasant, nor be agitated upon obtaining what is unpleasant.
Steady-minded, undeluded, the knower of Brahman, established in Brahman.

One should not rejoice—that is, one should not experience elation—upon obtaining or attaining something pleasant and desired; nor should one be agitated upon obtaining or attaining something unpleasant and undesired. For it is those who perceive the self as being merely the body that experience joy and despondency upon encountering the pleasant and the unpleasant; this is not so for one who perceives the pure self alone, because for such a person, the encounter with the pleasant and the unpleasant is impossible.

Furthermore, he whose intellect is steady—possessing a firm and doubt-free understanding that the one Self is the same and faultless in all beings—is undeluded and free from delusion; such a knower of Brahman as described stands in Brahman, being a non-doer of action, meaning one who has renounced all actions. (BhG 5.20)
Furthermore, one who is established in Brahman,
with a self unattached to external contacts, finds that happiness which is within the Self.
With his self united through yoga with Brahman, he enjoys imperishable bliss.

Regarding "external contacts" (*bāhyasparśeṣu*): they are external and they are contacts, thus "external contacts. They are called "contacts" (*sparśāḥ*) because they are touched; these are the objects such as sound and the rest. In those external contacts, he whose self—that is, his internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—is unattached is "one whose self is unattached. Being devoid of affection for sense-objects, he finds—that is, he obtains—the happiness that exists in the Self. This is what is meant.

He whose self (ātman)—that is, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—is joined with the yoga of Brahman; "yoga" here means meditative absorption (samādhi) in Brahman, and thus "joined with the yoga of Brahman" means concentrated and engaged therein. He experiences—that is, attains—imperishable happiness. Therefore, one who desires imperishable happiness in the Self should withdraw the senses from the fleeting pleasure derived from external objects; this is the meaning. || BhG 5.21 ||
o)O(o Furthermore, one should turn away from this:
for those enjoyments born of contact are indeed the very source of suffering.
They have a beginning and an end, O son of Kuntī; the wise man does not delight in them.

For since those enjoyments—that is, experiences—born of contact, arising from the contact between the sense organs and their objects, are indeed sources of suffering because they are produced by ignorance; for internal and other types of suffering are seen to have that very [contact] as their cause. Just as it is in this world, so it is understood to be in the next world as well, due to the use of the word "indeed" (*eva*). Having realized that not even a trace of pleasure exists in *saṃsāra*, one should withdraw the senses from the mirage of sensory objects.

Not only are these sources of suffering, but they also have a beginning and an end; the beginning of enjoyments is the contact between the senses and their objects, and their end is the separation from them. Therefore, because they exist only for a middle moment, they are impermanent—this is the meaning. O Kaunteya, the wise person, the discerning one who has realized the truth of the supreme reality, does not take delight in those enjoyments. For it is only among the utterly deluded that attachment to sense-objects is seen, as in the case of animals and the like.

Furthermore, this fault is the most grievous adversary to the path of excellence, the cause for the attainment of all misfortune, and difficult to ward off; therefore, one must exert great effort in its avoidance. Thus the Blessed One said:
"He who is able here itself, before the release from the body..."
That man who restrains the impulse arising from desire and anger is disciplined; he is happy.

He who is able—that is, capable—of enduring and withstanding [the impulses] while still living here, prior to the release of the body, meaning until death; the setting of death as the limit is because the surge arising from desire and anger is inevitable for one who lives, for it has infinite causes; the meaning is that as long as there is death, one must not feel secure.

Desire (*kāma*) is that thirst or craving which arises toward a pleasant object—whether it be perceived through the senses, heard, remembered, or previously experienced—that serves as a cause of happiness. Anger (*krodha*) is that aversion toward things disagreeable to oneself—causes of suffering—which are being seen, heard, or remembered. That surge of energy from which both desire and anger arise is called the "surge born of desire and anger" (*kāmakrodhodbhavo vegaḥ*).

The impulse arising from desire is characterized by signs such as horripilation, eyes and face beaming with joy, and so forth, and consists of an agitation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The impulse arising from anger is characterized by signs such as trembling of the limbs, perspiration, biting of the lips, and bloodshot eyes. That man who is able—that is, capable—to endure, to withstand, that impulse born of desire and anger, he is a disciplined yogi and a happy man in this world.
And in what state, established in Brahman, does one attain Brahman? To this the Blessed One says:
"He who is happy within, whose recreation is within, and likewise he whose light is indeed within."
That yogi, having become Brahman, attains the extinction in Brahman.

He who has internal happiness—whose happiness is within his own self—is "one whose happiness is internal" (*antaḥsukha*). Likewise, he whose delight, pleasure, or sport is only within the self is "one whose delight is internal" (*antarārāma*). Similarly, he whose light—that is, illumination—is only within the self is "one whose light is internal" (*antarjyotis*). Such a yogi, having become Brahman while still living here, attains and reaches the extinction in Brahman—the bliss of liberation (*nirvāṇa*) within Brahman.
Furthermore, O Brahmin, what do the sages, whose taints are exhausted, attain— namely, the nirvana of Brahman?
Having severed duality, with self-restrained minds, they are devoted to the welfare of all beings.

The sages who possess right vision attain the Brahman-nirvāṇa, which is liberation—those renunciants whose taints are exhausted, whose sins are destroyed, who are faultless, whose dualities are severed, whose doubts are dispelled, whose selves are restrained, whose senses are controlled, and who are devoted to the welfare of all beings; that is to say, they are intent on the well-being and favor of all creatures, meaning they are non-violent.
Furthermore,
for those ascetics who are free from desire and anger and whose minds are restrained—
For those who have realized the Self, the state of Brahman and liberation lie close at hand.

For those ascetics and renunciants who are free from desire and anger—desire and anger being "kāmakrodhau," and those who are separated from them; for those of restrained mind, meaning those whose internal organs (the *antaḥkaraṇa*) are controlled; for those who have known the Self (*viditātmanām*), meaning those by whom the Self has been realized or known, that is, those of right vision—for them, whether living or dead, there exists on both sides the extinction in Brahman (*brahmanirvāṇam*), which is liberation. || BhG 5.26 ||

o)O(o It has been stated that for renunciants established in right vision (*samyag-darśana*), there is immediate liberation. Furthermore, the Blessed One has declared at every step—and will declare again—that *karmayoga*, when performed by dedicating all states of being to the Lord Brahman, leads to liberation through the sequence of purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*), attainment of knowledge, and the renunciation of all actions. Now, intending to explain in detail *dhyānayoga*—which is the internal means (*antaraṅga*) to right vision—the Lord taught these verses which serve as its aphorisms (*sūtra*):
"Having placed the external objects of touch outside, and the gaze between the eyebrows..."
Having made the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal, moving within the nostrils.
The sage who has restrained his senses, mind, and intellect, who is intent on liberation,
and from whom desire, fear, and anger have departed— he is indeed liberated forever.

Having made external the objects of touch, such as sound and the rest—meaning that those objects like sound which have been brought inside the intellect through the doors of the ears and so forth—one does not think of them; thus, sound and the other objects, being external, remain truly outside. Having thus placed them outside, the phrase "and having fixed the eyes between the eyebrows" is to be supplied. Likewise, one should make equal the prāṇa and apāna breaths moving within the nostrils.

One whose senses, mind, and intellect are restrained—that is, one for whom the senses, the mind, and the intellect are controlled—is "one whose senses, mind, and intellect are restrained. A sage (*muni*) is so called because of his contemplation; he is a renunciant. Being solely intent upon liberation (*mokṣaparāyaṇa*), even while remaining in the body, he is one for whom liberation alone is the supreme goal (*param ayana*), the highest resort; such a sage would be one who is solely intent upon liberation.

One who is free from desire, fear, and anger—desire, fear, and anger being collectively termed "icchābhayakrodha"—is one from whom these have departed; he is "vigatecchābhayakrodha. He who always conducts himself in this manner is a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) and is indeed liberated. For him, no further liberation remains to be accomplished.
Knowing Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord of all worlds, and the Friend of all beings, one attains peace. (BhG 5.29)

Thus, it is said what is to be known by one whose mind is thus concentrated: having known Me as Nārāyaṇa—the enjoyer of sacrifice and austerity (yajña-tapas) in the form of the agent of sacrifices and austerities and in the form of the deity; the Great Lord of all worlds, the supreme ruler of all worlds; the friend of all beings, who benefits all living creatures without expectation of any return; who dwells in the heart of all beings; the supervisor of the fruits of all actions; and the witness of all cognitions—one attains peace, that is, the cessation of the entire cycle of worldly existence. || BhG 5.29 ||

Thus ends the fifth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya) and disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter Six:
Now begins the sixth chapter.
(Śaṅkarācārya’s Commentary:

At the end of the immediately preceding chapter, the verses beginning with "Having placed the objects of touch outside" [Gītā 5.27], which serve as aphorisms for the yoga of meditation—an internal means toward perfect knowledge—were taught. This sixth chapter is now commenced as a commentary (*vṛtti*) upon those [aphorisms]. In this regard, since action is an external limb of the yoga of meditation, and because action must be performed by the qualified householder until he becomes capable of ascending to the yoga of meditation, the text praises that action.

Now, one might ask: for what purpose is this demarcation between ascending to the yoga of meditation established, given that prescribed action is indeed to be performed as long as one lives? No; for there is the specific qualification: "For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means" (Gītā 3.3). Furthermore, because for one who has already ascended, only tranquility (*śama*) is enjoined. If both tranquility and action were intended to be performed by both the seeker and the ascended, then the distinction and separate specification made by the terms "for the seeker" and "for the ascended"—differentiating the respective objects of tranquility and action—would be meaningless.

If it is argued that among those in the stages of life (*āśramin*), some are desirous of ascending to yoga (*yogam ārurukṣu*) while others have already ascended (*ārūḍha*), and that for the rest there is neither the desire to ascend nor the state of having ascended—therefore, with reference to them, the qualification "of the one desirous of ascending and the one who has ascended" and the subsequent distinction are indeed appropriate—it is not so. This is because of the statement "of that very person" (*tasyaiva*), and because of the repeated mention of "yoga" in the phrase "of the one who has ascended to yoga" (*yogārūḍhasya*). Thus, for that very person who was previously desirous of ascending to yoga, once he has ascended, tranquility (*śama*) alone is to be practiced.

It is stated that the cause is for the sake of the fruit of yoga; therefore, there is no attainment of the obligation to perform any action for as long as one lives. This is also evident from the statement regarding one who has fallen away from yoga.

If yoga were prescribed for a householder who performs ritual actions (*karmī*) in the sixth chapter, then even for one who has fallen away from yoga, the fear of destruction—that he would attain the course of action, namely the fruit of action—would be untenable. For an action that has been performed, whether optional (*kāmya*) or obligatory (*nitya*), necessarily brings about its own fruit, since liberation is eternal and thus not something to be produced. Furthermore, we have already stated that because an obligatory action is understood through the authority of the Veda, it must have a fruit;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the Veda having no purpose.

Furthermore, the statement regarding "falling away from both" would not be meaningful if action were [entirely] existent, because there would be no possibility of a cause for falling away from action. If it is argued that since one has renounced the performed action to the Lord, the fruit of the action does not accrue to the agent, we say no; for it is logical that renunciation to the Lord is a cause for an even greater fruit. If it is argued that it is solely for the sake of liberation—namely, that the renunciation of one's own performed actions to the Lord, when accompanied by yoga, leads only to liberation and not to any other fruit—[we respond as follows].

If it is argued that, because he has fallen away from yoga, the apprehension of his destruction is indeed appropriate with respect to him, we say no; for there is an injunction for the renunciation of action in the words: "Solitary, with mind and self controlled, free from desire and possessions, remaining in the vow of celibacy" (Gītā 6.10, 14). Furthermore, the statement "free from desire and possessions," and so forth, is not compatible with a householder. Moreover, the question regarding one who has fallen away from both would be logically inconsistent.

If it is argued that by the term "unattached" (anāśrita), the status of being a renunciant (saṃnyāsin) and a yogi is stated only for the performer of ritual action (karmin), and that the status of being a renunciant and a yogi is thereby prohibited for one who has abandoned the sacrificial fire (niragni) and is inactive (akriya), we say no. This is because the passage is intended as a praise of the renunciation of the desire for fruits regarding ritual action, which is an external limb (bahiraṅga) with respect to the yoga of meditation (dhyānayoga).

A renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) and a yogi are not merely one who is without sacrificial fires and without ritual action; what then? Even a performer of action (*karmī*), having renounced attachment to the fruits of action and practicing the yoga of action for the sake of purifying the mind, becomes both a renunciant and a yogi—thus he is praised. Furthermore, it is not possible for a single sentence to simultaneously praise the renunciation of attachment to the fruits of action and prohibit the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*).

Furthermore, the Blessed One does not deny the status of renunciation (*saṃnyāsitva*) and yoga (*yogitva*) prescribed for one who is truly a renunciant—devoid of fire and action—in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and Yoga-śāstras. Moreover, it would contradict his own words [to do so], for he says: "Having renounced all actions with the mind... he remains neither acting nor causing to act" (Gītā 5.13), and "silent, content with whatever comes... (Gītā 12.19).

The Blessed One has shown his own words in various places, such as: "He who is homeless and steady-minded" (Gītā 12.19), "the man who, having abandoned all desires, moves about free from longing" (Gītā 2.71), and "one who has renounced all undertakings" (Gītā 12.16). A prohibition of the fourth stage of life would contradict these; therefore, for a sage desiring to ascend to yoga—

For one who has entered the householder stage, the performance of rites such as the *agnihotra*—when carried out without regard for their fruits—attains the status of a means for ascending to the yoga of meditation by way of purifying the *sattva*. Thus, he is praised as both a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) and a yogi:
"He who performs the action that must be done without depending on the fruit of action—he is a renunciant and a yogi; neither he who lacks the sacred fires, nor he who is inactive [is so]. (BhG 6.1)

"Not dependent" (*anāśrita*) means not resting upon anything. Upon what? Upon the fruit of action—the result of actions is "karmaphala," and he is not dependent on that; the meaning is that he is devoid of thirst for the fruit of action. For whoever has thirst for the fruit of action becomes dependent on the fruit of action. But this one is the opposite of that; therefore, he is "not dependent on the fruit of action. Being such as this, he performs—that is, carries out—the duty, the obligatory work which is the opposite of optional rites, such as the *agnihotra* and so forth.

Whosoever is such a performer of action is distinguished from other performers of action. With this very meaning, He says: "He is both a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) and a yogi. Renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) means total relinquishment; he who possesses that is a renunciant. Yoga is the concentration of the mind; he who possesses that is a yogi. One endowed with such qualities is to be so regarded. It should not be thought that only one who is without the sacred fires and without ritual action is a renunciant and a yogi.

One from whom the fires that constitute the limbs of ritual action have departed is "niragni" (one without fires). And one for whom actions—such as austerity, charity, and so forth—which do not employ fire as a means are non-existent, is "akriya" (one without action).

Now, an objection may be raised: "In the Śruti, Smṛti, and Yoga-śāstras, it is well known that the state of being a renunciant (saṃnyāsin) and a yogin belongs only to one who is without fire and without ritual action; how then can it be stated here—contrary to established usage—that the state of being a renunciant and a yogin belongs to one who possesses fire and performs ritual action? This is not a fault, because both states are intended to be attributed [to such a person] through a certain figurative application (guṇavṛtti).

How is that so? Renunciation (*saṃnyāsitva*) consists in the renunciation of the intention for the fruits of action, while the state of being a yogi (*yogitva*) consists in the performance of action as an auxiliary to yoga and the abandonment of the intention for the fruits of action—which is a cause of mental distraction. Thus, both are used in a secondary sense. To show that primary renunciation and the state of being a yogi are not what is intended here, He says: "Know that which they call renunciation, O Pāṇḍava, to be yoga;
for no one who has not renounced intention can be a yogi. (BhG 6.2)

That which is characterized by the renunciation of all actions and their fruits—the ultimate renunciation (*paramārtha-saṃnyāsa*)—is what those learned in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* call "renunciation" (*saṃnyāsa*). Know, O Pāṇḍava, that Yoga, which is characterized by the performance of action, is that very same ultimate renunciation; understand this. In response to the inquiry as to what kind of similarity is accepted between Karma-yoga, which is characterized by worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*), and ultimate renunciation, which is characterized by its opposite, withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), so that the latter's nature may be attributed to the former, this is said: there indeed exists a similarity between Karma-yoga and ultimate renunciation by way of the agent.

For he who is a renunciant in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-saṃnyāsī*) renounces the mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) regarding all actions and their fruits—the cause of desire which is the motive for worldly engagement—by virtue of having abandoned all means of action. This practitioner of *karma-yoga* as well, while indeed performing action, renounces the mental construction regarding the fruit. Intending to demonstrate this point, [the Lord] said: "Because no one whatsoever," that is, no practitioner of action (*karmī*), being a yogi possessed of concentration, can be "one whose mental construction has not been renounced"—that is, one by whom the mental construction or intention (*abhisandhi*) has not been renounced or abandoned.

It comes to pass; the meaning is that it does not fail to come to pass. Because the intention for fruit (*phala-saṃkalpa*) is a cause of distraction of the mind, therefore, whatever person is an agent who has renounced the intention for fruit, he would be a yogi, possessed of concentration, with an undistracted mind. The intended meaning is that this is because the intention for fruit, which is the cause of mental distraction, has been renounced.

Because one performs action as a limb of yoga, or because one abandons the intention for the fruits of action—which is a cause of mental distraction—one is called both a "yogi" and a "sannyāsin"; this is what is intended here. (BhG 6.2)

Thus, with reference to the commonality of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) by way of the agent in both ultimate renunciation and the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), it was stated for the purpose of praising karma-yoga that "that which they call renunciation, know that to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava" (Gītā 6.2). Having praised karma-yoga—which is independent of fruits—as being renunciation because it is an external means to the yoga of meditation (*dhyānayoga*), he now demonstrates that karma-yoga is a means to the yoga of meditation: "For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the cause."
For that very person who has ascended to yoga, tranquility is said to be the means.

The meaning is: for one who "desires to ascend" (ārurukṣoḥ)—that is, one who wishes to climb but has not yet climbed, being unable to remain established in the yoga of meditation (dhyānayoga). For whom is he such a seeker? For the sage (muni), which means for one who has renounced the fruits of action. What does he desire to ascend to? Yoga. Action is said to be the cause, the means. But for that same person once they have "ascended to yoga," tranquility (śama)—that is, peace, the cessation from all actions—is said to be the cause, the means for one who has ascended to yoga. This is the meaning.

To the extent that one ceases from actions, to that same extent the mind of one who is free from exertion and has conquered the senses becomes concentrated. This being so, he quickly becomes established in yoga. And thus it was said by Vyāsa:
"There is no wealth for a Brahmin such as oneness, equanimity, and truthfulness."
"Virtue, steadfastness, laying aside the rod of punishment, uprightness, and the gradual withdrawal from all activities"—thus [it is said]. (BhG 6.3)
Now, it is said when one becomes established in yoga:
"When indeed one is attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions..."
When one has renounced all volitional constructions, then one is said to have ascended to yoga.

When the yogi, with his mind composed in samādhi, does not become attached—meaning he does not form the notion that they ought to be performed—to sense-objects (the objects of the senses, such as sound and so forth) nor to actions (whether obligatory, occasional, optional, or prohibited), because he perceives no purpose in them; he is one who has renounced all mental constructs (sarvasaṃkalpasaṃnyāsī), meaning one whose nature it is to renounce all mental constructs that serve as causes for desires for objects in this world or the next.

"One who has ascended to yoga" means one who has attained yoga; this is what is said at that time. From the statement "one who has renounced all mental constructs" (*sarvasaṃkalpasaṃnyāsī*), the meaning is that one should renounce all desires and all actions. For all desires have their root in mental constructs; as the Smṛti says: "Desire indeed has its root in mental construct; sacrifices arise from mental construct" (Manu 2.3);
and "O Desire, I know your root; you are born from mental construct.
I shall no longer mentally construct you, and thus you shall not exist for me" (Mahābhārata 12.177.25). Etc.

Furthermore, upon the renunciation of all desires, the renunciation of all actions becomes established. This is because of such scriptural passages as: "As is one's desire, so is one's resolve; as is one's resolve, so is the action one performs" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5), and from such traditional texts as: "Whatever a living being does, that is the movement of desire" (Manu Smṛti 2.4). And this follows from reason as well: for when all volitions are renounced, no one is even capable of moving.
Therefore, by the statement "one who has renounced all volitions," the Blessed One causes one to abandon all desires and all actions.

When one has thus ascended to yoga, then by that means the self has been uplifted from the cycle of existence, which is a mass of misfortunes. Therefore, one should uplift the self by means of the self; one should not let the self sink down.
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

One should lift oneself up from the ocean of *saṃsāra* in which one is submerged; "thence upward" means one should raise oneself, that is, one should attain the state of being established in yoga. One should not cause oneself to sink, nor lead oneself downward, nor cause oneself to go down. For the self alone is the friend of the self; indeed, there is no other friend who can lead to liberation from *saṃsāra*. Even a friend is actually an obstacle to liberation, because he is a locus for the bonds of affection and the like.

Therefore, the restriction is appropriate: "The self alone is indeed the friend of the self. The self alone is the enemy or foe. Even that external enemy who causes harm is one instigated by the self; thus, the restriction "the self alone is the enemy of the self" is indeed appropriate.

It has been said: "The self alone is the friend, the self alone is the enemy of the self. In this regard, it is now stated what the characteristics of the self are when it is its own friend, and what the characteristics are when it is its own enemy:
"The self is the friend of that self by whom the self has been conquered by the self."
But for one who lacks self-control, the self itself would behave like an enemy in the state of being an enemy.

The self is the friend of that self; for him, that self is the friend by whom the very self has been conquered. "Self" here refers to the aggregate of the body and the senses; the meaning is: by whom [the senses] have been brought under control, i.e., one who has conquered the senses. But for the non-self—that is, for one who has not conquered the self—the self itself would exist in the state of an enemy, in the condition of an adversary. The meaning is: just as a non-self (an external enemy) is harmful to oneself, so too the self would act to the detriment of oneself, like an enemy.
For one who has conquered the self and is tranquil, the Supreme Self is fully composed amidst cold and heat, pleasure and pain, as well as honor and dishonor.

For one who has conquered the self—that is, for that renunciant whose self (the aggregate of the body and senses) is conquered by him, and who is tranquil, meaning whose internal organ is serene—the Supreme Self remains concentrated; the meaning is that It exists manifest as his very own Self. Furthermore, he should be the same toward cold and heat, pleasure and pain, as well as toward honor and dishonor—that is, toward respect and insult.
One whose self is satisfied with knowledge and realization, who is steadfast and has conquered the senses,
for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same— he is called a yogi who is disciplined.

One whose self—the internal organ—is satisfied by knowledge and realization; "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the thorough understanding of the categories taught in the scriptures, while "realization" (*vijñāna*) is the personal experience of those very things known through scripture in that same manner. One whose self has become satisfied by both that knowledge and realization, having attained the conviction of "enough," is "one whose self is satisfied by knowledge and realization. Such a person becomes "immovable" (*kūṭastha*), meaning unshakable. And he is one who has conquered the senses. He who is such as this is called, or described, as "yoked" (*yukta*), that is, composed in meditation.
That yogi for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal is one who regards a clod, a stone, and gold as the same; he is "one for whom a clod, a stone, and gold are equal."
Furthermore:
"Toward friends, allies, noble ones, neutrals, mediators, enemies, and kinsmen..."
One who possesses a mind of equanimity toward both the virtuous and the wicked is preeminent.

The half-verse beginning with "suhṛt" (friend) constitutes a single compound word. A *suhṛt* is one who helps without expecting a return; a *mitra* is one who is affectionate; an *ari* is an enemy; an *udāsīna* is one who sides with neither party; a *madhyastha* is one who desires the welfare of both opposing sides; a *dveṣya* is one who is personally disliked; and a *bandhu* is a relative. Regarding all these—whether they are virtuous and followers of the scriptures, or sinful and performers of forbidden acts—one should maintain an even mind toward them all.

"Who is he whose mind is not occupied with 'what is my duty?'"—this is the meaning. "He is distinguished" (viśiṣyate), or alternatively, "he is liberated" (vimucyate) is another reading. The meaning is that among all those who have ascended to yoga, this one is the best. || BhG 6.9 ||
Therefore, for this reason, in order to attain the supreme fruit,
the yogi should constantly discipline himself while staying in solitude.
Alone, with mind and self controlled, free from desire and without possessions.

The yogī, the meditator, should constantly and at all times yoke—that is, concentrate—his self, his internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), while staying alone and without a companion in a secluded place such as a mountain cave; by the qualifying terms "staying in seclusion" and "alone," the meaning is that he should do so after having renounced the world (saṃnyāsa). With his mind and body restrained—the mind being the internal organ and the body being the physical frame—he, whose mind and body are controlled, being free from expectations (nirāśīḥ) and devoid of thirst (vītatṛṣṇaḥ), and without possessions (aparigrahaḥ)—meaning, even while being a renunciant, having abandoned all belongings—should practice yoga. || BhG 6.10 ||

Now, the rules regarding posture, diet, conduct, and so forth—which serve as the means for one practicing yoga—must be stated, as well as the characteristics of one who has attained yoga and its fruits; therefore, this section begins. Among these, the posture is first described:
"Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place..."
Neither too high nor too low, it should be covered with cloth, a deerskin, and kusha grass, one over the other.

Having established for oneself a firm and motionless seat—neither too high nor too low—in a place that is clean, pure, and secluded by nature or through ritual preparation; and that seat should have cloth, a deerskin, and kusha grass as its upper layers—that is, a seat upon which cloth, deerskin, and kusha grass are placed in ascending order. Here, the sequence of the cloth and the other items is reversed from the order of recitation.
Having established [the image] there, what should one do? Having made the mind one-pointed therein, with the activities of the mind and senses restrained.
Having sat down on his seat, he should practice yoga for the purification of the self.

Having sat down there on that seat, one should practice yoga. How? Having withdrawn [the mind] from all objects and having made the mind one-pointed, with the activities of the mind and senses restrained—meaning he whose activities of the mind and senses (citta and indriyas) are controlled—he should practice yoga. For what purpose should he practice yoga? He says: for the purification of the self, that is, for the sake of purifying the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). || BhG 6.12 ||
The external posture has been described. Now, it is explained how the body is to be maintained: holding the body, head, and neck erect, motionless and steady.
Fixing his gaze on the tip of his own nose and not looking around in any direction.

"Keeping the body, head, and neck erect"—that is, the body, head, and neck together; holding them straight and motionless. For one who holds [them] straight, movement may still occur; therefore, he specifies "motionless," meaning having become steady. "Gazing at the tip of his own nose"—having performed the act of looking, that is, seeing, properly. The word *iva* (as if) should be understood as elided. For gazing at the tip of one's own nose is not what is intended here.

What then? It is the convergence of the gaze of the eyes. And that is intended as being dependent upon the concentration of the internal organ (manas). If the mere looking at the tip of one's own nose were intended, the mind would be concentrated on that very spot, not on the Self. For he will later state that the concentration of the mind is upon the Self in the words, "having made the mind established in the Self. Therefore, by the elision of the word *iva* (as if), the convergence of the gaze of the two eyes itself is called "looking intently. And "not looking at the quarters" means avoiding the looking toward the directions. (BhG 6.13)
Furthermore:
"With a tranquil self, free from fear, and established in the vow of celibacy,"
Having restrained the mind, with the mind fixed on Me, disciplined and intent on Me, he should sit.

"With a tranquil mind" (*praśāntātmā*): he whose inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is exceedingly peaceful is "one with a tranquil mind. "Free from fear" (*vigatabhīḥ*): one who is devoid of dread. "Abiding in the vow of celibacy" (*brahmacārivrate sthitaḥ*): the vow of a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) consists of service to the teacher, eating alms-food, and so forth; he is established in that. The meaning is that he should be a performer of those practices.

Furthermore, having restrained the mind—that is, having withdrawn the fluctuations of the mind—one whose mind is fixed on Me, the Supreme Lord, is "maccittaḥ"; being thus "yuktaḥ," or concentrated, he should sit, or remain seated. He becomes "matparaḥ," meaning one for whom I am the supreme goal. A certain person who is full of passion may have his mind fixed on a woman, yet he does not regard the woman alone as the supreme goal; rather, he regards the king or Mahādeva as such. But this person has his mind fixed on Me and I am his supreme goal.
Now, the fruit of yoga is being described:
"Thus constantly engaging the self in yoga, the yogi of restrained mind..."
He attains peace, which culminates in Nirvana and abides in Me.

Practicing yoga and performing concentration in this manner according to the prescribed method, the yogi—whose mind is *niyatamānasaḥ*, meaning one whose mind (*mānasa*) or internal organ (*manaḥ*) is restrained and controlled—attains peace (*śāntim*), which culminates in liberation (*nirvāṇaparamām*). Liberation (*nirvāṇa*) is *mokṣa*; that peace for which liberation is the ultimate goal is "culminating in liberation. He attains that peace which culminates in liberation, which is established in me (*matsaṃstham*), meaning dependent upon me. || BhG 6.15 ||
Now, the regulation regarding food and other matters for the yogin is stated: "But yoga is not for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all."
O Arjuna, neither for one who is habitually prone to excessive sleep nor for one who does not sleep at all.

For one who eats too much—that is, eating beyond the measure of food appropriate for oneself—there is no yoga; nor is there yoga for one who does not eat at all. As the Śruti declares: "That food which is commensurate with the self protects it and does not harm it; that which is more harms it, and that which is less does not protect it. Therefore, a yogi should not eat more or less than the amount of food commensurate with his own self.

Alternatively, for a practitioner who eats in excess of the measure of food prescribed in the Yoga scriptures, there is no yoga. For it has been said: "One should leave half of the seasoned food, one-third for water, and one-fourth for the movement of air," and so forth; such is the prescribed measure.
Likewise, O Arjuna, yoga does not come to one who is habitually addicted to excessive sleep, nor indeed to one who stays awake for too long.
Furthermore, it is said: "How does yoga come about?
For one who is moderate in food and recreation, moderate in activity during their duties,"
For one whose sleep and waking are disciplined, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.

For one whose food and recreation are regulated: "food" (*āhāra*) is that which is taken in, namely nourishment; "recreation" (*vihāra*) is moving about, namely walking; he for whom these two are "regulated," meaning restricted to a fixed measure, is "one whose food and recreation are regulated. Likewise, for one whose activity is regulated: he whose activity in performing actions is "regulated," meaning restricted.

Likewise, for one whose sleep and awakening are regulated—meaning for whom both sleep and awakening are disciplined and occur at their proper times—for the yogi who is moderate in food and recreation, disciplined in his exertion in actions, and disciplined in sleep and awakening, yoga arises which is the destroyer of suffering; that is to say, it is called the "destroyer of suffering" because it destroys all sufferings, meaning that yoga becomes the cause of the exhaustion of all the miseries of saṃsāra. ||BhGS_6.17||
Now, it is said: when is one considered to be disciplined? When the controlled mind abides in the Self alone.
When one is free from longing for all desires, then one is said to be disciplined.

When the mind—being *viniyata*, meaning specifically restrained, controlled, and having attained one-pointedness—abandons reflection on external objects and abides in the Self alone; that is to say, it attains stability within its own nature. When the yogi is *niḥspṛhaḥ*, meaning his longing or thirst for all desires regarding seen and unseen objects has departed, then at that time he is said to be *yuktaḥ*, concentrated in samādhi. (BhG 6.18)
An analogy is given for that concentrated mind of the yogi:
"Just as a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker— that is remembered as the simile."
For the yogi whose mind is restrained, as he practices yoga for the self.

Just as a lamp, well-lit and placed in a windless spot—in a place devoid of wind—does not flicker or move; that is the simile by which it is compared, so it is remembered and considered by those who know yoga and perceive the movement of the mind. It refers to the self of the yogi whose mind is restrained, whose internal organ is controlled, who is practicing yoga—that is, who is practicing meditative concentration (samādhi). This is the meaning. || BhG 6.19 ||
Thus, when the mind— having become one-pointed through the power of yoga practice and resembling a lamp in a windless place— comes to rest, restrained by the cultivation of yoga;
And wherein, beholding the Self by means of the self, one finds contentment within the self.

When, at which time, the mind ceases—that is, it comes to rest, being restrained from all sides and suppressed through the practice of yoga, the performance of yoga—and when, at that very time, seeing and perceiving the Self, the Supreme Consciousness whose nature is light, by means of the Self, which is the internal organ purified by samādhi, one finds satisfaction, attaining contentment within one's own Self.
Furthermore,
that absolute happiness which is beyond the senses is to be grasped by the intellect.
Wherein he knows [the Self], and being established therein, he does not deviate from reality.

"Ultimate" means that which becomes absolutely final; thus, "ultimate" has the sense of being infinite. That which is "grasped by the intellect" (*buddhigrāhya*) is grasped by the intellect alone, independent of the senses; thus, "grasped by the intellect" means it is beyond the senses and transcends the range of the senses, having been produced without an external object. He knows—that is, he experiences—such happiness at that time when this wise one, established in the nature of the Self, does not move away from it; in reality, he does not fall away from the true nature of reality. || BhG 6.21 ||
Furthermore: "And having obtained which, one considers no other gain to be superior to it."
Established in which, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering.

Having attained that, having reached that self-attainment, one does not think or consider that there is any other gain, any further acquisition, superior to it; moreover, established in that reality of the Self, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering characterized by the falling of weapons and the like.

One should know that specific state of the self, characterized by the attributes beginning with "wherein the mind comes to rest," as Yoga, which is defined as the disjunction from the union with suffering.
That yoga must be practiced with determination by one whose mind is free from despondency.

One should know—that is, one should understand—that "the disjunction from the union with suffering" means that union with sufferings is "union with suffering," and the separation from that is "disjunction from the union with suffering. One should know—that is, one should understand—that this very disjunction from the union with suffering is designated as "yoga" by virtue of its contrary definition. Having thus concluded the discussion on the fruit of yoga, the necessity of practicing yoga is stated once more through a renewed undertaking, for the purpose of prescribing certainty and freedom from despondency as the means for achieving yoga.

That yoga, which has the aforementioned fruit, must be practiced with certainty and resolute determination by one whose mind is undiscouraged—*anirviṇṇa* means not *nirviṇṇa*, or "discouraged. What is that? It is the mind; the meaning is: by a mind or consciousness free from despondency.
Furthermore:
Having abandoned all desires born of volitional thought without exception, [one remains].
Having restrained the entire collection of senses from all sides by the mind alone, ||BhG_6.24||

Having abandoned all desires—which are born of volition, meaning those desires for which volition is the source—completely and without remainder; and furthermore, having restrained the entire collection of the senses on all sides by means of the mind itself endowed with discrimination.
Gradually, by means of the intellect held with firmness, one should attain cessation;
having fixed the mind within the Self, one should not think of anything at all.

One should gradually, and not suddenly, bring about cessation—that is, one should effect withdrawal—by means of what? By means of the intellect (buddhi). Of what kind? "Seized by steadfastness" (dhṛtigṛhītayā); that is to say, by the intellect held by fortitude (dhairya), meaning it is endowed with firmness. Having made the mind "established in the Self" (ātmasaṃstham)—meaning established in the Self, such that the Self alone is everything and there is nothing other than that—one should not think of anything at all. This is the supreme method of Yoga.
In this regard, when the yogi has thus begun to fix the mind upon the Self,
from whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away—
Then, having restrained it from this and that, one should bring it under control within the Self alone.

From whatever cause—be it sound or any other object—from which the mind, being restless and exceedingly fickle, and for that very reason unstable, issues forth or goes out, from each and every such cause, such as sound and so on, one should restrain it by investigating the true nature of those respective objects, thereby rendering them mere appearances through the cultivation of detachment, and thus bring this mind under control within the Self alone.
One should bring it under one's own control. Thus, through the power of the practice of yoga, the mind of the yogi becomes tranquil within the Self alone.
For supreme happiness comes to this yogi whose mind is perfectly tranquil,
whose passion has been stilled, who has become one with Brahman, and who is free from taint.

He whose mind is perfectly tranquil—that is, one whose mind is exceedingly calm—is "one of tranquil mind"; to such a yogi, indeed, supreme happiness approaches, that is, comes near. He is one whose passion (*rajas*) has been stilled, meaning one for whom the dust of afflictions such as delusion (*moha*) and the like has been destroyed; he is "become Brahman," that is, liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), possessing the firm conviction that "all is indeed Brahman"; he is "Brahman-become," free from taint, being devoid of merit, demerit, and the like.
Thus constantly disciplining the self, the yogi, freed from all taint,
easily attains the infinite bliss that consists in contact with Brahman.

Thus practicing in the manner described, the yogi, free from obstacles to yoga, being always and at all times devoid of stain—that is, free from sin—easily, without effort, attains and pervades that supreme, unsurpassed bliss which is the touch of Brahman, a bliss whose contact is with the Supreme Brahman, and which exists beyond all extremes. ||BhGS_6.28||

Now, that fruit of yoga which is the vision of the oneness of Brahman— the cause of the cessation of all transmigratory existence— is demonstrated: "The Self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the Self."
One whose self is disciplined by yoga perceives with equal vision everywhere.

One whose self is disciplined through yoga—one whose internal organ is concentrated—beholds his own Self abiding in all beings, situated within all beings, and beholds all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, as having attained oneness with himself; he is one who sees the same everywhere, for he possesses the vision—that is, the knowledge—of the identity of Brahman and the Self, which is equal and without distinction toward all beings, from Brahmā down to the stationary, even though they are diverse.
The fruit of this vision of the oneness of the Self is now stated: "He who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me,"
I am never lost to him, nor is he ever lost to me.

He who sees Me as Vāsudeva, the Self of all, everywhere in all beings, and sees the entire multitude of beings beginning with Brahmā within Me, the Self of all—for him who thus perceives the oneness of the Self, I, the Lord, do not vanish; I shall not become invisible to him. And he does not vanish from Me; that wise man does not become invisible to Me, Vāsudeva, because of our identity as one single Self.
For one's own self is indeed dear to oneself; and because I am the very one who perceives the unity of the Self in all.
Having thus restated the right vision that constitutes the meaning of the preceding verse, its fruit, liberation, is now described:
"He who, established in unity, worships Me as dwelling in all beings..."
In every way, even while acting, that yogi abides in me.

In every way and by all means, even while acting, the yogin who possesses right vision abides in Me, the supreme state of Viṣṇu; he is eternally liberated—this is the meaning: he is not obstructed by anything on the path toward liberation.
Furthermore,
O Arjuna, he who, by means of the analogy of himself, sees equality everywhere—
Whether in happiness or in suffering, that yogi is considered supreme.

*Ātmaupamyena*: that by which one's own self (*ātman*) is compared by oneself is *upamā* (comparison); the state of that comparison is *aupamya*. By means of that *ātmaupamya*, O Arjuna, he who sees equally—that is, with equality—toward all beings everywhere, what does he see as equal? It is said: "Just as happiness is desired by me, so too is happiness agreeable to all living beings. The word *vā* is used in the sense of *ca* (and).

Or rather, just as whatever suffering is disagreeable and undesirable to me, so too is suffering, undesirable, and disagreeable to all living beings; thus, by means of the analogy of oneself (*ātmaupamya*), one views pleasure and pain, the agreeable and the disagreeable, with equality toward all beings. One who does not act disagreeably toward anyone—that is, one who is non-violent (*ahiṃsaka*)—is the yogi who is established in right vision (*samyag-darśana*). Such a person is considered and intended to be the supreme, most excellent among all yogis.
Observing that this yoga characterized by right vision, as previously described, is difficult to accomplish, Arjuna, desiring to hear the certain means for its attainment,
said: "O Madhusūdana, this yoga which has been taught by You through equanimity— "
Because of its restlessness, I do not perceive its steady stability.

O Madhusūdana, regarding this yoga which has been described by You as equality and equanimity, I do not perceive—that is, I do not attain—a steady and immovable state within it, because of the restlessness of the mind. What [state]? A firm and unshakable stability.
That is not established,
for the mind, O Kṛṣṇa, is restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate.
I consider its restraint to be as difficult as that of the wind.

The mind is indeed restless. "Kṛṣṇa" is a form derived from the root *kṛṣ*, meaning "to draw. He is called Kṛṣṇa because He draws away (removes) the defects of His devotees, such as sin; thus, "O Kṛṣṇa" is His vocative address. For the mind is restless—not only exceedingly restless, but also turbulent (*pramāthi*), having the nature of agitating. It agitates the body and the senses, throwing them into distraction and bringing them under its own control. Furthermore, it is powerful (*balavat*), being very strong and impossible for anyone to restrain, due to its being difficult to ward off.

Furthermore, it is firm and as difficult to cut as a serpent made of thread. I consider the restraint—that is, the cessation—of such a mind to be as difficult as that of the wind; the intention is that I consider it even more difficult than the restraint of the wind.
The Blessed Lord said: It is exactly as you say, O mighty-armed one; there is no doubt that the mind is restless and difficult to restrain.
But by practice, O son of Kuntī, and by dispassion, it is mastered.

Without doubt, there is no uncertainty regarding this: "The mind is restless and difficult to restrain," O mighty-armed one! However, by means of practice—practice being the repeated occurrence of similar mental impressions upon some stage of consciousness—and by means of dispassion—dispassion being the absence of craving resulting from the cultivation of seeing the defects in the enjoyment of seen and unseen objects—the movement of the mind in the form of distraction is seized. By that dispassion, the mind is grasped, restrained, and suppressed; such is the meaning.
Furthermore, for one whose self is unrestrained, yoga is difficult to attain by that unrestrained self; this is my conviction.
But by one who has mastered the self and strives through the proper means, it is possible to attain.

For one whose self—the internal organ—is uncontrolled due to a lack of practice and dispassion, that person is "one of uncontrolled self"; by such a person of uncontrolled self, yoga is difficult to attain; it is to be reached with great hardship—this is my conviction. But for one who is "of controlled self"—that is, one whose self, or mind, has been brought under control through practice and dispassion—for him, being of controlled self and striving further, making renewed effort, yoga can be attained through the means already described.

In this regard, Arjuna spoke out of fear for the destruction of one who, having undertaken the practice of yoga, has renounced the actions that cause the attainment of this world and the next, yet has not attained right vision— the means to liberation which is the fruit of yoga-perfection— such that at the time of death his mind wavers from the path of yoga: "One who is endowed with faith but lacks self-control, whose mind has wavered from yoga..."
O Kṛṣṇa, failing to attain perfection in yoga, what goal does one go to?

One who is diligent but lacks effort on the path of yoga, yet is endowed with faith and a conviction in its reality, whose mind wavers from yoga at the time of death—such a person, having lost his memory and failed to attain the perfection of yoga, that is, the fruit of yoga which is right vision, what goal does he go to, O Kṛṣṇa?
O mighty-armed one, I hope that he, being without support and bewildered on the path to Brahman, does not perish like a scattered cloud, having fallen away from both and lost his way.

Does someone, having fallen away from both—the path of action and the path of yoga—not perish like a scattered cloud, being without support and without refuge, O mighty-armed one, while deluded on the path of Brahman, the way to the attainment of Brahman? Or does he not perish? BhG 6.38.
O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to sever this doubt of mine completely;
for indeed, no one other than you is capable of being the dispeller of this doubt.

O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to sever and remove this doubt of mine completely. For there is no other seer or god besides you who is capable of—indeed, it is not possible—that he should be the one to sever and destroy this doubt; therefore, the meaning is that you alone ought to sever it. || BhG 6.39 ||
The Blessed One said:
O Pārtha, for him there is no destruction either in this world or in the next.
For no one who performs good deeds, my dear, ever goes to an evil state.

O Pārtha, for him there is no destruction either in this world or in the other world beyond. Destruction means obtaining a birth inferior to one's previous state; that does not exist for one who has fallen from yoga. For no doer of good, O dear one, ever attains a miserable or contemptible state. "Dear one" (*tāta*) is said of a father because he extends himself through his son; likewise, a son is called "dear one" as he is the very self of the father, and a disciple is also called a "son" because he does not go astray.
But what happens to him?
Having reached the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds and having dwelt there for eternal years—
One who has fallen from yoga is born into the house of the pure and the prosperous.

The renunciant who has set out upon the path of yoga, having by his own capacity reached and traversed the worlds of the doers of merit—those who have performed sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice—and having dwelt there for eternal, perpetual years, is born at the exhaustion of those enjoyments in the house of the pure, who act according to the teachings, and the prosperous, who possess great power, should he fall from yoga.
Or else he is born into a family of wise yogis;
for such a birth as this is indeed more difficult to obtain in this world.

Or else, he is born—not from a family of the prosperous, but from another family of poor yogis who are wise and intelligent. For this birth, in the family of poor yogis, is more difficult to attain and more difficult to reach than the former kind of birth in this world, namely such a birth as this in a family possessing the aforementioned qualities.
Because there he regains that same connection with the intellect belonging to his previous body.
And from that point on, O joy of the Kurus, he strives even more for perfection.

There, in the family of yogis, he regains that same application of the intellect—that union with the intellect (buddhi-saṃyoga)—which pertained to his previous body (paurvadehika). And from that previously performed latent impression (saṃskāra), O joy of the Kurus, he strives—that is, he exerts effort—further and more intensely for the sake of perfect attainment (saṃsiddhi).
How is it that there is a conjunction with the intellect of a previous body? To this it is said:
"For by that very same prior practice, he is led away even against his will."
Even one who merely desires to know yoga transcends the Brahman of sound.

That practice which was performed in a previous birth is "prior practice"; by that very [practice], being powerful, he is carried toward perfection, for even though he is one fallen from yoga (*yogabhraṣṭa*) and lacks self-control. If no karma characterized by unrighteousness (*adharma*) and so forth—which is stronger than the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born of the practice of yoga—has been performed, then he is carried away by the latent impression produced by the practice of yoga.

If unrighteousness (*adharma*) is committed with greater force, it indeed overcomes even the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born of yoga; however, upon the exhaustion of that [unrighteousness], the yoga-born impression begins its own effect spontaneously. The meaning is that there is no destruction of it, even though it has endured for a long time.

Therefore, even a renunciant who has fallen from yoga—even one who, though desiring to know the true nature of yoga, has merely set out upon the path of yoga—by virtue of his capacity transcends, surpasses, and casts off the "Word-Brahman," which is the fruit of performing the rituals prescribed in the Vedas; how much more so one who, having understood yoga, remains steadfast in it and practices it?
And for what reason is the state of a yogi superior?
Because a yogi who strives with effort, having his impurities completely cleansed, [attains the goal].
Having attained perfection through many births, he then reaches the supreme goal.

"Striving with effort" means striving intensely. Therein, the wise yogi, whose sins are completely purified—that is, whose impurities are cleansed—and who has attained perfection through many births—having accumulated a certain collection of impressions (saṃskāra) in various births and being perfected by that accumulation made over many births—thereby attaining right vision, goes to the supreme, most excellent goal. || BhG 6.45 ||
Since this is so, therefore the yogi is superior to the ascetics; he is also considered superior to the men of knowledge.
The yogi is superior even to the men of action; therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi.

"The yogi is superior to the ascetics; he is also considered superior to those possessed of knowledge—where 'knowledge' here means proficiency in the meaning of the scriptures—and even superior to those who perform ritual acts—such as the Agnihotra sacrifice and the like. Therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi. (BhG 6.46)
"Even among all yogis, he who, with his inner self absorbed in Me,
worships Me with faith— he is deemed by Me to be the most disciplined."

Among all yogis—even those devoted to the meditation on Rudra, the Ādityas, and others—he who worships and serves Me with an inner self (the internal organ) absorbed in Me, Vāsudeva, being full of faith and possessing conviction, is considered by Me to be the most disciplined (yuktatama), meaning he is exceedingly united [with Me]. This is My intention.

Thus ends the sixth chapter of the commentary on the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-pūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering mendicant teacher (Paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya). ||6||
Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter 7:
Now begins the seventh chapter, titled "The Yoga of Knowledge and Realization."
(Śaṅkara’s Commentary:
"Of all yogis as well, he who worships Me with his inner self absorbed in Me, full of faith—he is deemed by Me to be the most disciplined. [Gītā 6.47]
Having thus introduced the seed of the inquiry, the Blessed Lord, desiring himself to explain what His own true nature is and how one’s inner self may become absorbed in Him, said:
"O Pārtha, with your mind attached to Me, practicing yoga and taking refuge in Me, hear how you shall know Me fully and without doubt. (BhG 7.1)

He whose mind is attached to Me—the Supreme Lord endowed with the attributes to be described hereafter—is "one whose mind is attached to Me" (*mayyāsaktamanāḥ*). O Pārtha! "Practicing yoga" (*yogaṃ yuñjan*) means performing the concentration of the mind. "Taking refuge in Me" (*madāśrayaḥ*) means one for whom I alone, the Supreme Lord, am the refuge.

For whoever is desirous of some human goal resorts to some means for its accomplishment—be it the Agnihotra sacrifice, austerity, or charity—but this yogi resorts to Me alone as his support; having abandoned all other means, he becomes one whose mind is attached to Me alone.

Listen as I speak that by which you, being such as you are, shall know me—without any doubt—as the Blessed Lord, endowed with all my complete and total qualities of majesty, power, strength, sovereignty, and so forth, exactly as I am. BhG 7.1.
And that knowledge concerning Me, together with its full realization, I shall declare to you in its entirety.
Having known which, nothing else remains here to be known.

I shall declare to you this knowledge, along with its realization—that is, accompanied by direct experience—in its entirety and without omission. He praises that intended knowledge in order to attract the listener's attention: "Having known which knowledge, there remains nothing else here further to be known as a means for achieving the goals of human life; it is not left over. The meaning is that he who knows My true nature becomes all-knowing.
Therefore, because it yields such a distinguished fruit, this knowledge is difficult to attain. (BhG 7.2)
How so? It is said:
Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection.
Even among those who strive and have attained perfection, only some know me in truth.

Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives—that is, exerts effort—for perfection; and even among those who strive and have attained perfection—meaning those who indeed strive for liberation—scarcely anyone knows Me in truth, as I truly am.
Having made the listener receptive through this encouragement, he says:
"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, and intellect,"
This nature of mine, called egoism, is divided eightfold.

"Earth" refers to the subtle element (*tanmātra*) of earth, not the gross [element], because of the statement that "primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is divided eightfold. Likewise, water, fire, air, space, and mind are also said to be merely subtle elements. By "mind," the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*), which is the cause of the mind, is understood. By "intellect" (*buddhi*), the principle of the Great One (*mahat-tattva*), which is the cause of the ego-principle, is meant. By "ego-principle," the unmanifest (*avyakta*) conjoined with ignorance (*avidyā*) is intended.

Just as food mixed with poison is called "poison," so too the unmanifest primal cause (avyakta-mūlakāraṇa), when possessed by the latent impression of egoism (ahaṃkāra-vāsanā), is called "egoism" (ahaṃkāra) because it is the instigator of egoism. Indeed, in the world, egoism alone is seen to be the seed of all activity. Thus, this aforementioned Nature (prakṛti)—which is my own sovereign power of illusion (māyā-śakti)—is divided eightfold; that is, it has undergone differentiation.
But know, O mighty-armed one, that there is another, higher nature of Mine, distinct from this, which is the life-force by which this entire world is sustained.

This other [nature] is inferior—base, impure, productive of evil, and consisting of the bondage of saṃsāra. Know that other than this aforementioned one, there is My supreme (parā) nature, which is pure, My very self, the individual soul (jīva), characterized as the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and the cause of the maintenance of life, O mighty-armed one; by which nature, having entered within, this world is sustained.
Understand that all beings have this as their source;
I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe.

"Those whose womb is this"—understand and know that all beings have as their womb these two natures (*prakṛti*), characterized as the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), which are both higher and lower. Since my nature is the womb—the cause—of all beings, therefore I am the origin (*prabhava*) or birth, and likewise the dissolution (*pralaya*) or destruction, of the entire world. The meaning is that, by means of these two natures, I, the omniscient Lord, am the cause of the world.
Therefore, O Dhanañjaya, there is nothing whatsoever higher than Me.
All this is strung upon me, like clusters of gems on a thread.

Other than Me, the Supreme Lord, there is no other cause whatsoever—nothing exists; the meaning is that I alone am the cause of the universe, O Dhanañjaya. Since this is so, therefore all beings and this entire world are strung upon Me, the Supreme Lord—meaning they are woven through, permeated, and threaded together like a cloth on long threads, or like clusters of jewels on a string.
By what specific qualities are you distinguished such that all this is woven upon you? It is said:
"O son of Kuntī, I am the taste in the waters; I am the radiance in the moon and the sun."
The syllable Om among all the Vedas, the sound in space, and virility in men.

"I am the taste"—that which is the essence of the waters is taste; the meaning is that the waters are woven upon me, who have become that taste. It is the same everywhere. Just as I am the taste in the waters, so am I the radiance in the moon and the sun. The *praṇava*, the syllable *oṃ*, is [the essence] in all the Vedas; all the Vedas are woven upon me, who have become that *praṇava*. Likewise, sound is the essential element in space (*kha*); space is woven upon me, who am that sound.
Similarly, "manliness" (*pauruṣam*) is the nature of the person (*puruṣa*), from which the perception of manhood arises in men; men are woven upon me, who am that manliness.
I am the fragrance in the earth and the radiance in the fire;
I am the life-force in all beings and the austerity in ascetics.

I am the pure and fragrant scent in the earth; the earth is woven into me, who have become that scent. The purity of the scent is shown in the earth by its very nature, for the purpose of indicating the purity of taste and other qualities in water and the other elements. However, the impurity of scents and so forth depends on ignorance, moral conduct, and the like, arising from contact with specific material elements for those in the cycle of transmigration. And I am the heat and the light in the fire.
Likewise, I am the life-force in all beings; that by which all beings live is life-force. And among ascetics, I am austerity; in that austerity, the ascetics are woven upon me.
Know me, O Pārtha, to be the eternal seed of all beings;
I am the intellect of the intelligent and the splendor of the splendid.

Know Me, O Pārtha, to be the eternal and ancient seed that causes the sprouting of all beings. Furthermore, I am the discerning power of the intellect—the faculty of discrimination belonging to those possessed of intelligence—and I am the radiance, the boldness, of those who possess it.
And I am the strength of the strong, devoid of desire and attachment;
