I am the desire in beings that is not contrary to dharma, O bull of the Bharatas.

I am strength, capacity, and vigor among the powerful; and that strength is free from desire and attachment (*kāmarāga*). "Desire and attachment" means *kāma* and *rāga*. *Kāma* is [the longing] for objects closely associated with craving (*tṛṣṇā*), while *rāga* is the passion for objects already attained. I am that strength and vitality which is devoid of those two—desire and attachment—and serves merely for the maintenance of the body and so forth, but not that which is the cause of craving and passion for transmigrating beings. Furthermore, it is not contrary to *dharma*.

O bull of the Bharatas, that desire which is not opposed to the dharma and the meaning of the scriptures—that desire for living beings and creatures, such as the objects of food and drink intended merely for the maintenance of the body—that desire am I.
Furthermore, whatever states of being there are— whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)— [all arise from the Self].
Know them to be from Me alone; yet I am not in them, and they are not in Me.

Whatever states of being, whatever entities—whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika) arising from *sattva*, or characterized by passion (rājasa) arising from *rajas*, or characterized by darkness (tāmasa) arising from *tamas*—whatever states whatsoever are born to living beings through the power of their own karma, know that all of them without exception are born from Me alone. Even though they are thus born from Me, nevertheless I am not dependent on them nor subject to their control, as is the case with worldly transmigrators; rather, they are under My control and dependent on Me.

The Blessed One displays His compassion by saying that the world does not recognize Me—the Supreme Lord who am thus constituted, whose nature is eternally pure, awakened, and liberated, who am the Self of all beings, devoid of qualities, and the cause of burning away the seed of the defects of transmigratory existence. And for what reason is this ignorance of the world? It is said: "By these three states consisting of the *guṇas*, this entire world [is deluded]."
Deluded, he does not recognize Me, who am beyond these and immutable.

By these aforementioned entities—consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), which are modifications of the qualities and take the form of passion, hatred, delusion, and so forth—all this world, the entire host of living beings, is deluded; having been brought to a state of non-discrimination, it does not recognize Me. [It does not know] Me as being beyond these aforementioned qualities, distinct from them, and different from them, and as imperishable—that is to say, devoid of decay and free from all transformations of state such as birth and the rest.
But how, then, does one transcend this divine illusion (māyā) of Viṣṇu, which consists of the three qualities? It is said:
"For this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the qualities, is indeed difficult to overcome."
Those who take refuge in me alone cross over this illusion.

Because this aforementioned Māyā of Mine—which consists of the Guṇas—is divine, belonging to Me, the Lord Viṣṇu, and is indeed My very nature; and because it is "difficult to overcome," meaning that its passing beyond or transcendence is achieved with great difficulty—this being so, those who, having renounced all duties, take refuge in Me alone, the wielder of Māyā, who am their own Self, with their whole being, they cross over this Māyā which deludes all beings; that is to say, they are liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra. || BhG 7.14 ||
If those who have taken refuge in you cross over this illusion, why do all people not take refuge in you alone? To this it is replied:
"The evil-doers, the deluded, the lowest of men, do not take refuge in me."
Their wisdom carried away by illusion, they have taken refuge in a demonic nature.

The foolish evildoers—those who commit sinful deeds, the lowest of men, the most base among humanity—do not take refuge in me, the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa. Their wisdom has been carried away by my illusory power (māyā), their intellects being utterly deluded; they have indeed resorted to a demonic disposition characterized by violence, falsehood, and the like.
Furthermore, O Arjuna, those best of men who perform meritorious deeds— those virtuous people worship Me in four ways.
The distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom, O bull of the Bharatas.

O Arjuna, O bull of the Bharatas, four kinds of virtuous people—those who have performed meritorious deeds—resort to and serve Me: the distressed, who is seized by affliction, overcome by thieves, tigers, disease, and so forth; the seeker, who desires to know the true nature of the Blessed One; the seeker of wealth, who longs for riches; and the man of knowledge, who understands the reality of Viṣṇu.
Among them, the one who possesses knowledge, who is constantly disciplined and devoted to the One alone, is preeminent;
for I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to Me.

Among those four, the man of knowledge (*jñānī*)—who knows reality (*tattvavit*)—is ever-disciplined (*nityayukta*) because he knows reality; and he possesses single-minded devotion (*ekabhakti*), since he perceives no other object of worship. Therefore, that man of single-minded devotion is distinguished—that is, he attains excellence or superiority, meaning he excels. For I am the Self (*ātman*), and as such I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge. Indeed, it is well known in the world that the Self is dear.
Therefore, because the man of knowledge is His very Self, Vāsudeva is dear to Him; this is the meaning. And that man of knowledge, being indeed my very Self, O Vāsudeva, is exceedingly dear to Me.
In that case, are the three beginning with the distressed (ārta) not dear to Vāsudeva? No. What then?
All these are indeed noble; however, the man of knowledge (jñānī), in my opinion, is My very Self.
For he, being disciplined in soul, is established in me alone as the unsurpassed goal.

All these three are indeed noble and excellent; the meaning is that all are dear to Me. For no devotee of Mine is ever unloved by Vāsudeva. However, the distinction is that the man of knowledge is exceedingly dear. Why is that? To this He says: "But the man of knowledge is My very Self, not other than Me"—this is My conviction, My settled opinion.

The meaning is that the man of knowledge, being thus disciplined and concentrated in mind—thinking "I am indeed the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva and none other"—has set out to ascend, that is, he has begun to go toward Me alone, the Supreme Brahman, the unsurpassed goal to be reached.
Furthermore, the man of knowledge is praised:
at the end of many births, the possessor of knowledge attains Me.
He who perceives Vāsudeva as all—such a great-souled one is very difficult to find.

At the end—that is, at the conclusion—of many births whose purpose was the purification of knowledge, the possessor of knowledge, having attained mature wisdom, realizes Me, Vāsudeva, the inner Self, through direct perception. How? By realizing that "Vāsudeva is everything. He who thus attains Me, Nārāyaṇa, the Self of all, is a Great Soul (mahātman). There is no other equal to him, nor any superior. Therefore, he is very difficult to find, as it has been said: "Among thousands of men... (BhG 7.19).
The reason for the failure to realize that "the Self alone is everything, [namely] Vāsudeva," is stated as follows:
"Those whose knowledge has been carried away by various desires resort to other deities."
Adhering to this or that specific rule, they are constrained by their own inherent nature.

Those whose discernment has been stolen away by various desires for objects such as sons, cattle, and heaven, resort to other deities; that is, they attain deities other than Vāsudeva, their own Self. Adhering to—meaning taking recourse to—this or that specific rule well-known for the worship of a deity, they are constrained by their own nature, that is, by their individual disposition consisting of particular impressions acquired in previous births.
And among those seekers of desire, whosoever desires to worship with faith whatever form [of a deity] they are devoted to, [I grant that faith].
I bestow that very same unwavering faith upon each person according to their own inclination.
Whichever devotee, possessed of faith, desires to worship and honor whichever form of a deity he chooses, I make firm and stabilize that very same unshakable faith of that seeker.

By whatever disposition one has previously been engaged, and whichever form of a deity one desires to worship with faith, being endowed with that very faith, one strives for the propitiation of that [deity].
And from that, he obtains his desires, for they have indeed been ordained by me alone.

Endowed with that faith ordained by Me, he strives—that is, exerts himself—for the propitiation, the worship, of that particular form of the deity. And from that deity, once she has been propitiated, he obtains his desired objects; these are indeed ordained and fashioned by Me alone, the Supreme Lord, who is omniscient and knows the distribution of the fruits of actions. For since those desires have been ordained by the Blessed Lord, the meaning is that he necessarily obtains them.
If one analyzes the word as "hitān," then the quality of being beneficial must be understood as applied figuratively to desires; for desires are never truly beneficial to anyone.
Because they are undiscriminating regarding the operation of the means and are possessed of desire, therefore the fruit of those small-minded ones becomes finite.
Those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods; my devotees, however, come to me as well.

But the fruit of those of small intelligence—those of little wisdom—is perishable and comes to an end. "Worshippers of the gods go to the gods": those who sacrifice to the gods are called "worshippers of the gods," and they go to the gods. My devotees, however, come to Me as well. Thus, although the effort is equal, they do not take refuge in Me alone for the sake of the infinite fruit. "Alas! How truly painful this is!"—thus the Blessed One displays His compassion.
"For what reason do they not take refuge in me alone? To this it is said:
"The unintelligent think of me, who am unmanifest, as having attained manifestation."
Failing to recognize my supreme, immutable, and unsurpassed nature.

The meaning is this: the undiscerning—those lacking discrimination who do not know my supreme state, which is the nature of the Supreme Self—think of Me, though I am the eternally established Lord, as having now attained manifestation and clarity after being unmanifest and without light; they think thus because they do not know My imperishable, immutable, and unsurpassed (anuttama) nature.
It is said: "What is the cause of that ignorance?"—
I am not manifest to everyone, being veiled by my own yoga-māyā.
Deluded, this world does not recognize me, the unborn and immutable.

"I am not manifest to the whole world; I am manifest only to those who are My devotees"—this is the intended meaning. "Enveloped by *yogamāyā*": *yoga* is the conjunction or arrangement of the *guṇas*; that itself is *māyā*, hence *yogamāyā*. Enveloped by that *yogamāyā*, i.e., concealed—this is the sense. For this very reason, this deluded world does not recognize Me, the unborn and immutable.
"I know all beings that have passed away, those that are present, O Arjuna, and those yet to come; but no one knows Me."

That *yogamāyā* by which the world does not recognize me, being veiled by it—that *yogamāyā* of mine, though it is mine, does not obstruct the knowledge of me, the Lord who am the wielder of *māyā*. It is just as the *māyā* of any other magician does not obstruct his own knowledge. Since this is so, therefore, O Arjuna, I know—indeed, I perceive—all beings that have passed away, those that exist now, and those that are yet to be; but no one knows me, except for my devotee who has taken refuge in me alone.
Precisely because of the absence of the realization of the Self, he does not resort to Me.
But by what obstruction to the knowledge of My true nature are all beings, even as they are being born, obstructed such that they do not know Me? In response to this inquiry, He says:
"By the delusion of the pairs of opposites arising from desire and aversion, O Bhārata."
All beings fall into delusion at the time of creation, O scorcher of foes.

"Arising from desire and aversion": desire and aversion are "icchādveṣau"; that which arises from these two is "icchādveṣasamuttha," and by that "icchādveṣasamutthena. When there is an expectation for a specific term [to answer "by what?"], he says this: "by delusion regarding the pairs" (*dvandvamohena*). Delusion caused by the pairs is "dvandvamoha," and by that. Those very same desires and aversions—mutually opposed like cold and heat, having as their objects pleasure and pain along with their causes, and being experienced by all beings at the appropriate time—are designated by the word "pair" (*dvandva*).

In this regard, whenever desire and aversion acquire their own nature through the attainment of pleasure and pain, along with their causes, they then produce delusion (*moha*)—which is the cause that obstructs the arising of knowledge regarding the object of the ultimate reality of the self—for all beings, by means of bringing one's own wisdom (*prajñā*) under their control. For indeed, knowledge of things as they truly are does not arise even regarding external objects for one whose mind is enslaved by the defects of desire and aversion.

What more need be said? For one whose intellect is possessed by those two and who is utterly deluded, knowledge does not arise regarding the inner self due to many obstacles. Therefore, O Bhārata, by that delusion of the pairs of opposites born from desire and hatred...

O scion of Bharata’s lineage, O scorcher of foes, all beings, being deluded, go toward—enter into—delusion, that state of infatuation, at the time of creation, that is, at the time of birth. The meaning is that all beings, while being born, are born under the very sway of delusion. Since this is so, therefore all beings, their wisdom obstructed by that delusion of the pairs of opposites, are deluded and do not know Me as their own Self.
For this very reason, they do not worship Me as their own Self.
To show the intended meaning— namely, who are those liberated from this delusion of duality who, having known You according to the scriptures, worship Your own self— I shall speak:
"But for those people of meritorious deeds, whose evil has come to an end..."
Freed from the delusion of dualities, they worship me with firm resolve.

But for those people whose evil has come to an end, reached its conclusion, and is exhausted—those who possess meritorious deeds, in whom merit exists as the cause of the purification of their being—those performers of meritorious deeds, being freed from the delusion of the pairs (dvandvamoha), that is, freed from the aforementioned delusion of the pairs, they worship Me, the Supreme Self, with firm vows.
Thus, having attained certain knowledge through the vow of total renunciation that "the reality of the supreme goal is exactly so and not otherwise," they are called those of firm vows.
For what purpose do they worship? It is said: "Those who, taking refuge in Me, strive for liberation from old age and death."
They know that Brahman, the whole of the supreme self, and all of action in its entirety.

Those who, having taken refuge in Me, the Supreme Lord, for the sake of liberation from old age and death—that is, for the purpose of being released from old age and death—strive with their minds concentrated on Me, they know that which is the supreme Brahman; they know the entire totality of the inner self (adhyātma), the reality pertaining to the individual soul, and they know all action in its entirety.
Those who know Me as the one with the elemental beings and the divine, and also as the one with the sacrifice—
even at the time of departure, they know Me with concentrated minds.

Those who know Me as "with the elemental and the divine"—that is, together with the elemental (adhibhūta) and the divine (adhidaiva)—and those who know Me as "with the sacrifice," that is, together with the sacrificial (adhiyajña), they know Me even at the time of departure, at the time of death; for their minds are disciplined, meaning their consciousness is concentrated.

Thus ends the seventh chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakācārya).
Bhagavad Gītā 8:
Now begins the discourse on the Imperishable Brahman, titled "The Instruction on the Imperishable Brahman."
The Eighth Chapter (with the commentary composed by the venerable Śrīmac-Śaṅkarācārya Bhagavatpāda)

With the words beginning "They know that Brahman in its entirety," the Blessed One has provided the seeds for Arjuna’s questions. Therefore, for the purpose of asking about those matters, Arjuna said:

"What is that Brahman? What is the inner self (adhyātma)? What is action, O Supreme Person? And what is declared to be the objective world (adhibhūta)? What is called the divine (adhidaiva)? (BhG 8.1)
Who is the Lord of Sacrifice here in this body, O Madhusūdana?
And how are You to be known at the time of death by those of self-restraint?
To provide a sequential resolution to these questions, the Blessed Lord said:
"The supreme imperishable Brahman is called the Self-nature (svabhāva), which is termed the Adhyātma."
The creative emission that brings about the origin of beings and their states is designated as action (karman).

The Imperishable (akṣara) is that which does not perish; it is the Supreme Self, according to the Vedic scripture: "Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.9). Furthermore, the syllable *oṃ* is not to be understood here, because it is distinguished by the subsequent qualification: "The single-syllabled Brahman is *oṃ*" (Gītā 8.13). Moreover, the qualification "supreme" (*paramam*) is more appropriately applied to the Imperishable Brahman, which is beyond all comparison. It is the very nature of that same Supreme Brahman to exist as the inner self (*pratyagātman*) within every body.

One's own state is "svabhāva" (intrinsic nature), which is called "adhyātma" (the internal). That reality which, with reference to the self—that is, the body—proceeds as the inner self and culminates in the supreme Brahman, is "svabhāva," and is designated by the term "adhyātma. "Bhūtabhāvodbhavakara" means that which brings about the arising of the state of beings; "bhūtabhāva" is the state of beings, "udbhava" is its arising, and that which effects this is "bhūtabhāvodbhavakara"—that is to say, it is the cause of the production of the reality of beings.

*Visarga* is relinquishment—the renunciation of substances such as cooked rice (*caru*) and sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) for the sake of the deity. This very sacrifice, characterized by relinquishment, is designated as "action" (*karman*), meaning it is expressed by the word *karman*. For from this [sacrifice], which serves as the seed, all beings—both stationary and moving—arise through the sequence of rain, food, and so forth.
The perishable state is the *adhibhūta* (the field of elemental beings), and the *puruṣa* is the *adhidaivata* (the field of the divine).
I alone am the *adhiyajña* (the field of sacrifice) here in this body, O best of embodied beings.

"Adhibhūta" is that which exists with reference to the class of living beings (*prāṇijāta*). What is this? It is the "perishable" (*kṣara*), so called because it perishes; it is a "state of being" (*bhāva*), meaning any entity whatsoever that possesses birth. "Puruṣa" is so called because everything is filled by him, or because he dwells within the body (*puri*); he is Hiraṇyagarbha, who resides within the sun and is the sustainer of the instruments of all living beings—he is *adhidaivata*.

The presiding deity of sacrifice (*adhiyajña*) is the deity named Viṣṇu, who presides over all sacrifices, according to the Vedic scripture: "Viṣṇu is indeed sacrifice" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.7.4). That Viṣṇu is indeed myself. In this context, I am the presiding deity of whatever sacrifice exists within this body. For sacrifice, being accomplished by means of the body, is inherent in the body; thus, O best among the sustainers of the body, it has the body as its locus.
And at the time of death, whoever departs casting off the body while remembering Me alone,
attains My state; there is no doubt about this.

At the time of the end, at the time of death, whoever departs—leaving behind and casting off the physical body—while remembering Me alone, Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, he attains My own state, the Vaiṣṇava reality. There is no doubt whatsoever in this matter as to whether he does or does not attain it.
This rule does not apply to me alone. What then?
Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end, [that state one attains].
O son of Kuntī, one who is constantly permeated by that very state goes to that very state.

Whatever state of being—whatever specific deity—one remembers and contemplates while abandoning and relinquishing the body at the end, at the time of death when the vital breaths depart, to that very state remembered one goes, and to no other, O son of Kuntī; for one who is "always permeated by that state"—that state belonging to him is "his state," and he by whom it has been cultivated through constant recollection and practice is "one who is always permeated by that state."
Since, therefore, the final meditation is the cause for attaining another body,
remember Me at all times and fight.
With mind and intellect dedicated to me, you shall come to me alone, without doubt.

Therefore, at all times remember me according to the scriptures; and while fighting, perform your duty in battle. You, whose mind and intellect are offered to me, Vāsudeva—you, being one whose mind and intellect are thus offered to me, shall come to me alone, just as you have remembered me. Of this there is no doubt; no uncertainty exists in this matter.
Furthermore:
"With a mind disciplined by the yoga of practice, not wandering elsewhere,"
Contemplating the supreme divine Person, O Pārtha, he goes to Him.

By means of that mind of the yogi which is joined with the yoga of practice—that is, a mind occupied solely with Me as the object of the surrender of the heart, characterized by the recurrence of a uniform cognition uninterrupted by heterogeneous cognitions, and which is thus disciplined through that practice and yoga.

"With a mind that does not go elsewhere"—that is, one whose nature is not to wander to another object; with such a mind that does not go elsewhere, O Pārtha, meditating upon—that is, reflecting upon the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher—the Supreme, Unsurpassed Person, who is divine, existing in the celestial solar orb, one goes, one attains Him. ||BhGS_8.8||
And what kind of Person does he go to? It is said:
the ancient seer, the instructor.
He who should meditate upon that which is subtler than the subtle,
the sustainer of all, whose form is inconceivable,
whose color is like the sun, and who is beyond darkness; BhG 8.9.

Whoever should meditate upon—that is, reflect deeply upon—the Seer, the one of far-reaching vision, the Omniscient, the Ancient, the Primeval, the Instructor, the Ruler of the entire world; subtler than even the subtle, more minute than the minute; the Ordainer and Disposer of all the various fruits of action, who distributes them to living beings in their manifold variety; and whose form is inconceivable, meaning that although his form exists, it is not fixed and cannot be conceived by anyone.

"Of solar hue" means that whose color (nature) is like that of the sun—namely, the constant light of consciousness; "beyond darkness" means beyond the blinding darkness of delusion characterized by ignorance. The connection with the preceding verse is: "he goes, meditating upon Him."
Furthermore,
at the time of departure, with a steady mind...
Endowed with devotion and indeed by the power of yoga,
having properly fixed the vital breath between the eyebrows,
he attains that supreme, divine Person.

At the time of departure—that is, at the time of death—one who is endowed with devotion (*bhakti*), which means joined with worship, and also endowed with the power of yoga (*yogabala*)—the meaning being that one is joined with the power of yoga characterized by the stability of the mind produced by the accumulation of impressions born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—with a steady mind, free from wavering, [attains the Supreme].

Having first brought the mind under control within the lotus of the heart, and then, by means of the upward-moving channel (ūrdhvagāminī nāḍī), having caused the vital breath (prāṇa) to enter and remain between the eyebrows through the gradual conquest of the stages (bhūmi-jaya), that wise yogi, being thus perfectly vigilant, attains—that is, reaches—that Supreme Person who is higher than the highest, characterized as "the Seer, the Ancient," and so forth; He is divine, consisting of light. || BhG 8.10 ||

[The objection that Brahman is attained merely by following the path of yoga even without the knowledge of Brahman having thus arisen, is addressed as follows: Furthermore, the Blessed One provides a description of the Brahman intended to be realized by means of the method about to be taught—a Brahman qualified by attributes such as being "that which the knowers of the Vedas speak of"—in the words:
"That Imperishable which the knowers of the Vedas speak of."
That goal which ascetics free from passion enter,
and desiring which they lead a life of celibacy—
that state I shall declare to you in brief.

That which does not perish is the "imperishable" (*akṣara*), the indestructible; so say those who know the Vedas, those who understand the meaning of the Vedas. For the Śruti declares: "O Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas speak of this very imperishable as 'not gross, not subtle,' and so forth. They speak of it by negating all specific attributes. Furthermore, when perfect insight is attained, ascetics—those whose nature is striving, renunciants from whom passion has departed (*vītarāga*)—enter into it, that is, they merge into it.

And that which they practice—that is, they observe—the life of a student (*brahmacarya*) under a teacher desiring to know the Imperishable (the ellipsis being "the Imperishable"), that state, that state called the Imperishable which is to be reached, I shall declare—that is, I shall speak—of it to you in brief; "brief" (*saṃgraha*) means a summary, by that, [I shall speak] in summary. || BhG 8.11 ||

"Venerable sir, if someone among men should meditate upon the syllable *oṃ* until the end of his life, which world indeed does he conquer by that? To him he said: "Satyakāma, this *oṃ*-syllable is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman," and having begun thus, [he continues] with the passage: "But he who meditates upon the supreme Puruṣa by means of this very syllable *oṃ* consisting of three measures (*trimātra*), he is led up to the world of Brahman by the Sāmans," and so forth.
And having begun with the statement, "Other than dharma, other than adharma" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.14), it continues:
"That goal which all the Vedas proclaim,
and which all austerities declare."
Desiring that which they seek, they practice the holy life;
I shall tell you that state in brief: it is "Om. [KaṭhU 1.2.15]

By such statements as these, it has been taught that the meditation (*upāsana*) upon the syllable *oṃ*—which is intended for those of dull or mediocre intellect as a means of realizing the Supreme Brahman, either as its designator (*vācaka*) or as a symbol (*pratīka*) like an image—yields the fruit of liberation at a later time; and this very same point applies here as well to the Supreme Brahman introduced in the passages, "the ancient seer, the ruler" (Gītā 8.9) and "that Imperishable which the knowers of the Veda declare" (Gītā 8.11), according to the form previously described.

The meditation upon the syllable *oṃ*, which serves as the means for practice and yields the fruit of liberation at a later time, along with the concentration (*dhāraṇā*) of yoga, must be explained; and whatever else follows incidentally or by way of further elaboration—this is the purpose for which the subsequent portion of the text is commenced:

"Having restrained all the gates [of the senses] and having fixed the mind within the heart, placing the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the head, he remains established in the concentration of yoga. (BhG 8.12)

Having restrained all the gates—that is, having controlled all those gates—and having fixed the mind in the heart, that is, having brought it to a standstill within the lotus of the heart and rendered it motionless; then, with the mind thus mastered, having ascended upward through the channel (nāḍī) that goes upwards from the heart and having placed his vital breath (prāṇa) in the head, he is established in the practice of yoga, intent upon maintaining the concentration of yoga.
And in that very state, holding fast to the single-syllable Brahman "Om," uttering it while remembering Me.
He who departs, casting off the body, goes to the supreme goal.

Uttering—that is, pronouncing—the single-syllabled Brahman, the syllable *oṃ*, which is the designator of Brahman; and while recollecting—that is, contemplating—Me, the Lord, who am the referent of that syllable, he who departs—that is, dies—leaving behind and abandoning the body, the physical frame (the phrase "leaving the body" serves to qualify the act of departing, meaning the soul's departure occurs by the abandonment of the body and not by the destruction of its own nature), he thus goes—that is, attains—the supreme, most excellent goal.
Furthermore,
he who constantly remembers me at all times with an undistracted mind—
I am easily attained, O Pārtha, by that yogi who is constantly disciplined.

"One whose mind is not directed elsewhere" (*ananyacetāḥ*) means one whose consciousness is not fixed on any other object. "The yogi who constantly"—that is, at all times—"remembers Me," the Supreme Lord. By "constantly" (*nityaśaḥ*) is meant uninterruptedness; by "always" (*satatam*) is meant long duration. It does not mean for six months or a year. What then? The meaning is: he who remembers Me with uninterrupted continuity throughout his entire life.

I am easily attained with ease by that yogi who is ever-disciplined, O Pārtha—that is, by the yogi whose mind is always concentrated. Since this is so, therefore, being single-minded, one should remain ever-concentrated on Me.
What would result from your accessibility? It is said: listen to what happens through my accessibility. Having come to me, there is no rebirth—that abode of suffering which is impermanent.
The high-souled ones, having attained the supreme perfection, do not return.

Having come to me—that is, having approached me, the Lord—and having attained my own nature, they do not obtain, they do not undergo, rebirth, which is to say, a new birth. What kind of rebirth do they not undergo? To answer this, he states its qualification: it is a "dwelling-place of suffering," meaning the abode or support of sufferings such as those that are internal (ādhyātmika) and so forth; for in it, sufferings are lodged, thus it is a dwelling-place of suffering. It is not merely a dwelling-place of suffering, but also impermanent, its very nature being unstable.

Great-souled ascetics do not undergo such rebirth again, having attained—that is, reached—the supreme and most excellent perfection known as liberation; however, those who do not attain Me return once more.
But what about those who have attained something other than you—do they return again? It is said:
"O Arjuna, all worlds, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return."
But having come to Me, O Kaunteya, there is no rebirth.

"Up to the world of Brahmā" (*brahmabhuvana*): that in which beings come into existence is called a "world" (*bhuvana*). The world of Brahmā is the *brahmabhuvana*; the meaning is the realm of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). Up to the world of Brahmā—that is, including the world of Brahmā—all worlds are subject to return, having the nature of returning again. But, O Arjuna, son of Kuntī, for one who has attained Me alone, there is no further birth, no further arising.
Why, then, do the worlds, including the world of Brahmā, involve a return? Because they are limited by time. How so?
"Those who know that the day of Brahmā extends for a thousand yugas..."
Those people who know day and night understand that the night ends after a thousand yugas, and so does the day.

That day of Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, the Virāj, has for its limit a thousand yugas—that is, a day whose end consists of a thousand yugas. They know his night also to be of the same duration as the day, ending after a thousand yugas. Who knows this? He says: "Those who know day and night," meaning those people who know the calculation of time. Since they are thus limited by time, they belong to worlds that involve return.
That which occurs during the day and the night of Prajāpati is now described: from the Unmanifest, all manifest beings come forth at the arrival of the day.
At the arrival of night, they dissolve back into that very same state known as the unmanifest.

From the Unmanifest comes the Unmanifest, which is the state of sleep of Prajāpati. From that Unmanifest, all manifested beings—characterized as both stationary and moving—come forth; they are manifested, meaning they emerge at the arrival of the day, that is, at the time of the day's arrival, during the period of Brahmā’s awakening. Likewise, at the arrival of night, during the period of Brahmā’s sleep, all manifested beings dissolve back into that very same previously mentioned state known as the Unmanifest.

In order to avoid the faults of [the soul] experiencing the results of actions not performed or the loss of those performed, and to demonstrate the fruitfulness of the scriptures concerning bondage and liberation; and because this collection of beings, being subject to the latent impressions of karma rooted in afflictions such as ignorance, comes into existence repeatedly and then perishes involuntarily—it is for the purpose of demonstrating dispassion toward such saṃsāra that he says this:
"This very same collection of beings, having come into existence again and again, dissolves."
At the arrival of night, O Pārtha, it prevails inevitably; at the arrival of day, it prevails.

This very same collection of beings, this aggregate of entities characterized as both stationary and moving, which existed in the previous kalpa, is not different from this one. Having come into being again and again at the arrival of day, it dissolves repeatedly at the arrival of night, at the end of the day, being helpless and lacking independence. O Pārtha, it comes forth—that is, it is born—helplessly indeed at the arrival of day.

The means for attaining that imperishable (akṣara) which was introduced has been pointed out in such passages as, "Om, the single-syllabled Brahman" (Gītā 8.13). Now, with the desire to define the very nature of that imperishable, this is said: "But beyond that unmanifested is another eternal being, unmanifested and distinct from the unmanifested," indicating that one must proceed by this path of yoga to reach it.
He who does not perish even when all beings perish.

"Other" (*para*) means distinct and different. From what? From that which was previously mentioned. The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to specify the distinction of the desired Imperishable (*akṣara*) from the Unmanifest (*avyakta*). "Being" (*bhāva*) refers to the Supreme Brahman known as the Imperishable. Since there is the possibility of similarity even while being distinct, he says "other" (*anya*) in order to exclude that. "Other" means of a different character. And that is unmanifest, beyond the range of the senses. It has been stated: "other than that."

Why, then, is he "other"? The intention is that he is a different, distinct entity from the previously mentioned unmanifest (avyakta), characterized by ignorance, which serves as the seed for the multitude of beings. He is eternal (sanātana), ancient; that entity does not perish even when all beings, beginning with Brahmā, perish.
He who is unmanifest is called the Imperishable; they speak of Him as the supreme goal,
attaining which they do not return— that is My supreme abode.

That which is called the "unmanifest" and the "indestructible"—they speak of that very unmanifest state, designated as the indestructible, as the supreme, most excellent goal. Having reached that supreme state, they do not return to worldly existence; that is my abode, my supreme station—the meaning is the highest step of Viṣṇu.
The means for attaining that [Self] is now stated:
"That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by unswerving devotion."
In whom all beings abide, and by whom all this is pervaded.

The *puruṣa* is so called because he dwells within the city (*puri*) of the body, or because of his fullness. He is the Supreme, O Pārtha; he is the highest, beyond whom there is nothing else. He is to be attained through unswerving devotion characterized by knowledge, directed toward the Self. Within that *puruṣa* abide all beings—that is, all effects—for an effect indeed exists within its cause. By that *puruṣa* this entire world is pervaded, just as jars and other objects are pervaded by space.

Since the northern path must be described for the sake of the realization of Brahman by the yogins under discussion—those whose intellects are absorbed in Brahman through the *praṇava* and who partake in liberation at a later time—the verse beginning with "At what time" (*yatra kāle*) is spoken to present the intended meaning; furthermore, the mention of the path of return is spoken for the purpose of praising the other path:
"But at what time the yogins [attain] non-return and indeed return..."
I shall describe that time at which those who have departed proceed [to their destination], O bull of the Bharatas.

The phrase "at which time they depart" is to be connected with what follows later in the verse. "At which time" (*yatra*) means at that particular time; "non-return" (*anāvṛtti*) refers to the absence of rebirth, and "return" (*āvṛtti*) is its opposite. The term "yogins" (*yoginaḥ*) refers both to practitioners of yoga and to performers of ritual action (*karmiṇaḥ*); however, the performers of action are called "yogins" figuratively because of their engagement in the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), as indicated by the qualifying term "of yogins. O bull of the Bharatas, I shall declare that time—at which time the yogins who have departed and died attain non-return, and at which time those who have departed attain return.
He has described that time as fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice.
Departing from there, those people who know Brahman go to Brahman.

Agni is the deity presiding over time; likewise, Jyotis is also the deity presiding over time. Alternatively, Agni and Jyotis are deities exactly as they are heard in the text. However, there is a frequent designation where "that time" refers to the time itself, as in the case of a "grove of mango trees" (*āmravana*). Similarly, Ahaḥ is the deity presiding over the day; Śukla is the deity of the bright fortnight; and the six months of the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*)—there too, it is established elsewhere that the deity itself constitutes the path (*BAU* 4.3.4). This principle is settled.

On that path, those who have died while traveling proceed toward Brahman—those who know Brahman, those who worship Brahman, and those people devoted to the meditation on Brahman. The phrase "in due order" is the completion of the sentence. For there is no going or coming for those who possess immediate liberation and are established in right vision; according to the Śruti: "His vital breaths do not depart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6). Their vital breaths are indeed merged in Brahman; they consist of Brahman and have become Brahman itself.
Smoke, night, likewise the dark fortnight, and the six months of the sun's southern course.
And having attained the lunar light there, the yogi returns.

Smoke is night, as well as the deities presiding over smoke and night; likewise, "the dark" refers to the deity of the dark fortnight; and "the six months of the southern course" refers, as before, to the deity itself. Having attained the lunar light—the fruit arising from the moon—the yogi who performs sacrifices and other rites, having enjoyed that [result], returns again to this world upon its exhaustion.
These two paths of the world, the bright and the dark, are indeed considered eternal.
By one a man goes to non-return; by the other he returns again.

The "white and black" refers to the white and the black paths. It is called "white" because it illuminates through knowledge; it is called "black" because of the absence of that [knowledge]. These two paths, the white and the black, belong to those qualified for knowledge and action—that is, they are the destinations for those so designated—not for the entire world indiscriminately. They are "eternal," meaning constant, because worldly existence is eternal; this is the intended view. Among them, by one—the white—one goes to non-return; by the other—the remaining one—one returns again and again.
Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogin whatsoever is deluded.
Therefore, at all times, be disciplined in yoga, O Arjuna.

Knowing these two paths as they have been described—O Pārtha, that one leads to transmigratory existence and the other to liberation—not even a single yogin is deluded. Therefore, O Arjuna, at all times remain disciplined in yoga and composed in mind.
Listen to the greatness of that yoga,
which is found within the Vedas, the sacrifices, and indeed in ascetic penances.
Having understood all this, the yogi transcends whatever fruit of merit is prescribed for gifts and attains the supreme, primordial state.

When the Vedas have been properly studied, when sacrifices have been performed with excellence, when austerities have been well-practiced, and when gifts have been duly bestowed—whatever fruit of merit, the "fruit of merit" (puṇyaphala), has been prescribed for these by the scripture, he transcends, passing beyond, all that collection of fruits.

Having understood this and having correctly grasped the meaning stated by way of the resolution of the seven questions, and having practiced it, the yogi attains—that is, reaches—the supreme, most excellent, divine station. "The first" means that which exists at the beginning, the causal Brahman.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Imperishable Brahman," in the commentary on the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakas.
Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter 9:
Now begins the yoga known as the King of Sciences and the King of Secrets.
The Ninth Chapter (Śāṅkara Bhāṣya):

In the eighth chapter, the yoga of concentration (*dhāraṇā-yoga*) with attributes was taught by means of the channels (*nāḍī*) and other gateways; and its fruit was specified as the attainment of Brahman at a later time through the sequence beginning with fire and light, characterized by non-return. To dispel the doubt that liberation is attained only in this manner and not otherwise, the Blessed Lord said:
But I shall declare to you, who are free from carping, this most secret knowledge together with realized wisdom, by knowing which you shall be liberated from evil.

This knowledge of Brahman—which has been stated and will be stated in the preceding chapters—is referred to as "this" by bringing it to mind. The word *tu* (but/however) is for the purpose of specifying its distinction. This alone is perfect knowledge, the direct means for attaining liberation, according to such scriptural and traditional texts as: "Vāsudeva is all" (Gītā 7.12), "All this is indeed the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2), and "One only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).

It is not otherwise; for from such scriptural passages as, "But those who know it otherwise than this become subjects of other kings and possess perishable worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2), and others, it is clear. To you, who are free from malice (*anasūye*), I shall proclaim—that is, I shall speak—that which is most secret, that which is most to be guarded. What is that? Knowledge. Of what nature is it? It is accompanied by realized wisdom (*vijñāna*), joined with direct experience. Having known—that is, having attained—that knowledge, you will be liberated from evil, from the bondage of saṃsāra.
And this is the royal science, the royal secret; it is this supreme purifier.
This dharma is directly perceivable, easy to perform, and leads to the imperishable.

It is the king of sciences (*rājavidyā*), because it possesses an excellence of brilliance; for this knowledge of Brahman shines forth with preeminence above all other sciences. Likewise, it is the king of secrets (*rājaguhyam*), the most secret of all secrets. It is the supreme purifier (*pavitram*); this knowledge of Brahman is the highest cause of purification among all purifying things.

It reduces to ashes in a mere moment even the karma accumulated over many thousands of births, including both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), along with its very roots; therefore, what need is there to speak of its purifying power? Furthermore, it is "directly perceived" (*pratyakṣāvagama*), meaning that its realization occurs through direct perception, just like pleasure and so forth. While it is observed that even one possessing many virtues may be opposed to *dharma*, knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*) is not contrary to *dharma*; rather, it is "conducive to *dharma*" (*dharmya*), meaning it does not deviate from *dharma*.

Even so, one might think that [this knowledge] could be accomplished with difficulty; therefore, he says: "It is very easy to perform," like the discernment of gems. In this regard, it is observed that other actions which require little effort and are easily accomplished yield small fruits, whereas those that are difficult to perform yield great fruits. Since this [knowledge] is easily accomplished, one might conclude that its fruit would eventually be exhausted; hence he says: "imperishable" (*avyayam*). It is "imperishable" because, unlike worldly action, it has no exhaustion in terms of its fruit. Therefore, self-knowledge is to be trusted. (BhG 9.2)
Furthermore, O scorcher of foes, those men who have no faith in this dharma—
Failing to reach Me, they return to the path of the cycle of death.

Lacking faith, devoid of trust, they are atheists regarding both the nature and the fruit of this dharma of self-knowledge; they are doers of evil who have adopted the secret doctrine of the Asuras—the view that the self is nothing more than the body. These sinful men, thirsting for life, are faithless. "O scorcher of foes!"—meaning that without attaining Me, the Supreme Lord (for there is no doubt regarding the attainment of Me), they fail to reach even mere devotion, which is a specific path to My attainment. They return; that is, they certainly continue [in the cycle of rebirth].

Where? On the path of the cycle of death; "mṛtyu-saṃsāra" means the cycle of existence joined with death, and its "path" is the route leading to rebirth as hell-beings, animals, and so forth—the meaning is that they remain on that very path. (BhG 9.3)
Having turned Arjuna’s attention toward him by means of praise, he said:
"By me, whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded."
All beings abide in Me, yet I do not abide in them.

By me—that which is my supreme state—this entire world is pervaded, by me whose form is unmanifest (*avyaktamūrtinā*). "Unmanifest form" means that my own nature (*svarūpa*) is not manifest; I am he whose form is unmanifest, that is to say, whose nature is beyond the range of the senses. In me, who am of unmanifest form, all beings—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—are situated (*matsthāni*). For no being whatsoever can function in the world of empirical experience if it is devoid of a self (*nirātmaka*).

Therefore, they abide in Me; that is, they exist through Me by virtue of My being their Self. Hence it is said, "they abide in Me. Because I alone am the Self of those beings, it appears to those of deluded intellect that I abide in them. Therefore I say: "Nor do I abide in those beings. For, due to the absence of any contact like that of material objects, I am even more internal than space itself. Indeed, an entity that is non-contacting can never abide as something contained within another.
Precisely because of this lack of contact, beings do not abide in Me; behold My divine yoga!
My Self, the source of all beings, sustains all beings but does not dwell within them.

Nor do the beings, beginning with Brahmā, reside within Me. Behold My *yoga*—My sovereign power (*aiśvara*), meaning the true nature of My self as a sovereign. Thus, scripture demonstrates My state of non-attachment due to My lack of contact: "Unattached, for He does not cling" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26). Behold this other wonder: though unattached, I am the sustainer of beings; yet I do not abide within beings.

Because it has been shown by the reasoning already stated that it is impossible for [the Self] to reside within the elements; how then is it said, "This is my Self"? Having distinguished the aggregate of the body and so forth, and having superimposed the notion of "I" upon that [aggregate], one designates it as "my Self" in accordance with worldly understanding, but not because one knows—as the world does—that the Self is something other than the Self. Likewise, He is the "Creator of Beings" (bhūtabhāvana), meaning He brings beings into existence (bhāvayati) by producing or nourishing them.
Establishing the meaning stated by the two preceding verses through an illustration, he says:
"Just as the great wind, omnipresent and eternal, resides in space,"
In the same way, understand that all beings abide in Me.

Just as in the world the wind, which is situated in space and always remains in space, moves everywhere—being all-pervading and great in its extent—so too, understand and discern that these [elements] abide in Me, who am all-pervading like space, without any attachment whatsoever. BhG 9.6.
In this way, O son of Kuntī, all beings remain within me during the time of their existence, just as the wind remains in space; at the end of that time, those same beings return to my own nature.
At the end of the aeon, I again emit them at the beginning of the aeon.

O son of Kuntī, at the end of a kalpa, at the time of dissolution, all beings go to my lower, inferior nature, which consists of the three guṇas; then, at the time of creation, at the beginning of a kalpa, I send forth those beings again, I produce them as before.
Thus, taking hold of my own nature, which is characterized by ignorance, I manifest again and again.
This entire multitude of beings, being powerless under the sway of material nature, [is deluded].

Having taken hold of—having brought under my control—my own nature (prakṛti), I repeatedly emit this entire present multitude of beings, this collection of creatures born from nature, which is powerless and not independent, being rendered subject to others by defects such as ignorance, and remaining under the sway of nature—that is, under the sway of its own inherent nature.
"In that case, since You, the Supreme Lord, ordain this diverse multitude of beings, would You not be connected with merit and demerit caused by those acts? To this, the Blessed One said:
"And those actions do not bind Me, O Dhanañjaya."
Sitting as if indifferent, unattached to those actions.

And those actions which cause the unequal creation of the multitude of beings do not bind me, the Lord, O Dhanañjaya. He states the reason for my lack of connection with those actions: "seated like one indifferent," meaning seated like some indifferent person who is an onlooker, because the Self is changeless; "unattached," meaning free from attachment to the fruits [of action] and devoid of the conceit, "I am doing these actions."

Therefore, for others as well, the absence of the conceit of agency and the absence of attachment to results are the causes of non-bondage; otherwise, the deluded person is bound by actions like a silkworm—this is the intended meaning.
In this regard, it is stated that "I project this multitude of beings while remaining as if indifferent," which appears contradictory; therefore, to resolve that, he says:
"Under my supervision, Nature produces the moving and the unmoving."
By this cause, O son of Kuntī, the world revolves.

By Me, acting as the supervisor—whose nature is pure consciousness alone and who is changeless—My Māyā, which consists of the three guṇas and is characterized as ignorance (avidyā), the primordial nature (prakṛti), brings forth the world of moving and non-moving beings. Thus says the Vedic mantra:
"The one God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings."
"The overseer of karma, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, absolute and devoid of qualities" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11).

O son of Kuntī, by this cause, this motive—namely, this state of being the witness—the world, including all things moving and unmoving and consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest, revolves through all its states. For every activity of the world has as its motive the attainment of the status of being an object of sight; indeed, [activity] culminates in cognition, beginning with such thoughts as: "I shall enjoy this," "I see this," "I hear this," "I experience pleasure," "I experience pain," "for that purpose I will do this," or "I will know this. It ends only when it reaches the finality of cognition.

The mantra beginning with "He who is its supervisor in the highest heaven" (Ṛgveda 8.7.17.7; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.8.9) and others demonstrate this meaning. Consequently, since there is no other conscious being apart from the one God—who is pure consciousness acting as the supervisor of all and who, in the ultimate sense, has no connection to any enjoyment—there is no other enjoyer. Therefore, regarding the question "For what purpose is this creation?", both the question and the answer are untenable, as expressed in: "Who truly knows? Who here can declare? (Ṛgveda 10.129.6).

This is known from such Vedic mantra passages as, "From where was this born? From where did this creation proceed? (Ṛgveda 8.7.17.8), and it has been shown by the Blessed One: "Knowledge is covered by ignorance; thereby living beings are deluded" (Gītā 5.15).
Thus, though I am of the nature described— eternally pure, enlightened, omniscient, and the Self of all living beings—
the deluded disregard me because I have assumed a human form.
Failing to recognize my supreme nature as the Great Lord of all beings.

The deluded, lacking discrimination, disregard Me—those fools who treat with contempt and show me disrespect. They do not know My supreme state, the highest reality of the Self which is like the ether, even more internal than the ether, and which has resorted to a human body—that is, which functions through a human form. Thus, they do not know Me as the Great Lord of all beings, their very own Self.
And therefore, by harboring such a sense of disregard for Me, those wretched ones are ruined.
How so?
"Futile are their hopes, futile their actions, futile their knowledge, and devoid of discernment they are."
They have taken refuge in a delusive nature that is both demonic and asuric.

Those whose hopes are vain are "moghāśāḥ"—those for whom their expectations and aspirations are in vain. Likewise, they are "moghakarmāṇaḥ," meaning those whose actions—such as the performance of the *agnihotra* and other rites—are rendered utterly fruitless; because of their disregard for the Blessed One, that is, their contempt for Him who is their very own Self, their actions become merely vain and result-less. Similarly, they are "moghajñānāḥ," meaning those whose knowledge is vain and fruitless; even their knowledge would be entirely without result.

The intention is that they become devoid of discernment and lacking in discrimination. Furthermore, they take refuge in—that is, they resort to—a Rākṣasa nature, which is the natural disposition of Rākṣasas, and an Āsura nature, which is the natural disposition of Asuras; it is deluding, causing infatuation, and asserting that the body is the self. The meaning is that they become performers of cruel deeds, habitually saying such things as, "Cut! Pierce! Drink! Eat! Seize the property of others! This is in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "Those worlds are called non-celestial" (Īśa Upaniṣad 3).

Furthermore, those who possess faith and have set out upon the path to liberation characterized by devotion to the Blessed One— those high-souled ones, O Pārtha, who have taken refuge in my divine nature (māṃ... daivīṃ prakṛtim āśritāḥ).
They worship with undivided minds, having known the imperishable source of all beings.

But those of great resolve, O Pārtha, whose minds are not petty, having known Me—the Lord, the divine nature of the gods characterized by tranquility, self-control, compassion, faith, and so forth—worship and serve Me with single-minded devotion, their hearts fixed on no other, knowing Me as the imperishable source of all beings, including the elements such as ether and all living creatures.
How so?
By constantly glorifying me, striving with firm resolve.
And bowing to me with devotion, they worship me, ever-disciplined.

Constantly and at all times glorifying me, the Blessed One, whose nature is Brahman; striving—that is, exerting themselves through virtues characterized by the withdrawal of the senses, tranquility, self-control, compassion, non-violence, and so forth; firm in their vows—those whose vow is firm, steady, and unshakable; and bowing down to me, the Self dwelling in the heart, they worship and serve me, being ever-devoted with devotion.
It is now stated by what various means they worship:
"Others also, sacrificing with the sacrifice of knowledge, worship me."
As one, as distinct, and manifoldly with faces turned in every direction.

By the sacrifice of knowledge—that is, by that very sacrifice which has the Blessed Lord as its object—others, abandoning other forms of worship, worship Me, the Lord; and they worship with that knowledge through the vision of ultimate reality, seeing the Supreme Brahman as one alone in its unity. And some worship Him through differentiation, regarding that same Blessed Lord Viṣṇu as existing in distinct forms such as the Sun, the Moon, and so forth.

Some worship that very Blessed One, who exists in many ways as the one whose face is everywhere and who is the universal form (viśvarūpa), as that universal form whose face is everywhere, in many ways—that is, in many modes.
If they worship You through many different modes, how is it that they worship You alone? To this, He says:
"I am the sacrifice (*kratu*); I am the oblation (*yajña*); I am the ancestral offering (*svadhā*); I am the medicinal herb (*auṣadha*)."
I am the mantra; I alone am the clarified butter, I am the fire, and I am the oblation.

I am *kratu*, the various types of Vedic rituals; I alone am *yajña*, the Smārta rites. Furthermore, I am *svadhā*, the food offered to the ancestors. I am *auṣadha*, that which is eaten by all living beings—the common term for grain such as rice and barley. Alternatively, *svadhā* refers to food common to all living beings, while *auṣadha* refers to medicine intended for the alleviation of disease. I am the *mantra*, that by which oblations are given to the ancestors and the deities.
I alone am the clarified butter and the oblation; I am the fire, that fire into which the oblation is poured when offered; and I am the act of offering, the oblation itself.
Furthermore:
"I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer, and the grandfather."
The object of knowledge, the purifier, the syllable Om, as well as the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus—these are [the Vedas].

I am the father, the progenitor of this world; the mother, the one who gives birth; the sustainer, the ordainer of the fruits of action for living beings; the grandfather, the father of the father; the object to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable Om, and also the Rig, Sama, and Yajur Vedas.
Furthermore,
he is the goal, the sustainer, the lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, and the friend.
I am the source, the dissolution, the support, the storehouse, and the imperishable seed.

He is the goal, the fruit of karma; the sustainer and nourisher; the lord and master; the witness of the deeds done and undone by living beings; the abode in which living beings dwell; the refuge for the afflicted; and the remover of the suffering of those who have sought his protection.

He is a benefactor who acts without expectation of a return favor; He is the source (*prabhava*) from which the world originates, and the dissolution (*pralaya*) into which it is absorbed; likewise, He is the locus (*sthāna*) in which it subsists, and the repository (*nidhāna*)—the storehouse for living beings to enjoy at a later time; He is the seed (*bīja*), the cause of growth for all things subject to germination; and He is imperishable (*avyaya*) because He exists as long as saṃsāra endures, for nothing ever germinates without a seed.
Furthermore, since germination is observed to be constant, it is understood that the continuity of the seed never ceases.
Furthermore,
I heat [the world], and I withhold as well as release the rain.
I am indeed both immortality and death, O Arjuna, and both being and non-being.

"Having become the sun, I heat [the world] with certain fierce rays; with certain rays I send forth rain; having sent it forth, I withhold it again with certain rays; and after eight months, I send it forth again during the rainy season. I am the nectar of the gods and death for mortals. Whatever exists in relation to something else is 'being' (sat), and its opposite is 'non-being' (asat); I am that, O Arjuna.
But the Blessed One is not absolutely non-existent, nor is He Himself the effect or the cause, or being and non-being."

Those knowers of wisdom who worship and meditate upon Me through the previously mentioned methods of cessation— through the sacrifices consisting of the realization of oneness, difference, and so forth— they attain Me alone, according to their respective understanding. But those ignorant ones who desire objects of desire, the followers of the three Vedas who drink the soma juice and are purified of sin—
Having sacrificed with rituals, they pray for the way to heaven;
having attained merit, they enjoy the divine pleasures of the gods in the celestial realm of the Lord of the Gods.

The knowers of the three Vedas—those who know the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas—worship me in the form of the gods beginning with Vasu; they are "Soma-drinkers" (somapāḥ), so called because they drink the Soma juice, and by that very drinking of Soma they are purified of sin, their impurities cleansed. Having worshipped me through sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, they pray for the heavenly state—the going to heaven, where heaven itself is the goal. And having attained and reached the world of the Lord of Gods, the abode of Śatakratu, they enjoy the divine, super-physical pleasures of the gods, which exist in heaven.
Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world,
they enter the world of mortals when their merit is exhausted.
Thus, those who have resorted to the dharma of the three Vedas and desire objects of desire obtain the state of going and returning.

Having enjoyed that vast and extensive heavenly world, they enter—the word "enter" meaning they descend—into the world of mortals when their merit is exhausted. Thus, in the manner described, those who have resorted solely to the dharma of the three Vedas, which is Vedic ritual action, and who desire objects of desire (kāmakāmāḥ)—meaning they long for desires—obtain only going and coming; that is, going and returning. The meaning is that they do not obtain any independence anywhere.
But those people who, free from desire and possessing right vision, worship Me with undivided thought— those who devote themselves to Me;
For those who are constantly devoted to Me, I provide for their acquisition of what they lack and the preservation of what they possess.

Those people who, being renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*), worship Me by meditating upon Me as their very Self—having realized that the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa is non-different and not separate from them—I carry their *yoga-kṣema*; that is, I bring about *yoga*, which is the attainment of what has not yet been attained, and *kṣema*, which is the preservation of what has been attained. Since it is My opinion that "the man of knowledge is indeed My own Self" (Gītā 7.18) and "he is dear to Me" (Gītā 7.17), they have become My very Self and are dear to Me. Thus, for those who perceive the supreme reality and are constantly devoted—that is, those who are ever-exerting—I provide both yoga and kṣema.

[Arjuna asks: "But does the Blessed One not indeed carry the *yogakṣema* (acquisition and preservation) of other devotees as well? [The Lord replies: "It is true that He indeed carries it. However, this is the distinction: those other devotees themselves also strive for their own *yogakṣema* for their own sake; but those who perceive no other [than Me] do not strive for *yogakṣema* for their own sake. For they do not harbor greed for their own life or death; they have taken refuge in the Blessed One alone. Therefore, the Blessed One Himself carries their *yogakṣema*. (BhG 9.22)
[Objection: But if you yourself are indeed every other deity as well, then those devoted to them worship you alone. [Reply: True, it is so;
even those who are devotees of other deities and worship them, being endowed with faith—
They too, O son of Kuntī, sacrifice to me alone, though not according to the prescribed rule.

Even those who are devotees of other deities—being devoted to other gods, they sacrifice and worship them, endowed with and following faith, that is, the conviction of their existence—they too, O Kaunteya, sacrifice to me alone, though in an improper manner; "improper" means preceded by ignorance—that is the meaning of "sacrificing in an improper manner."
Why is it said that they sacrifice without following the prescribed rule? Because I am indeed the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices.
But they do not recognize Me in truth; therefore, they fall.

For I am indeed the deity and the enjoyer, as well as the Lord, of all sacrifices—both those prescribed by the Vedas (*śrauta*) and those prescribed by the Smṛtis (*smārta*). Indeed, it has been said: "Sacrifice has Me as its master; I alone am the Adhiyajña here" (Gītā 8.4). Yet they do not know Me truly and as I am. Therefore, having sacrificed according to rites that are contrary to the injunctions, they fall away—they deviate from the fruit of the sacrifice.
Even for those who worship other deities not according to the prescribed rules because of their devotion to them, the fruit of their sacrifice is nonetheless inevitable. How so?
"Those devoted to the gods go to the gods; those devoted to the ancestors go to the ancestors."
Those who worship the spirits go to the spirits; those who sacrifice to me also come to me.

Those whose vow is the gods—those for whom the vow (niyama), discipline, and devotion are directed toward the gods—go to the gods. Those whose vow is the ancestors—those devoted to the ancestors who are intent on rites such as the *śrāddha*—go to the ancestors, such as the Agniṣvāttas and others. Those who worship spirits—worshippers of spirits such as Vināyaka, the hosts of Mothers, the Four Sisters, and so forth—go to the spirits. Those who sacrifice to me—the Vaiṣṇavas whose habit is to sacrifice to me—go to me alone.
The meaning is that even though the exertion is equal, because they do not worship me due to ignorance, they become partakers of small fruits.
Not only does my devotee obtain the infinite fruit characterized by non-return, but I am also easy to worship. How so? "Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water..."
Therefore, I eat what is offered with devotion by one whose self is purified.

Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—even that which consists of a leaf and so forth, offered with devotion, brought forward with devotion—I accept and partake of it from the self-restrained one of purified intellect. (BhG 9.26)
Since this is so, therefore:
whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, and whatever you give;
Whatever austerity you perform, O son of Kuntī, do that as an offering unto Me.

Whatever you do as spontaneously obtained, whatever you eat, and whatever you offer in sacrifice—whether performing Vedic or Smṛti rites—whatever you give away or bestow upon Brahmins and others such as gold, food, clarified butter, and so forth, and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī, perform that as an offering unto Me, a dedication to Me.
Listen to what happens to you as you act in this way:
by means of the fruits of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, you will thus be liberated from the bonds of karma.
With your self disciplined by the yoga of renunciation, you shall be liberated and come to Me.

By means of actions that have auspicious and inauspicious fruits—those actions which have auspicious and inauspicious, desired and undesired results—by those bonds of action (karmabandhana), where actions themselves are the bonds, by such bonds of action, you will be liberated while thus making this surrender unto Me.

This is what is called the yoga of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-yoga*): it is renunciation because of the surrendering of actions to Me, and it is yoga because of that very [surrender]. You, whose inner organ (*ātman*)—that is, your mind—is joined with this yoga of renunciation, being thus liberated from the bonds of action even while living, shall attain Me upon the falling away of this body; you will come to Me.
"In that case, the Blessed One possesses attachment and aversion, since he favors devotees and not others. To this it is said:
"I am equal toward all beings; to Me there is none hateful and none dear."
But those who worship me with devotion, they are in me and I am also in them.

I am equal toward all beings; there is none hateful to Me and none dear. Just as fire does not remove the cold for those standing at a distance, yet removes it for those who approach it—so do I favor those who are devoted, and not others. But those who worship Me, the Lord, with devotion, they abide in Me by their very nature, and not because of any passion on My part. And I also abide in them by their very nature, and not in others.
It is not by this that I harbor hatred toward them.
Listen to the greatness of devotion to Me:
even if one of very wicked conduct worships Me with undivided devotion, [he becomes righteous].
He indeed should be considered righteous, for he has rightly resolved.

Moreover, even if one is of very evil conduct—meaning one whose behavior is exceedingly wicked and utterly contemptible—if he worships Me with undivided devotion, being possessed of exclusive devotion, he is to be regarded as indeed righteous; he is to be known as such, for he has rightly resolved, since his determination is directed toward what is good.
Having cast off external misconduct through the power of right internal resolve, he quickly becomes a man of dharma and attains eternal peace.
O son of Kuntī, declare it with certainty: my devotee does not perish.

He quickly and swiftly becomes one whose nature is dharma, possessing a mind fixed on dharma alone. Constantly and eternally, he attains peace and tranquility. Listen to the ultimate truth, O Kaunteya: make this firm promise—that my devotee, who has surrendered his inner self to Me, never perishes.
Furthermore,
O Pārtha, even those who may be of low birth, by taking refuge in me—
Women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras—they too attain the supreme goal.

For, O Pārtha, by taking refuge in me—that is, by accepting me as their support—even those who may be of "sinful birth"—those whose birth is sinful, meaning those of low or wicked origin—go to the supreme goal, the highest state. Who are they? He says: women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras; even they attain that supreme destination.
How much more so, then, O Brahmins, meritorious ones, and royal sages who are my devotees!
Having reached this world which is impermanent and full of suffering, worship Me.

How much more so, then, for the meritorious Brahmins born of merit, and likewise for the royal sages (*rājarṣis*)—those who are both kings and sages. Since this is so, having reached this world—the human realm which is impermanent, momentary in its destruction, and devoid of happiness—you should worship and serve Me, having obtained this human state which is difficult to attain and is the means for accomplishing the goals of human life.
How so?
Set your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me.
Thus, having disciplined yourself and making Me your supreme goal, you shall come to Me alone.

He whose mind is fixed on me, Vāsudeva—be such as you are, one whose mind is on me (*manmanā*); likewise, be my devotee (*madbhakta*); be a sacrificer to me (*madyājī*), having the habit of sacrificing to me; and bow down to me alone. Having united and concentrated your mind, you shall come to me alone, the Lord. Thus, "you shall come to me," who am the Self (*ātman*)—for I am the Self of all beings and the supreme goal (*parā gatiḥ*), the ultimate refuge (*param ayanaṃ*)—this is the connection with the preceding word. The meaning is: being one for whom I am the supreme resort (*matparāyaṇaḥ*).

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Royal Science and the Royal Secret," in the commentary on the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakas.
Bhagavad Gītā 10:
Now begins the tenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Manifestations."
(Commentary by the venerable Śrīmacchaṅkarācārya):

In the seventh chapter, as well as in the ninth, the true nature (*tattva*) and the manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) of the Blessed One were revealed. Now, those various states (*bhāvāḥ*) in which the Blessed One is to be meditated upon must be declared. Furthermore, although the true nature of the Blessed One has already been stated, it must be explained again because it is difficult to comprehend; therefore, the Blessed One said:
"O mighty-armed one, listen once more to my supreme word."
That which I, desiring your welfare, shall speak to you who are well-disposed toward me.

Listen once more, O mighty-armed one, again to my supreme word, which reveals the unsurpassed Reality; for you, who take delight in my speech and drink it as if it were nectar, I shall speak out of a desire for your welfare.
To the question, "For what purpose shall I speak?", he says:
"Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know my origin."
For I am indeed the source of the gods and of the great seers in every respect.

Neither the hosts of gods, beginning with Brahmā, know Me; they do not understand Me. What is it that they do not know? My *prabhavam*—my power, my majesty, or the excellence of my sovereign capacity; or else, my *prabhavam*, meaning my origin or birth. Nor do the great seers, such as Bhṛgu and others, know Me. Why is it said that they do not know? Because I am the *ādiḥ*, the cause, of both the gods and the great seers in every way and in all respects.
Furthermore,
he who knows me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds;
He who is undeluded among mortals is liberated from all sins.

He who knows Me as unborn and beginningless—for I am the source of the gods and the great seers (maharṣis), and no other origin for Me exists—therefore I am unborn and beginningless; he who knows Me, the unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds, the Fourth (turīya) who is devoid of ignorance and its effects, remains undeluded, free from delusion, and is liberated from all sins, whether committed intentionally or unintentionally, among mortals. || BhG 10.3 ||
For this reason as well, I am the Great Lord of the worlds:
intelligence, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forgiveness, truth, self-restraint, and tranquility.
Happiness and suffering, existence and non-existence, as well as fear and fearlessness.

Intellect (*buddhi*) is the capacity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) to comprehend subtle and other objects; for they say that one who possesses this is "intelligent" (*buddhimān*). Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the comprehension of categories such as the Self (*ātman*). Absence of delusion (*asaṃmoha*) is activity preceded by discrimination regarding present objects to be understood. Forbearance (*kṣamā*) is the state of an undisturbed mind when one is reviled or struck.

Truth (*satya*) is speech uttered exactly as it has been seen or heard, and as it has been personally experienced, for the purpose of transferring that understanding to the intellect of another. Self-restraint (*dama*) is the pacification of the external senses; tranquility (*śama*) is the pacification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Pleasure (*sukha*) is delight; pain (*duḥkha*) is affliction. Existence (*bhava*) is arising; non-existence (*abhāva*) is its opposite. Fear (*bhaya*) is terror, and fearlessness (*abhaya*) is its contrary. || BhG 10.4 ||
Non-violence, equanimity, contentment, austerity, charity, fame, and infamy—
these various states of beings arise from Me alone.

Non-violence is the non-affliction of living beings. Equanimity is even-mindedness. Contentment is satisfaction and the sense of sufficiency regarding acquisitions. Austerity is the infliction of bodily hardship preceded by the restraint of the senses. Charity is the distribution [of wealth] according to one's capacity. Fame is renown caused by righteousness; infamy, however, is renown caused by unrighteousness. These aforementioned states—intellect and the rest—arise for beings, that is, for living creatures, from Me alone, the Lord, in their various and manifold forms, in accordance with their own past actions.
Furthermore,
O great seers, there were seven ancient ones as well as four Manus.
Those who were born from my mind through my nature are these progeny in the world.

The seven great seers, Bhṛgu and the others, who belong to the past; and the four Manus, well known as the Sāvarṇas—these were of my own nature, possessed of a disposition directed toward me, and endowed with Vaiṣṇava power.
