They were born as my mind-born sons, produced by me from my mind alone. From these Manus and great seers, this creation of living beings, characterized by the mobile and the immobile, has come forth in this world.
He who knows in truth this glory and this yoga of Mine is united with unshakable yoga; of this there is no doubt.

He who knows in truth—that is, according to reality and as it truly is—this aforementioned manifestation (vibhūti), extension (vistāra), and yoga—the application (yukti) of my own nature, or alternatively, the power of yogic sovereignty, omniscience, and that which is born of yoga (yogaja)—is joined with, or connected to, unwavering and unshakable yoga, characterized by the stability of right vision (samyag-darśana). There is no doubt in this; there is no uncertainty regarding this matter.
By what kind of unshakable yoga is one joined? It is said:
"I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds."
Thinking thus, the wise, endowed with devotion, worship me.

I am the Supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva, the source and origin of the entire world. From Me alone proceeds the entire world in its modified form, characterized by maintenance, destruction, activity, and the experience of results. Thinking thus, the wise—those who have realized the truth of the supreme reality—worship and serve Me, being endowed with *bhāva*; that is to say, they are joined with *bhāva*, which means a state of contemplation or a deep attachment to the truth of the supreme reality.
Moreover,
with their minds fixed on Me and their lives surrendered to Me, they enlighten one another.
And constantly speaking of me, they are satisfied and they rejoice.

With their minds fixed on Me—those whose minds are on Me; with their life-breaths gone to Me—those whose life-breaths, such as the eyes and other senses, have reached and attained Me; that is to say, they have withdrawn their faculties into Me. Alternatively, "with their life-breaths gone to Me" means "with their very existence centered in Me. Awakening one another and making each other understand, and speaking of Me who am distinguished by attributes such as knowledge, power, and valor, they are satisfied—they attain complete contentment—and they rejoice—they find delight—as if in union with a beloved.
To those devotees who, being virtuous, worship Me in the ways described above— those who worship Me with love and are ever steadfastly devoted to Me— [I grant their constant devotion].
I bestow upon them that yoga of discernment by which they come unto Me.

For those who are constantly engaged, eternally devoted, and have desisted from all external desires—those who worship and serve Me; for what reason? Not for the sake of seeking anything, as he says: "with love as the motive. Love (*prīti*) means affection (*sneha*); the meaning is: for those who worship Me preceded by such affection.

I give, I bestow, the yoga of wisdom (*buddhiyoga*). Wisdom is right vision (*samyagdarśana*) concerning My true nature; the yoga by means of that is the "yoga of wisdom. By which yoga of wisdom—characterized by right vision—they attain Me, the Supreme Lord, who am their very Self, realizing Me as the Self? They are those who worship Me through such modes as fixing the mind on Me.
In response to the inquiry— "For what purpose, or for whom, do you grant the yoga of wisdom that destroys the cause of the obstruction to attaining You?"— He says:
"Out of compassion for them alone, I [dispel] the darkness born of ignorance."
Abiding within their very being, I destroy [their ignorance] with the shining lamp of knowledge.

Out of compassion for them—meaning for the sake of their welfare—I, abiding within their very self-nature (the internal organ or latent disposition), destroy the darkness of delusion, which is born of ignorance, arises from lack of discrimination, and is characterized by false cognition. I do this with the lamp of knowledge, which takes the form of discriminative discernment, is anointed with the oil of devotion and grace, and is fanned by the wind of intent devotion to Me.

The meaning is: by means of the lamp of knowledge—which possesses the refinement resulting from the practice of celibacy and other disciplines; which abides in wisdom; which has its support in an internal organ characterized by dispassion; which stands in a windless chamber with the mind turned away from sense objects and untainted by the stains of attachment and aversion; and which is radiant with right vision born of meditation performed with constant one-pointedness.
Having heard of the Lord’s majesty and yoga as described, Arjuna said:
"You are the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Abode, and the Ultimate Purifier."
The eternal, divine Person, the primordial God, unborn and all-pervading.

You are the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, the Supreme Abode, the Supreme Splendor, the Pure, the Purifier, the Most Excellent, and the Most Preeminent. You are the Eternal, Constant Person, the Divine one born in heaven, the Primordial God existing before all gods, the Unborn, the All-pervading Lord whose nature is to pervade.
All the seers, as well as the celestial seer Nārada, speak of you in this way.
Asita, Devala, and Vyāsa, and you yourself have told me this.
The sages Vasiṣṭha and all the others say this of you; likewise the celestial sage Nārada, and Asita Devala says exactly so, as does Vyāsa, and you yourself tell me the same.
I consider all this that you tell me, O Keśava, to be the truth;
for neither the gods nor the demons, O Blessed One, know your manifestation.

All this that has been spoken by the seers and by you, O Keśava, I consider to be truly and indeed the truth; for neither the gods nor the demons, O Blessed One, know your manifestation or your origin, as you tell me.
Since you are the origin of the gods and others, therefore,
O Supreme Person, you alone know yourself by yourself.
O creator of beings, O Lord of beings, O God of gods, O Lord of the universe!

You alone know Yourself by Yourself as the Lord, possessed of unsurpassed power consisting of knowledge, sovereignty, strength, and other attributes! O Puruṣottama! O Bhūtabhāvana—the nourisher of all beings! O Bhūteśa—the ruler of all beings! O Devadeva—O God of gods! O Jagatpati—O Lord of the universe!
You ought to speak in full of Your divine self-manifestations,
by which manifestations You abide pervading these worlds.

You ought to speak and tell [them] in their entirety; for divine are Your self-manifestations. Those which are the manifestations of the Self, You ought to speak of them—those manifestations by which, through the expansions of Your own majesty, You abide pervading these worlds.
O Yogi, how may I know You by constantly meditating upon You?
In what various manifestations, O Blessed One, are You to be contemplated by me?
How may I know You, O Yogin, as I constantly contemplate You? In what various states and objects am I to meditate upon You and reflect on You, O Blessed One?
O Janārdana, speak again in detail of your own yoga and majesty;
for there is no satiety for me as I drink in this nectar.

O Janārdana—[the word *janārdana* being a form derived from the root *ar*, meaning "to go," because You cause the *asuras* (those who are the enemies of the gods) to go to hell and other such realms]—tell me again in detail Your own yoga, Your specific power of mastery over yoga, and the full extent of Your manifestations (*vibhūti*), as well as the objects to be meditated upon.
For there is no satiety for me as I listen to the nectar of words issuing from Your mouth. (BhG 10.18)
The Blessed Lord said:
"Come now, I shall declare to you my divine self-manifestations."
I have declared this only in its principal aspects, O best of the Kurus; there is no end to my full extent.

"Come now, I shall describe to you those divine manifestations of Myself—which exist in heaven—that are My own glories (vibhūtayaḥ), O best of the Kurus! I shall describe them according to their importance, mentioning each principal manifestation as it preeminently stands out; for it is not possible to describe them exhaustively even in a hundred years, since there is no end to the extent of My glories. This is the meaning.
In this regard, first of all, listen:
O Guḍākeśa, I am the Self dwelling within the heart of all beings.
I am the beginning, the middle, and indeed the end of all beings.

I am the Self, the innermost Self, O Guḍākeśa—Guḍākā meaning sleep, and he who is the lord (īśa) of that is Guḍākeśa; the meaning is "one who has conquered sleep," or alternatively, "one with thick hair. Abiding in the heart, which is the abode of all beings—I, the Self, the innermost Self, am to be meditated upon constantly. By one who is unable to do so, I am to be contemplated in the subsequent states. For I alone am the beginning—the cause—of beings, as well as their middle, their duration, and their end, their dissolution.
And thus am I to be meditated upon as Viṣṇu among the Ādityas, the radiant Sun among the luminaries.
Among the Maruts I am Marīci; among the stars I am the Moon.

Among the twelve Ādityas, I am the Āditya named Viṣṇu; among luminaries, I am Ravi, the radiant one endowed with rays. Among the Maruts—the various classes of the Marut deities—I am he who is named Marīci; and among the constellations, I am Śaśin, the Moon.
Among the Vedas, I am the Sāmaveda; among the gods, I am Vāsava;
among the senses, I am the mind; and among beings, I am consciousness.

Among the Vedas, I am the Sāmaveda; among the gods, such as the Rudras and Ādityas, I am Vāsava, Indra; and among the eleven senses, beginning with the eyes, I am the mind—that mind which consists of resolve and doubt. Among beings, I am consciousness—the mental modification of the intellect (buddhi) that is eternally manifest within the aggregate of the body and the organs.
Among the Rudras, I am Śaṅkara; among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, I am the Lord of Wealth (Kubera);
among the Vasus, I am Pāvaka; and among the peaked mountains, I am Meru.
Among the eleven Rudras, I am Śaṅkara; among the Yakṣas and Rakṣasas, I am their lord, Kuvera; among the eight Vasus, I am Pāvaka the fire; and among the peaked mountains, I am Meru.
And know me, O Pārtha, to be Bṛhaspati, the chief among domestic priests;
among army commanders I am Skanda, and among bodies of water I am the ocean.

And know Me, O Pārtha, as Bṛhaspati—the chief and foremost among the domestic priests and royal chaplains; for he is indeed the principal priest of Indra. Among generals and army commanders, I am Skanda, the commander of the celestial hosts. Of lakes—that is, those bodies of water excavated by divine power—I am the ocean.
Among the great seers, I am Bhṛgu; among words, I am the single syllable Om.
Among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of silent recitation; among immovable things, I am the Himalayas.

Among the great seers, I am Bhṛgu; among words characterized by their syllables, I am the single syllable Om. Among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of silent recitation; among immovable things that possess stability, I am the Himalaya.
Among all trees, I am the Aśvattha; among divine seers, Nārada;
among Gandharvas, Citraratha; and among perfected beings, the sage Kapila.

Among all trees, I am the Aśvattha; among the divine seers (devarṣis), I am Nārada—those who, being gods, attained the status of seers through their vision of the mantras—and among them, I am Nārada. Among the Gandharvas, I am the Gandharva named Citraratha. Among the Siddhas—those who have attained from birth a preeminence in dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—I am the sage Kapila.
Know me as Uccaiḥśravas among horses, born of the nectar;
as Airāvata among lordly elephants, and as the king among men.

Among horses, know me to be Uccaiḥśravas by name, the king of horses; know me as having arisen from the nectar, produced during the churning for the sake of the nectar. Among lordly elephants, the masters of elephants, know me to be Airāvata, the offspring of Irāvatī—this "know me" is understood to carry over. And among men, human beings, know me to be the king, the lord of men. BhG 10.27.
Among weapons, I am the thunderbolt; among cows, I am the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhuk; I am Kandarpa, the progenitor; and among serpents, I am Vāsuki.

Of weapons, I am the thunderbolt born from the bones of Dadhīci; of milch-cows, I am Kāmadhuk, the cow of Vasiṣṭha who milks all desires—or rather, I am the common cow of plenty that milks every wish. Of progenitors, I am Kandarpa, the god of love; of serpents, I am Vāsuki, the king of snakes.
Among the Nāgas I am Ananta; among the aquatic creatures I am Varuṇa;
among the ancestors I am Aryaman; and among those who exercise restraint, I am Yama.

Among the Nāgas, I am Ananta; among the distinguished Nāgas, I am the King of the Nāgas. Among the aquatic creatures, I am Varuṇa; among the deities of the waters, I am the King. Among the ancestors, I am he named Aryaman, the King of the ancestors. Among those who exercise restraint, I am Yama.
Among the Daityas I am Prahlāda; among those who mete out time, I am Time;
among wild beasts I am the king of beasts, and among birds I am Vainateya.

Among the Daityas, the descendants of Diti, I am known by the name Prahlāda; among those who calculate, I am Time, the reckoning of those who perform calculation. Among beasts, I am the king of beasts, the lion or the tiger; and among birds, I am Vainateya, Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā.
Among purifiers I am the wind; among wielders of weapons, I am Rāma;
among fish I am the makara; and among flowing streams I am the Gaṅgā.

Among those that purify, I am the wind; among wielders of weapons, I am Rāma, the son of Daśaratha; among aquatic creatures such as fish, I am the species known as the Makara; and among flowing streams, I am the Jāhnavī, the Gaṅgā.
I am the beginning, the end, and also the middle of all creations, O Arjuna; among sciences, I am the science of the Self, and among those who debate, I am the logic of debate.

I am the beginning, the end, and also the middle of all creations—of all emanations, O Arjuna; I am their origin, their sustenance, and their dissolution. Although it was stated at the outset that I am the beginning and the end of "beings" (bhūtāni) specifically as those presided over by individual souls, the distinction here is that I am the beginning and end of the entire process of creation itself. Among sciences, I am the science of the Self (adhyātmavidyā), because it is the primary means for attaining liberation. Among disputants, I am the debate (vāda), because it is the primary means for determining the truth; therefore, I am that.
By way of the speakers, the term "those who debate" (pravadatām) here refers specifically to the different types of discourse: discussion (vāda), wrangling (jalpa), and cavil (vitaṇḍā).
Among letters, I am the letter *a*; and among compounds, I am the copulative (*dvandva*).
I alone am inexhaustible time; I am the Ordainer whose face is turned everywhere.

Among letters, I am the letter *a*; among compounds, I am the *dvandva* compound, which is the preeminent among all types of compounds. Furthermore, I am the inexhaustible time known as the moment (*kṣaṇa*) and so forth; or rather, as the Supreme Lord, I am the Time even of time. I am the Ordainer who dispenses the fruits of action for the entire world, facing in every direction—omnipresent.
I am death that carries away all, and I am the origin of those things yet to be;
among women, I am fame, fortune, speech, memory, intelligence, steadfastness, and forgiveness.

Death is of two kinds: that which takes away wealth and the like, and that which takes away life. Of these, that which takes away life is called "all-taking" (*sarvahara*); the meaning is: "I am that. Alternatively, the Supreme Lord is the "all-taker" (*sarvahara*) because He takes away everything at the time of dissolution; I am He. "Udbhava" means excellence or prosperity; I am the cause for its attainment. Of whom? Of those who are destined for the future—that is, of those whose welfare is yet to come and who are fit to attain excellence.

Among women, I am fame, fortune, eloquence, memory, intelligence, fortitude, and forbearance—these I am, the most excellent of women, by whose mere connection with their reflection people consider themselves to have achieved their life's purpose.
Likewise, among the Sāmans I am the Bṛhat-sāman; among meters, I am the Gāyatrī.
Among months I am Mārgaśīrṣa, and among seasons I am the flower-bearing spring.

Likewise, among the Sāmans I am the Bṛhat-sāman, which is the foremost. Among the meters (chandas), I am the Gāyatrī; the meaning is that among the Ṛks distinguished by meters such as the Gāyatrī and others, I am the Gāyatrī-Ṛk. Among the months I am Mārgaśīrṣa, and among the seasons I am Vasanta, the flower-producer.
Of those who practice deception, I am gambling; of the radiant, I am splendor;
I am victory; I am resolve; and of those possessed of strength, I am strength.

I am gambling, characterized by the playing with dice and the like, among those who practice deception; I am the splendor of the splendid; I am victory among victors; I am resolve among the resolute; and I am the goodness of the virtuous, of those possessed of the quality of purity (sattva).
Among the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva; among the Pāṇḍavas, Dhanañjaya.
Among the sages I am Vyāsa; among the poets, the poet Uśanas.

Among the Vṛṣṇis and Yādavas, I am this very Vāsudeva; among the Pāṇḍavas, you yourself are Dhanañjaya. Among the sages—those of reflective nature who know all things—I am Vyāsa; and among the poets, who possess far-reaching vision, I am the poet Uśanas.
Of those who subdue, I am the rod; of those who seek victory, I am statesmanship;
of secrets, I am silence; and of the wise, I am knowledge.

Among those who subdue, I am the rod of punishment; I am the chastiser of the unsubdued. Among those desiring victory, I am statesmanship. And among secrets, I am silence. Among the wise, I am knowledge.
Moreover, O Arjuna, I am the seed of all beings;
there exists no being, whether moving or unmoving, that can exist without me.

Furthermore, O Arjuna, that which is the seed and the cause of growth for all beings—that I am. For the purpose of concluding this section, He speaks this summary of His manifestations: "There is no being, whether moving or unmoving—whether mobile or immobile—that could exist without Me. For that [being] would indeed be soulless and void, as it would be deprived of and abandoned by Me. Therefore, the meaning is that everything has Me as its Self. (BhG 10.39)
There is no end to my divine manifestations, O scorcher of the foe;
this detailed exposition of my glory has been declared by me only in brief.

O scorcher of the foe, there is no end to the expansion of my divine manifestations. For it is not possible for anyone to describe or even to know the full extent of the divine manifestations of the Lord, who is the Self of all. However, this detailed account of my manifestation has been declared by me only in brief, as a mere partial indication.
Whatever being possesses majesty, splendor, or power,
know that to be born from but a fragment of My splendor.

Whatever being exists in the world that is possessed of majesty, endowed with power, glorious, or even exalted—whether "glory" (śrī) means Lakṣmī herself, or whether it means accompanied by her, or endowed with enthusiasm—know each of those to have arisen from a portion of My, the Lord's, splendor; know that which has its origin in a single part or division of My splendor to be such.
Or rather, what is the use of this extensive knowledge of yours, O Arjuna?
Sustaining this entire universe with but a single fraction of Myself, I remain as the world.

Or rather, O Arjuna, what would be the use of knowing much more of this kind and the like, since it would remain incomplete for you? Listen, however, to the matter being stated in its entirety: having specially pervaded—that is, having performed a firm stabilization of—this entire world with one part, that is, with one limb, or one foot, in the form of all beings. And thus says the Vedic mantra: "All beings are but one foot of Him" (Ṛgveda 8.4.17.3). Thus I stand.

Thus ends the tenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya).
Bhagavad Gītā 11:
Now the Eleventh Chapter.
The Yoga of the Vision of the Cosmic Form (with the commentary composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Bhagavatpāda).

The divine manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) of the Blessed One have been described. Having heard there the statement of the Blessed One, "Pervading this entire universe, I stand with but a single portion" (Gītā 10.42), Arjuna, desiring to directly perceive that primordial, sovereign form which is the very self of the world, spoke.
By those words which You have spoken for my benefit— this supreme secret concerning the inner self— this delusion of mine has vanished.

"For the sake of my grace—for the purpose of favoring me—this supreme, unsurpassed, secret, and hidden discourse concerning the inner self (*adhyātma*), which is the subject of the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self, has been spoken by You; by that speech of Yours, this delusion of mine has departed. The meaning is that my undiscriminating intellect has been dispelled. (BhG 11.1)
Furthermore,
the origin and dissolution of beings have indeed been heard by me in detail.
And from you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, [I have heard] of your imperishable majesty as well. BhG 11.2.

"Origination" (bhava) is birth, and "dissolution" (apyaya) is destruction; these two, origination and dissolution, of living beings have indeed been heard by me from you in detail, not in brief. From you—that is, from your presence. O lotus-petal-eyed one! One whose eyes are like the petals of a lotus is "lotus-petal-eyed"; O lotus-petal-eyed one! Furthermore, the state of being a Great Soul (māhātmya), which is imperishable and undecaying—this too has been heard [by me], as the word "heard" is understood to carry over [from the previous verse]. || BhG 11.2 ||
"It is even so as you have said of yourself, O Supreme Lord.
I desire to see your divine form, O Supreme Person."

"It is exactly so and not otherwise, O Supreme Lord, just as you have described yourself; nevertheless, O Supreme Person, I desire to see Your divine Vaiṣṇava form, endowed with knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor."
If you think, O Lord, that it is possible for me to see that,
then, O Master of Yoga, show me your imperishable self.

O Lord! O Master! O Lord of Yoga!—you are the master (īśvara) of those who possess yoga (yogins); therefore, O Lord of Yoga, since I am exceedingly desirous to see [that form], for my sake, show Yourself, the Imperishable. (BhG 11.4)
Thus urged by Arjuna, the Blessed One said:
"Behold, O Pārtha, my forms by the hundreds and by the thousands."
Of various kinds, divine, and of diverse colors and forms.

Behold my forms, O Pārtha! By the hundreds and by the thousands—meaning in great numbers—and they are of various kinds, manifold in their nature; divine, meaning celestial and non-material; and of various colors and shapes—those forms whose colors, such as blue, yellow, and so forth, are diverse and distinct, and whose shapes, that is, specific arrangements of limbs, are likewise varied. || BhG 11.5 ||
Behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, as well as the two Aśvins and the Maruts;
behold, O Bhārata, many wonders never seen before.

Behold the twelve Ādityas, the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the Maruts who consist of seven groups of seven; likewise, behold many other wonders, O Bhārata, never before seen in the world of men by you or by anyone else.
Not only this much alone;
behold today, all this entire world, with its moving and unmoving beings, situated here in one place.
And whatever else you wish to see within my body, O Guḍākeśa.

Behold now, O Guḍākeśa, the entire universe in its totality, including all that is moving and unmoving, situated here in one place—within my very body. And whatever else you may doubt, such as victory or defeat, or what you have said, "Whether we shall conquer them, or whether they shall conquer us" (Gītā 2.6), you may see even that if you so desire.
However,
you are not able to see me with these very eyes of yours.
I give you divine vision; behold my sovereign yoga.

But you are not able to see Me, who possess this universal form, with these very eyes of yours—your own natural eyes. However, that divine eye with which you may be able to see, that divine eye I give to you. With that, behold My sovereign yoga—the meaning is, My supreme power of yoga as the Lord.
Saṃjaya said:
Having spoken thus, O King, Hari, the great lord of yoga, then—
He revealed to Pārtha his supreme sovereign form.

Having spoken thus in the manner described, immediately thereafter, O King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Hari Nārāyaṇa—the Great Lord of Yoga (Mahāyogeśvara), being both great and the Lord of Yoga—revealed, he showed, to Pārtha, the son of Pṛthā, his supreme form, the sovereign Universal Form (Viśvarūpa).
With many mouths and eyes, displaying many wonders,
adorned with many divine ornaments, and wielding many uplifted divine weapons.

"Having many mouths and eyes" means that form in which there are many mouths and many eyes; "having many wonderful sights" means that form in which there are many wonderful, astonishing appearances; likewise, "having many divine ornaments" means that in which there are many divine ornaments.
Likewise, "divyānekodyatāyudham" means that in which there were many divine weapons, such as swords and others, raised up; this is to be connected with the preceding verb "darśayāmāsa" (he showed).
Furthermore:
wearing divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine perfumes and unguents;
The Lord who consists of all wonders, infinite, with faces on every side.

He showed him—that Lord who wears divine garlands and garments (divyamālyāmbaradharam), meaning He by whom divine garlands (mālya) and flowers as well as divine garments (ambara) and clothes are worn; who is anointed with divine perfumes (divyagandhānulepanam), meaning He whose anointing with divine scents is divine; who consists of all wonders (sarvāścaryamayam), meaning He who is composed primarily of every marvel; who is infinite (anantam), meaning He who has no end; and who faces in all directions (viśvatomukham), meaning He whose face is everywhere because He has become the Self of all beings. "Arjuna saw Him" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Furthermore, as for the radiance of the Blessed One Viśvarūpa, a simile for it is this: it would be like the simultaneous rising of a thousand suns in the sky.
If that light were similar to the light of that Great-Souled One, it would be so.

Whether in the atmosphere or in heaven, if there were a thousand suns—a thousand suns—arising simultaneously, the light of that thousand suns arising together would be similar only to the light of that Great-Souled One in his Universal Form; or rather, it would not be so, for the light of the Universal Form alone excels it—this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore,
within that [Self], the entire universe, though divided manifoldly, is situated as one.
Then the son of Pāṇḍu beheld [all this] within the body of the God of gods.

There, in that single universal form, Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, then beheld the entire world situated as one, yet divided manifoldly according to the distinctions of gods, ancestors, humans, and so forth, within the body of Hari, the God of gods.
Then Dhananjaya, overcome with wonder and his hair standing on end,
bowed his head to the God and spoke with palms joined in reverence.

Then, having seen him, Dhanañjaya was filled with wonder; overcome by that wonder, his hair stood on end, and he became one whose body-hairs were thrilled. Having bowed down—performing a profound salutation—and being deeply humbled, he spoke with his head to the God who bears the universal form, with palms joined in reverence for the purpose of paying homage.
"How so? Manifesting his own experience by saying, 'I see that universal form which was shown by you,' Arjuna said:
"O God, I see the gods in Your body."
Likewise, all the hosts of various beings,
Brahmā the Lord seated upon his lotus-throne,
all the ṛṣis, and the divine serpents.

I see, O Lord, I perceive within Your body all the gods, as well as the hosts of various classes of beings—meaning the multitudes of diverse stationary and moving entities with their manifold forms; furthermore, I see Brahmā, the four-faced lord and ruler of creatures, seated upon his lotus-throne (the meaning being that he is seated on Mount Meru, which is like the pericarp of the earth-lotus);
and I see all the sages, such as Vasiṣṭha and others, as well as the divine serpents, such as Vāsuki and others, who dwell in heaven.
I see You on all sides with many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes, possessing infinite forms.
O Lord of the Universe, O You of universal form, I see neither Your end, nor Your middle, nor again Your beginning.

I see you with many arms, stomachs, mouths, and eyes—he who has many arms, stomachs, mouths, and eyes is "anekabāhūdaravaktranetra," and I see you, that one with many arms, stomachs, mouths, and eyes. I see you everywhere, on all sides, as the one of infinite forms—he whose forms are infinite is "anantarūpa," and I see you, that one of infinite forms. I see neither end—end meaning a limit—nor middle; "middle" refers to the space between two ends.
But I do not perceive Your beginning, nor do I perceive Your end, O God; I do not perceive Your middle, nor again do I perceive Your beginning, O Lord of the Universe, whose form is the universe!
Furthermore,
[I see] him wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and holding a discus.
I behold You as a mass of splendor blazing on all sides, difficult to gaze upon, with the brilliance of a flaming fire and the sun, immeasurable in every direction.

I see You, the wearer of a crown—*kirīṭin*, meaning one who possesses a *kirīṭa*, a specific kind of head ornament; likewise, the wielder of the mace—*gadin*, meaning one for whom a mace (*gadā*) exists; likewise, the wielder of the discus—*cakrin*, meaning one who possesses a discus (*cakra*). I see You as a mass of splendor—a heap of radiance, blazing on all sides—one who possesses radiance in every direction (*sarvatodīptimant*); I see You, who are difficult to behold, from every side, everywhere.

"You, whose splendor is like the radiance of a blazing fire and the sun—'analārkau' means fire and sun; 'dīptau analārkau' means the two blazing fires and suns; 'dīptānalārkayoḥ' means of those two blazing fires and suns; 'dyutir iva dyutiḥ' means whose splendor, that is, brilliance, is like their radiance—you are 'dīptānalārkadyuti'. To You, who possess such a splendor like that of a blazing fire and the sun, and who are 'aprameya'—that is, not measurable, meaning impossible to be fully delimited—I bow. (BhG 11.17)
From this very observation of your power of yoga, I infer that you are the Imperishable, the Supreme, who is to be known.
You are the supreme treasure-house of this entire universe;
You are the imperishable protector of the eternal dharma; You are considered by me to be the ancient Puruṣa.

You are the Imperishable (*akṣara*), meaning that which does not decay; You are the Supreme Brahman to be known—that is, to be realized—by those seeking liberation. You are the supreme, most excellent repository (*nidhāna*) of this entire universe; "repository" means that in which everything is deposited, signifying the ultimate support. Furthermore, You are the Undecaying (*avyaya*), for no decay exists in You. You are the Protector of the Eternal Dharma (*śāśvatadharman-goptā*); "eternal" (*śāśvata*) means existing perpetually, referring to the eternal or constant Dharma, and You are its protector.
You are considered by me to be the eternal, ancient, supreme Puruṣa. || BhG 11.18 ||
Furthermore,
he is without beginning, middle, or end, and possesses infinite vigor.
I behold You with infinite arms, with eyes like the moon and the sun, with a mouth of blazing fire,
scorching this entire universe with Your own splendor.

"Anādimadhyāntam" means that for you there is no beginning, middle, or end; thus, you are "anādimadhyānta," and [I bow] to you, who are without beginning, middle, or end. "Anantavīryam" means that there is no end to your power; thus, you are "anantavīrya," and [I bow] to you, who are of infinite power. Likewise, "anantabāhum" means that you have infinite arms; thus, you are "anantabāhu," and [I bow] to you, who are of infinite arms.

I behold you, whose eyes are the moon and the sun—that is, you whose two eyes are the moon and the sun—possessing the moon and the sun as your eyes; I behold you, whose mouth is the blazing fire—that is, you whose mouth is that which is both blazing and the consumer of oblations—possessing a mouth of blazing fire; scorching this entire universe with your own splendor.
For this space between heaven and earth,
as well as all the directions, is pervaded by you alone.
O Great-Souled One, seeing this wondrous and fierce form of yours, the three worlds are deeply distressed.

Indeed, this space between heaven and earth, the intermediate region, is pervaded by you alone who bear all forms; and all the directions are pervaded as well. Having seen—having perceived—this wondrous, astonishing, and fierce form of yours, which is cruel, the three worlds, the triad of worlds, are deeply distressed, terrified, or shaken. O Great-Souled One! O You of noble nature! *Bhagavad Gītā 11.20*

Now, the Blessed One, having set out to demonstrate the absolute victory of the Pāṇḍavas in order to resolve Arjuna’s doubt— which was previously expressed as, "Whether we shall conquer, or whether they shall conquer us" (Gītā 2.6)— observes him and says: "Moreover,
these hosts of gods are indeed entering into you."
Some, filled with fear, utter words with palms joined;
having said "May it be well," the hosts of great seers and perfected ones praise you with abundant hymns of praise.

For these warriors fighting here—the hosts of gods such as the Vasus who have descended in human form to remove the burden of the earth—are seen entering you; they enter you while being observed. Among them, some, being terrified, praise you with palms joined in reverence, while others are unable even to flee.

When battle is imminent, having observed omens such as portents, the hosts of great seers and perfected beings—those multitudes of maharṣis and siddhas—saying, "May there be well-being for the world," praise You with abundant and complete hymns of praise.
Furthermore:
the Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and those who are the Sādhyas—
The Viśvedevas, the Aśvins, the Maruts, and the Uṣmapās;
the hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas— all of them gaze upon you, utterly amazed.

The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and those who are the Sādhyas; the hosts beginning with the Rudras; the Viśvedevas and the two gods, the Aśvins; the Maruts and the Pitṛs who drink the steam; and the hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas—the Gandharvas such as Hāhā and Hūhū, the Yakṣas such as Kubera, the Asuras such as Virocana, and the Siddhas such as Kapila—all these hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas behold You, filled with wonder, having attained a state of amazement. They all, indeed, gaze upon You. (BhG 11.22)
Because your form is great, with many mouths and eyes;
O mighty-armed one, having seen You with many arms, thighs, and feet, with many bellies and many formidable tusks, the worlds are thus distressed, as am I.

Your form is great and of immense proportions; it has many mouths and eyes—that form in which there are many faces and eyes is "many-mouthed-and-eyed. O mighty-armed one! It has many arms, thighs, and feet—that form in which there are many arms, thighs, and feet is "many-armed-thighed-footed. Furthermore, it has many bellies—that in which there are many bellies is "many-bellied."

Having seen such a form—terrible with many fangs, distorted by its many fangs—the worldly beings, that is, the creatures of the world, were struck with terror and shaken by fear; and so was I as well.
In this regard, the reason is this:
[he sees] a blazing [fire] touching the sky, possessing many colors.
Indeed, O Viṣṇu, seeing you with your mouth wide open and your large eyes blazing, my inner self is deeply distressed; I find neither fortitude nor peace.

"Touching the sky" means touching the heavens; "blazing" means flaming; "multicolored" means you in whom there are many terrifying colors and various shapes—that you, the multicolored one; "with gaping mouths" means you in whom there are gaping, wide-open faces—that you, with gaping mouths.

Having seen You, whose eyes are blazing and wide—meaning You, in whom the eyes are blazing (dīpta), i.e., inflamed, and wide (viśāla), i.e., expansive—I, with my inner self deeply distressed, meaning my mind (the inner self) being greatly pained and terrified, find no steadiness (dhṛti), that is, no fortitude, nor do I obtain peace (śama), which is the calming of the mind and its satisfaction. O Viṣṇu! (BhG 11.24)
Why?
Because your faces are terrible with fangs.
Having seen these forms resembling the fire of cosmic destruction, I no longer know the directions nor do I find peace;
be gracious, O Lord of Gods, Abode of the Universe! (BhG 11.25)

Having seen—that is, having perceived—your faces, which are formidable with tusks, distorted by tusks, and resembling the fire of time (the fire that burns the worlds at the end of an aeon), I have lost my sense of direction; I am bewildered as to the distinction between east and west. Therefore, I find no peace—I obtain no happiness. Hence, be gracious, O Lord of gods, O Abode of the Universe!
The apprehension I had regarding defeat from them has now vanished;
for these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra are [now] with you.
All together with the hosts of kings—
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and that son of a charioteer (Karna),
along with our own chief warriors as well.

"And these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Duryodhana and the others, are entering [the mouth] in haste"—this is the connection with the distant verb. All together, joined with the multitudes of rulers of the earth (*avanipāla*)—those who protect the earth (*avani*), that is, the world—they enter along with those hosts. Furthermore, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Karṇa the son of a Sūta, as well as those [others], together with our own chief warriors, the foremost among combatants, such as Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the rest.
Moreover,
your mouths are entering [the body] with great haste.
Terrifying and formidable with their fangs bared,
some are seen caught between the gaps of the teeth, their heads crushed to powder.

Hastening, filled with haste, they enter Your mouths; what kind of mouths? Terrifying, formidable, and fearsome, with tusks that are gaping. Moreover, some are seen and perceived among those who have entered the mouths as if being eaten like meat, stuck between the teeth, with their heads—their upper parts—pulverized and reduced to dust.
How do they enter the openings? To this he says:
"Just as the many currents of water of rivers [enter the ocean]."
Just as rivers flow toward the ocean alone,
so do these heroes of the world of men enter your blazing mouths.

Just as the many and numerous currents of water—the various velocities and surges of the flowing rivers—rush toward and enter the ocean headlong; even so, these heroes of the world of men, Bhīṣma and the others, who are valiant in the human realm, enter your blazing and radiant mouths.
For what purpose do they enter, and how? To this he says: "Just as moths [enter] a blazing fire..."
They enter with full force for their destruction;
even so, O Lord, these worlds enter your mouths with full force for their destruction.

Just as moths, those winged insects, enter a blazing, flaming fire for their destruction with full force—those whose speed, that is, their motion, has become intense—so too do these creatures enter your mouths for their destruction with full force.
But you, moreover,
are licking [the world], devouring it on all sides.
Filling all the worlds with Your blazing mouths and the entire universe with Your splendors, Your fierce radiance shines forth, O Viṣṇu.

You lick—that is, you taste—swallowing them in by drawing them entirely within from all sides; you pervade and fill the entire world together with its extremities through your blazing, radiant faces. Furthermore, O Viṣṇu, whose nature is all-pervading, your fierce and cruel splendors scorch—that is, they exert their heat.
Since you are thus of such a fierce nature, therefore tell me: who are you, appearing in this terrible form?
Homage be to you, O best of gods; be gracious!
I desire to know you, the Primordial One, for I do not understand your manifestation.

Tell me, declare to me who you are, you of such fierce form and cruel appearance. Homage be unto you, O best of gods, O foremost of deities; be gracious, show favor. I desire to know you specifically—to know you as the primordial one, existing from the beginning—for I do not understand your activity, that is, your purposeful movement.
The Blessed One said:
"I am Time, the destroyer of worlds, now fully grown."
Engaged here in the destruction of the worlds,
even without you all these warriors who stand arrayed in the opposing armies shall cease to exist.

I am Time, the destroyer of worlds; "the destroyer of worlds" means one who brings about the destruction of all worlds. Having increased—that is, having reached full maturity—listen to the purpose for which I have increased: I have set out at this time to gather together, that is, to annihilate, the worlds.

Even without you, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and all the others whom you fear will cease to exist. They stand in the opposing ranks—in "opposing ranks" (pratyanīkeṣu) meaning in the ranks arrayed against each individual rank (anīkam anīkaṃ prati)—those warriors who have taken their positions as combatants in the enemy forces.
Since this is so,
therefore arise and obtain glory.
"Having conquered your enemies, enjoy a prosperous kingdom;
these have already been slain by me alone—
be merely the instrument, O Savyasācin."

Therefore, arise! Attain the glory that Bhishma and the other great car-warriors—invincible even to the gods—have been defeated by Arjuna; for that is obtained solely through merit. Having conquered your enemies, Duryodhana and the rest, enjoy a prosperous kingdom, free from rivals and thorns. These have already been slain by me alone; they have certainly been deprived of their lives beforehand. You be merely the instrument.
O Savyasācin! Arjuna is called Savyasācin because he can discharge arrows even with his left hand, the savya.
Droṇa and Bhīṣma, Jayadratha and Karṇa, as well as other heroic warriors—
"Kill those who have already been slain by me; do not be distressed.
Fight, and you shall conquer your enemies in battle."

And as for Droṇa, the Blessed One points out each and every warrior of whom Arjuna had apprehension, saying, "He has been slain by me. In this regard, the grounds for apprehension concerning Droṇa and Bhīṣma are well known. Droṇa was indeed the preceptor of the science of archery (*dhanurveda*), endowed with divine weapons (*divyāstra*), and especially his own teacher and most venerable superior. Bhīṣma, moreover, possessed the power of death at will, was endowed with divine weapons, and had engaged in single combat with Paraśurāma without being defeated.

Likewise, Jayadratha; for his father is performing penance with the thought, "Whoever shall strike off the head of my son, his own head shall also fall to the ground. And Karṇa, the son of the Sun, is born of a maiden and is endowed with the unfailing *vāsavadattā* spear; therefore, he is designated by that very name. "Slay those who have been slain by me, using me merely as an instrument. Do not be distressed; do not harbor fear of them. Fight, and you shall conquer your rivals and enemies—Duryodhana and the others—in battle.
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard these words of Keśava,
With palms joined in reverence, trembling, and bowing down again and again, Arjuna, wearing the diadem, spoke to Kṛṣṇa with a faltering voice, utterly terrified.

Having heard these words previously spoken by Keśava, the wearer of the crown (Arjuna), with palms joined in reverence, trembling and shaking, paid homage and spoke again to Kṛṣṇa with a faltering voice—due to being overcome by fear and the impact of grief, as well as by the surge of affection; and because his eyes were filled with tears, his throat was constricted by phlegm.

And thus, "sagadgadam" means that which is accompanied by a faltering of speech—that is, a dullness or slowness of sound; this qualifies the act of speaking, meaning he spoke words with a faltering voice. Furthermore, being "bhītabhītaḥ"—that is, having a mind repeatedly overcome by fear—he bowed down, becoming humble. The word "āha" (he said) is to be connected with the distant verb [praṇamya].
Arjuna said:
It is fitting, O Hṛṣīkeśa, that by your glorification...
The world rejoices and is filled with devotion;
the Rākṣasas flee in fear in all directions,
and all the hosts of Siddhas bow down in reverence.

"It is fitting; what is that? By hearing Your praise—that is, by hearing the proclamation of Your majesty—O Hṛṣīkeśa! that the world rejoices, attains great delight; that is fitting, such is the meaning. Alternatively, 'fitting' (*sthāne*) is an adjective qualifying the object: the Blessed One is a fitting object for joy and so forth, because He is the Lord, the Self of all, and the friend of all beings. Likewise, that [the world] becomes enamored and attains passion—that too should be explained as being the object."

Furthermore, the *rākṣasas*, overcome with fear, flee in all directions; and that is appropriate. All the hosts of *siddhas*—the assemblies of perfected beings such as Kapila and others—bow down and offer salutations; and that too is appropriate. (BhG 11.36)
He shows the reason why the Blessed One is an object of joy and so forth:
"And for what reason, O Great-Souled One, should they not bow down to you?"
To the one greater even than Brahmā, the primordial creator;
O infinite Lord of gods, abode of the universe, You are the Imperishable, that which is both being and non-being, and that which is beyond them.

And for what reason, O Great-Souled One, should they not bow down—that is, pay homage—to you, who are more venerable (garīyase), that is, weightier? Because you are the primordial creator (ādikartā), the cause even of Brahmā, the Golden Womb (Hiraṇyagarbha); therefore, [they should bow] to the Primordial Creator. How could they not pay homage? Thus, the meaning is that you are the worthy object (arhaḥ), the proper locus for joy and the like, as well as for salutation. O Infinite One, Lord of Gods, Abode of the World, you are that Supreme Imperishable (akṣaram) which is heard of in the Vedāntas.

What is that? It is "being" (sat) and "non-being" (asat). "Being" is that which exists; "non-being" is that regarding which the cognition "it does not exist" arises. That syllable (akṣara) has being and non-being as its limiting adjuncts (upadhāna), by means of which it is metaphorically designated as "being" and "non-being. In the ultimate sense, however, that syllable which those who know the Vedas speak of is beyond both being and non-being: "That syllable which the knowers of the Veda declare" (Gītā 8.11). The intention is that you alone are that, and nothing else.
Once again he praises him:
"You are the primordial god, the ancient Puruṣa."
You are the supreme repository of this entire universe;
you are the knower and that which is to be known, and the highest abode.
By you, O you of infinite forms, the whole world is pervaded.

You are the *Ādideva* because of being the creator of the world; you are the *Puruṣa*, so called because you dwell within the city (*puri*) of the body; you alone are the *Purāṇa*, the ancient one, and the supreme (*parama*) repository (*nidhāna*) of this entire universe, for in it—such as at the time of the great dissolution—all the world is deposited. Furthermore, you are the knower (*vettā*), the perceiver of everything that is to be known. And whatever is to be known, worthy of being known, that too are you, as well as the supreme abode (*dhāma*), the highest station of Viṣṇu. By you the entire universe is pervaded (*tataṃ*). O you of infinite forms! No end (*anta*) is found to your forms.
Furthermore,
you are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, and Śaśāṅka.
You are Prajāpati and the Great-Grandfather;
salutations, salutations be unto you a thousand times,
and yet again, further still, salutations, salutations unto you!

You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa the lord of the waters, Śaśāṅka the moon, Prajāpati, Kaśyapa and the others, and the Great-Grandfather (prapitāmaha)—that is to say, the father of even the Grandfather (pitāmaha), the father of Brahmā. Salutations, salutations unto You a thousand times; and again, yet once more, salutations, salutations unto You. The suffix *kṛtvasuc* is used to express the counting of repetitions in the practice of performing salutations many times.
By saying "and again, yet once more," he demonstrates his own lack of satisfaction due to the intensity of his faith and devotion.
Likewise,
salutations to you from the front and also from behind.
Homage be unto You from every side, O All!
You possess infinite power and immeasurable prowess;
You pervade all, and therefore You are the All.

Salutations to you from the front, in the eastern direction; and salutations to you from behind, even from your rear—let there be salutations to you from every side, in all directions, to you who abide everywhere. O Sarva! You whose vigor is infinite and whose prowess is immeasurable—one whose vigor (*vīrya*) is endless and whose prowess (*vikrama*) is limitless. *Vīrya* is capability; *vikrama* is valor. For even someone who possesses vigor may not exert himself in matters such as slaying an enemy, or may be of feeble prowess.

But you, possessing infinite power and immeasurable prowess, are Anantavīryāmitavikrama. Since you pervade—that is, you completely and perfectly encompass—the entire world with your single self, therefore you are "all" (sarva). The intended meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from you.
Since I have offended you through ignorance of your greatness, I have spoken to you impetuously, considering you my friend.
"O Kṛṣṇa! O Yādava!
O Friend!"—this was said by me out of negligence or even out of affection, because I did not know this greatness of yours.

Thinking and perceiving [Arjuna] as a friend of equal age, and having overcome him by force through a contrary understanding—what was said [by the ignorant one], namely "O Kṛṣṇa! O Yādava! O Friend!"—was spoken by an ignorant, deluded person who did not know. What did he not know? To this he says: "Your majesty," that is, Your greatness, this universal form of the Lord. The connection is to be understood as a grammatical coordination (vaiyadhikaraṇya), meaning "not knowing this majesty of Yours. If the reading is *tava imam* ("this of Yours"), then it is indeed a case of grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
Whether out of negligence, through a distracted mind, or even out of affection—affection being a confidence born of love—it is for that reason also that I have spoken.
And as for the fact that you were treated with disrespect for the sake of mockery regarding your dwellings, beds, seats, and meals;
Or even alone, O Acyuta, in Your presence, I seek forgiveness from You, the immeasurable one.

And when you have been treated with disrespect or humiliated for the sake of mockery—that is, for the purpose of derision—where? In matters of wandering, lying down, sitting, and eating. "Wandering" (*vihāra*) means walking about; "lying down" (*śayyā*) means reclining; "sitting" (*āsana*) means staying seated; and "eating" (*bhojana*) means consuming food. In these matters of wandering, lying down, sitting, and eating, you were alone and out of sight, and thus you were treated with disrespect and humiliated.

Or else, O Acyuta! "In Your presence"—the word *tat* (that) being used as an adverb meaning "directly" or "before Your eyes"—I beg forgiveness for all those multitudes of offenses committed against You; I ask You, the immeasurable One who transcends all means of knowledge, to grant me pardon.
Since you are the father of the world, both moving and unmoving.
You are his worshipful one and his most venerable teacher;
there is no one equal to you, much less anyone superior, even throughout the three worlds, O You of incomparable power.

You are the father, the progenitor, of the world—the multitude of living beings, both moving and unmoving, stationary and animate. You are not merely the father of this universe; you are also worthy of worship, for you are the Guru, the most venerable. Why are you more venerable? He says: there is none equal to you. Indeed, two Lords cannot coexist, because if there were many, the practical functioning of the world would be impossible. Thus, even another being equal to you is simply not possible.

How much less could there be another superior to You, even throughout all the three worlds? O You of incomparable power! That by which something is measured is a "measure" (pratimā); since no such measure exists for Your power, You are one whose power is incomparable (apratimaprabhāva). O You of incomparable power—the meaning is, O You of unsurpassed power.
Since this is so,
therefore, having bowed down and composed the body,
I seek to propitiate you, the Lord worthy of praise;
as a father for his son, as a friend for a friend,
as a lover for his beloved, so may you, O God, deign to forgive me.

Therefore, having bowed down—that is, having paid homage by holding my body low—I seek to propitiate you, the Lord, the Ruler, the one worthy of praise. Furthermore, just as a father forgives the transgression of a son, or a friend the transgression of a friend, or as a lover forgives the transgression of a beloved, even so, O God, it behoves you to endure—that is, to bear with and forgive—my offense. ||BhGS_11.44||
Having seen what was never seen before, I am thrilled;
yet my mind is deeply distressed by fear.
O God, show me that very form;
be gracious, O Lord of gods, O Abode of the Universe!

Never before have I seen this universal form of yours, nor has anyone else ever seen it; having seen it, I am filled with joy, yet my mind is distressed by fear. Therefore, O Lord, show me that very form which was my friend. Be gracious, O Lord of gods, O Abode of the Universe, you who are the dwelling place of the world!
I wish to see you likewise, wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and with a discus in hand.
In that very form with four arms, O you of universal form, become thousand-armed!

I desire—that is, I pray—to see You as you were before: wearing a crown (*kirīṭin*), possessing a mace (*gadin*), and with a discus in Your hand (*cakrahasta*). Since this is so, therefore, O Thousand-armed One! appear in that very form as the son of Vasudeva, with four arms; O Universal Form! appear in Your present universal form. The meaning is: having withdrawn the universal form, appear in that very same form.
Perceiving that Arjuna was afraid, the Blessed Lord withdrew his universal form and, consoling him with affectionate words, said:
"O Arjuna, this [vision] has been shown to you by me in my grace."
This supreme form has been shown by My own power—
consisting of light, universal, infinite,
and primordial— which has never been seen before by anyone other than you.

By me, being pleased—“pleased” meaning possessing a mind of grace toward you—by me thus being pleased, O Arjuna! this supreme form, the universal form, has been shown to you through my own yoga, that is, by the power of my own sovereignty. It is composed of light, consisting mostly of splendor; it is the entire universe, infinite, without end, existing from the beginning, primordial—a form of mine which has never been seen before by anyone other than you.
He praises him, saying: "By the sight of my form, you have indeed become one who has achieved his purpose; for it cannot be attained through Vedic knowledge, sacrifices, study, or gifts."
Nor can I be seen in such a form in the world of men by anyone other than you, O hero of the Kurus, through ritual acts or through fierce austerities.

Not by Vedic sacrifices or by the study of the four Vedas—since the study of sacrifice is already accomplished through the study of the Vedas themselves, the separate mention of the "study of sacrifice" is intended to indicate the *understanding* of sacrifice—not by gifts such as the *tulāpuruṣa* and others, nor by ritual acts such as the *agnihotra* and other Śrauta rites, nor even by severe austerities such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* and other harsh and formidable penances; such is the nature [of the path] as it has been shown.
I, who possess this universal form, cannot be seen in this manner by anyone other than you in the world of men, O hero of the Kurus.
Let there be no distress in you, nor any state of confusion, upon seeing this terrible form of mine such as this.
Free from fear and with a joyful mind, behold once more this very form of mine.

Let there be no distress for you, let there be no fear, and let there be no state of bewilderment—that is, no confusion of mind—upon seeing and perceiving such a terrible form as this which has been shown by me. With your fear departed and your mind filled with joy, behold once again that very four-armed form of yours, bearing the conch, discus, and mace; behold this form which is dear to you.
Saṃjaya said:
Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva—
The Great-Souled One again showed his own form and, assuming once more a gentle appearance, comforted him who was terrified.

Having spoken these words to Arjuna who was in such a state, Vāsudeva again showed his own form born in the house of Vasudeva; and the Great-Souled One, having once more assumed a gentle body with a serene form, comforted him who was terrified.
Arjuna said:
O Janārdana, having seen this gentle human form of yours, [I am restored to my normal state].
Now I have become composed in mind and have returned to my natural state.

"O Janārdana, having seen this human form of yours, which is my friend, serene, and gentle, I have now—at this very moment—become restored; that is, I have become possessed of consciousness, with a tranquil mind, and have returned to my own nature."
The Blessed Lord said: You have seen this form of mine which is very difficult to behold.
Even the gods are constantly longing for a vision of this form.

"Sudurdarśam" means that its vision is very difficult to obtain; this form of mine which you have seen—even the gods always and at all times long for a vision of this form of mine. The intention is that although they desire to see it, they have not seen it as you have, nor will they see it.
Why?
Because "Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen [in this way]."
It is indeed possible for such a one to see me as you have seen me.

Neither by the Vedas—the four Vedas of Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan—nor by intense austerity such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances, nor by gifts such as cows, land, or gold, nor by sacrifice or worship can I, who am of such a nature as has been shown, be seen in the manner that you have seen Me.
But how, then, am I possible to be known? It is said:
"But by unswerving devotion, O Arjuna, I who am of such a nature can be known."
To know, to see, and to enter [Me] in truth, O scorcher of the foe.

To the question, "By what kind of devotion? he says: "by undivided" (*ananyayā*), meaning not separate; that devotion which never at any time exists apart from the Blessed One is "undivided" devotion. That devotion by which nothing other than Vāsudeva is perceived through any of the senses is "undivided" devotion; by such devotion, O Arjuna, I—who am of this nature, in the form of the Cosmic Body—am capable of being known through the scriptures.
O scorcher of foes, it is not merely to know through scripture, but also to see—that is, to realize it in its true essence—and to enter into and attain liberation.

Now, the essential meaning of the entire Gītā scripture, which concerns the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) and is to be practiced, is stated in summary: "Performing my work, having me as the supreme goal, devoted to me, and free from attachment."
He who is free from enmity toward all beings, O Pāṇḍava, he comes to me.

"Matkarmakṛt" means one who performs my work; "my work" (*matkarma*) refers to action for my sake, and he who performs that is "one who performs my work. "Matparamaḥ": a servant performs his master's work, yet he does not regard the master as the supreme goal or destination to be attained after death. This person, however, being "matkarmakṛt," attains me alone as the supreme goal; thus he is "matparamaḥ"—he for whom I am the supreme, the ultimate goal. He is "matparamaḥ" because I am his supreme, highest refuge.

Likewise, my devotee worships Me alone in every way—with his whole being and with all his energy; thus he is "my devotee. He is "free from attachment," meaning free from attachment—attachment being affection or fondness—to wealth, children, friends, wife, and the circle of kinsmen. He is "without enmity," meaning devoid of hostility toward all beings, even toward those who are intent on doing him extreme harm. Such a devotee of Mine comes to Me.
I alone am his supreme goal; there is no other goal whatsoever. This instruction, which is desired by you, has been taught by me. O Pāṇḍava! Thus [ends the chapter].

Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya). ||11||
Bhagavad Gītā 12:
Now begins the twelfth chapter, named "The Yoga of Devotion."
(Commentary by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Bhagavatpāda):

In the chapters beginning with the second and ending with the chapter on manifestations (*vibhūti*), the meditation upon the Supreme Self, the Imperishable Brahman, from whom all specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) have been destroyed, has been taught. Furthermore, the meditation upon Īśvara—who possesses the limiting adjunct of *sattva* endowed with all yogic powers and omniscience—has been taught in various places. However, in the chapter on the Cosmic Form (*viśvarūpa-adhyāya*), your own universal form, which is divine and the very self of the entire universe, was shown by You solely for the purpose of meditation.
Having shown that [vision], You said, "He who performs actions for Me" (Gītā 11.55), and so forth. Therefore, with a desire to know which of these two positions is superior, Arjuna said:
"But among those who are thus constantly disciplined and worship You as the Bhakta, and those who worship the Imperishable and the Unmanifest—of these, who are the best knowers of yoga? (BhG 12.1)

The word "thus" (*evam*) refers back to the meaning stated in the immediately preceding verse by the words "performing my work" (*matkarmakṛt*) and so forth. "Thus constantly disciplined" (*evaṃ satatayuktāḥ*) means being engaged in the aforementioned matters, such as the service of the Blessed One, with uninterrupted concentration. Those devotees who, having no other refuge, worship—that is, meditate upon—you in the form of the Universal Manifestation (*viśvarūpa*) as it has been shown.

And those others who, having abandoned all desires and renounced all actions, worship that imperishable Brahman as previously described—which, because it is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is unmanifest and beyond the reach of the senses; for whatever is within the range of the senses is called "manifest" (*vyakta*), since the root *añj* has that as its object—whereas this imperishable is the opposite of that, and is distinguished by the attributes being stated in the sequel: among these two groups, which are the best knowers of yoga? That is to say, which are the most excellent practitioners of yoga? (BhG 12.1)

The Blessed Lord said: Let those who are worshippers of the Imperishable, who possess right vision, and whose desires have ceased, remain for now. What is to be said regarding them, I shall explain later. But as for the others, who, having fixed their minds on Me, worship Me with constant discipline—
Endowed with supreme faith, they are considered by Me to be the most disciplined.

Those devotees who, having fixed and concentrated their minds upon Me, the Supreme Lord of universal form, worship Me—the omniscient Lord of all yogas and the best of things, whose vision is freed from the darkness of afflictions such as attachment—remaining ever-disciplined according to the principle of the meaning of the verse stated at the end of the immediately preceding chapter, and endowed with supreme, most excellent faith; they are My thought, they are intended by Me as the most perfectly disciplined.
For they pass their days and nights with their minds incessantly fixed on Me; therefore, it is appropriate to say that they are the most perfect among the disciplined.
Are the others not most disciplined? No; however, hear what is to be said regarding them:
"But those who worship the Indestructible, the indefinable, the unmanifest..."
All-pervading, inconceivable, immovable, unchanging, and eternal.

But those who [meditate] on the Imperishable, which is indefinable because, being unmanifest (*avyakta*), it cannot be defined as being within the range of words; therefore, it is "indefinable. It is "unmanifest" because it is not manifested by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); they "worship it completely," that is, they worship it all around. What is called "worship" (*upāsana*) is this: having approached proximity to the object of worship by making it the focus of one's attention according to the scriptures, one remains for a long time in a continuous flow of identical mental impressions, like a stream of oil; that is what they call "worship."

He states the qualification of the Imperishable (*akṣara*): "all-pervading like space" (*sarvatragaṃ vyomavat*), meaning it is all-encompassing; and "inconceivable" (*acintya*) because of its unmanifest nature. For whatever falls within the range of the senses can be conceived by the mind; since this is the opposite, the Imperishable is inconceivable. "Fixed" (*kūṭastha*): in common worldly usage, the word *kūṭa* is well known in such expressions as "an object with visible qualities but hidden faults" (*dṛśyamānaguṇam antardoṣaṃ vastu kūṭam*), or "a forged document" (*kūṭarūpam*), or "perjury" (*kūṭasākṣyam*). Thus, that which is of the nature of a forgery is called *kūṭa*.

Likewise, that which is well-known in such passages as "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10) and "My Māyā is difficult to cross" (Bhagavad Gītā 7.14)—namely, that which possesses many seeds of saṃsāra beginning with ignorance (avidyā) and is characterized by internal defects, being denoted by terms such as 'Māyā' and 'the Undifferentiated' (avyākṛta)—is the 'Kūṭa'.

That which abides in that Kūṭa is 'Kūṭastha', meaning it stands as the presiding witness over it. Alternatively, it is 'Kūṭastha' because it stands like a heap (rāśi); for this very reason, it is immovable (acala). Because it is immovable, it is therefore 'dhruva', meaning eternal. || Bhagavad Gītā 12.3 ||
Having fully restrained the collection of senses and possessing equal intelligence toward all,
those who delight in the welfare of all beings attain Me alone.

Having fully restrained—that is, having properly controlled and withdrawn—the aggregate of the senses, those who possess equal intellect (*samabuddhi*)—meaning those whose intellect is the same or equal toward the attainment of the desirable and the undesirable—at all times, everywhere, they, being thus disposed and devoted to the welfare of all beings, attain Me alone. It need not be said further that "they attain Me," for it has already been stated: "But the man of knowledge is My very self; this is My opinion."
For it is not appropriate to speak of being most disciplined or least disciplined regarding those who exist as the very nature of the Blessed One.
However,
for those whose minds are attached to the unmanifest, their affliction is greater.
For the path to the Unmanifest is attained with difficulty by those who possess bodies.

The affliction is greater. Although the affliction is indeed great for those devoted to their duties and so forth, the affliction is even greater for those whose nature is the Imperishable (akṣara), who perceive the ultimate reality, and who are motivated by the abandonment of the conceit of being the body. "Those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest" means those whose minds are fixed on the Unmanifest; for that goal which consists of the Imperishable is difficult to attain by embodied beings who possess the conceit of being the body. Because the goal consisting of the Imperishable is the Unmanifest, it is attained with difficulty by those who identify with the body.
Therefore, their affliction is greater. We shall explain later the conduct of those who worship the Imperishable. ||BhGS_12.5||
But those who, having renounced all actions unto Me, are devoted to Me, and worship Me, meditating on Me with a yoga that is indeed one-pointed; BhG 12.6.

But those who, having surrendered all actions unto Me, the Lord, being "intent on Me"—meaning those for whom I am the supreme goal—and being thus single-minded (ananya), worship Me by means of yoga, that is, through meditative absorption (samādhi), meditating upon and contemplating Me, the Self, the God of universal form, from whom nothing else exists as an object of support—[they too reach Me]. || BhG 12.6 ||
What of them?
Of them I am the deliverer from the ocean of mortal transmigration.
I am not far from those whose minds are absorbed in me, O Pārtha.

For those who are solely intent on my worship, I am the Lord and their deliverer. Why? To this He says: "From the ocean of the cycle of death. The cycle of existence (saṃsāra) conjoined with death is "the cycle of death" (mṛtyu-saṃsāra); that itself is like an ocean because of its difficulty in crossing. From that ocean of the cycle of death, I become their deliverer before long. What then? Immediately, O Pārtha, for those whose minds are absorbed in Me—those whose minds are absorbed in, that is, concentrated upon, My universal form (viśvarūpa). They are "those whose minds are absorbed in Me. (BhG 12.7)
Since this is so, therefore fix your mind on Me alone; establish your intellect in Me.
From this time forward, you shall dwell in Me alone; of this there is no doubt.

Fix—place—the mind, which consists of volition and doubt, upon Me alone, the Lord who am the universal form; fix and settle the intellect, which performs determination, upon Me alone. Then hear what will happen to you: you shall dwell—you will certainly abide—with Me as your very self after the fall of this body; of this there is no doubt; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
But if you are unable to fix your mind steadily on Me,
then seek to reach Me, O Dhanañjaya, by the yoga of constant practice.

Now, if you are unable to fix and establish your mind upon me in such a way as I have described—steadfast and immovable—then afterwards, through the yoga of practice (*abhyāsa-yoga*), seek and strive to attain me in my universal form. Practice is the repeated fixing of the mind on a single object after having withdrawn it from all other directions; the yoga preceded by that is characterized by meditative concentration (*samādhāna*). Through that yoga of practice, O Dhanañjaya, desire to reach me.
If you are unable even to practice, be intent on performing actions for Me;
by performing actions for My sake, you shall attain perfection.

If you are unable even to practice—that is, if you are incapable—then become one for whom my work is supreme (*matkarmaparama*). "My work" (*matkarman*) means action performed for My sake; "one for whom that is supreme" (*tatparamaḥ*) means one for whom My work is the primary focus. Even without practice, by performing actions solely for My sake, you will attain perfection through the gateway of the purification of the mind, yoga, and the attainment of knowledge.
But if you are unable even to do this, take refuge in my yoga and then renounce the fruits of all actions, with your self controlled.

Furthermore, if you are unable to perform even that which was described as the supremacy of my action—that performance consisting of the renunciation of actions performed for me, having taken refuge in my yoga—then, taking refuge in that yoga of mine, perform the renunciation of the fruits of all actions (sarvakarmaphalatyāga), that is, the relinquishing of the results of all works; immediately thereafter, do so while being self-controlled, meaning with a restrained mind. (BhG 12.11)
Now he praises the renunciation of the fruits of all actions:
"Knowledge is indeed better than practice; meditation is superior to knowledge."
From meditation comes the renunciation of the fruits of action; from renunciation, peace follows immediately.

Knowledge is indeed more excellent—that is, more praiseworthy—than the former. Why? Because it arises from practice preceded by discrimination (*viveka*). Even compared to that knowledge, meditation (*dhyāna*) preceded by knowledge is superior. It follows [from the context] that renunciation of the fruits of action is superior even to the meditation of one who possesses knowledge. Thus, for one who possesses the aforementioned qualifications, peace—that is, tranquility—will occur immediately after the renunciation of the fruits of action; it does not depend upon any further interval of time.

For one who is ignorant and engaged in action, when unable to perform the means previously taught, the renunciation of the fruits of all actions is taught as the means for attaining the highest good (*śreyas*), but not from the very beginning. Therefore, by teaching that each subsequent stage is superior—starting with "Knowledge is indeed better than practice" (*jñānaṃ hi abhyāsāt*)—the renunciation of the fruits of all actions is praised, because it is heard in scripture as something to be practiced when one is unable to carry out the fully perfected means.

By what similarity does it possess the nature of praise? When it is said, "When all are completely liberated," immortality is stated through the abandonment of all desires; that is well known. And all desires are the fruits of rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti. Furthermore, for the wise man established in meditation, there is peace immediately upon their renunciation. Thus, because the commonality of abandoning all desires exists in the abandonment of the fruits of action by the ignorant, this praise of the abandonment of the fruits of all actions is intended to inspire enthusiasm based on that similarity.

Just as the ocean was drunk by the Brahmin Agastya, and thus even present-day Brahmins are praised because of their commonality with the quality of being Brahmins, so too has the superiority of Karma-yoga as a means to the highest good been declared through the renunciation of the fruits of action.

In this context, having relied upon the distinction between the self and the Lord, Yoga was described as the concentration of the mind upon the Lord who possesses the universal form (*viśvarūpa*), as well as the performance of action for the sake of the Lord. Now, by indicating that the effects of ignorance persist even in one who is "unable even to do this" (Gītā 12.11), He demonstrates that Karma-yoga is not appropriate for the worshiper of the Imperishable (*akṣara*) who perceives non-difference; likewise, He shows that the worship of the Imperishable is not appropriate for the practitioner of Karma-yoga.

Having stated that those who worship the Imperishable (akṣara) possess independence in attaining liberation by saying, "They come to Me alone" (Gītā 12.4), He has shown that for others there is dependence on the Lord due to their lack of autonomy, as expressed in "I am their deliverer" (Gītā 12.7). For if they were considered to have become the very Self of the Lord because of their vision of non-difference, then they would be of the very nature of the Imperishable; in that case, the statement regarding the act of delivering them would be inappropriate.

Since the Blessed Lord is the absolute well-wisher of Arjuna, He teaches him the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) which is devoid of right vision and characterized by the perception of duality; for no one, having known the Self as the Lord through valid means of knowledge, would desire to become subordinate to anyone else, as that would be a contradiction. Therefore, [the Lord] proceeds with the intention: "I shall declare the collection of attributes beginning with 'one who is not hateful toward any being,' which is the direct cause of immortality for those renunciants who worship the Imperishable, are established in right vision, and have abandoned all desires."
One who is not a hater of any being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from the sense of "mine" and free from egoism, equal in pleasure and pain, and patient; BhG 12.13.

"Non-hating" (*adveṣṭā*) means one who does not hate; he does not hate anything, even that which causes suffering to himself, for he perceives all beings as his own self. "Friendly" (*maitraḥ*) means having the state of a friend (*mitrabhāva*); he acts with friendliness, thus he is friendly. And likewise, "compassionate" (*karuṇaḥ*): compassion (*karuṇā*) is pity or mercy toward those in distress; one who possesses that is compassionate, bestowing fearlessness upon all beings—this is the meaning of a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*). "Free from possessiveness" (*nirmamaḥ*) means devoid of the notion of "mine. "Free from egoism" (*nirahaṃkāraḥ*) means from whom the notion of "I" has departed.

One who is equal in pain and pleasure is "samaduḥkhasukhaḥ"—one for whom the two, pain and pleasure, do not give rise to aversion or attachment. One who is patient (kṣamī) is possessed of forbearance; even when reviled or struck, he remains entirely unperturbed.
The yogi who is always content, self-controlled, firm in resolve,
and whose mind and intellect are dedicated to Me— that devotee of Mine is dear to Me.

He is always and constantly content, having conceived a sense of sufficiency regarding both the gain and loss of what is necessary for the maintenance of the body; likewise, he is content whether there is the acquisition of excellent things or the opposite. The yogi is ever concentrated in mind (*samāhitacitta*). He is self-controlled (*yatātmā*), meaning his nature is restrained. He is firm in resolve (*dṛḍhaniścaya*); that is, one whose determination and resolve regarding the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is firm and stable is "firm in resolve."
