"One whose mind and intellect are offered unto Me": the mind consists of volition and doubt, while the intellect is characterized by determination; he is one for whom these two are offered—that is, established—only in Me, that renunciant is "one whose mind and intellect are offered unto Me. Such a devotee of Mine is dear to Me. Indeed, it was indicated in the seventh chapter that "I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to Me"; that is now being elaborated here.
He by whom the world is not agitated and who is not agitated by the world, and who is free from joy, envy, fear, and anxiety— he, too, is dear to Me.

He who, as a renunciant, does not cause the world to tremble—that is, he does not cause it to feel agitation, distress, or perturbation—and likewise he who is not himself agitated by the world; who is free from joy, envy, fear, and agitation—joy being the exaltation of the internal organ upon obtaining what is dear, characterized by signs such as horripilation and the shedding of tears; envy being intolerance; fear being terror; and agitation being anxiety—he who is liberated from these is dear to Me.
He who is free from expectations, pure, skillful, impartial, free from distress,
and has renounced all undertakings— he who is my devotee is dear to me.

Free from expectation (*anapekṣaḥ*) regarding objects of desire such as the connection between the body, the senses, and their objects; pure (*śuciḥ*), endowed with both external and internal purity; skillful (*dakṣaḥ*), capable of immediately and correctly responding to tasks as they arise; indifferent (*udāsīnaḥ*), being an ascetic who does not take the side of anyone, whether friend or foe; free from distress (*gatavyathaḥ*), meaning free from fear; and one who has renounced all undertakings (*sarvārambhaparityāgī*)—those things which are undertaken [are called *ārambhāḥ*].
All undertakings here are actions motivated by desire for the enjoyment of fruits in this world and the next; he whose nature it is to renounce these, being my devotee, is dear to me.
Furthermore,
he who does not rejoice, does not hate, does not grieve, and does not desire—
He who has renounced both the auspicious and the inauspicious and is full of devotion—he is dear to me.

He who does not rejoice upon obtaining what is desirable, nor hates upon obtaining what is undesirable, who does not grieve at the separation from the beloved, nor craves for what has not been attained; he whose nature it is to renounce both auspicious and inauspicious actions—that devoted one who thus renounces the auspicious and the inauspicious is dear to Me.
He is the same toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor;
he is the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and is free from attachment.
He is equal toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor, respect and contempt, cold and heat, pleasure and pain; and he is entirely free from attachment in all circumstances.
Furthermore,
he is equal in both blame and praise, silent, and content with whatever comes his way.
The man who is homeless, steady-minded, and full of devotion is dear to Me.

He for whom blame and praise are equal; "blame and praise" refers to *nindā* and *stuti*. He who regards these two as equal is one for whom blame and praise are equal (*tulyanindāstuti*). He is silent (*maunī*), meaning he possesses silence and has his speech restrained. He is contented (*saṃtuṣṭa*) with whatever serves merely as a means for the maintenance of the body. As it has been said: "Clothed in anything whatsoever, fed by anything whatsoever, and sleeping anywhere at all—the gods know him to be a Brāhmaṇa. (Mahābhārata 12.245.12).

Furthermore, "homeless" (aniketa) means one for whom no fixed abode, residence, or dwelling place exists; this is according to other Smṛtis such as, "not in a house," and so forth. "Steadfast-minded" (sthiramati) means one whose mind is steady, having the ultimate reality as its object. Such a man, possessed of devotion, is dear to Me.

The collection of duties for those renunciants who are devotees of the Imperishable, who have desisted from all seeking, and who are established in the knowledge of the supreme truth— beginning with the verse, "One who is not hateful toward any being" (Gītā 12.13)— is here concluded:
"But those who fully attend to this nectar of dharma as it has been described..."
Those devotees who are full of faith, regarding Me as the supreme goal, are exceedingly dear to Me.

But those renunciants who worship—that is, practice—this aforementioned nectar of dharma (dharmyamṛtam), which is consistent with dharma because it is the cause of immortality, being full of faith and regarding Me as the Supreme; who have Me as their supreme goal, meaning they hold Me—the Self that is the Imperishable—as their unsurpassed ultimate resort; and who are My devotees, having taken refuge in the highest form of devotion characterized by knowledge of the Supreme Truth—they are exceedingly dear to Me.

Having explained what was indicated by the statement, "For the man of knowledge is exceedingly dear to Me" (Gītā 7.18), it is here concluded with the words, "Those devotees are exceedingly dear to Me. Since one who practices this nectar of dharma as described becomes exceedingly dear to the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the Supreme Controller, therefore this nectar of dharma must be practiced with effort by one desiring liberation who wishes to go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu; such is the meaning of the passage. (BhG 12.20)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya).

Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter 13 [Note: The numbering of this chapter does not correspond to standard editions. The Blessed Lord said: I shall declare that which is to be known, and that which, when known, brings liberation from all bonds—beginningless Brahman, called both the Manifest (Vyakta) and the Unmanifest (Avyakta). The unmanifest is said to be indestructible; its end is not perceived. Its opposite is called the destructible, which consists of all beings. The eternal, immutable Supreme Being is distinct from this. He is the indestructible within the destructible, and He is called the Supreme Self (Kṣetrajña). Thus, this body is called the Field (Kṣetra); and he who knows it is called the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña) by those who perceive the distinction between the two. Know Me, O Pārtha, as the Knower of the Field in all fields. The knowledge of the Field and the Knower of the Field is what I consider to be true knowledge. What that Field is, what its nature is, what its modifications are, and from what cause they arise; and who He is, and what His powers are—hear now that from Me in brief. All the sages, as well as the Vedas, have sung of this in various ways, using many different hymns and diverse expressions. In brief, this body is said to consist of the five elements, egoism, intellect, the unmanifest, and the ten senses, along with the mind as the eleventh. Desire, hatred, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, intelligence, and fortitude—these, briefly stated, constitute the Field and its modifications. Humility, sincerity, harmlessness, patience, uprightness, service to the teacher, purity, steadfastness, self-control; Dispassion toward the objects of sense, absence of egoism, perception of the misery and evil of birth, death, and old age in bodily existence; Non-attachment, absence of self-identification with son, wife, home, and the like, and constant even-mindedness amid desirable and undesirable events; Unswerving devotion to Me through single-minded yoga, resorting to secluded places, distaste for the society of men; Constancy in the knowledge of the Self, and the perception of the goal of the knowledge of reality—this is declared to be wisdom (Jñāna), and whatever is contrary to it is ignorance (Ajñāna). That which is the object of wisdom, what that is, hear now from Me in truth: it is the Supreme Brahman, without beginning, neither being nor non-being. It has hands and feet on all sides, eyes, heads, and faces everywhere; it possesses ears everywhere in the world, and it exists enveloping all. Possessing the splendor of the sun and excelling even the moon in brilliance, it exists pervading everything, sustaining all beings, and devouring them again. It is said to be beyond the darkness; wisdom is its form, and it stands as the heart of all beings. It is the light of lights, and it is said to be beyond all darkness. Wisdom is gained by meditation, by the one-pointedness of the senses, and by the practice of self-restraint; it is attained by those who see the truth, perceiving the Self within themselves. Standing outside as well as inside all beings, moving and yet unmoving, it is undivided, yet appears as if divided among beings. It is the sustainer, the ruler, and the beloved of all beings; it is the witness, the consciousness, the absolute, free from attributes, and established in the hearts of all. By devotion to Me, one may know this directly, in its essence, and then enter into Me; this is the certain conclusion reached by the science of Sāṅkhya. But by devotion through the yoga of action, one may attain Me even while remaining in this world; for I am the goal of those who worship Me with single-minded yoga. Even those who, endowed with faith, worship other deities, they too worship Me alone, though in an irregular manner. I am indeed the enjoyer of all sacrifices and the Lord of all the worlds, yet these ignorant ones do not recognize Me as I truly am. The fourfold orders of men and the four stages of life, created according to their qualities and actions, proceed from Me alone, yet I am not the agent of them, nor do they belong to Me. Understand Me as the inexhaustible source of all beings, and yet I am not the cause of the creation of beings; they do not exist in Me. Just as the great wind, moving everywhere, takes refuge in space, so too all beings take refuge in Me at the time of dissolution. At the end of a kalpa, all beings enter My own nature; and at the beginning of a kalpa, I send them forth again. Having presided over My own nature, I send forth again and again all this multitude of beings, powerless under the sway of nature. Nor does this wisdom bind Me, O descendant of Bharata, seated as I am, transcending the three guṇas, and free from attachment and aversion. Under the guise of nature, the three guṇas—sattva, rajas, and tamas—bind the immutable embodied soul in the body. Of these, sattva, being pure, illuminates all and is free from disease; it binds by attachment to happiness and by attachment to knowledge, O sinless one. Rajas, possessing the nature of passion, is the source of thirst and attachment; it binds the embodied soul by attachment to action. But tamas, born of ignorance, deludes all embodied beings; it binds by negligence, indolence, and sleep. Sattva attaches one to happiness, rajas to action, and tamas, veiling wisdom, attaches one to negligence. Rajas and tamas are overcome by sattva; know that tamas is overcome by rajas; and rajas and sattva are overcome by tamas, when each prevails. When the light of wisdom shines forth from all the gates of the body, then one may know that sattva prevails. Greed, activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness, and longing—these arise when rajas prevails, O best of the Bharatas. Darkness, stagnation, negligence, indolence, and delusion—these arise when tamas prevails, O joy of the Kurus. If the embodied soul attains the departure when sattva prevails, then he goes to the stainless worlds of those who know the highest. Attaining the departure during the prevalence of rajas, one is born among those attached to action; and departing during the prevalence of tamas, one is born in the wombs of the ignorant. The fruit of a meritorious deed is said to be pure and stainless, belonging to sattva; the fruit of rajas is pain, and the fruit of tamas is ignorance. From sattva arises wisdom, from rajas greed, and from tamas come negligence, delusion, and even ignorance. Those who abide in sattva go upward; those of the nature of rajas stay in the middle; and those of the nature of tamas, being base, sink downward. When the seer perceives no agent other than the gunas, and understands that which is beyond the gunas, he enters into My being. Transcending these three gunas, which constitute the source of the body, the immortal, fearless Puruṣa attains immortality, O son of Kuntī. He who hates none, is friendly and compassionate to all, free from possessiveness and egoism, even-minded in pain and pleasure, and forgiving; To whom praise and blame are equal, who is content with anything, who is homeless, steady-minded, and possessed of firm resolve, and whose devotion to Me is fixed—he transcends the gunas. For one who transcends the three gunas, who has conquered the body, and who is devoted to the Imperishable, the unchanging Supreme Self, there is no rebirth. He who, having fixed his mind upon the Imperishable, the Unmanifest, the Omnipresent, the Immutable, and the Support of all, does not think of anything else; He who, having equanimity toward all beings, neither grieves nor desires, and who is even-minded in honor and dishonor, is fit for the state of Brahman. When the wise man remains equanimous amidst the pairs of opposites, is free from attachment, and remains balanced in sorrow and joy, he is fit for the state of Brahman. When his mind is withdrawn from external contacts, and he finds delight only in the Self within himself, he is fit for the state of Brahman, having become tranquil. One who moves about without attachment, with the mind and senses controlled, and who abandons all undertakings, is said to be fit for the state of Brahman. When one casts off here and now both what is pleasant and what is unpleasant, he becomes, by that very fact, fit for the state of Brahman. For the Brahman-state is free from desire and devoid of dualities; it is the end of all action, and is defined as tranquility. Now begins the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Field and the Knower of the Field."

(Commentary by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Bhagavatpāda): In the seventh chapter, two natures (*prakṛti*) of the Lord were indicated: the lower one, consisting of the three *guṇas* and divided eightfold, which is the cause of transmigratory existence; and the higher, other [nature], which is the individual soul (*jīva*), characterized as the Lord who is the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*). By means of these two natures, the Lord attains the state of being the cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe. Now, the Chapter on the Field (*kṣetrādhyāya*) is commenced in order to determine the true nature of the Lord who possesses those two natures, by way of defining the two natures characterized as the Field and the Knower of the Field.

In the immediately preceding chapter, beginning with the words "One who is not hateful toward any being" (Gītā 12.13) and continuing until the conclusion of that chapter, it was stated how those renunciants who possess knowledge of reality abide—that is, what their state of perfection (*niṣṭhā*) is like. Now, this chapter is commenced for the purpose of explaining by what knowledge of reality they are endowed such that, through the practice of the aforementioned duties, they become dear to the Blessed One.

And primordial nature (prakṛti), which consists of the three guṇas, having transformed into the forms of all effects, instruments, and objects, combines with the Puruṣa in the form of the body, senses, and so forth, for the purpose of the Puruṣa’s experience and liberation. This very combination is this body.
Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "O son of Kuntī, this body is called the field (kṣetra)."
Those who know this call him the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).

The word "this" (*idam*), expressed by a pronoun, is specified as "the body" (*śarīram*). O Kaunteya! It is called "field" (*kṣetram*) because it protects from injury (*kṣata-trāṇāt*), because it perishes (*kṣayāt*), because it wastes away (*kṣaraṇāt*), and because the fruits of action are produced within it as in a field (*kṣetra-vat*). The word "iti" has the sense of the word "evam" (thus); thus, it is designated—that is, it is spoken of—as "the field."

He who knows—that is, discerns—this body as the field, making it an object of knowledge from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head through either innate or taught cognition, perceiving it part by part; him, the knower, they call, they declare, the "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*). The word *iti* here has the same meaning as the word *evam* (thus), as before. They say, "He is the knower of the field. Who? Those who know those two—the field and the knower of the field—are the "knowers thereof" (*tadvidaḥ*).
Thus, the field and the Knower of the Field have been described. Is it to be understood that they are to be known by this much knowledge alone? No, it is said:
"And know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O Bhārata."
That which is the knowledge of the field and the knower of the field—that, in my opinion, is true knowledge.

Know Me also as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Supreme Lord characterized as previously described, who is not subject to transmigratory existence. The intention is this: know that Knower of the Field—who, in all fields, is differentiated by the various limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the many fields from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—as being devoid of all distinctions of limiting adjuncts and beyond the reach of words and concepts such as "being" or "non-being."

O Bhārata! Since there remains nothing else within the scope of knowledge apart from the true nature of the field, the knower of the field, and the Lord, therefore that knowledge by which the field and the knower of the field—both of which are the objects of knowledge—are made the objects [of cognition], that knowledge is considered, according to my intention as the Lord Viṣṇu, to be perfect knowledge (samyag-jñāna).

Now, if it is argued that there is only one Lord in all fields (*kṣetra*) and no other enjoyer exists apart from Him, then it follows that the Lord Himself is subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*). Alternatively, since there would be no transmigrating being other than the Lord, it would follow that transmigratory existence itself does not exist. Both of these are undesirable, because they would render the scriptures concerning bondage, liberation, and their causes purposeless, and because they would contradict means of valid cognition such as direct perception. For, by direct perception, transmigratory existence—characterized by pleasure, pain, and their causes—is indeed apprehended.

Furthermore, because the diversity of the world is perceived, the cycle of transmigration (saṃsāra) is inferred to have merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma) as its cause. All of this is untenable if the Self and the Lord are one. Not so; for it is tenable due to the distinction between knowledge and ignorance. These two are far apart, opposite, and divergent: "That which is ignorance and that which is knowledge" (KaṭhU 1.2.4). Likewise, a contradictory difference in the fruits of those two objects—knowledge and ignorance—is also specified: "The beneficial (śreyas) and the pleasant (preyas)" (KaṭhU 1.2.2).

The domain of knowledge (*vidyā*) is the higher good (*śreyas*), whereas the lower good (*preyas*) is the product of ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus Vyāsa says: "Now, these two paths... and so forth, as well as "These indeed are the two paths," and so forth. Furthermore, two goals have been declared here; and it is understood from *śruti*, *smṛti*, and reasoning that ignorance, along with its effects, must be abandoned by means of knowledge. As for the *śruti* passages: "If one has known this here, then there is truth; if one has not known this here, there is great ruin" (Kena Upaniṣad 2.5).
"Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here; there is no other path for the journey," [TaittĀ 3.12] "the knower does not fear anything from any quarter. [TaittU 2.9]

But for the ignorant, there are such scriptural passages as: "Then fear comes upon him" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7), "Remaining in the midst of ignorance" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.5), "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9), and "He who thinks 'He is one and I am another' does not know; he is like an animal to the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10). Conversely, "He who knows the Self becomes all this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10), and "When [the Self] is like a skin... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.20)—such passages exist by the thousands.

And there are scriptural traditions (*smṛti*) such as: "Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; by that, living beings are deluded" (Gītā 5.15); "In this very world, rebirth is conquered by those whose minds are established in equanimity" (Gītā 5.19); and "For seeing the same everywhere" (Gītā 13.29), and so forth.
And according to reason (*nyāya*):
[one should avoid] snakes, the tips of *kuśa* grass, and likewise a well.
"Having understood this, men avoid it; some fall into it through ignorance. Behold the fruit of knowledge, how exceedingly distinguished it is! [Mbh 12.201.17] Thus it is said.

And thus, it is understood that the ignorant person, possessing the notion of a self in the body and so forth, impelled by passion, hatred, and the like, performs righteous and unrighteous deeds, and is born and dies; whereas those who perceive the self as distinct from the body and so forth, through the cessation of engagement in righteous and unrighteous deeds dependent upon the abandonment of passion, hatred, and the like, are liberated—this cannot be denied by anyone on the basis of reason.

This being so, although the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is indeed the Lord himself, he appears as if subject to transmigratory existence due to the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) created by ignorance (*avidyā*), just as the Self appears to have the nature of the body and so forth. For it is well known among all living beings that the certain identification of the Self with the body and other non-Self objects is produced by ignorance, just like the mistaken perception of a person in a tree-trunk. Yet, by this much, the attributes of the person do not belong to the tree-trunk, nor do the attributes of the tree-trunk belong to the person.

Likewise, it is not logical that consciousness is a property of the body, nor that qualities such as being composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion—which belong to the body—are properties of the conscious self. This is because there is no difference in their being produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), just like old age and death. If it is argued: "No, because the cases are not equal," [we reply: in the case of the post and the person, both are merely objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) which are superimposed (*adhyasta*) upon one another by the knower through ignorance. However, in the case of the body and the self, there is a mutual superimposition between two things that are respectively object and subject of knowledge (*jñeya-jñātṛ*). Thus, the illustration is not equivalent.

If it is argued that, for this reason, even though they are objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), the attributes of the body belong to the knower, the Self (*ātman*), we say no; for that would entail the consequence of [the Self] being insentient and so forth. For if the attributes of the knowable field (*kṣetra*)—such as pleasure, pain, delusion, desire, and the like—belonged to the knower, then one would have to state the specific reason why some attributes of the knowable field, such as pleasure and the like, belong to the Self as superimpositions of ignorance (*avidyādhyāropita*), while others, such as old age and death, do not. There exists an inference that they do not belong to it, because they are superimpositions of ignorance, just like old age and death, and because they are things to be abandoned (*heya*) or things to be accepted (*upādeya*), and so on.

This being so, transmigratory existence—characterized by agency and enjoyership—is situated in the object of knowledge and is superimposed upon the knower through ignorance; therefore, the knower is not affected in the least by it. It is just as the sky is not affected by such qualities as having a surface or being soiled, though these are superimposed upon it by the ignorant. This being the case, even though the Blessed Lord, the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), exists in all fields, not even a trace of his being subject to transmigratory existence is to be suspected. For nowhere in the world is it observed that anyone is benefited or harmed by a quality superimposed through ignorance.

As for what was said—that the illustrative example is not analogous—that is incorrect. Why? Because it is only the commonality of being a mere superimposition (*adhyāsa*) due to ignorance (*avidyā*) that is intended as the point of similarity between the example and the subject; that [commonality] does not fail. As for your thought that [the analogy] fails in the case of the knower, its lack of exclusivity (*anaikāntikatva*) has already been demonstrated by means of old age and other such factors.

If it is argued that the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field) is subject to transmigratory existence because of possessing ignorance (*avidyā*), we say no; for ignorance is of the nature of darkness (*tāmasa*). Indeed, a cognition characterized by darkness is ignorance, because its essence is obscuration; it either apprehends things erroneously, gives rise to doubt, or consists of non-apprehension. This is because these do not exist when the light of discrimination is present, and because the three forms of ignorance—non-apprehension and the rest—are observed only when there is a defect such as cataracts, which is dark in nature and obscuring.

To this it is said: "In that case, ignorance (*avidyā*) must be a property of the knower. No; for defects such as cataracts (*taimirikatva*) are observed in the eye, which is an instrument (*karaṇa*). As for your thought that ignorance is a property of the knower, and that the state of being a transmigrating soul (*saṃsāritva*) consists precisely in the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) possessing the property of ignorance—therefore, what was stated [by you], that the Knower of the Field is indeed the Lord (*īśvara*) and not a transmigrator, is incorrect—that is not so. For it is seen that defects such as erroneous perception reside in the instrument, namely the eye.

Neither the apprehension of objects in a distorted manner nor the defects such as cataracts (timira) that cause it belong to the grasper; for when the cataract is removed by the refinement of the eye, they are no longer seen in the grasper. Thus, just as it is not a property of the grasper, so too in all cases, non-apprehension, distorted cognition, and doubt—along with their causes—must belong only to some instrument (karaṇa), and not to the knower, the *kṣetrajña*. Furthermore, because these are objects of consciousness, like the light of a lamp, they cannot be properties of the knower.

Precisely because it is an object of cognition, it must be cognized by something distinct from its own self; for even in the state of liberation (*kaivalya*), which is characterized by the disjunction of all instruments of perception, no proponent of any philosophical school accepts that the Self possesses defects such as ignorance (*avidyā*). If the Self, as the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), were [inherently] like the heat of fire...

Since this is the nature of the Self, there can never be a separation from it. Furthermore, because the Self is immutable, all-pervading like space, and formless, conjunction with or disjunction from anything else is logically impossible; thus, the eternality of the Knower of the Field's lordship (īśvaratva) is established. This is also confirmed by scriptural statements concerning the Lord, such as: "Because of being beginningless, because of being devoid of qualities" (Gītā 13.31).

If it is argued that this being so, there would be the fault of the scriptures becoming useless and so forth due to the absence of transmigratory existence and a transmigrating self, we say no. For this fault is admitted by everyone. Indeed, a fault accepted by all proponents of the self (*ātmavādin*) need not be remedied by anyone alone. How is it accepted? For the absence of the conventional usage of "transmigratory existence" and "transmigrating self" in the case of liberated selves is desired by all proponents of the self alike; yet they do not admit that the fault of the scriptures becoming useless and so forth applies to those [liberated ones].

Likewise, for us, even though the knowers of the field (kṣetrajña) are one with the Lord, let the scriptures be purposeless [from the ultimate standpoint]; yet they possess purpose within the domain of ignorance (avidyā). Just as for all dualists, the scriptures and so forth have purpose only during the state of bondage and not in the state of liberation, so it is here.

[Objection: Surely, for all dualists, the states of bondage and liberation of the self are real entities from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Therefore, since there exists that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be attained, along with the means thereto, the scriptures and so forth would possess purpose and validity. However, for the non-dualists (*advaitins*), because duality is not ultimately real and because the state of bondage of the self is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*) and thus not ultimately real, the scriptures and so forth would be purposeless due to a lack of a valid object (*nirviṣayatva*). [Reply: This is not so, because it is logically impossible for the self to undergo a change of states.

If, first of all, the states of bondage and liberation of the self were to occur, they would have to be either simultaneous or successive. They cannot be simultaneous because of their mutual contradiction, just as staying and moving cannot coexist in one and the same thing. As for their being successive, are they causeless or with a cause? If they were causeless, it would follow that liberation is impossible. If they were with a cause, since such a cause does not exist inherently, it follows that they are not ultimately real. And this being the case, there would be a abandonment of your own tenet.

Furthermore, when determining the sequence between the states of bondage and liberation, the state of bondage must be conceived as preceding it; yet that [state] would be both beginningless and finite, which contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Likewise, the state of liberation would have to be accepted as having a beginning and being infinite, which likewise contradicts valid means of knowledge. Moreover, it is impossible to establish the permanence of that which possesses states and undergoes transition from one state to another. Now, if one does not conceive of a distinction between the states of bondage and liberation in order to avoid the fault of impermanence—

Therefore, even for the dualists, defects such as the futility of the scriptures are indeed unavoidable; thus, since the situation is the same, this defect need not be refuted by the proponent of non-duality.

Nor is the scripture purposeless, because the scripture has as its subject those persons who are not yet enlightened, according to their established [ignorance]. For the ignorant indeed perceive the fruit and the cause—which are non-self—as the Self, whereas this is not the case for the enlightened. For when the enlightened perceive the Self as distinct from the fruit and the cause, it is impossible for them to perceive those two as "I," that is, as the Self. Indeed, even one who is utterly deluded, such as a madman, does not perceive identity between water and fire, or between shadow and light; how much less so, then, one who possesses discrimination?

Therefore, the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions does not apply to one who perceives the Self as distinct from both the fruit and the cause. For when someone is enjoined to a certain action with the words, "Devadatta, you do this," a person standing nearby, even while hearing that injunction, does not think, "I, Viṣṇumitra, am enjoined. Such a realization would only occur if there were a failure to grasp the distinction between the subject of the injunction and the object of the injunction; the same applies to the fruit and the cause.

[Objection: Is it not indeed appropriate that the understanding of the subject matter of the scripture should be based on ordinary worldly relations—even when there is the realization of the Self as distinct from the body, its causes, and its fruits—given that one thinks, "I am impelled toward what has desirable fruits and causes, and I am restrained from what has undesirable fruits and causes"? Just as, for example, fathers, sons, and others, despite perceiving their mutual difference as selves, still understand the meaning of injunctions and prohibitions directed at one another? [Reply: No.

Because the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding the cause and the fruit is established even prior to the realization of the view of a separate Self; for it is one who has already understood the meaning of injunctions and prohibitions who realizes the Self’s distinctness from the cause and the fruit, not one previously. Therefore, it is established that the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions has as its domain the ignorant person.

If it is argued that, because those who perceive the self as distinct from the body would not engage in such acts as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*) [Āp. ŚrS. 10.2.1], while those who view the body and so forth as the sole self would likewise not engage, there is therefore an absence of an agent and the scriptures would be purposeless—this is not so. For engagement and withdrawal are possible precisely according to what is conventionally accepted. To begin with, the knower of Brahman, who perceives the identity of the Lord and the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*), does not engage in action.

Likewise, even one who propounds selflessness does not fail to act on the grounds that there is no other world; rather, having inferred the existence of a self through the fact that the hearing of scriptures prescribing injunctions and prohibitions would otherwise be inexplicable, such a person—who is ignorant of the specific nature of the self but has developed a thirst for the fruits of action—engages in activity out of faith. Thus, [the existence of a self] is not perceived by everyone. Therefore, the scriptures are not purposeless.

If it is argued that because those who possess discernment (*vivekin*) are seen to abstain from action, the scriptures would become useless since those who follow them would likewise abstain, we say: no. This is because discernment arises only in some individuals; for among many living beings, only a rare few might possess discernment, just as is the case now. Furthermore, the deluded do not follow the discerning, because activity is dependent upon defects such as passion (*rāga*) and the like, as is observed in activities such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), and because activity proceeds from one's own nature (*svabhāva*). For it has been said: "But it is nature that acts" (Gītā 5.14).

Therefore, saṃsāra is merely ignorance (avidyā), pertaining only to the object as it is perceived. Ignorance and its effects do not belong to the isolated Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). Furthermore, false knowledge is not capable of defiling an ultimate reality; for the water of a mirage cannot turn a salt-flat into mud by means of moisture. Likewise, ignorance can do nothing to the Knower of the Field. It is for this reason that it has been said: "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field," and "Knowledge is enveloped by ignorance" (Gītā 5.15).

Now, why is it that even among the learned there is this notion—"I am thus," "this is mine"—as if they were worldly transmigrators? Listen: this is their so-called learning, which consists in perceiving the Self as being nothing other than the field (*kṣetra*). If, however, they were to perceive the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) as changeless, then they would not desire enjoyment or action, thinking, "may this be mine. For enjoyment and action are themselves modifications. This being the case, the ignorant person engages in activity because of a desire for results.

Furthermore, for the wise person who perceives the self as changeless, since there is an absence of desire for results, activity is untenable; thus, when the functioning of the aggregate of causes and effects ceases, it is figuratively described as "cessation."

Furthermore, let someone else possess this kind of "wisdom": "The Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is indeed the Lord (*īśvara*). The Field (*kṣetra*) is something other than that, being the object of the Knower of the Field alone. But I am a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*), subject to pleasure and pain. The cessation of my transmigration must be achieved through the knowledge of the Field and the Knower of the Field, and by directly realizing the Lord—the Knower of the Field—through meditation, and by abiding in His very nature. He who understands in this way, and he who teaches it, is not the Knower of the Field.

He who, thinking thus, says, "I shall establish the meaningfulness of the scripture regarding both saṃsāra and liberation," is a false scholar. Being himself deluded, he destroys his own self and deludes others as well, because he is devoid of the traditional transmission of the meaning of the scriptures; he does so by discarding what is heard [in the texts] and imagining what is not heard. Therefore, one who does not know the tradition should be disregarded like a fool, even if he is a knower of all the scriptures.

As for what was said—that if the Lord were one with the individual knower (kṣetrajña), he would become subject to transmigratory existence (saṃsāritva); and if the individual knowers were one with the Lord, there would be an absence of transmigratory beings, leading to the consequence of the non-existence of transmigratory existence—these two faults have been answered by the acceptance of the distinction between knowledge (vidyā) and ignorance (avidyā). How so? Because the ultimate reality, which is the object of that [knowledge], is not defiled by a defect imagined through ignorance. And thus the illustration has been shown: a desert region is not turned into mud by the water of a mirage.

The fault of the undesirable consequence that cyclic existence would not exist because of the non-existence of a transmigrating being has also been refuted by the demonstration that both cyclic existence and the transmigrating being are constructed by ignorance.

If it be argued that the very possession of ignorance is the defect of transmigratory existence for the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), and that the resulting states of happiness, suffering, and so forth are perceived through direct experience—[we reply: no. For whatever belongs to the object of knowledge is a property of the Field (*kṣetra*); since the Knower of the Field is the subject of knowledge, it is impossible for him to possess defects produced by that [Field]. Whatever collection of defects you impute to the Knower of the Field while he does not actually possess them, because those are logically established as objects of knowledge, they are necessarily properties of the Field alone, not properties of the Knower of the Field.

And the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is not defiled by that, because a conjunction between the object of knowledge and the knower is impossible. For if there were such a conjunction, its very status as an object of knowledge would be untenable. If ignorance, suffering, and so forth were attributes of the Self, how, my friend, could they be perceived through direct experience? Or how could they be attributes of the Knower of the Field?

When it is established that the entire field (*kṣetra*) is the object of knowledge and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is the subject who knows, then to assert that ignorance, suffering, and so forth are attributes of the knower of the field—that is, qualities belonging to the *kṣetrajña*—and that these are perceived through direct experience, is a contradiction stated solely on the basis of a reliance upon mere ignorance.

Here it is asked: "To whom does that ignorance belong? [The answer is: "It belongs to him by whom it is perceived. [Objection: "By whom is it perceived? To this it is said: The question "To whom does ignorance belong? is meaningless. How so? If ignorance is perceived, you also perceive its possessor. And when the possessor is apprehended, the question "To whom does it belong? is not appropriate. For when one who possesses cows is apprehended, the question "Whose are the cows? does not become meaningful.

Is it not the case that the illustration is dissimilar? Since cows and their owner are perceptible, their relationship is also perceptible; therefore, the question is pointless. It is not so with ignorance and its possessor, for they are not perceptible, such that the question would be pointless. Even if the relationship between ignorance and the ignorant one were known through something imperceptible, what would be gained by you? Since ignorance is the cause of misfortune, it ought to be abandoned. He who possesses ignorance will abandon it.

[Objection: "Surely ignorance belongs to me alone. [Reply: Then you must know ignorance as well as the self that possesses it. [Objection: "I do know them, but not through direct perception (pratyakṣa). [Reply: If you know them through inference (anumāna), how is the apprehension of their relationship possible? For at that time, a relationship between you, the knower, and ignorance—which has become an object of knowledge—cannot be apprehended, since the knower is occupied solely with ignorance as its object. Nor is it possible for there to be another cognition, distinct from the primary one, which could grasp the relationship between the knower and ignorance, nor could there be a further cognition having that [relationship] as its object.

Because it would lead to an infinite regress. If the connection between the knower and the object of knowledge were itself known by another knower, then yet another knower would have to be postulated, and for that one another, and for that one another—an infinite regress that cannot be avoided. However, if ignorance is the object of knowledge, or whatever else is the object of knowledge, it is simply an object of knowledge; likewise, the knower is simply a knower and does not become an object of knowledge. And when this is so, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who is the true knower, is not affected in the least by ignorance, suffering, and the like.

Is it not the case that this very same fault remains—namely, that the knower is a field (*kṣetra*) possessed of defects? No; for the status of being a knower is merely a figurative designation (*upacāra*) applied to that which is of the nature of consciousness itself and is changeless. Just as the action of heating is figuratively attributed to fire by virtue of its mere heat, so it is here. Thus, the Blessed One has shown that the absence of the nature of action, agent, and fruit in the Self is inherent to it; rather, it is only action, agency, and so forth, superimposed through ignorance (*avidyā*), that are figuratively attributed to the Self.

Likewise, this has been shown in various contexts such as [Gītā 2.19]: "He who knows him as the slayer," [Gītā 3.27]: "Actions are performed in every way by the qualities of *prakṛti*," and [Gītā 5.15]: "He does not take on the sin of anyone," and so forth. We have explained it accordingly, and we shall demonstrate it further in subsequent sections.

Well then! Since the nature of action, agent, and fruit does not exist in the Self by its own nature, and since it is merely superimposed through ignorance, it follows that ritual acts are to be performed only by the ignorant, and not by the wise. This is indeed correct; we shall demonstrate this very point under the verse, "For one who bears a body, [it is] not possible" (18.11). Furthermore, we shall show it specifically in the section summarizing the meaning of the entire scripture, under the verse, "O Kaunteya, the supreme steadfastness in knowledge" (18.50), where we shall treat it in brief. Enough with this extensive elaboration; thus the discussion is concluded.

This summary verse—beginning with "That field, what it is," and so forth—is presented as a recapitulation of the subject matter of the Chapter on the Field (*kṣetrādhyāya*), which was taught in the verse beginning with "This body" (*idaṃ śarīram*). For it is proper to present a summary of the meaning one intends to explain.
Thus: "That field, what it is, of what nature, what its modifications are, and from whence it arises..."
Hear from me in brief who he is and what his power is.

He refers by that pronoun "that" to what was indicated as "this body. And he refers to what was indicated as "this field" by the phrase "of what kind," meaning of what nature it is through its own attributes. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction. "Yadvikāri" means that which undergoes modification; "yataḥ" means from which [cause] and "yat" means that effect which is produced—this is the completion of the sentence.

And as for that Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) who has been pointed out—he is "of such power," meaning he possesses those powers which are capacities produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Listen from my words to that true nature of the Field and the Knower of the Field as it has been specifically described, in brief—that is, in summary. The meaning is: having heard it, retain it in your mind.
He praises that true nature of the field and the knower of the field which he intends to expound, for the purpose of stimulating the listeners' interest:
"It has been sung by the seers in many ways, separately, in various Vedic meters."
And also by means of the words of the Brahma-sūtras, which are reasoned and definitive.

It has been sung—that is, described—in many ways and in various manners by the sages, such as Vasiṣṭha and others; it has been sung separately and with discernment through diverse meters, such as the Ṛg-veda and others, and in manifold states and various modes.

Furthermore, "by the words of the Brahma-sūtras"—the *brahmasūtra* are those statements that indicate Brahman; they are called "words" (*padaiḥ*) because by them one proceeds, goes, or knows. It follows that by these very [words] the true nature of the field and the knower of the field has been sung. By such words of the Brahma-sūtras as "One should meditate [on Him] as the Self alone," the Self is known.
They are "possessed of reason" (*hetumat*), meaning they are joined with logic, well-determined, free from doubt, and capable of producing a firm conviction. (BhG 13.4)
To Arjuna, who had become inclined toward praise, the Blessed One said: "The great elements, egoism, intellect, and the unmanifest alone..."
The senses are eleven, and the objects of the senses are five.

The *mahābhūtāni* (great elements) are both "great" because they pervade all modifications and "elements" (*bhūtāni*) because they are subtle. However, their gross forms will be designated by the term "objects of the senses. *Ahaṃkāra* (ego) is the cause of the great elements, characterized by the notion of "I. The cause of *ahaṃkāra* is *buddhi* (intellect), characterized by determination (*adhyavasāya*). Its cause is the *avyakta* (unmanifest) itself; it is not manifest (*vyakta*), hence it is called *avyakta*, the unevolved, the power of the Lord (*īśvara-śakti*), as it has been said: "My *māyā* is difficult to overcome."

The word *eva* (only) has the sense of restriction regarding the primordial nature (*prakṛti*): "the primordial nature is divided into only this many [eightfold]. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of a conjunction of divisions. The senses (*indriyāṇi*) are ten: the five beginning with hearing are the organs of cognition (*buddhīndriyāṇi*) because they produce cognition; the five beginning with speech and hands are the organs of action (*karmendriyāṇi*) because they accomplish action. Those are ten. And one. What is that? The mind (*manaḥ*), which consists of volition and so forth, is the eleventh. And the five objects of the senses—the spheres such as sound and the rest. These, the Sāṃkhyas declare, are the twenty-four principles (*tattva*).

Now, regarding those things which the Vaiśeṣikas call the "qualities of the self," the Blessed One declares that these too are indeed attributes of the field (kṣetra) and not of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña): desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, consciousness, and fortitude.
This field has been briefly described along with its modifications.

Desire (*icchā*) is that by which, having previously perceived an object of a certain kind as a cause of pleasure, one, upon perceiving another object of that same kind, desires to take hold of it because it is a cause of pleasure. This desire is a property of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇadharma*), and because it is an object of knowledge (*jñeyatvāt*), it is the field (*kṣetra*). Likewise, aversion (*dveṣa*): having experienced an object of a certain kind as a cause of pain, one, upon perceiving another object of that same kind, feels aversion toward it. This aversion, being an object of knowledge, is likewise the field.

Likewise, pleasure (*sukha*), which is favorable and consists of a serene state of being, is indeed the field (*kṣetra*) because it is an object of knowledge. Pain (*duḥkha*), which is of a contrary nature, is also the field because it too is an object of knowledge. The "conglomeration" (*saṃghāta*) is the collection of the body and the senses; within that, the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) becomes manifest, like fire in a heated lump of iron. Consciousness (*cetanā*) is that which is permeated by the flavor of the reflection of the self's consciousness (*ātma-caitanya-ābhāsa-rasa-viddhā*); and that too is the field because it is an object of knowledge. Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is that by which the body and senses, when they have reached a state of exhaustion, are sustained.

And that [body] is the "field" because it is an object of knowledge. The mention of desire and so forth is for the purpose of indicating all the attributes of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). Therefore, he concludes by saying "this": "This field," along with its modifications—that is, together with the modifications such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest—has been briefly declared or described.

That aggregate of various elements born from the field, which was stated to be "this body is the field" (Gītā 13.2), has been explained as the field (*kṣetra*) divided into the distinctions of the great elements and so forth, ending with fortitude (*dhṛti*). As for the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), whose specific characteristics will be described later—the realization of that powerful Knower of the Field brings about immortality—the Blessed Lord himself will describe him with his specific attributes in the passage beginning with, "I shall declare that which is to be known" (Gītā 13.12).

Now, however, the Blessed Lord prescribes that group of means for attaining that knowledge—characterized by humility and so forth—which, when present, makes one fit and qualified for the realization of that which is to be known; and intent upon which the renunciant is called one established in knowledge. Because they are the means to knowledge, He designates this group beginning with humility as "knowledge" itself:
Humility, unpretentiousness, non-violence, forbearance, uprightness, service to the teacher, purity, steadfastness, and self-control. (BhG 13.7)

Humility (*amānitva*) is the absence of the state of pride; pride is the praising of oneself, and its absence is humility. Freedom from ostentation (*adambhitva*) is the absence of hypocrisy, which is the public display of one's own religious duties. Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the non-affliction of living beings. Forbearance (*kṣānti*) is the absence of agitation when encountering the offenses of others. Straightforwardness (*ārjava*) is the state of being upright, the absence of crookedness. Service to the teacher (*ācāryopāsana*) is the attendance upon the teacher—who instructs in the means to liberation—through acts such as listening with reverence.

Purity (*śauca*) is the washing away of bodily impurities with earth and water; and internal purity is the removal of the impurities of passion and the like from the mind through the cultivation of their opposites. Steadfastness (*sthairya*) is the state of being firm, consisting of having made a firm resolve for the path to liberation alone. Self-restraint (*ātmavinigraha*) is the restraining of that aggregate of causes and effects—which is denoted by the word "self" and acts as its own adversary—by checking its natural tendency to proceed everywhere and confining it solely to the right path.
Furthermore: detachment from the objects of the senses and indeed the absence of egoism;
The contemplation of the defects of suffering inherent in birth, death, old age, and disease.

Vairāgya (dispassion) is the state of detachment toward the objects of the senses—sound and so forth—which are both seen and unseen enjoyments. Anahaṃkāra is simply the absence of egoism. Janmamṛtyujarāvyādhiduḥkhadoṣānudarśana is the observation of the defects in each of these, beginning with birth and ending with suffering: namely, birth, death, old age, diseases, and sufferings. Regarding birth, the defect is the emergence through the gateway of the womb while dwelling in the embryo; the observation (*anudarśana*) of that is its contemplation. Likewise, there is the observation of the defects in death.

Likewise, in old age, there is the observation of the defects consisting in the obstruction of wisdom, power, and vitality, as well as being treated with contempt. Likewise, in diseases such as headaches and the like, there is the observation of their defects. Likewise, in sufferings caused by internal, elemental, and divine factors—or rather, suffering itself is the defect, which is the "defect of suffering," and the observation of this [defect] in birth and so forth is as previously described: birth is suffering, death is suffering, old age is suffering, and diseases are suffering.

Because they are the cause of suffering, birth and the rest are suffering, but not because they are suffering by their very nature. Thus, through the perception of the defect of suffering in birth and the rest, detachment arises toward the enjoyment of objects such as the body and the senses. Thereafter, the instruments (the senses) turn toward the inner self for the sake of the vision of the Self. In this way, the perception of the defect of suffering in birth and the rest is called "knowledge" because it is a cause of knowledge. || BhG 13.8 ||
Furthermore: non-attachment and lack of clinging toward children, wife, home, and so forth;
And constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant.

Non-attachment (*asakti*) is the absence of attachment; attachment is merely a sense of fondness for objects that cause clinging. Non-attachment is the absence of such attachment. Attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*) is indeed a specific form of attachment characterized by the identification of oneself with another. For example: "When another is happy or miserable, I alone am happy or miserable; when he lives or dies, I alone live or shall die. Where does this occur? He says: "In children, wife, home, and so forth."

"Among sons, wives, homes, and—by the inclusion of the word 'etcetera'—among other things that are extremely dear, such as the group of servants and so forth; and both of these [the former and the latter] are called 'knowledge' because they serve the purpose of knowledge. Furthermore, there is constant equanimity of mind, which is the state of having an equal mind. Where? In the occurrence of the desirable and the undesirable—the occurrences or attainments of both the desirable and the undesirable—in those occurrences of the desirable and the undesirable, there is always an equal state of mind. One does not rejoice in the occurrence of the desirable, nor does one become agitated in the occurrence of the undesirable. And this constant equanimity of mind is knowledge. (BhG 13.9)
Furthermore,
there is unswerving devotion to me through the yoga of exclusive concentration.
Dwelling in solitary places and a lack of delight in the assembly of people. BhG 13.10.

When there is [devotion] toward Me, the Lord, through *ananya-yoga*—that is, through non-dual meditative absorption (*apṛthak-samādhi*)—the conviction that "there is nothing else superior to the Blessed Vāsudeva; therefore, He alone is our refuge" constitutes *ananya-yoga*, which is a firm and unerring intellect. Devotion (*bhakti*) is worship by means of that [intellect], being non-deviating (*avyabhicāriṇī*), meaning it does not have the nature of wavering. And that [devotion] is knowledge. It consists in resorting to a secluded place.

A secluded place (*vivikta-deśa*) is one that is isolated by its very nature or by its conditioned state—such as being free from impurities and the like, or devoid of snakes, tigers, and so forth—and is a location such as a forest, a riverbank, or a temple. One whose habit is to resort to such a place is a "resortant of secluded places" (*vivikta-deśa-sevī*); the state of being such is "the practice of resorting to secluded places. For it is in secluded places that the mind becomes serene; because of that, the cultivation of the Self and other [principles] arises in solitude. Therefore, resorting to secluded places is called knowledge (*jñāna*). Dislike (*aratih*) means a lack of delight in the assembly of people.

The assembly or gathering of common people who are devoid of refinement and undisciplined is called *janasaṃsat*. It is not the assembly of those who possess refinement and are disciplined, because such an assembly is conducive to knowledge. Therefore, detachment from the assembly of common people is "knowledge" (*jñāna*), since its purpose is the attainment of knowledge.
Furthermore:
"Constancy in the knowledge of the inner self, and the vision of the goal that is the knowledge of reality."
This is declared to be knowledge; ignorance is that which is otherwise than this.

"Constancy in the knowledge of the inner self" (*adhyātmajñānanityatva*): Knowledge concerning the self and so forth is "knowledge of the inner self"; constancy is the state of being constant toward that. True knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) is the cause for the ripening of the cultivation of the means to knowledge, such as humility (*amānitva*) and the rest. Its "object" (*artha*) is liberation, which is the cessation of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). "Vision of the object of true knowledge" (*tattvajñānārthadarśana*) is the contemplation of that [liberation]. For it is only when one perceives the fruit of true knowledge that there arises engagement in the practice of its means.

This, beginning with non-pride and ending with the vision of the truth of the meaning of knowledge, has been declared as "knowledge" because it serves the purpose of knowledge. Ignorance (ajñāna) is that which is other than this aforementioned [knowledge], being its opposite: pride, hypocrisy, violence, lack of forbearance, crookedness, and so forth; this is to be understood as ignorance for the sake of its avoidance, since it is the cause of the progression of saṃsāra. || BhG 13.11 ||
In response to the inquiry, "What is that which is to be known by means of the knowledge [previously] described?", he says:
"I shall declare that which is to be known, knowing which one attains immortality."
The supreme Brahman is without beginning; it is said to be neither being nor non-being.

But surely, the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), such as humility (*amānitva*) and so forth, are not by means of them that the Knowable is known. For humility and the like are never seen to be the delimiters (*paricchedaka*) of any object whatsoever. And in every case, it is observed that only that knowledge which has a particular thing as its object is the delimiter of that very knowable object. Indeed, one thing is not perceived by a knowledge whose object is something else, just as fire is not perceived by a knowledge whose object is a jar. This is not a fault; for we have already stated that they are called "knowledge" because they are the instrumental causes (*nimitta*) of knowledge.

And because it is a cooperative cause for knowledge: that which is to be known (*jñeya*)—that which ought to be known—I shall declare, that is, I shall explain thoroughly and correctly. What is its fruit? To attract the listener by means of such praise, he says: "Having known that which is to be known, one attains immortality (*amṛta*)," the meaning being that one does not die again. "Without beginning" (*anādimat*): that which has a beginning is "with beginning" (*ādimat*); that which does not have a beginning is "without beginning. What is that? It is the supreme, unsurpassed Brahman, which is the subject under discussion as "that which is to be known."

In this regard, some divide the compound as *anādimat-param*, arguing that since the meaning has already been expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the addition of the possessive suffix *-mat-* would be redundant and undesirable. They further demonstrate a specific meaning: "That whose supreme power (*parā śakti*) is called Vāsudeva—that is *matparam*. It is true that in this way there would be no tautology, provided such a meaning is possible.

But that meaning is not possible, because Brahman is intended to be made known precisely through the negation of all specific attributes, as in the statement: "It is said to be neither being nor non-being. To demonstrate the possession of specific powers and yet to negate those specific attributes is a contradiction. Therefore, although the possessive suffix *matup* has the same meaning as a *bahuvrīhi* compound, its use here is for the sake of completing the verse. Having drawn [the listener] toward the subject by means of an incentive—namely, "The knowable, which has immortality as its fruit, will be spoken of by me"—he says: "That knowable is not said to be being, nor is it said to be non-being."

Objection: Having proclaimed with great preparation and a loud voice that "I shall declare the Knowable," you have stated something inconsistent when you say, "That which is not existent is called non-existent. Response: No, what was said is indeed consistent. How so? For in all the Upanishads, the Knowable—Brahman—is indicated solely through the negation of specific attributes, such as "not this, not this" (BU 2.3.6) and "neither gross nor subtle" (BU 3.8.8), because it is beyond the reach of speech, such that one cannot say "this is it."

Is it not the case that there is no such thing which is not denoted by the word "exists"? If it is not denoted by the word "exists," then it is not an object of knowledge (*jñeya*). And it is a contradiction to say that it is an object of knowledge and yet is not denoted by the word "exists. It is certainly not non-existent, because it is not an object of the cognition of non-existence.

Is it not the case that all cognitions are indeed accompanied by the notions of "existence" or "non-existence"? This being so, the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) would also have to be either the object of a cognition accompanied by the notion of existence, or the object of a cognition accompanied by the notion of non-existence. No; because, due to its being beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*), it is not the object of cognitions accompanied by either of those two notions. For whatever object is accessible to the senses, such as a jar and the like, that may be the object of a cognition accompanied by the notion of existence, or it may be the object of a cognition accompanied by the notion of non-existence.

However, this [reality] must be understood as being beyond the reach of the senses; because it is accessible through verbal testimony (*śabda*) alone as its sole means of valid cognition, it is not an object of a cognition that conforms to both [subjective and objective] cognitions like a jar or similar things. Therefore, it is said to be neither existent nor non-existent.

As for what was said—that "that which is to be known is called neither existent nor non-existent" is a contradiction—it is not a contradiction, because of the Śruti: "It is indeed other than the known, and moreover above the unknown" (KenU 1.3). If it is argued that even this Śruti has a contradictory meaning—just as in the case of beginning the sacrificial hall for a sacrifice and then saying, "Who indeed knows whether he exists in that world or not? (TaittS 6.1.1)—we say no.

Because the scriptural statement regarding [Brahman] being other than both the known and the unknown is intent upon establishing an object that must necessarily be known, the passage beginning with "If in this" and so forth is merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) supplementary to an injunction. Furthermore, for the sake of logical consistency, Brahman is not denoted by such terms as "existent" (*sat*) or "non-existent" (*asat*).

For every word, when employed to illuminate an object and heard by listeners, conveys its meaning by means of genus (*jāti*), action (*kriyā*), quality (*guṇa*), or relation (*saṃbandha*), depending upon the apprehension of convention (*saṃketa*); it does not do so otherwise, for such a thing has never been observed. For example: "cow" or "horse" is by way of genus; "cooks" or "reads" is by way of action; "white" or "black" is by way of quality; "wealthy" or "owner of cows" is by way of relation. But Brahman does not possess a genus; therefore, it is not denotable by words such as "existent" (*sat*) and the like.

Nor is it possessed of qualities, such that it could be denoted by a word expressing a quality, because it is devoid of qualities. Nor is it expressible by a word signifying action, because it is actionless, according to the scriptural text: "Partless, actionless, tranquil" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19). Nor is it related to anything else, because of its oneness. And since it is non-dual, beyond the reach of objects, and is the Self itself, it is logical that it cannot be expressed by any word whatsoever, as also stated in such scriptural passages as: "From which words turn back" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9).

Because it is not the object of the word or the notion "existent," there may be a doubt regarding its non-existence; therefore, in order to dispel that doubt by demonstrating the existence of the Knowable through the medium of the adjuncts of the organs of all living beings, [the Lord] says:
"It has hands and feet everywhere; it has eyes, heads, and faces everywhere."
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, it stands encompassing all.

"Having hands and feet everywhere": that which is to be known is "having hands and feet everywhere," meaning it has hands and feet on all sides. The existence of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is manifested through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the organs of all living beings. And the Knower of the Field is designated by means of the limiting adjunct of the field (*kṣetra*). Furthermore, the field is divided in many ways by hands, feet, and so forth. The entire collection of specific distinctions produced by the differences of the field's limiting adjuncts is merely illusory for the Knower of the Field; thus, by removing those [adjuncts], its state of being the object of knowledge is stated. It is said: "It is neither existent nor non-existent."

Although the form produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is false, it is spoken of as being like a property of the object of knowledge (*jñeyadharma*), having been conceptually constructed for the sake of comprehending its existence; thus it is said, "hands and feet everywhere," and so forth. For there is this statement of those who know the tradition: "The non-proliferated (*niṣprapañca*) is made manifest through superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and negation (*apavāda*). Hands, feet, and the rest, which are perceived everywhere as belonging to all bodily parts, are the effects of their own respective causes—the presence of the power of the object of knowledge. Thus, they are figuratively called "signs" (*liṅga*) of the existence of the object of knowledge.

The rest should be explained in the same way. That Knowable is "having hands and feet everywhere. It has eyes, heads, and faces on all sides; that which possesses eyes, heads, and faces on every side is "having eyes, heads, and faces everywhere. It is "possessing ears everywhere"; *śruti* means the sense of hearing—that which possesses it is "possessing ears. In the world, among the multitude of living beings, it stands pervading and encompassing everything.

This verse is commenced for the purpose of ensuring that there be no suspicion that the object of knowledge possesses those [attributes], due to the superimposition of the sense organs such as the hands and feet which serve as its limiting adjuncts (upādhi):
"It appears through the qualities of all the senses, yet it is devoid of all senses."
It is unattached yet the sustainer of all; devoid of qualities, yet the experiencer of the qualities.

It manifests as the qualities of all the senses; and "all those senses" refers to the ears and so forth, known as the organs of perception and the organs of action, as well as the internal organs—the intellect (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*)—since they are equal in being limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for the object of knowledge. Thus, they are included by the term "all the senses."

Moreover, since even the ears and other external organs possess the status of being limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) only by way of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the Self shines forth through all the qualities of the senses—which serve as adjuncts for both the internal and external organs—such as determination (*adhyavasāya*), volition (*saṃkalpa*), hearing, and speaking. Thus, the meaning is that the Knowable (*jñeya*) appears as possessing the qualities of all the senses, as if engaged in the activities of all the senses; this is in accordance with the Śruti: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7).

For what reason, then, is it not perceived as being active? To this he says: "devoid of all sense organs," meaning it is devoid of all instruments of action. Therefore, that object of knowledge is not active through the operations of the instruments. As for this mantra: "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper; He sees without eyes and hears without ears" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19), and so forth.

This is intended to demonstrate that the Knowable possesses the power to assume qualities in accordance with the adjuncts of all the sense organs; it is not, however, intended to show that it directly possesses activities such as moving and so forth. The meaning of this mantra is like the meaning of the mantra beginning with "The blind man found a jewel" (TaittĀ 1.11). Since the Knowable is devoid of all instruments, it is therefore unattached, being free from all connection. Even though it is so, it nevertheless supports all things.

For everything has its locus everywhere, because it is followed by the cognition of existence; indeed, even mirages and the like do not exist without a locus. Therefore, it sustains all, as it is said: "it bears everything. Furthermore, there is this other gateway for attaining the reality of the Knowable: that Knowable is devoid of the *guṇas*—that is, it is free from the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; nevertheless, it is the enjoyer of the *guṇas*, meaning that Knowable is the experiencer and perceiver of the *guṇas*—namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—which, through the medium of sound and the other sense objects, transform into the forms of pleasure, pain, and delusion. This is the meaning.
Furthermore,
it exists both outside and within all beings, as that which is unmoving and indeed that which is moving.
Because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; it is both far away and near.

With reference to the body—which is imagined through ignorance as the Self and extends outward to the skin—that very body is made the limit and is called "outside. Likewise, with reference to the inner Self (pratyagātman), taking the body itself as the limit, it is called "inside. When both "outside" and "inside" are mentioned, the possibility of their non-existence in the middle might arise; therefore, this is said: "both the unmoving and the moving. Even that which appears as the body, whether moving or unmoving, is only the Knowable, just as the appearance of a snake is only the rope.

If that which is non-moving were indeed moving, and if all objects of empirical usage were knowable, why would this not be known by everyone? To this it is said: It is true that it appears as everything; nevertheless, it is subtle like space. Therefore, because of its subtlety, even though it is knowable in its own form, it is unknowable to the ignorant. For the wise, however, it is eternally known through such authoritative means as "All this is indeed the Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6) and "All this is indeed Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.1).
It is far away because it is unknown, since it cannot be attained by the ignorant even in ten million billion years; yet it is near, because it is the very Self of the wise.
Furthermore:
"And it is undivided, yet it exists as if divided among all beings."
And that Knowable is the sustainer of beings, as well as their devourer and their progenitor.

And it is undivided, yet like space it is one, though it appears as if divided within each body, because it is perceived only within bodies. It is the sustainer of beings, for it supports all living entities during the time of their existence; it is the devourer at the time of dissolution, having the nature of swallowing them; and it is the source of manifestation at the time of creation, having the power to bring them forth, just as a rope is the basis for the false conception of a serpent.
Furthermore, if something exists everywhere yet is not perceived, is it then darkness? No. What is it then?
It is said to be the light of even lights, beyond darkness.
Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is attainable through knowledge—this dwells within the heart of every being.

That which is to be known is the light even of the luminaries such as the sun; for the luminaries like the sun shine only when kindled by the light of the self’s consciousness, according to such scriptural passages as, "By whose splendor the sun shines, kindled by his brilliance" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.9), and "By its light all this is illumined" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.14). This is also supported by the Smṛti, such as, "The light that resides in the sun" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.12), and so forth. It is said to be beyond darkness—that is, untouched by ignorance.

To encourage one who has become despondent through the thought that knowledge and so forth are difficult to attain, He says: "Knowledge is humility and the rest"; "the Knowable is that which I shall declare," as stated in Gītā 13.12 and following; "that which is to be reached by knowledge" is called "reachable by knowledge" because the Knowable itself, when known, becomes the fruit of knowledge; whereas while it is being known, it is the "Knowable. All three of these abide—specifically situated—in the heart, that is, in the intellect (buddhi) of every living being;
for it is precisely therein that this triad is discerned. || BhG 13.17 ||
This verse is commenced for the purpose of summarizing the meaning as it has been stated:
"Thus, the field, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, have been described in brief."
Having understood this, my devotee attains to my own state of being.

Thus, the field (*kṣetra*)—beginning with the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and ending with sustenance (*dhṛti*); likewise, knowledge (*jñāna*)—beginning with humility (*amānitva*) and ending with the vision of the reality of the meaning of truth (*tattvajñānārthadarśana*); and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*)—beginning with "that which is to be known" (*jñeyaṃ yat tat*) and ending with "it is said to be beyond darkness" (*tamasaḥ param ucyate*)—has been declared in brief, that is, in summary. For this much indeed is the entire meaning of the Vedas and the meaning of the *Gītā*, stated here in its conclusion.

Who is qualified for this right vision? It is said: My devotee—whose entire being is surrendered to Me, the Lord, the omniscient supreme teacher Vāsudeva, and whose intellect is permeated with the realization that whatever he sees, hears, or touches is indeed the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva—that devotee of Mine, having understood this aforementioned right vision, attains my state; "my state" (madbhāva) means the state of the Supreme Self, and for that purpose he becomes fit, meaning he goes to liberation.

In that seventh chapter, two natures (*prakṛti*) of the Lord were presented—the higher and the lower, characterized as the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). It was also stated: "All beings have these as their source" (Gītā 7.7). Now, the following point is explained: how is it that all beings have these two natures, the field and the knower of the field, as their source? "Know both nature and the person (*puruṣa*) to be indeed beginningless."
And know that both the modifications and the qualities arise from Prakṛti.

Know that both *prakṛti* (nature) and *puruṣa* (the individual self) are the two *prakṛtis* of the Lord. Know those two, *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, to be beginningless (*anādi*), meaning they have no beginning. Because the Lord is eternal, it is logical that His two *prakṛtis* should also be eternal. Indeed, the very nature of the Lord’s lordship consists in possessing these two *prakṛtis*. Through these two *prakṛtis*, the Lord is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world; these two, being beginningless and real, are the cause of *saṃsāra*.

Some explain *nādī* as *anādī* using a *tatpuruṣa* compound; by this, it is said that the causality of God (*īśvara*) is established. However, if primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*) alone were eternal, then the world would be produced by them alone, and God would not have the status of being the creator of the world. That is incorrect.
