And by all the Vedas, I alone, the Supreme Self, am to be known as the object of knowledge.

The meaning is that I am the author of the Vedānta—that is, the author of the tradition concerning the meaning of the Vedānta—and I alone am the knower of the Vedas, as well as the knower of the meaning of the Vedas.

The brief summary of the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of the Blessed Lord, known as Nārāyaṇa, who is conditioned by specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), has been stated in the passage beginning with, "That splendor which resides in the sun" (Gītā 15.12). Now, however, the subsequent verses are commenced with the desire to determine the true nature (*tattva-svarūpa*) of that very same Lord when He is free from all adjuncts (*nirupādhi*) and absolute (*kevala*), being distinguished by the adjuncts of the perishable (*kṣara*) and the imperishable (*akṣara*). In this regard, having grouped together all the subject matter of the preceding and following chapters into three categories, He says:
"These two persons exist in the world: the perishable and the imperishable."
All beings are the perishable; the Immutable is called the Imperishable.

These two persons, being distinguished as separate, are spoken of in the world of *saṃsāra* as follows: one group is the *kṣara*, so called because it perishes (*kṣarati*), meaning it is subject to destruction. The other person is the *akṣara*, which is the opposite of that; it is the Lord’s power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*), the seed of origin for the person called *kṣara*, and the substratum for the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the desires and actions of the many transmigrating beings—it is called the *akṣara-puruṣa*.

Who are those two persons? The Blessed Lord Himself explains: "The perishable (kṣara) is all beings," meaning the entire aggregate of modifications. "The immutable (akṣara) stands like a peak (kūṭastha)"—that is, it stands firm like a mountain peak. Alternatively, *kūṭa* means illusion (*māyā*), speech, falsehood, or crookedness; these are synonyms. It is called *kūṭastha* because it exists in the form of various kinds of illusions, speech, and so forth. Because it is the endless seed of transmigratory existence, it does not perish and is therefore called the imperishable (*akṣara*).

Distinct from these two— the perishable and the imperishable— is another, characterized differently and untouched by the defects of the two limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the perishable and the imperishable; this Supreme Person (uttama-puruṣa), whose nature is eternally pure and awakened, is declared to be the Supreme Self (paramātman).
He who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them as the imperishable Lord.

The Supreme Person, however, is another who is entirely distinct from these two and is the most excellent; He is called the *Paramātman* (Supreme Self) because He is supreme (*parama*) in relation to the selves created by ignorance such as the body and so forth, and because He is the inner conscious self (*ātman*) of all beings. Thus He is declared and described in the Vedāntas as the *Paramātman*. He is further specified as the one who, having entered and pervaded the three worlds known as Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar by means of His own power of consciousness and strength, sustains them—He sustains and upholds them by His mere existence as the essential nature.
"Imperishable" (avyaya) means that no decay (vyaya) exists for him; who is he? The Lord, the omniscient one known as Nārāyaṇa, whose nature is to rule.

The name "Puruṣottama" is well-known for the Lord as described above. By demonstrating the meaningfulness of this name through its established etymology, the Blessed One reveals Himself as the unsurpassed Lord, saying: "Since I transcend the perishable and am even superior to the imperishable."
Therefore, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person.

Since I have transcended the perishable—that is, I have gone beyond the tree of worldly illusion known as the *aśvattha*—and since I am even higher than the imperishable, which is the seed of the tree of worldly illusion, I am therefore the most excellent (*uttama*), the most sublime, or the highest. Because of this superiority over both the perishable and the imperishable, I am celebrated and renowned in the world and in the Veda as "Puruṣottama. Thus do my devotees know me; poets also record this name in their poetry and other works, and they praise me by this designation, "Puruṣottama."
Now, the fruit for one who knows the Self as it has been described is stated:
He who, undeluded, thus knows Me as the Supreme Person—
O Bhārata, that all-knowing one honors me with his whole being.

O Bhārata, he who—being free from delusion, that is, devoid of confusion—knows Me, the Lord, endowed with the aforementioned attributes, in the manner described, as "This am I," the Supreme Person; he, knowing all by means of his entire self, is all-knowing, and he worships Me, who abide in all beings, with his whole being, as the Self of all.
In this chapter, having explained the knowledge of the reality of the Lord which has liberation as its fruit, he now praises it:
"O sinless one, this most secret teaching has been declared by me."
Having understood this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that is to be done.

Thus, this is the most secret, the most to be guarded, the ultimate mystery—what is that? It is the scripture (*śāstra*). Although the entire scripture known as the *Gītā* is being spoken of, nevertheless, this very chapter alone is here called "the scripture" for the sake of praise, because of the context; for the entire meaning of the *Gītā* scripture has been stated in summary in this chapter. Not only the meaning of the *Gītā* scripture, but the entire meaning of the Vedas is also fully concluded here.

"He who knows that is a knower of the Vedas" (Gītā 15.1), and it has also been said, "By all the Vedas, I alone am to be known" (Gītā 15.15). This has been declared and spoken by me, O sinless one! Having understood this scripture according to the meaning as it has been shown, one would become wise; not otherwise. And one becomes one who has accomplished his duty, O Bhārata—by whom the duty (kṛtya) that was to be performed has been performed, he is one who has accomplished his duty (kṛtakṛtya).

The meaning is that whatever must be performed by a Brāhmaṇa born of a distinguished birth becomes fully accomplished once the reality of the Blessed Lord is known. The intention is that otherwise, no one’s duty can ever be brought to completion; for it has been said: "All action in its entirety, O Pārtha, culminates in knowledge" (Gītā 4.33).
Indeed, this is the complete equipment for the birth of a Brāhmaṇa in particular:
"Having attained this, a twice-born man is truly one who has fulfilled his purpose, and not otherwise" (Manu 12.93).
And such is the word of Manu. Since you have heard this supreme reality from Me, therefore, O Bhārata, you have attained your purpose.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakas.
Bhagavad Gītā 16:
Now begins the yoga known as the "Discrimination between the Divine and Demoniacal Natures."
Chapter Sixteen (The Commentary composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Bhagavatpāda).

In the ninth chapter, the dispositions (*prakṛti*) of living beings were indicated as being divine, demoniacal, and rakshasa. To demonstrate these in detail, this chapter begins with the words, "Fearlessness, purity of heart," and so forth. Among them, the divine disposition leads to liberation from transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), while the demoniacal and rakshasa lead to bondage; therefore, the divine disposition is presented for adoption, and the other two for avoidance. Regarding this, the Blessed Lord said:
Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, charity, self-restraint, sacrifice, study of the scriptures, austerity, and uprightness; BhG 16.1.

Fearlessness is the absence of timidity. Purity of being (*sattva-saṃśuddhi*) is the complete purification of the inner organ (*sattva*); the meaning is that it consists of conduct characterized by a state of pure being, which involves the total avoidance of deceiving others, guile, falsehood, and so forth, in all worldly dealings. Steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga-vyavasthiti*) means that "knowledge" is the understanding of categories such as the Self through scripture and the teacher, while "yoga" is the attainment of direct self-realization regarding those understood objects through one-pointed concentration and the withdrawal of the senses and other faculties.

The firm establishment (*vyavasthiti*) in those two—knowledge and yoga—is their steadfastness, that is, being devoted to them. This is said to be the primary divine [nature], which is characterized by *sattva*. Giving (*dāna*) is the distribution of food and other things according to one's capacity. Self-restraint (*dama*) is the pacification of the external organs. He will later describe the pacification of the internal organ as tranquility (*śānti*). Sacrifice (*yajña*) includes the Vedic (*śrauta*) rites such as the *agnihotra*, as well as the Smṛti-based (*smārta*) rites such as the sacrifice to the gods. Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) is the recitation of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Austerity (*tapas*) refers to the bodily and other types to be described later. Straightforwardness (*ārjava*) is the state of being upright at all times. (BhG 16.1)
Furthermore: non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility, and absence of backbiting;
Compassion for all beings, freedom from greed, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness. BhG 16.2.

Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the non-injuring of living beings, the avoidance of causing them pain. Truthfulness (*satya*) is speech that corresponds to reality as it is, avoiding what is unpleasant or false. Absence of anger (*akrodha*) is the pacification of anger when one has been reviled or struck by others. Renunciation (*tyāga*) is the act of relinquishment (*saṃnyāsa*), since giving (*dāna*) has already been mentioned previously. Tranquility (*śānti*) is the calming of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Freedom from malice (*apaiśuna*) is the absence of backbiting. Malice (*paiśuna*) is the exposing of another's faults to others; the absence of that is freedom from malice.

Compassion is pity for living beings who are suffering. Non-covetousness is the absence of agitation in the senses when they are in proximity to their objects. Gentleness is softness and lack of cruelty. Modesty is a sense of shame. Lack of fickleness is the state of not engaging the speech, hands, feet, and so forth, when there is no purpose. (BhG 16.2)
Furthermore:
energy, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, non-malice, and lack of excessive pride;
These divine perfections belong to one who is born to them, O Bhārata.

*Tejas* (splendor) is self-confidence, not merely the glow of the skin. *Kṣamā* (forbearance) is the non-arising of internal agitation when one is reviled or struck; we have stated that *akrodha* (absence of anger) is the pacification of such agitation once it has arisen—such is the distinction between forbearance and the absence of anger. *Dhṛti* (fortitude) is a specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that prevents despondency when the body and senses have fallen into a state of exhaustion, by which the organs and the body are sustained so that they do not succumb.

Purity (*śauca*) is twofold: external, consisting of cleansing with earth and water, and internal, which is the clarity of the mind and intellect, the absence of the turbidity of illusion, passion, and the like. Such is the twofold purity. Non-malice (*adroha*) is the absence of the desire to kill others, that is, non-violence (*ahiṃsana*). Lack of excessive pride (*nātimānitā*): "excessive pride" (*atimāna*) is excessive conceit; one who possesses this is "excessively proud" (*atimānī*). The state of being so is "excessive pride" (*atimānitā*). The absence of that is "lack of excessive pride," meaning the absence of the notion of one's own extraordinary worthiness of honor.

These qualities, beginning with fearlessness and ending with this [list], belong to one who is born into perfection. Of what kind of perfection? It means belonging to one who is born for divine perfection—that is, one who possesses the excellence of the gods, who is worthy of divine glory, and whose future is auspicious—O Bhārata!
Now,
the demonic nature is described:
hypocrisy, arrogance, excessive pride, anger, and even harshness.
And ignorance, O Pārtha, belongs to one born for the demonic nature.

Hypocrisy (*dambha*) is the display of the banner of righteousness (*dharmadhvajitva*). Arrogance (*darpa*) is the haughtiness caused by learning, wealth, kinsmen, and so forth. Excessive pride (*atimāna*) has been described previously. Anger (*krodha*) and harshness (*pāruṣya*), which is indeed harsh speech—for example, calling one who has eyes "one-eyed," one who is handsome "ugly," or one of noble birth "of low birth," and so on. Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the lack of discriminative knowledge, a false cognition regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, and other such matters. O Pārtha, for one who is "born" (into this state)—to the question "born into what?", he says—it is the demonic nature (*āsurī saṃpat*); the meaning is that of one born into the nature of the *asuras*.
The function of these two types of perfection is now stated:
the divine perfection is considered to lead to liberation, while the demonic perfection leads to bondage.
Do not grieve, O Pāṇḍava; you are born endowed with divine nature.

The divine endowment (*daivī saṃpat*) leads to liberation from the bondage of *saṃsāra*. Conversely, the demonic endowment (*āsuri saṃpat*)—as well as the Rākṣasa endowment—is considered and intended to be a fixed bond for the purpose of binding. When this had been stated, the Blessed One, perceiving Arjuna’s internal state of reflection in the form of the inquiry, "Am I endowed with the demonic endowment, or am I endowed with the divine endowment?", said: "Do not grieve; do not give way to sorrow."
"You have been born with divine fortune; you are born with distinguished marks. The meaning is: "You are destined for future prosperity," O son of Pāṇḍu!
There are two types of created beings in this world: the divine and the demoniac.
The divine has been described at length; now hear from me, O Pārtha, about the demoniac.

The two creations of beings (*bhūtasarga*) refer to the two types of creation of beings, that is, of human beings. They are called "the two creations of beings" because they are created as beings endowed with the two-fold nature of divine and demonic prosperity (*saṃpad*). This is based on the Vedic scripture: "Verily, there were two classes of offspring of Prajāpati: the gods and the asuras" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.1). In this world—that is, in *saṃsāra*—this is appropriate, since all things are established as being twofold.

What are those two types of creation of beings? It is said: "The divine and the demonic. He states the purpose for restating what has already been mentioned: "The divine creation of beings—fearlessness, purity of being," and so forth—has been proclaimed and described at length, in various detailed ways; however, the demonic has not been described at length. Therefore, for the sake of its avoidance, O Pārtha, listen to and comprehend the demonic as it is being spoken by me in detail.
Until the conclusion of this chapter, the demonic nature (*āsurī saṃpat*) is demonstrated as a qualification of living beings; for it is possible to effect its abandonment through direct perception.
Thus: "And the demonic people know neither the path of engagement nor the path of withdrawal."
Neither purity, nor right conduct, nor truthfulness is found in them.

Asuras do not know engagement—that activity directed toward the accomplishment of a human goal which ought to be performed—nor do they know withdrawal, which is its opposite, from that cause of harm from which one must desist. They do not merely fail to understand engagement and withdrawal; in them neither purity nor right conduct nor truth exists. For Asuras are indeed impure, ill-behaved, deceitful, and speakers of untruth.
Furthermore,
they say that this world is unreal, without foundation, and without a Lord.
How could anything else arise except from mutual interaction, having desire as its cause?

"Just as we are mostly false, so this entire world is unreal; and it is without foundation, for it has neither dharma nor adharma as its foundation—thus it is 'without foundation'. Those Asura people said that the world is "without a Lord" (*anīśvara*), meaning that there exists no ruling Lord who takes account of dharma and adharma; therefore, they say the world is without a Lord.

Furthermore, everything in this world has arisen from the mutual union of men and women impelled by desire; what else could it be? "Caused by desire" (*kāmahaituka*) means having desire as its cause. What other cause for the world exists? There is no other cause such as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth. This is the Lokāyata view that for living beings, desire alone is the cause of the world.
Holding fast to this view, their souls ruined and their intellects small,
they arise as performers of cruel deeds, enemies of the world for its destruction.

Holding fast to this view, relying upon it, those of ruined souls—those whose very nature is destroyed and who have fallen away from the means of attaining the next world—possessing little intelligence (those whose intellect is limited to the objects of the senses), they arise, they come into being as performers of fierce deeds, performers of cruel deeds, and those whose nature is violence. The connection is that they arise for the destruction of the world; the meaning is that they are enemies, harmful to the world.
And they,
resorting to desire— which is difficult to satisfy— are possessed by hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance.
Having grasped false attachments out of delusion, they engage in impure vows.

Relying upon and clinging to various desires—which are difficult to satisfy and impossible to fulfill—those possessed of hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance (dambha-māna-mada), having grasped and adopted false notions and impure resolutions through delusion and lack of discrimination, they proceed in this world with impure vows; those whose vows are impure are called "impure-vowed" (aśuci-vrata).
Furthermore,
they have resorted to immeasurable anxiety that lasts until the end of the dissolution of the universe.
They are intent on the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, convinced that this is all there is.

And they are possessed of immeasurable anxiety—that anxiety whose limit cannot be measured is "immeasurable," and they have resorted to that which ends in dissolution, that is, death; the meaning is that they are constantly intent on anxiety. They are devoted solely to the enjoyment of desires; "desires" (kāmāḥ) are those objects of sense such as sound and so forth because they are desired, and they are "devoted solely to the enjoyment of them. Their minds are resolved thus: "This alone is the supreme human goal, namely, the enjoyment of desires. They are certain that this is all there is.
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope and devoted to desire and anger,
they strive for the sake of sensual enjoyment to accumulate wealth by unjust means.

Bound by hundreds of snares of hope—hope itself being the snares—and thus restrained and dragged from all sides, those who have made desire and anger their supreme resort strive and exert themselves for the sake of the enjoyment of desires, not for the sake of dharma; that is to say, by unjust means such as seizing the property of others. For what purpose? For the accumulation of wealth, for the amassing of riches. (BhG 16.12)
And such was their intention:
"This has been gained by me today; this desire shall be attained."
"This exists, and this wealth of mine shall exist again."

"This wealth has been obtained by me today; this other thing I shall obtain, which will fulfill my heart's desire and satisfy my mind; this I possess, and this too shall be mine in the coming year—through that wealth, I shall become famous as a rich man. ||BhGS_16.13||
"This enemy has been slain by me, and I shall slay others as well;
I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, powerful, and happy. (BhG 16.14)

"This invincible enemy named Devadatta has been slain by me; I shall also slay others, even those who are wretched. What can these miserable ones do? In every respect, there is no one equal to me. How so? I am the lord, I am the enjoyer; in every way I am successful and endowed with sons and grandsons; I am not merely a human being, but I alone am powerful and happy, while others have been cast down as a burden upon the earth. (BhG 16.14)
"I am wealthy and of noble birth; who else is equal to me?
I shall sacrifice, I shall give gifts, and I shall rejoice"—thus are they deluded by ignorance. (BhG 16.15)

"Possessed of wealth," "of noble birth"—meaning one whose lineage for seven generations has been endowed with Vedic learning and other such qualities—by that [status] too, there is no one equal to me. Who else is like or equal to me? Moreover, "I shall sacrifice"—by means of sacrifice I shall surpass others; "I shall give"—to actors and the like; "I shall rejoice"—I shall attain an excess of joy. Thus, deluded by ignorance—that is, bewildered by ignorance—they have fallen into various states of non-discrimination.
Perplexed by manifold thoughts, enveloped in the net of delusion,
and attached to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, they fall into an impure hell.

"Perplexed by manifold thoughts" means they are variously bewildered by many thoughts of the kinds already mentioned; "enveloped in the snare of delusion" means that delusion (*moha*)—which is non-discrimination or ignorance—is like a snare because it is of the nature of an obscuration, and they are completely covered by it; "addicted to the enjoyment of sense-objects," being seated right there in them, their sins accumulated thereby, they fall into the impure hell, such as Vaitaraṇī and others.
Self-conceited, stubborn, and filled with the intoxication of wealth and pride, they perform sacrifices under the guise of religion, yet out of hypocrisy and contrary to scriptural injunctions.

"Self-conceited" means those who have been honored by themselves alone on account of their own excellence in all virtues, and not by the virtuous. "Arrogant" means those whose minds are unbending. "Possessed of the intoxication of wealth and pride" means possessed of both pride and intoxication caused by wealth; [they] perform sacrifices with "sacrifices in name only"—that is, sacrifices consisting of mere names—out of hypocrisy, under the guise of righteousness, and contrary to the rules, lacking the prescribed limbs and procedures as ordained by the injunctions. (BhG 16.17)
Resorting to egoism, power, arrogance, lust, and anger,
they hate Me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others, being full of envy.

Egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is the act of egoizing (*ahaṃkaraṇa*). It is that by which one conceives of the self as qualified by qualities—both existing and non-existing—that have been superimposed upon it, thinking "I am. This egoism, known as ignorance (*avidyā*), is most painful; it is the root of all defects and the source of all unwholesome activities. Likewise, there is power (*bala*), which is the cause of overcoming others and is accompanied by desire and passion (*kāmarāga*).

Arrogance—by whose arising one transgresses dharma—is a particular defect residing in the internal organ (antahkarana). Desire refers to objects such as women; anger refers to undesirable objects. They have resorted to these and other great defects. Furthermore, they hate Me, the Lord, who am the witness of the intellect and actions within their own bodies and in the bodies of others. "Hate" means transgressing My command; acting thus, they are envious, unable to tolerate the virtues of those established on the path of truth.
Those hateful and cruel ones, the lowest of men in the worlds, I incessantly hurl into inauspicious demonic wombs alone.

I cast those who are hostile to me—those cruel haters of the virtuous who stand as adversaries to the true path, those lowest of men who, due to their possession of unrighteousness and fault, perform inauspicious deeds—into the very paths of wandering through many hells within the cycles of worldly existence; I cast those inauspicious ones perpetually and continuously into the wombs of tigers, lions, and the like, which are predominantly characterized by cruel actions and belong to the demonic realm. This is the connection [of the verse].
Having entered the womb of an asura, deluded from birth to birth,
they do not attain Me, O son of Kuntī, but from there go to the lowest state.

Having entered—that is, having attained—the demonic womb, these deluded and undiscriminating ones are born life after life in wombs abounding in darkness; descending further, these deluded ones go to an even lower state, a most degraded condition, O Kaunteya, without reaching—that is, without attaining—Me, the Lord. The phrase "without reaching Me" does not imply any possibility of reaching Me at all; rather, it means that they fail to reach the path of the virtuous taught by Me.

This summary of the entire demonic nature (*āsuryā saṃpat*) is now stated, within which all the infinite varieties of demonic nature are included; by abandoning which, one abandons them all, and which is the root of every misfortune—that is described as follows: "These three are the gates to hell, the ruin of the self."
Lust, anger, and likewise greed—one should therefore abandon these three.

This threefold, three-pronged gateway to hell is the destroyer of the self; for by entering this very gateway, the self perishes—it becomes unfit for any human goal. Therefore it is said, "the gateway that destroys the self. What is that? Desire, anger, and likewise greed. Therefore, one should abandon these three; since this is the gateway that destroys the self, one should renounce this triad beginning with desire.
This is a praise of renunciation:
O son of Kuntī, a man who is liberated from these three gates of darkness [attains the highest state].
He practices what is for his own welfare; from that, he goes to the supreme goal.

Freed from these, O son of Kuntī—by these doors of darkness, which are the gates to hell characterized by suffering and delusion, namely desire and the rest—a man who is liberated from these three practices and performs; what? His own highest good (śreyas). That which he previously did not practice because it was obstructed, he now practices due to its removal. Then, by practicing that, he goes to the supreme goal, which is liberation as well.

The scripture is the authority for all this—the avoidance of the demonic nature and the practice of what is beneficial. Both of these can be accomplished through the standard of the scripture, and not otherwise. Therefore, he who disregards the injunctions of the scripture and acts according to his own whims—
He attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.

He who, having cast aside the injunctions of the scripture—the Veda—which are the means for discerning what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, namely the prescriptions and prohibitions, acts according to his own will, being impelled by desire, does not attain perfection, which is fitness for the goals of human life; nor does he find happiness in this world, nor the supreme goal, whether it be heaven or liberation.
Therefore, the scripture is your authority for determining what ought to be done and what ought not to be done;
having understood what is prescribed by the ordinances of the scripture, you should perform your duty here.

Therefore, the scripture is the authority for you as a means of knowledge regarding the determination of what ought to be done and what ought not to be done—that is, the determination of duty and non-duty. Hence, having known and understood that which is declared by the scriptural injunction—where "vidhi" (injunction) means "vidhāna" (prescription), and "śāstravidhāna" refers to the scripture itself as the prescription characterized by such rules as "one should do" or "one should not do"—you ought to perform here that which is your own duty as stated therein. The word "here" is used to indicate the sphere of one's qualification for action. || BhG 16.24 ||

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya).
Bhagavad Gītā 17: Now follows the yoga of the classification of the threefold faith.
Chapter Seventeen.
Having received the seed of his question from the Lord’s statement, “Therefore, the scripture is the authority” (Gītā 16.24), Arjuna said:
“Those who, casting aside the injunctions of the scripture, perform sacrifice endowed with faith...”
But what, O Kṛṣṇa, is their final goal: goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), or darkness (tamas)?

Whosoever, without distinction, having cast aside and abandoned the scriptural injunction—the ordinance of the scriptures, the mandate of the Śruti and Smṛti treatises—worship and honor the gods and other deities while being endowed with faith, that is, possessed of a conviction rooted in the belief in the scriptures; those who, not seeing any scriptural injunction characterized by Śruti or Smṛti, worship the gods and others solely out of faith based merely on observing the conduct of their elders.

Those who, having abandoned the injunctions of the scriptures, perform sacrifice here while being endowed with faith, are understood by the phrase "those who... having abandoned the scriptural injunctions, sacrifice. However, those who, despite perceiving some scriptural injunction, abandon it and worship gods and others in a manner contrary to the rules, are not included here among "those who... having abandoned the scriptural injunctions, sacrifice. Why? Because of the qualifying attribute "being endowed with faith."

It is impossible to imagine that those who, while actually seeing some scripture devoted to the rules for the worship of gods and others, would nevertheless discard it due to a lack of faith and yet proceed with faith in the worship of gods and others prescribed therein; therefore, the previously stated interpretation alone is correct regarding the passage: "Those who, discarding the scriptural injunction, sacrifice endowed with faith... (Gītā 17.1).

They are so perceived. But what is the ultimate state (*niṣṭhā*) of those who are thus constituted, O Kṛṣṇa—is it *sattva*, or *rajas*, or *tamas*? Does their final abiding consist in *sattva*, or rather in *rajas*, or else in *tamas*? What is meant by this is: is that worship of them, directed toward the gods and others, *sāttvika*, or is it *rājasa*, or perhaps *tāmasa*? (BhG 17.1)
"The Blessed One said: "This question concerns a general subject and does not deserve an answer without further analysis.
The faith of embodied beings is of three kinds; it is born of their own nature."
It is of three kinds—sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa; hear now about it.

Faith is threefold, of three kinds, regarding that steadfastness about which you inquire. For embodied beings—that is, for those possessing bodies—it is born of their own nature (*svabhāvajā*). The impressions (*saṃskāra*) of dharma and so forth formed in previous births, which become manifest at the time of death, are called "nature"; faith born from that is "born of nature. That which is *sāttvikī* arises from *sattva* and has as its object the worship of gods and the like. That which is *rājasī* arises from *rajas* and has as its object the worship of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and the like. That which is *tāmasī* arises from *tamas* and has as its object the worship of pretas, piśācas, and the like.
Listen and take to heart this threefold faith as it is being described.
This very faith is of three kinds according to one's nature; for everyone, O Bhārata, faith arises in accordance with their character.
This person consists of faith; whatever his faith is, that indeed he is.

O Bhārata, the faith of every living being arises in accordance with their nature and in conformity with their internal organ, which is endowed with specific mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). If this is so, what would follow from it? It is said: "This person—the transmigrating individual soul (*jīva*)—consists of faith; he is composed primarily of faith. How so? Whatever one's faith is—that is, whatever kind of faith a particular *jīva* possesses—that very *jīva* is of that same nature, corresponding precisely to his faith.

And thus, since the steadfastness in *sattva* and the other *guṇas* is to be inferred from their effects as signs—namely, the worship of gods and so forth—he says: "Those characterized by *sattva* worship the gods; those characterized by *rajas*, the yakṣas and rākṣasas."
Other people, characterized by darkness (tāmasa), worship the spirits of the departed (pretas) and hosts of elemental beings (bhūtagaṇas).

Those established in goodness (sāttvika), being devoted to purity, worship the gods; those characterized by passion (rājasa) worship the yakṣas and rākṣasas; and other people, characterized by darkness (tāmasa), worship the spirits of the dead, hosts of elemental beings, the Seven Mothers, and so forth.

Thus, by their effects, those who abide in *sattva* and the other *guṇas* have been determined in relation to the abandonment of scriptural injunctions. Among them, only one in a thousand becomes established in *sattva*, being devoted to the worship of the gods and so forth; for the most part, however, living beings abide in *rajas* and *tamas*. How so?
"Those people who perform terrible austerities not ordained by the scriptures..."
Endowed with hypocrisy and egoism, and possessed by the force of desire and passion.

Those people who perform and carry out asceticism that is not ordained by the scriptures—not even ordained by the scriptures—terrible, causing pain to living beings and to themselves, are possessed of hypocrisy and egoism. "Hypocrisy and egoism" means *dambha* and *ahaṃkāra*; those joined with these two are "possessed of hypocrisy and egoism. They are "endowed with the power of desire and attachment": *kāma* and *rāga* are "desire and attachment"; the power produced by them is "the power of desire and attachment," and those endowed with that are "endowed with the power of desire and attachment."
Those mindless ones who emaciate the collection of elements within the body,
as well as Me who dwell within the body— know them to be of demonic resolve.

Emaciating—that is, making lean—the aggregate of elements (bhūtagrāma), which is the collection of instruments residing within the body, and being devoid of discrimination (acetasaḥ), they likewise emaciate Me, Nārāyaṇa, who resides within the body as the witness of their actions and intellect. To neglect My instruction is itself to emaciate Me. Know them to be of demonic resolve (āsuraniścaya)—those whose resolve is demonic; "know them" is the instruction for the purpose of avoiding them. (BhG 17.6)

Here, the preference for foods—distinguished into three groups such as those that are savory, unctuous, and so forth—by persons of *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* natures is demonstrated in due order. This is done so that, by means of the sign of one’s own excessive delight in specific foods such as the savory and unctuous, one may recognize one's own *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, or *tāmasa* nature; and having recognized this, one may avoid foods characterized by *rajas* and *tamas* while adopting those characterized by *sattva*.

Likewise, the demonstration that sacrifices and other acts are also of three kinds according to the distinction of the qualities such as *sattva* is for this purpose: so that, having understood the *rājasa* and *tāmasa* types, one might indeed abandon them and practice only those that are *sāttvika*. To this end, He says:
"Moreover, food is dear to everyone in three ways;
likewise, sacrifice, austerity, and charity. Hear now this division of them. (BhG 17.7)

Furthermore, for every living being who eats, food is dear and desired in three ways; likewise are sacrifice, austerity, and charity. Listen now to this distinction of those—food and the rest—which is about to be described.
Food that increases life, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and joy, which is savory, oleaginous, substantial, and agreeable to the heart, is dear to those of sattva.

Longevity, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and joy—these are "longevity, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and joy"; [the foods] that cause their increase are "those which increase longevity, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and joy. And those foods are savory (rasya), meaning endowed with flavor; unctuous (snigdha), meaning possessing oiliness; stable (sthira), meaning they remain for a long time in the body; heart-pleasing (hṛdya), meaning dear to the heart; and they are "foods dear to the sāttvika," meaning desired by one of a sāttvika nature.
Bitter, sour, salty, excessively hot, pungent, dry, and burning foods are dear to those of the rajasic nature; they bring about pain, grief, and disease. (BhG 17.9)

Regarding the phrase "bitter, sour, salty, very hot, pungent, dry, and burning," the word *ati* (excessively) is to be applied to all [the qualities] beginning with bitter—thus, "excessively bitter" (*atikaṭu*), "excessively pungent" (*atitīkṣṇa*), and so forth. Bitter, sour, salty, very hot, pungent, dry, and burning—these foods are dear to the passionate person (*rājasa*). They are "givers of pain, grief, and disease" (*duḥkha-śoka-āmaya-pradāḥ*), meaning they bestow pain, grief, and disease.
Food that is stale, tasteless, putrid, and decomposed, as well as that which is leavings and impure— such food is dear to those of tamasic nature.

*Yātayāma* means half-cooked; for that which lacks potency is already expressed by the term "devoid of essence" (*gatarasa*). *Gatarasa* means separated from its flavor. *Pūti* means foul-smelling. *Paryuṣita* refers to that which has been cooked and then kept overnight. *Ucchiṣḷa* is what remains after eating. *Amethya* is food unfit for sacrifice. Such food is dear to those of a *tāmasa* nature. (BhG 17.10)
Now, sacrifice is said to be of three kinds: that sacrifice which is performed according to scriptural injunction by those who do not desire its fruits;

Speech that does not cause agitation to living beings, that does not cause suffering, which is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial—that is, pleasant and beneficial in terms of both visible and invisible purposes—is what is meant. Speech is qualified by these attributes such as "not causing agitation" and so forth; the word "and" (ca) serves to aggregate these qualifying attributes. If speech employed for the purpose of convincing another were deficient in even one or two of these qualities—truthfulness, pleasantness, benefit, and non-agitation—it would not constitute the austerity of speech (*vāṅmaya-tapas*).

Likewise, if truthful speech lacks any one of the others, or two, or three, it does not constitute austerity of speech. Similarly, if pleasant speech lacks any one of the others, or two, or three, it does not constitute austerity of speech. Likewise, if beneficial speech lacks any one of the others, or two, or three, it does not constitute austerity of speech.

What, then, is that austerity? That speech which is truthful, non-agitating, pleasant, and beneficial—that is austerity consisting of speech. For example: "Be peaceful, my child; practice sacred study and yoga, and thus it will be for your highest good. Clarity of mind (*manaḥprasāda*) is the tranquility of the mind; it is the attainment of lucidity, which they call gentleness (*saumyatva*) or cheerfulness (*saumanasya*). It is a function of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that is to be inferred from its effects, such as the clarity of the face and so forth. As for silence (*mauna*), although it is a restraint of speech, it is preceded by the restraint of the mind; thus, by means of the effect, the cause is expressed: silence is the restraint of the mind. The restraint of the mind that is the very object of speech is silence; this is the distinction. Purity of disposition is the absence of deceitfulness when dealing with others; this is called mental austerity. (BhG 17.16)

Penance performed for the sake of honor (*satkāra*)—that is, for the purpose of being praised as "this ascetic is a true Brahmin"—for the sake of respect (*māna*), such as rising from one's seat and saluting, and for the sake of worship (*pūjā*), such as washing the feet, offering reverence, and providing a bed; that penance performed with hypocrisy is declared here to be *rājasa*, unstable because its fruit is merely occasional, and unsteady. That austerity which is performed with a deluded grasp—that is, with a resolve devoid of discrimination—and out of self-torment, for the sake of destroying or annihilating another, is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).

that gift which is given with the thought "it ought to be given" to one who provides no benefit;

Giving that gift which is bestowed with the thought "it simply ought to be given"—whether to one who does no service and is unable to return the favor, or even to one who is capable [of returning it]—but is given without expectation of anything in return; and which is given at a sacred place such as Kurukṣetra and the like, at an auspicious time such as the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti) and the like, and to a worthy recipient (pātra) such as one who knows the six Vedāṅgas or has mastered the Vedas—that gift is declared to be sāttvika. || BhG 17.20 ||
But that gift which is given for the sake of a return favor, or again with a view toward a fruit,

But that gift which is given for the sake of a return favor—thinking, "This person will repay me at some time"—or with the aim of its fruit, thinking, "There will be an unseen result from this gift for me," and which is given again after being mentally directed [toward a specific goal], being afflicted and joined with weariness—that gift is declared to be *rājasa*.
That gift which is given at an improper place and time, and to unworthy recipients,

A gift given at an improper place and time—given in an unsuitable location, one that is impure and crowded with barbarians, unclean persons, and the like; given at an improper time, one not renowned as a cause of merit and devoid of special occasions such as the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti); and given to unworthy recipients, such as fools, thieves, and so forth—or even when the excellence of place and other factors is present, a gift given without respect, lacking kind words, washing of feet, worship, and the like, being given with contempt and involving the humiliation of the recipient—that gift is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). || BhG 17.22 ||
This instruction is now being stated for the purpose of ensuring the excellence of sacrifice, charity, austerity, and so forth:

"Oṃ Tat Sat"—such is the designation (*nirdeśa*). It is called a "designation" because it is by means of this that [Brahman] is designated. This threefold designation of Brahman is recorded and contemplated in the Vedāntas by those who know Brahman. By means of that threefold designation, the Brāhmaṇas and the Vedas and sacrifices were ordained and created in the past, in ancient times; thus it is said for the purpose of praising the designation. (BhG 17.23)

Therefore, having uttered—that is, pronounced—"Om," the acts of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity, which constitute the very nature of such rites as sacrifices and the like, proceed at all times and in every way as prescribed by rule and enjoined by scripture for those who speak of Brahman, that is, for those whose habit is the discourse on Brahman.
Without aiming for a fruit, those who desire liberation perform sacrifices, acts of austerity, and various acts of charity.

"Without aiming for that"—that is, having uttered the designation "That" (tad), which refers to Brahman, and without aiming for the fruit of sacrificial and other rites; "sacrificial and ascetic acts" (yajña-tapas-kriyāḥ)—meaning sacrificial acts and ascetic acts, as well as various acts of giving characterized by the bestowing of land, gold, and so forth—are performed and accomplished by those desiring liberation, those seeking liberation, the seekers of freedom (mumukṣubhiḥ).

The application of the two words *tat* and *śabda* has been explained. Now, the application of the word *sat* is being stated: the term *sat* is employed in the sense of existence (*sadbhāva*) and in the sense of goodness (*sādhubhāva*).

That state which exists in sacrifice, in the performance of sacrificial rites, in austerity, and in charity—that is called "the Real" (sat) by the wise. And action for that purpose—action intended for sacrifice, charity, and austerity; or rather, action intended for that which has the three aforementioned names, namely, action intended for the Lord (īśvara)—is designated simply as "the Real."

Thus, this action—whether sacrifice, charity, austerity, or the like—even if it is of a non-sattvic nature and deficient in quality, becomes endowed with qualities and sattvic when performed with faith by employing the three designations of Brahman.

And since everything is accomplished there and everywhere by making faith the primary factor, therefore: "Whatever is offered in sacrifice, given as a gift, or performed as austerity, if done without faith..."
It is called "non-existent," O Pārtha, for it exists neither here nor after death.

An oblation offered without faith, a gift given to Brahmins without faith, austerity practiced without faith, and likewise whatever is performed such as praise and salutation without faith—all that is said to be "unrighteous" (asat), O Pārtha, because it lies outside the path of the means for attaining Me. And even though it involves great effort, it leads neither to fruit after death nor to any purpose in this world, because it is censured by the virtuous.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya).
Arjuna said:
O mighty-armed one, I desire to know the true nature of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), and also that of relinquishment (*tyāga*), separately, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O slayer of Keśin. 18.1.

O mighty-armed one, O Hṛṣīkeśa (Lord of the senses), O Keśiniṣūdana (Slayer of Keśin)—by which name the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva is addressed by Arjuna because He destroyed a certain demon named Keśin who appeared in the guise of a horse—I desire to know the reality, that is, the true nature or essence, of *saṃnyāsa*—meaning the word "renunciation"—and also of *tyāga*—meaning the word "abandonment"—separately, that is, through their mutual distinction.

The words "renunciation" (saṃnyāsa) and "relinquishment" (tyāga) have been mentioned here and there, but their precise meanings have not been fully unraveled in the preceding chapters. Therefore, for the sake of providing a definitive resolution to Arjuna’s inquiry, the Blessed Lord said: the Blessed Lord said.
The wise understand the renunciation of optional rites to be *saṃnyāsa*;
the discerning declare the relinquishment of the fruits of all actions to be *tyāga*.

Some wise men, the learned, know the meaning of the word *saṃnyāsa* to be the renunciation (*nyāsa*) of optional rites such as the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), which have been established as things to be performed; whereas the discerning scholars declare that the meaning of the word *tyāga* (renunciation) is the abandonment of the fruit—which, though it arises through one's own connection to them—of all obligatory and occasional rites that are being performed. This is what they call *tyāga*.

If the meaning intended is either the renunciation of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) or the renunciation of their fruits, then in every respect, mere renunciation would be the single meaning of the words *saṃnyāsa* and *tyāga*, and they would not have meanings belonging to entirely different categories, like the words "pot" and "cloth."

But is it not said that obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) actions have no fruit at all? How then can it be said that there is a renunciation of their fruit, as if one were renouncing the son of a barren woman? This is not a fault, because the Blessed One accepts that even obligatory actions possess fruit. For the Blessed One will say: "Unpleasant, pleasant, and mixed [fruits]" (Gītā 18.12), and "[these accrue] except for those who have renounced" (Gītā 18.12).

Indeed, by showing that the non-attachment to the fruits of action belongs exclusively to renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*), [the Lord] demonstrates that those who are not renunciants obtain the fruits of their obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) through the words, "It happens after death for those who do not renounce" (Gītā 18.12). "Some wise men say that action should be abandoned as if it were full of defects;
others say that the action of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity should not be abandoned. (18.3)

(18.3) That which is to be abandoned (*tyājya*) is that which ought to be relinquished because it possesses a fault (*doṣavat*); that is, whatever action (*karman*), since it is a cause of bondage. Alternatively, some wise men—learned scholars who rely on the perspective of the Sāṃkhya and other schools, including even those engaged in ritual action (*karmī*)—say that action is to be abandoned just as faults such as passion (*rāga*) and the like are abandoned. On the other hand, others say that in that very context, the actions of sacrifice, charity, and austerity are not to be abandoned.

Only those engaged in action (karmiṇaḥ) are qualified; these alternatives are intended with respect to them, and not with respect to renunciants who have risen above [action] and are established in knowledge. For those who were excluded from the qualification for action by the statement, "The steadfastness of the Sāṃkhyas in the yoga of knowledge was declared by Me previously," no such consideration applies.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that, just as those previously qualified for the path of action (*karmayoga*)—even though they were distinguished by their respective steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*)—are now considered here in this section on the summary of the meaning of all the scriptures, so too should the followers of Sāṃkhya, who are steadfast in knowledge (*jñāna*), be considered? [Reply: No, because for them the abandonment of the causes of delusion and suffering is impossible. The followers of Sāṃkhya do not perceive bodily affliction as a cause of suffering within the Self (*ātman*), since desire and the rest have been shown to be attributes of the field (*kṣetra*) alone.

Therefore, they do not abandon action out of fear of the suffering caused by physical exhaustion. Nor do they perceive actions as being within themselves, whereby they might abandon prescribed action out of delusion. Indeed, they renounce action by means of the qualities [of the constituents], thinking, "I do nothing at all. The manner of renunciation for the knower of reality has been described in such passages as, "Having renounced all actions with the mind" (Gītā 5.13).

Therefore, those others who are qualified for action but are not knowers of the Self, and whose renunciation is possible through delusion and fear of physical hardship—they alone are the tamasic and rajasic renunciators who are censured for the purpose of praising the renunciation of the fruits of action by those performers of work who are knowers of the Self, as in: "one who has abandoned all undertakings" (Gītā 14.25) and "the silent sage, content with whatever comes" (Gītā 12.19).

Furthermore, because the one who has transcended the qualities (*guṇātīta*) is specifically characterized as "homeless and steady-minded" (*aniketaḥ sthiramatiḥ*, Gītā 12.19), and because [the Lord] will later state, "That which is the supreme consummation of knowledge" (*niṣṭhā jñānasya yā parā*, Gītā 18.50), those renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) established in knowledge are not intended here. Rather, it is the renunciation of the fruits of action alone—which is designated as "renunciation" (*saṃnyāsa*) by virtue of its quality of being *sāttvika* in relation to *tāmasa* and other states—that is meant, and not the primary renunciation of all actions.

If it is argued that, because of the statement of a reason—"for one who bears a body" (Gītā 18.11)—it must be the primary [meaning] since the renunciation of all actions is impossible, we say no; for the statement of the reason is intended as praise. Just as in the passage, "From renunciation comes peace immediately" (Gītā 12.12), the renunciation of the fruits of action is merely praised—since it is prescribed for the ignorant Arjuna who is incapable of practicing the various aforementioned alternatives—so too this statement, "for one who bears a body it is not possible," is for the purpose of praising the renunciation of the fruits of action.

No one can demonstrate an exception to this position that "having renounced all actions with the mind, one remains neither acting nor causing others to act. Therefore, this alternative between renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and abandonment (*tyāga*) applies only to those who are qualified for ritual action (*karman*). However, as for the Sāṃkhyas who perceive the ultimate reality, their qualification lies solely in steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*), which is characterized by the renunciation of all actions, and not elsewhere; thus, they are not subject to this alternative.
This has been established by us in the passage beginning with "Know the imperishable" (Gītā 2.21) and in the third chapter and following.
In this regard, O best of the Bharatas, hear from Me the definitive conclusion concerning these various types of renunciation.
For renunciation, O tiger among men, is proclaimed to be of three kinds. (18.4)

(18.4) Hear my firm conclusion and grasp it from my words: regarding that renunciation—the distinction between renunciation (*tyāga*) and relinquishment (*saṃnyāsa*) as previously shown—O best of the Bharatas, O most excellent of the Bharatas, [I say this]. For renunciation—intending that the meaning expressed by the words "renunciation" and "relinquishment" is indeed one and the same—he says: "For renunciation..."

O tiger among men, renunciation and relinquishment—which are denoted by the words *tyāga* and *saṃnyāsa*—are proclaimed in the scriptures as being threefold, categorized according to the modes of *tamas* and so forth; that is, they are correctly described as being of three kinds for the qualified agent who performs action and lacks self-knowledge, but not for one who perceives the supreme reality. Since this matter is difficult to understand, no one other than Me is capable of explaining its true nature here. Therefore, hear from Me My divine resolve, which is the certain conclusion regarding the meaning of the scripture of the supreme truth.
What, then, is this resolution? He says: "The acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity must not be abandoned; they must indeed be performed.
Sacrifice, charity, and austerity are the purifiers of the wise. (18.5)

(18.5) Sacrifice, charity, and austerity—this threefold action is not to be abandoned; it must indeed be performed. Why? Because sacrifice, charity, and austerity are purifiers, bringing about purification for the wise who do not seek their fruits. However, even these actions should be performed having abandoned attachment and [the desire for] results.

"O Pārtha, it is my firm and supreme conviction that these actions—namely sacrifice, charity, and austerity, which have been declared to be purifying—must nevertheless be performed after abandoning attachment to them and renouncing their fruits; they are to be carried out; this is my settled and highest opinion. (18.6)

Having made the declaration, "Hear my certain conclusion in this matter" (Gītā 18.4), and having stated the reason—that [these actions] are purifying—the statement "even these actions must be performed" is precisely the conclusion of the declared meaning as "the settled, supreme opinion," not a statement of a new subject. This is because the use of the word "even" (*api*) is logically consistent with its proximity to the subject under discussion. The meaning of the word "even" is that even these actions—which are causes of bondage for one who is attached and seeks results—must be performed by one who desires liberation. It is not said "even these" in comparison to other types of actions.

Others, however, explain that because there is no fruit for obligatory (*nitya*) actions, the statement "having abandoned attachment and fruits" would be untenable; therefore, they argue that by the words "these also," those optional (*kāmya*) actions distinct from the obligatory ones are meant, implying that even these should be performed, let alone the obligatory sacrifices, gifts, and austerities. That is incorrect, because the fact that even obligatory actions possess fruit has been established here by such statements as, "Sacrifice, gift, and austerity are indeed purifiers" (Gītā 18.5).

For one who desires liberation and wishes to renounce even obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) out of fear that they might cause bondage, how could there be any inclination toward optional rites (*kāmyakarman*)? This is because such acts are condemned in the statement, "Action is far inferior" (Gītā 2.49), and because it is certain that optional rites cause bondage in the statement, "Other than action performed for the sake of sacrifice" (Gītā 3.9). Furthermore, the Vedas have as their domain the three *guṇas* (Gītā 2.45); those learned in the three Vedas, the drinkers of Soma, worship me [in this way] (Gītā 9.20); and when their merit is exhausted, they enter the world of mortals (Gītā 9.21).
And thus, because they are remote and separated [from the context], the designation "these also" does not apply to the optional rites (*kāmya*).
Therefore, for the ignorant person who is qualified [for action] and seeks liberation, the renunciation of obligatory duty (*niyata-karman*) is not appropriate.

The abandonment of that obligatory [duty] out of delusion is proclaimed to be *tāmasa* (of the nature of darkness). (18.7) However, the renunciation—that is, the abandonment—of obligatory, constant action is not possible for one who lacks knowledge, because its purifying quality is desired. Abandonment of that obligatory duty out of delusion, which is ignorance, is a contradiction: it is both "obligatory" (meaning it must necessarily be performed) and yet "is abandoned. Therefore, abandonment caused by delusion is proclaimed to be *tāmasa*; and since delusion is *tamas* (darkness), it is so designated.

If one abandons action merely because it is painful, out of fear of bodily exertion, he performs a renunciation that is characterized by passion (rājasa); he shall certainly not obtain the fruit of renunciation. 18.8.

If one should abandon action merely because it is "suffering," out of fear of bodily exertion or fear of physical pain, he performs a renunciation that is *rājasa*—produced by passion—and shall not obtain the fruit of renunciation; namely, he shall not at all obtain the fruit called liberation, which belongs to the renunciation of all actions preceded by knowledge.
What, then, is *sāttvika* renunciation? He says:
"O Arjuna, that obligatory action which is performed simply because it ought to be done..."
Having abandoned attachment as well as the fruit, that renunciation is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).

O Arjuna, that obligatory and constant action which is performed and accomplished simply because "it ought to be done," having abandoned attachment as well as the fruit—that is [the true nature of such action]. We have already stated that the Lord’s own words are the authority for the fact that these obligatory actions possess fruits. Alternatively, even though no fruit is explicitly heard of for an obligatory action, the ignorant person nonetheless assumes that the obligatory action, when performed, produces a fruit for the self, either in the form of self-purification (*ātmasaṃskāra*) or the avoidance of transgression (*pratyavāya-parihāra*).

In that regard, he rules out even that conceptualization by means of the phrase "having abandoned the fruit. Therefore, it was rightly said: "having abandoned attachment and the fruit. That renunciation—the abandonment of attachment and the fruit in obligatory duties—is considered *sāttvika*, meaning it is brought about by *sattva*. This is the intended meaning.

But surely, the renunciation of action (*karmaparityāga*) has been introduced as the threefold *saṃnyāsa*. Among those, the *tyāga* characterized as *tāmasa* and *rājasa* has already been described. How then can the abandonment of attachment and fruit be spoken of here as the third? It is like the case where it is said, "Three Brahmins have arrived; among them, two are knowers of the six Vedāṅgas, and the third is a Kṣatriya. This is not a fault, because it is intended as praise by virtue of the commonality of "abandonment" (*tyāgatva*). For there is indeed a commonality of the nature of abandonment between the renunciation of action and the abandonment of the intention for results.

In this context, by means of the censure of the abandonment of action as being characterized by *rajas* and *tamas*, the abandonment of attachment to the fruits of action is praised as being characterized by *sattva*, as it is said: "That renunciation is considered *sāttvika*" (Gītā 18.9).

But he who is qualified, having abandoned attachment and the desire for fruits, performs obligatory action; his internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), being unpolluted by passion for results and the like, becomes purified as it is refined by those obligatory actions. That purified [organ] becomes serene and capable of perceiving the Self. Now, for one whose internal organ has been purified through the performance of obligatory actions and who is oriented toward self-knowledge, it must be explained how that steadfastness may gradually be attained; thus he says: "He does not hate inauspicious action, nor is he attached to auspicious action."

The renouncer, endowed with purity of being (*sattva*), wise, and with doubts severed— (18.10)— does not hate an unwholesome, inauspicious, or desirable action that is a cause of worldly existence by way of initiating the body, thinking, "What is the use of this? Nor does he become attached— that is, he does not form an attachment of pleasure— to a wholesome, auspicious, or obligatory action, which is a cause of liberation because it is the means for the purification of *sattva*, the arising of knowledge, and steadfastness therein, thinking, "This is the cause of liberation."

Who, then, is this? A renouncer (*tyāgī*) is one who possesses that which was previously described as the renunciation of attachment and its fruit; he is the renouncer who, having abandoned attachment to action and its fruit, performs obligatory duties (*nityakarman*). But when does he neither hate unwholesome action nor become attached to wholesome action? It is said: "when permeated by *sattva*. When he is permeated—that is, pervaded or joined—by *sattva*, which is the cause of the discriminative knowledge of the Self and the non-Self.

And for this very reason, the wise man (*medhāvī*)—one who possesses *medhā*, that is, the wisdom characterized by self-knowledge—is one endowed with such insight. Precisely because of this wisdom, he has his doubts severed (*chinna-saṃśaya*); that is, he whose doubt produced by ignorance has been cut away by the certainty that "abiding in the true nature of the Self alone is the supreme means to the highest good, and nothing else whatsoever. Thus he is one whose doubts have been severed.

The person who is qualified—who, having purified his self through the gradual practice of *karmayoga* in the manner previously described, has awakened to the actionless Self as his own Self by virtue of its being free from modifications such as birth—attains the steadfastness in knowledge characterized by freedom from action (*naiṣkarmya*), remaining seated while mentally renouncing all actions, neither acting nor causing others to act. By this very verse, the purpose of the previously mentioned *karmayoga* has been stated.

Furthermore, for one who is qualified [for action], yet being an ignorant bearer of the body due to the identification of the self with the body, whose conviction is fixed on "I am the doer" because of the uncontradicted cognition of the self as an agent—for such a person, since the total renunciation of all actions is impossible, his qualification lies only in the performance of enjoined duties by abandoning the fruits of action, not in the abandonment of the actions themselves. To demonstrate this point, He said:
"For it is not possible for a bearer of the body to abandon actions entirely.
But he who abandons the fruit of action—he is called a renouncer. (18.11)

(18.11) For indeed, by one who "bears a body"—one who bears a body (*dehabhṛt*) is so called because he possesses the conceit of identifying the body with the self; this refers to the non-discriminating person, for the discriminating one has been turned away from the qualification for agency by such statements as, "Know the Indestructible" (Gītā 2.21). Therefore, by that ignorant bearer of a body, it is not possible to abandon—that is, to renounce—all actions without remainder, that is, completely.

Therefore, he who is ignorant yet qualified [for action], performing obligatory duties while renouncing the fruits of action—that is, one who has renounced the mere attachment to the fruits of action—is designated as a "renouncer" (tyāgī), even though he is still an agent; this is said with the intent of praise. Consequently, only one who perceives the supreme reality—who does not identify with the body and is free from the notion of the body being the self—is capable of effecting the renunciation of all actions without exception.
What, then, is that purpose which results from the renunciation of all actions? It is said:
the fruit of action is threefold—undesirable, desirable, and mixed.
It accrues after death for those who do not renounce, but never for those who have renounced.

(18.12) "Undesirable" refers to that characterized by hell, the animal kingdom, and so forth; "desirable" refers to that characterized by the world of the gods and so forth; and "mixed," which is a combination of the desirable and the undesirable, refers to that characterized by the human state. That threefold action is of these three kinds.

The definition of "fruit" (*phala*) is as follows: the fruit characterized by merit and demerit, produced through the operation of many external causal factors, created by ignorance, resembling an illusion or a magical conjuration (*indrajāla-māyā*), and causing great delusion—though it approaches the inner self as if real, it goes to dissolution and disappearance due to its worthlessness. Such is this fruit for those who do not renounce, the ignorant performers of ritual action who have not renounced from the perspective of ultimate truth, after death—that is, subsequent to the fall of the body.

But this is not the case for renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*)—namely, the *paramahaṃsa-parivrājakas* who are established solely in knowledge and are renunciants in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). For those established solely in right vision (*samyagdarśana*) never fail to uproot the seed of transmigratory existence, which consists of ignorance and the rest; such is the meaning. Therefore, the renunciation of all actions is possible only for those who perceive the ultimate reality, because actions, their factors, and their fruits are superimposed upon the Self by ignorance; however, for the ignorant person—who perceives the locus and other factors of action as being the Self itself—the renunciation of all actions is not possible.
He demonstrates this with the following verses:
"O mighty-armed one, learn from me these five causes declared in the Sāṃkhya system of definitive conclusion for the successful accomplishment of all actions. (18.13)

(18.13) "O mighty-armed one, learn from me these five causes that bring about [the results] which are about to be described. This is said for the purpose of focusing the mind on what follows and to demonstrate the distinct nature of the subject matter. He praises those causes as things to be known: *sāṃkhye* refers to the Vedānta, that scripture in which the categories (*padārthāḥ*) are enumerated (*saṃkhyāyante*). *Kṛtānte* is an epithet of that very same [Vedānta].

"Kṛta" refers to action; its "anta," meaning end or completion, where that occurs, is "kṛtānta," which is to say, the end of action. By the verses, "Whatever purpose there may be in a small reservoir" (Gītā 2.46) and "All action in its entirety, O Pārtha, culminates in knowledge" (Gītā 4.33), he shows that when self-knowledge has arisen, there is the cessation of all actions. Therefore, for the sake of that self-knowledge, in the Sāṃkhya—that is, in the Vedānta known as Kṛtānta—those [means] are proclaimed and taught for the sake of accomplishment, for the purpose of the completion of all actions. What are they? It is said:
The locus, the agent, and the various instruments,
as well as the diverse individual activities and destiny as the fifth factor in this regard...

The locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the substratum for the manifestation of desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, knowledge, and so forth; that locus is the body. Likewise, the agent is characterized by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), as is the enjoyer. The instruments (*karaṇa*) are the various kinds—of many types—such as the ear and others, for the perception of sound and so forth; they number twelve. And there are the diverse activities (*ceṣṭā*) of the vital airs (*vāyu*), such as *prāṇa* and *apāna*. Furthermore, there is the divine (*daiva*). Among these four, the fifth—which completes the group of five—is the sun and other factors that assist the eye and other senses.
Whatever action a person undertakes with his body, speech, and mind...
Whether it be righteous or contrary, these five are its causes.

(18.15) Whatever action a person undertakes or accomplishes through these three—body, speech, and mind—whether it be righteous, that is, in accordance with dharma and scripture, or contrary, that is, not in accordance with scripture and contrary to dharma; and even that which is the cause of mere existence, such as the act of blinking or other involuntary movements—that too is the effect of previously performed dharma and adharma. Thus, by the inclusion of both the "righteous" and the "contrary," all such actions are subsumed. These five, as described, are the causes and the instrumental factors for all action whatsoever.

[Objection: But since these [five], beginning with the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*), are the effectors of all actions, how can it be said that "one undertakes action through body, speech, and mind"? [Response: This is not a fault. All action characterized by injunctions and prohibitions has the triad of body and so forth as its primary means. Since seeing, hearing, and so on—which constitute the maintenance of life—are subordinate members of that [action], they too are included within the threefold aggregate and are thus said to be "undertaken through the body and so forth. Furthermore, even at the time of the fruit, [the action] is experienced through those very means which have them as their primary factors. Thus, there is no contradiction in the five alone being the causes.
This being so, he who, due to his unrefined intellect, perceives the self alone as the agent— that person of dull understanding does not see. 18.16.

The word "therein" (*tatra*) is connected with what has been previously mentioned. This being so—that is, when the action is to be accomplished by the five aforementioned causes—then "this being so" is connected as the cause for the state of having poor intellect. In that context, regarding the action being performed by means of those [causes] which are imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) as non-different from the Self, the ignorant person who perceives the Self alone, as pure and isolated, thinking "I alone am the doer," [is one of poor intellect].

Why? Because his intellect is unrefined (*akṛtabuddhi*) due to the lack of instruction in the principles taught by the teachers of Vedānta; even one who maintains that the Self is distinct from the body and so forth, yet perceives the Self alone as the agent, is likewise of unrefined intellect. Therefore, because his intellect is unrefined, he does not perceive the true nature of the Self or of action—this is the meaning. Consequently, he is "evil-minded" (*durmati*); he is called evil-minded because his mind is base, perverted, and corrupt, being the cause for his incessant engagement in birth and death.

Even though he sees, he does not see, just as one with a visual disorder sees many moons, or as one sees the moon moving when the clouds are moving, or as one seated in a vehicle perceives oneself moving while others are running.
Who, then, is the wise person who sees correctly? It is said:
he whose state of being is free from egoism, and whose intellect is not defiled.
Even having slain these worlds, he does not kill, nor is he bound. 18.17.

For one whose self has been refined by the logic of the teachings of the scriptures and the preceptor, there does not arise the state of egoism—the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) characterized by the thought "I am the doer. These very five factors, beginning with the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*), are imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) as the agents of all actions; [the wise person realizes]: "I am not the agent; rather, I am the witness of their operations, for 'He is without breath, without mind, pure, higher than the high Imperishable' (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2), absolute and changeless"—thus he perceives. This is the case for that Self whose internal organ (*buddhi*, *antaḥkaraṇa*) is thus transformed.

Being free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), he is neither stained nor possessed of latent tendencies (*anuśayin*). He whose intellect is not stained by such thoughts as "I did this; therefore I shall go to hell"—he is one of right understanding (*sumati*); he sees. Even having slain all these worlds—all these living beings—this means that he does not slay, he does not perform the act of killing, and he is not bound, nor is he connected with its result, the fruit of unrighteousness (*adharma*).

Is it not a contradiction to say, "even having killed, he does not kill," even if it is intended as praise? This is not a fault, for it is logically consistent in view of both the worldly and the ultimate perspectives. Relying on the worldly perspective—the notion that the body and so forth are the self expressed as "I am the killer"—he says, "even having killed. But relying on the ultimate perspective as it has been shown, he says, "he does not kill, nor is he bound. Both of these are indeed consistent.

[Objection: But surely the Self does indeed act by coming together with the locus and other factors, since the word "only" (*kevalam*) is used in the passage: "But [he who sees] the Self as the sole agent" (Gītā 18.16). [Reply: This is not a fault, because if the Self were of an unchanging nature (*avikriya-svabhāva*), its being joined with the locus and other factors would be impossible. For conjunction with others is possible only for that which possesses change (*vikriyāvat*); or else, agency could only belong to one that acts through such conjunction.

However, since there is no conjunction of the changeless Self with anything else, agency through association is not possible. Therefore, the inherent isolation (*kevalatva*) of the Self is its very nature, and the word "isolated" (*kevala*) is merely a restatement of this fact. Furthermore, the changelessness of the Self is well-established by Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning. As has been repeatedly demonstrated in the Gītā itself: "This is said to be unchangeable" (Gītā 2.25), "Actions are performed by the qualities alone," and "Even while dwelling in the body, one does nothing" (Gītā 13.31). Thus, [the Self's nature] is established.

And in the Śrutis, such as "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were," and so forth; and according to logic, the royal road is that the reality of the Self is partless, independent, and changeless. Even if one were to admit that the Self possesses modification, its own modification alone could belong to the Self, and not the actions of the substratum and so forth could have the Self as their agent. For the action of another cannot come to the Self without being performed by it. That which is brought about through ignorance does not belong to it.

Just as the nature of silver does not belong to mother-of-pearl, or as the surface-dirtiness perceived by the ignorant through ignorance does not belong to the sky, so too the modifications of the locus and so forth belong only to those [objects], not to the Self. Therefore, it is rightly said: "Because he is untainted by the notion of egoity, the wise man neither kills nor is bound."

Having established the proposition, "This one neither kills nor is killed" (Gītā 2.19), and having stated the soul's immutability through supporting statements such as, "It is not born" (Gītā 2.20), [the Lord] briefly declared at the beginning of the scripture that the knower is exempt from the obligation to perform action by saying, "He who knows it as indestructible" (Gītā 2.21). Having then expanded upon this throughout the middle section by addressing various incidental topics, He here concludes for the purpose of summarizing the entire meaning of the scripture: "The wise man neither kills nor is bound."

This being so, since the misconception of being a "possessor of a body" is untenable, the renunciation of all actions performed under the influence of ignorance becomes possible; thus it is established that for renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*), the threefold fruit of action—whether undesirable and so forth—does not come to pass. Conversely, for others, it does occur, and this is unavoidable. Thus has the meaning of the *Gītā* scripture been summarized.
