This very essence of the meaning of all the Vedas should be reflected upon and realized by those of sharp intellect and learning; accordingly, we have demonstrated it here and there through the division of topics in accordance with the logic of the scriptures.
Now, that which sets actions in motion is being stated: knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower—this is the threefold impulsion to action.
The instrument, the action, and the agent—this is the threefold aggregate of action. (18.18)

(18.18) Knowledge (*jñāna*) is that by which something is known; it is spoken of generally as pertaining to all objects. Likewise, the knowable (*jñeya*) is that which is to be known; that too is spoken of generally as being everything. Similarly, the knower (*parijñātā*) is the experiencer (*bhoktā*), characterized by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, these three—without distinction—are the threefold impetus for action (*karmacodanā*) that sets all actions in motion. For when these three—knowledge and the others—converge, the undertaking of all actions occurs, having as its purpose the rejection or acquisition [of things].

Then, that which has been commenced by the five [factors] beginning with the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*), having become threefold through the division of speech, mind, and body, is subsumed within the three categories beginning with the instrument (*karaṇa*). This is what is stated: the instrument (*karaṇa*) is that by which something is performed; it is external, such as the ear and so forth, and internal, such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. The object (*karman*) is that which is most desired by the agent and is pervaded by the agent's action. The agent (*kartṛ*) is the one who sets the instruments into operation, characterized by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Thus, there is a threefold collection of objects (*karmasaṃgraha*)—meaning it is "collected" (*saṃgṛhyate*) within these three types.

"Comprehension" (*saṃgraha*): the comprehension of action is "the comprehension of action" (*karmasaṃgraha*), for action is indeed contained within these three; therefore, this threefold comprehension of action [is explained].

Now, since all things—the action, the agent, and the fruit—are composed of the *guṇas*, the threefold division based on the distinctions of the *guṇas*—sattva, rajas, and tamas—must be stated; thus it begins:
"Knowledge, action, and the agent are each of three kinds according to the distinction of the *guṇas*."
"Knowledge and action are declared in the *Guṇasaṃkhyāna* [system]; hear them as they truly are.

(18.19) Knowledge and action—action being activity (*kriyā*), not the technical grammatical "object" (*karman*) defined as that which is most desired to be reached; nor is it the agent (*kartṛ*), who is the accomplisher of actions. The restriction "only threefold" is intended to demonstrate the absence of any other genus distinct from the qualities (*guṇa*). The meaning is: "according to the distinction of the qualities," namely, by way of the division into *sattva* and so forth. They are "declared," that is, spoken of, in the *Guṇasaṃkhyāna*, the scripture of Kapila. Furthermore, that scripture of *Guṇasaṃkhyāna* is indeed an authoritative source regarding the subject of the experiencer of the qualities.

Although there may be a contradiction regarding the subject of the oneness of Brahman in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), nevertheless, those followers of Kapila (*kāpila*) are experts in defining the operations of the primary and secondary qualities (*guṇa*); thus, their scripture is also cited here for the purpose of praising the meaning that is about to be explained, and so there is no contradiction. Listen to these [qualities] as they truly are, according to logic, and according to scripture—listen to those various types of knowledge and so forth produced by the differentiation of the qualities; the meaning is: "Apply your mind with concentration to the meaning that is about to be explained. First, the threefold nature of knowledge is stated.
That by which one perceives the one undecaying being in all beings, as undivided within the divided—know that knowledge to be *sāttvika*.

By that knowledge through which one perceives—that is, sees—as a single entity (*bhāva*)—the word *bhāva* here signifying a "thing"—among all beings from the unmanifest (*avyakta*) down to the stationary (*sthāvara*), [one perceives] that single reality of the Self (*ātma-vastu*); [one perceives it as] imperishable (*avyaya*), meaning it does not perish either by its own nature or by its own attributes, meaning it is immutable (*kūṭastha*); and one perceives that entity as undivided (*avibhakta*), meaning that reality of the Self is not divided among the various distinct bodies, being continuous like space.
Know that knowledge to be direct, right vision, pertaining to the non-dual Self, and characterized by *sattva*.
Those views which perceive duality are unreal, being *rājasa* and *tāmasa*; they do not lead directly to the cessation of *saṃsāra*.
However, that knowledge which [perceives] various entities as distinct—[is of a different nature].

Know that knowledge which perceives all beings as distinct—that is, with differentiation, as separate from one another in every body—is of the nature of passion (*rājasa*). This means that by which knowledge one perceives various entities as diverse, the self as manifold, and things of different kinds—meaning they possess distinct characteristics—that knowledge, existing within all beings, you should know to be *rājasa*, produced by the quality of *rajas*. (18.21)
But that which is attached to a single effect as if it were the whole, which is without cause, devoid of the true object, and trivial— that is declared to be tāmasa.

That knowledge (*jñāna*) which, as if total, as if complete, and as if having all things as its object, is attached to a single effect—whether the body or an external object such as an image—thinking, "The Self or the Lord is only this much; there is nothing beyond this"; just as the Nagnakṣapaṇakas and others hold that the *jīva* exists within the body and is of the same size as the body, or that the Lord is merely a stone or a piece of wood—such knowledge is attached to a single effect, is causeless (*ahaituka*), devoid of reason (*hetu-varjita*), and lacking the true nature of reality (*atattvārthavat*).

That which possesses an object contrary to reality—whereas a real object is an object of truth (*tattvārtha*) and that [truth] exists for it as its object of knowledge—is "possessing the object of truth" (*tattvārthavat*); that which does not possess the object of truth is "not possessing the object of truth" (*atattvārthavat*). Furthermore, it is "insignificant" precisely because it is causeless, or because its scope is limited, or because its fruit is meager. That is declared to be *tāmasa*. For such is the knowledge observed among ignorant beings who are characterized by *tamas*.
Now, the threefold nature of action is being stated: that which is performed as a duty, free from attachment, and without passion or hatred.

That action which is performed by one who does not desire its fruit is called *sāttvika*. (18.23) "Obligatory" means constant; "free from attachment" means devoid of clinging. "Performed out of passion and aversion" refers to that which is done by one impelled by passion and impelled by aversion; the opposite of that is "not performed out of passion and aversion. "By one who does not desire its fruit": one who desires a fruit is a "fruit-desirer," meaning one who thirsts for results; the action performed by an agent who is the opposite of that—that is, by one who does not desire its fruit—is called *sāttvika*.
But that action which is performed with a desire for rewards, or again with egoism,
and with great exertion— that is declared to be rājasa.

As for the statement "by one desiring objects of desire"—meaning by one who seeks the fruits of action—it is said "with egoism" (*sāhaṃkāreṇa*) [Gītā 18.25], not with reference to the knower of reality. What then? It is with reference to the worldly *śrotriya* who is devoid of egoism. For one who knows the Self and is devoid of egoism in the ultimate sense, there is no possibility of being a performer of actions characterized by a preponderance of desire and exertion. This is true even for a performer of *sāttvika* action; if he is a non-knower of the Self and acts with egoism, how much more so for those performing *rājasa* and *tāmasa* actions?

In the world, even a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) who does not know the Self is called "free from ego" (*nirahaṃkāra*), as in the expression, "This Brāhmaṇa is free from ego. Therefore, it was said [in the previous verse], "or with ego," only with reference to that [worldly usage]. The word *punaḥ* is for the purpose of completing the meter. That action which is performed with great exertion—that is, brought to completion by the agent through great effort—is declared to be *rājasa*. That action which is undertaken out of delusion, without regard for the consequences, loss, injury to others, or one's own human capacity, is called *tāmasa*. (18.25)

(18.25) That which follows after [an action] is called its *anubandha* (consequence); that *anubandha*, as well as *kṣaya*—meaning that action in which, when being performed, there is a loss of power or a loss of wealth—and *hiṃsā*, meaning injury to living beings; and disregarding *pauruṣa*, which is human effort, namely one’s own capacity such as "I am able to complete this task"—that action which, out of delusion (*moha*) or lack of discrimination (*aviveka*), is undertaken while disregarding these factors from consequence up to human effort, is said to be *tāmasa*, arising from *tamas*.
Now, the distinction between types of agents is stated:

"One who is free from attachment, who does not speak of 'I', who is endowed with fortitude and enthusiasm, and who remains unchanged in success and failure—such an agent is said to be *sāttvika* (of the nature of goodness). (18.26)

(18.26) *Muktasaṅgaḥ*: one by whom attachment (*saṅga*) has been abandoned or relinquished is *muktasaṅgaḥ*; *anahaṃvādī*: one whose nature is not to speak of "I"; *dhṛtyutsāhasamanvitaḥ*: endowed with steadfastness (*dhṛti*)—which is maintenance—and enthusiasm (*utsāha*)—which is exertion—one who is joined with these two is *dhṛtyutsāhasamanvitaḥ*; *nirvikāraḥ siddhyasiddhyoḥ*: unchanging in success or failure—that is, regarding the success or failure of the fruit of the action being performed, he is one who is motivated solely by the authority of the scriptures and not by passion for the result and so forth.
One who is free from change is so described. Such a doer as this is said to be of the nature of *sattva*.
A doer who is passionate, desirous of the fruits of action, greedy, violent by nature, impure, and possessed by joy and sorrow, is proclaimed to be of the nature of *rajas*. (18.27)

(18.27) *Rāgī*: one who possesses passion (*rāga*); that is, one who desires the fruits of action, meaning one who seeks the results of ritual acts; *lubdha*: greedy, having developed a craving for the wealth of others, or failing to renounce one's own wealth at sacred sites and the like; *hiṃsātmaka*: violent by nature, characterized by causing pain to others; *aśuci*: impure, devoid of both external and internal cleanliness; *harṣaśokānvita*: possessed of joy and sorrow—joy upon obtaining the desired and sorrow upon obtaining the undesired or losing what is dear—and thus joined with those two, joy and sorrow; and of that very same action...
Joy and sorrow arise from success and failure; he who is the agent joined with these two is proclaimed as *rājasa*.
Unrestrained, vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, malicious, lazy, despondent, and procrastinating—the agent is said to be *tāmasa*. (18.28)

(18.28) "Unfit" means not disciplined, lacking meditative concentration (*asamāhita*), ordinary, with an utterly unrefined intellect like that of a child, stubborn— like a staff, not bowing to anyone— deceitful, a master of concealment, malicious, intent on creating dissension among others, lazy, having a disposition toward inaction even regarding duties, despondent, full of dejection, always of a depressed nature, and procrastinating, one who delays necessary tasks for too long and is always slow by nature, thinking "today or tomorrow."
He who does not perform even that which ought to be done, even within a month—he who is such as this is called a Tāmasa agent.
Now hear, O Dhanañjaya, the threefold division of the intellect and of fortitude according to their qualities, being declared in its entirety and in detail. 18.29.

(18.29) "Listen to the threefold division of intelligence and of fortitude according to their qualities—that is, according to the qualities of *sattva* and so forth"—this is the introduction of the aphorism. It is being proclaimed, explained in its entirety without remainder, exactly as it is, in its distinctness and discrimination, O Dhanañjaya. He is called Dhanañjaya because he conquered abundant wealth, both human and divine, during his conquest of the quarters; thus Arjuna is Dhanañjaya.
[Listen also to] the path of action and the path of renunciation, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, fear and fearlessness.

That intellect which knows both bondage and liberation, O Pārtha, is Sāttvic. (18.30) "Engagement" (*pravṛtti*) means active involvement—the path of action that causes bondage and has as its object the injunctions prescribed by the scriptures. "Withdrawal" (*nivṛtti*) means cessation—the path of renunciation that causes liberation. Since they are mentioned in the same context as bondage and liberation, it is understood that engagement and withdrawal refer to the paths of ritual action and renunciation respectively. "What ought to be done and what ought not to be done" (*kāryākārye*) refers to what is enjoined and what is prohibited, whether worldly or Vedic; that is to say, the performance and non-performance of actions according to the understanding derived from the scriptures.

Of what? Of actions whose objects are seen or unseen, depending on place, time, and so forth. Regarding "fear and fearlessness": that from which one fears is "fear," such as thieves, tigers, and the like; that which is not fear is "fearlessness. "Fear and fearlessness" refers to the causes of fear and fearlessness concerning both seen and unseen objects—this is the meaning. That intellect (*buddhi*) which knows—that is, discerns—bondage along with its cause and liberation along with its cause, O Pārtha, is *sāttvika*. In this context, knowledge is a function (*vṛtti*) of the intellect, whereas the intellect itself possesses functions. Fortitude (*dhṛti*) likewise is simply a specific function of the intellect.
O Pārtha, that intellect by which one perceives dharma and adharma, as well as what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, incorrectly, is of the nature of passion (rājasī). 18.31.

O Pārtha, that intellect by which one does not discern, as they truly are and with certainty, the dharma enjoined by the scriptures and the adharma prohibited by them, nor what ought to be done and what ought not to be done—those very matters of action and non-action previously mentioned—it is rajasic.
O Pārtha, that intellect which, enveloped by darkness, regards adharma as dharma and perceives all objects in a perverted manner, is tamasic. (18.32)

(18.32) That which, being shrouded by darkness (*tamas*), considers what is unrighteous to be prescribed as righteous and knows it as such—that intellect, O Pārtha, is *tāmasī*. It perceives all objects—indeed, all things to be known—as contrary, perceiving them precisely as their opposites.
[Now, regarding *dhṛti*: that steadfastness (*dhṛti*) by which one maintains the activities of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses...
"That fortitude by which, through yoga, one holds fast the activities of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses without deviation—that, O Pārtha, is sattvic.

(18.33) The connection with the word "without deviation" (*avyabhicāriṇyā*) is with the distant term "by which fortitude" (*dhṛtyā yayā*). What does it hold fast? "The activities of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses"—that is, the mind (*manas*), the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and the senses (*indriya*); their activities are their movements. One holds fast, that is, restrains, them from engaging in paths contrary to the scriptures. For when they are held fast by fortitude, they do not concern themselves with paths that deviate from the scriptures. "Through yoga," meaning through *samādhi*; "without deviation," meaning constantly accompanied by *samādhi*.

This is what is meant: one sustains through yoga the activities of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses by means of a steadfastness (*dhṛti*) that is unswerving. That steadfastness which has such characteristics, O Pārtha, is *sāttvika*.
But that steadfastness by which one holds fast to duty, pleasure, and wealth, O Arjuna, desiring their fruits through attachment—that, O Pārtha, is *rājasa* steadfastness. (18.34)

(18.34) But that *dhṛti* by which one constantly holds fast in the mind the *dharma*, *kāma*, and *artha*—that is, *dharma*, *kāma*, and *artha*—and determines them as things to be performed, O Arjuna; and that person who, through attachment to whichever of these, such as *dharma* and so forth, becomes desirous of their fruits—that person’s *dhṛti*, O Pārtha, is *rājasī*. [That *dhṛti*] by which one holds fast to sleep, fear, sorrow, despondency, and even intoxication...
The dull-witted person does not relinquish that resolve, O Pārtha; it is considered *tāmasī* (of the nature of darkness).

(18.35) By which [resolve] a person of base intellect (*durmedhāḥ*), esteeming as his own high purpose sleep, drowsiness, fear, terror, grief, despondency, dejection, intoxication, and the pursuit of sense objects—acting like one intoxicated and constantly performing even intoxication itself as something to be done in the mind—does not relinquish it but rather maintains it; that resolve of his is considered *tāmasī*.
The threefold division of actions and agents according to the distinction of qualities has been stated. Now, the threefold division of the fruit, which is happiness, is being declared:
"But now, O bull of the Bharatas, hear from me of the three kinds of happiness, wherein one finds delight through practice and reaches the end of suffering. (18.36)

(18.36) Now hear of the threefold happiness; apply your mind to this, O bull among the Bharatas. Through practice—through familiarity and repetition—one finds delight, one attains joy in that experience of happiness wherein one reaches the end of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the definitive attainment of peace from suffering.
That which is like poison at first, but in its result is comparable to nectar.
That happiness is said to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika), born from the clarity of one’s own intellect. 18.37.

That happiness which is initially—first—at the moment of contact, at the commencement of knowledge, dispassion, meditation, and concentration, is of the nature of pain due to being preceded by extreme exertion, like poison; whereas the happiness arising from the maturation of knowledge, dispassion, and so forth, in its final transformation, is comparable to nectar—that happiness is declared by the wise to be *sāttvika*. It is born from the clarity (*prasāda*) of the intellect regarding the Self (*ātmabuddhiprasādaja*); "intellect regarding the Self" means the intellect directed toward the Self, and the "clarity" of that intellect is its stainlessness, its transparency like that of water. From that [clarity] it is born.

Or, "self-cognition" (ātmabuddhi) is the intellect whose object is the self or which has the self as its support; it is that which is born from the excellence of its clarity. Therefore, that is *sāttvika*.
That pleasure which, arising from the contact of the senses with their objects, is like nectar at first but becomes like poison in its transformation—that is remembered as *rājasa*. (18.38)

(18.38) That pleasure which arises from the contact of the sense objects with the senses is like nectar at first—at the initial moment—but in its consequence it is like poison. Because it is the cause of the loss of strength, vigor, beauty, wisdom, intelligence, wealth, and enthusiasm, and because it is the cause of unrighteousness (*adharma*) and the resulting hells and so forth, that pleasure is remembered as *rājasa* (passionate), being like poison at the end of its enjoyment. And that pleasure which is delusive for the self both at the beginning and in its aftermath...
That which arises from sleep, laziness, and negligence is declared to be tāmasa.

(18.39) That pleasure which is delusive—that is, which causes delusion of the self—in its beginning, its consequence, and at the time following its conclusion; which arises from sleep, laziness, and negligence—meaning it originates from those three—is declared to be tāmasa.
Now, a verse is commenced for the purpose of concluding this section:
"There exists nothing on earth, nor again in heaven among the gods, that is free from these three qualities born of material nature. (18.40)

(18.40) There is no such being on earth—whether among humans and other creatures, or any other thing lacking life—or again, any being in heaven among the gods, that could be free from or abandoned by these three qualities, such as *sattva* and the rest, which are born of *prakṛti*, produced from *prakṛti*; "there is no such [being]" is how it connects with what precedes.

The entire cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), characterized by action, agent, and fruit, consisting of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*), has been described as a calamity together with its root. This was expressed through the metaphor of a tree in passages such as "Rooted above" (*Gītā* 15.1), and further stated: "Having cut that [tree] with the firm weapon of detachment" (*Gītā* 15.3), and "Then that state is to be sought after" (*Gītā* 15.4).

And since, in that case, because everything consists of the three *guṇas*, the cessation of the cause of *saṃsāra* would be impossible, it must be explained how that cessation may occur; furthermore, the entire meaning of the *Gītā* scripture must be summarized, and it must be shown that this alone is the purpose of all the Vedas and Smṛtis to be practiced by those desiring the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). For this purpose, the passage beginning with "Of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas... is commenced:
"O scorcher of foes, the duties of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are distributed according to the *guṇas* born of their own natures. (18.41)

(18.41) Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas constitute the "brāhmaṇakṣatriyaviśaḥ"; [the Lord says] "of those brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras. The reason for not forming a compound with the śūdras is that, while they belong to a single caste, they lack the qualification for the Vedas. O scorcher of foes, actions have been divided and established through their mutual distinctions.

By what? By the qualities (guṇas) originating from their own nature (svabhāva). Nature is the primordial material cause (prakṛti) of the Lord, consisting of the three qualities (triguṇātmikā), which is Māyā; those qualities for which that is the source are "originating from their own nature. By these, the actions such as tranquility (śama) and so forth are distributed among the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes.

Alternatively, for the nature of a Brāhmaṇa, sattva is the source or cause; likewise, for the nature of a Kṣatriya, rajas with sattva as subordinate is the source; for the nature of a Vaiśya, rajas with tamas as subordinate is the source; and for the nature of a Śūdra, tamas with rajas as subordinate is the source—this is seen from the observation of the natures of the four [classes] as tranquility, sovereignty, desire, and delusion, respectively.

Alternatively, *svabhāva* (nature) refers to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) formed in previous births, which becomes manifest in the present life as being directed toward its own specific effects. Those qualities (*guṇas*) for which this nature is the source are "those originating from nature" (*svabhāvaprabhavā guṇāḥ*). This is because it is logically untenable for the manifestation of qualities to be without a cause. Furthermore, by stating "nature is the cause," a specific kind of cause is being adopted.

Thus, by these qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—which originate from nature and arise from primordial matter (*prakṛti*), actions such as tranquility (*śama*) and the rest are distributed according to their respective effects.

[Objection: But surely the duties such as tranquility (*śama*) and the rest, which are prescribed by the scripture for the Brāhmaṇas and others, are already distinguished by the scripture itself; why then is it said that they are "distinguished by the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva*"? [Reply: This is not a fault. Even by the scripture, the duties such as tranquility are distinguished for the Brāhmaṇas and others precisely with regard to their specific qualities like *sattva*, and not independently of those qualities. Thus, although these duties are distinguished by the scripture, they are also said to be "distinguished by the qualities. What, then, are those duties? It is said: Tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, forbearance, and uprightness.
Knowledge, realized wisdom, and faithfulness are the duties of a Brāhmaṇa, born of his own nature.

(18.42) Tranquility and self-restraint have meanings as previously explained; austerity is as described, consisting of bodily and other forms; purity has been explained; forbearance is patience; and uprightness is straightforwardness. Furthermore, knowledge and realized wisdom, along with faithfulness—the state of being a believer characterized by trust in the meanings of the scriptures—are the duties of the Brāhmaṇa caste, born of his own nature. That which was stated earlier—that [duties] are "divided according to the qualities arising from one's own nature"—is precisely what is meant here by the phrase "born of his own nature."
Heroism, majesty, firmness, dexterity, and not fleeing in battle, as well as generosity and the spirit of lordship— this is the duty of a Kshatriya, born of his own nature. 18.43.

Valor (*śaurya*) is the state of being a hero; energy (*tejas*) is boldness; fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the power of sustaining oneself, by which one remains undepressed in all circumstances when supported; skillfulness (*dākṣya*) is the state of being dexterous, the engagement in suddenly arisen tasks without confusion; and even in battle, it is the refusal to flee, the state of not turning one's back on enemies; generosity (*dāna*) is the open-handedness regarding things to be given; and lordliness (*īśvarabhāva*) is the state of being a lord, the manifestation of sovereign power.

With respect to those who are to be ruled, the duty of the Kṣatriya—the duty ordained for the Kṣatriya caste—is the duty of the Kṣatriya born of its own nature. Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are the duties of the Vaiśya born of his own nature. Service by its very nature is the duty of the Śūdra as well, born of his own nature. 18.44.

(18.44) Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade—agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade constitute "agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade. Agriculture (*kṛṣi*) is the tilling of the soil. Cattle-rearing (*gaurakṣya*): one who protects cows is a cowherd (*gorakṣa*); the state of being such is cattle-rearing, meaning the tending of livestock (*pāśupālya*). Trade (*vāṇijya*) is the work of a merchant, characterized by buying and selling; it is the duty of the Vaiśya caste, born of their own nature. Service (*paricaryā*), which consists of the nature of obedience, is likewise the duty of the Śūdra, born of his own nature.

The attainment of heaven is the natural fruit of these duties prescribed for each caste when they are properly performed, according to such Smṛti texts as: "Castes and stages of life, being devoted to their own duties, after dying and experiencing the fruit of their actions, then, by what remains [of that merit], obtain a birth distinguished by [excellent] country, caste, family, character, lifespan, learning, conduct, wealth, happiness, and intelligence" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.2.2.3); and because the Purāṇas record specific differences in the fruits of the worlds for those belonging to the castes and stages of life.
However, from another cause, there is this fruit which is about to be described.
Devoted to his own particular duty, a man attains perfection. Listen to how one who is intent on his own work finds success. 18.45.

Devoted to and intent upon his own respective duties according to the characteristics previously described, a person—the qualified individual—attains, through the performance of his own duty, *saṃsiddhi*, which is the state of fitness for the perfection of knowledge once impurities have been destroyed; that is, he reaches it. Is *saṃsiddhi* attained directly from the mere performance of one's own duty? No. How then? Listen to how and by what manner a person devoted to his own duty attains perfection:
"From whom proceeds the activity of beings, by whom all this is pervaded."
By worshipping Him with one's own duty, a human being attains perfection.

(18.46) For from Him—from the Inner Controller, the Lord—comes the activity, the origin, or the movement of all beings, living creatures; by that Lord this entire world is pervaded. By worshipping, honoring, and propitiating that Lord with one's own duty as previously described according to each social class, a human being attains perfection, characterized solely by fitness for steadfastness in knowledge.
Since this is so, therefore it is better to perform one's own duty, even if deficient, than to perform the duty of another well-performed.
One who performs the action prescribed by one's own nature incurs no sin. 18.47.

(18.47) One's own duty (*svadharma*)—meaning one's own prescribed duty—is better (*śreyān*), that is, more praiseworthy, than the duty of another. The word "even" (*api*) should be understood [to apply] to the phrase "even if deficient. That which is determined by nature (*svabhāvaniyata*) means fixed by nature; what was called "born of nature" is precisely what is meant here by "determined by nature. Just as poison does not cause harm to a worm born from poison, so too, performing an action determined by one's nature, one incurs no sin (*kilbiṣa*).

It has been said that one who performs action determined by his own nature incurs no sin, like a worm in poison; and that the duty of another is fraught with fear; and that for one who does not know the Self, "no one indeed remains even for a moment without performing action" (Gītā 3.5).
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, one should not abandon one's innate duty, even if it is flawed.
For all undertakings are enveloped by defect, as fire is by smoke. 18.48.

(18.48) *Sahaja* means that which arises simultaneously with birth. What is that? Action (*karman*), O son of Kuntī, one should not abandon even if it is defective, because it consists of the three *guṇas*. "All undertakings" (*sarvārambhāḥ*) refers to those things which are undertaken; this means all actions. From the context, whatever undertakings there may be—whether one's own duties (*svadharma*) or the duties of others (*paradharma*)—all of them are indeed covered by defect, just as fire is covered by its innate smoke, because they consist of the three *guṇas*; this "consisting of the three *guṇas*" is the reason here. Because they consist of the three *guṇas*, they are covered by defect.

Because there is fault even in performing the duties of another by abandoning one's own duty called "inherent" (*sahaja*), one is not at all liberated; moreover, the duty of another is fraught with fear. And since it is not possible for an ignorant person to abandon action entirely, the meaning is that one should therefore not renounce it.
Is it that one should not renounce because it is impossible to abandon action entirely? Or is it that there is a fault in abandoning inherent action? What follows from this? If...

Since it is impossible to abandon [it] entirely, one's innate action (sahaja-karma) should not be abandoned; thus, it is established that if it were possible to abandon it entirely, there would indeed be merit. This is true.

If it is argued that renunciation in its entirety is simply not possible, is the person (puruṣa) of a nature that is eternally active, as the *guṇas* are for the Sāṃkhyas? Or is action itself the agent, as the momentary aggregates (*skandhas*) are for the Buddhists? In either case, the renunciation of action in its entirety is not possible. Now, as for the third position: when it acts, the entity is active; when it does not act, that very same entity is inactive.

This being so, it is possible to abandon action entirely. However, this is the distinction regarding this third position: there is no eternally moving substance, nor is the action itself the agent. What then? Action arises while the substance remains stable, and having existed, it perishes. That pure substance persists as possessing power (*śaktimat*). Thus say the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas), and that very [substance] is the agent. What is the fault in this position?

But this very point is a defect, because this doctrine is non-Bhāgavata. How is this known? Because the Blessed Lord has said: "The being of the non-existent does not exist" (Gītā 2.16), and so forth. For according to the followers of Kaṇāda, there is the coming into being of the non-existent and the passing away of the existent; thus, this doctrine is non-Bhāgavata. If it is asked, "Even if it is non-Bhāgavata, what is the harm if it is consistent with logic? it is replied: This [doctrine] is indeed defective, because it contradicts all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

How so? If, first of all, a substance such as a dyad (dvyaṇuka) is absolutely non-existent prior to its production, and having been produced, remains for some time only to fall back again into absolute non-existence—then, this being the case, that which is non-existent arises as existent, and that which is existent falls into non-existence; non-being becomes being, and being becomes non-being.

In that regard, it is claimed that non-existence (*abhāva*), while being produced, is like the horn of a hare prior to its arising, and that it arises in dependence upon causes known as the inherent (*samavāyin*), the non-inherent (*asamavāyin*), and the instrumental (*nimitta*). However, it is not possible to say that "non-existence is produced and depends upon a cause," because non-existent things such as the horns of a hare are never observed. If, on the other hand, existent things (*bhāva*) such as jars arise, it can be understood that they arise in dependence upon some cause for their mere manifestation.

Furthermore, if both the non-existent and the existent were to exist [simultaneously], or if both were non-existent, no one would have confidence in any of the conventional practices involving means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*), because the certainty that "the existent is indeed existent" and "the non-existent is indeed non-existent" would be untenable.

Furthermore, they say that "it arises" means that a substance such as a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) enters into a relation with the existence (*sattā*) of its own causes. Prior to its arising it is non-existent; subsequently, depending upon the operation of its causes, it becomes connected with its own causes—the atoms—and with *sattā* by way of the relation characterized as inherence (*samavāya*). Being thus connected, it comes to exist as inherent in its causes.

In this regard, it must be asked: how could that which is non-existent have its own cause, or how could it have any relation with anything? For it is not possible, according to any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), to conceive of a barren woman’s son having his own cause or any relation with anything.

But surely the Vaiśeṣikas do not conceive of a relation for non-existence in this way. For they maintain that substances such as dyads (dvyaṇuka) possess a relation characterized by inherence in their own causes only when they already exist. No; for they do not admit existence prior to the relation. Indeed, the Vaiśeṣikas do not accept the existence of jars and the like prior to the operation of the potter, the stick, the wheel, and so forth. Nor do they maintain that clay itself merely undergoes the attainment of the form of a jar and the like.
Consequently, by process of elimination, it follows that they must accept the relation of that which is precisely non-existent.

[Objection: Is it not the case that even for a non-existent thing, a relation characterized by inherence (*samavāya*) is not contradictory? [Reply: No; because things such as the son of a barren woman are never observed. Even though non-existence is equal in all cases, a distinction must be stated regarding why the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of a jar or similar object has a relation with its own cause, whereas that of the son of a barren woman does not. A distinction cannot be shown by anyone through definitions such as "the non-existence of one," "the non-existence of two," "the non-existence of all," "prior non-existence," "non-existence after destruction" (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), "mutual non-existence" (*itaretarābhāva*), or "absolute non-existence" (*atyantābhāva*).

And in the absence of any distinction, it is the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the jar alone that, through the potter and other factors, attains the state of being a jar and becomes connected with the entity known as the potsherd; once so connected, it becomes fit for all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*). It is not, however, the subsequent non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) of the jar itself that is so, even though it too is a non-entity. Thus, while non-entities such as subsequent non-existence are never fit for worldly transaction, only the prior non-existence—which, in the form of substances such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), is subject to transactions such as production—is capable of such usage. This is the point.

This is inconsistent; for there is no distinction between them in terms of being non-existent, just as in the case of absolute destruction and non-existence (*atyantapradhvaṃsābhāva*). [Objection: But we do not say that prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) attains the state of being an entity. [Reply: In that case, it would be an entity attaining the state of being an entity—just as a jar attains the state of being a jar, or a cloth attains the state of being a cloth. This too is contrary to valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like the attainment of being an entity by non-existence. Furthermore, even the Sāṃkhya position regarding transformation (*pariṇāma*) does not differ from the Vaiśeṣika position, because it accepts the arising and destruction of previously non-existent properties (*dharma*).

Even if one accepts manifestation (*abhivyakti*) and concealment (*tirobhāva*), there remains a contradiction with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-virodha*) regarding whether these manifestation and concealment themselves exist or do not exist, just as before. By this, the claim that production and so forth are merely the specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of the cause itself is also refuted.

By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the one existent reality alone is conceptualized as manifold through ignorance (*avidyā*) by means of attributes such as arising and perishing, like an actor. This Bhāgavata doctrine was stated in the verse "The non-existent has no being" (*Gītā* 2.16), because the cognition of existence (*sat-pratyaya*) is invariable, whereas the cognitions of other [attributes] are variable.

How, then, is it that the renunciation of action in its entirety is not possible while the Self remains changeless? Whether the *guṇas* (qualities) are real entities or merely imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*), action is their property; therefore, it is only superimposed upon the Self by ignorance. Thus it was said: "For no one, even for a moment, is able to renounce [action] entirely."

But for the wise person, once ignorance has been removed by knowledge, it is indeed possible to renounce action entirely; for a remnant of that which was superimposed by ignorance cannot logically remain. Indeed, when the cataract is removed, no trace remains of the double moon or other such things superimposed by the vision of one suffering from ophthalmia. This being the case, such statements as "having mentally renounced all actions" (Gītā 5.13), "the man who is devoted to his own duty attains perfection" (Gītā 18.45), and "by worshipping Him through one's own duty, one attains perfection" (Gītā 18.46) become consistent.
And [as it is said in Gītā 18.46]: "The man attains...

Now, that perfection born of action which was described as characterized by fitness for steadfastness in knowledge, and its fruit—which is the perfection of freedom from action (*naiṣkarmya-siddhi*) characterized by steadfastness in knowledge—must be explained; thus the following verse is begun:
"One whose intellect is unattached everywhere, who has conquered the self, and from whom longing has departed..."
Through renunciation, he attains the supreme perfection of actionlessness.

(18.49) One whose intellect is unattached—that is, one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is free from attachment toward all things that cause it, such as son, wife, and so forth; one who has conquered the self—that is, one whose internal organ is mastered and brought under control; one who is free from longing—that is, one from whom desire or thirst for the body, life, and enjoyments has departed; he who is such a knower of the Self attains *naiṣkarmya-siddhi*, from which all actions have departed.

Through the realization of the Self as the actionless Brahman, he becomes free from action; the state of being so is *naiṣkarmya*. That *naiṣkarmya* is itself the perfection (*siddhi*), hence it is called *naiṣkarmyasiddhi*. Alternatively, it is the accomplishment or attainment of the state of being free from action, characterized by abiding in the nature of the actionless Self. That *naiṣkarmyasiddhi*, which is supreme—that is, most excellent, distinct from the perfections born of ritual action, and consisting in the state of immediate liberation—is attained through renunciation, that is, through right vision (*samyagdarśana*) or through the renunciation of all actions preceded by such vision.
He attains, he reaches. And thus it has been said: "Having renounced all actions with the mind, he sits neither acting nor causing action to be done" (Gītā 5.13).

For one who has attained the perfection characterized as previously described—produced by the performance of one's own duties in the form of worshiping the Lord—and for whom the discriminative knowledge of the Self has arisen, the manner in which the perfection characterized by *naiṣkarmya* (freedom from action), consisting of steadfastness in pure self-knowledge, comes about must be stated. Therefore, He says:
"Learn from Me how one who has attained perfection reaches Brahman."
"In brief, O son of Kuntī, this is the supreme culmination of knowledge" (18.50).

Having attained perfection through one's own duty by worshipping the Lord, one attains the perfection characterized by the fitness of the body and senses for steadfastness in knowledge—a perfection born of His grace. The phrase "having attained perfection" is a restatement intended for what follows.

What is that answer for the sake of which this restatement is made? It is said: "In whatever manner—that is, by way of steadfastness in knowledge—one attains Brahman, the Supreme Self, learn from My words that manner, the sequence for attaining steadfastness in knowledge; understand it with certainty. Is this in detail? No, He says: "Just briefly, in summary alone, O Kaunteya, learn how one attains Brahman."

In order to demonstrate, in its specific nature, that attainment of Brahman which was promised by this [statement], he says: "The culmination of knowledge is that which is supreme. *Niṣṭhā* means the final limit, the completion—this is what it signifies. Of what? Of the knowledge of Brahman. What is that which is supreme? It is of the same nature as the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*). What is that like? It is of the same nature as the Self. And what is that like? It is of the same nature as the Self has been described by the Blessed One, by the sentences of the Upaniṣads, and through logical reasoning.

Is it not the case that cognition has the form of the object, but the object is not the cognition, nor is the Self ever held anywhere to possess form? But surely the Self’s possession of form is heard in such scriptural passages as "of the color of the sun," "consisting of light," and "self-luminous. No; for those statements serve to negate the nature of darkness. Since the negation of forms such as substance and quality would imply that the Self is of the nature of darkness, the statements beginning with "of the color of the sun" (Gītā 8.9) are intended to negate that very nature of darkness.

Furthermore, because there is a specific negation of form in the term "formless" (*arūpa*), and because it is not an object of perception—as seen in such passages as, "His form does not stand within the range of vision; no one sees him with the eye" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.20), and "without sound, without touch" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.15)—it is therefore untenable to claim that knowledge has the Self as its form.

How, then, is there knowledge of the self (*ātman*)? For whatever object a cognition has, that cognition takes on the form of that object. And it has been stated that the self is formless (*nirākāra*). If both the cognition and the self are formless, how can there be an establishment based on the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of them? No; because the self is established as being absolutely pure, extremely transparent, and extremely subtle. And since the intellect (*buddhi*) is established as possessing purity and so forth just like the self, it is possible for it to manifest as the reflection of the form of the self's consciousness.

The mind is a reflection of the intellect (*buddhi*); the senses are reflections of that [mind]; and the body is a reflection of the senses. Therefore, worldly people form the view of the Self (*ātman*) with respect to the body alone. Furthermore, the Materialists (*Lokāyatika*), who maintain that consciousness resides in the body, say: "The person is the body characterized by consciousness. Likewise, others maintain that consciousness resides in the senses; others that it resides in the mind; and others that it resides in the intellect. Beyond even that, some have accepted as the Self the internal, unmanifest state called the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*), which is the condition of ignorance (*avidyā*).

In all cases, from the intellect (*buddhi*) down to the body, the appearance of the self’s consciousness (*ātmacaitanya-ābhāsatā*) is the cause of the delusion regarding the self; therefore, knowledge concerning the self need not be enjoined. What, then, is to be done? Only the cessation of the superimposition (*adhyāropaṇa*) of non-self entities such as name and form (*nāmarūpa*) must be accomplished. Furthermore, the realization of the self’s consciousness must be accomplished, because [the self] is perceived as being qualified by the forms of all objects superimposed through ignorance (*avidyā*).

For this very reason, the Buddhist Vijñānavādins have maintained that no entity exists apart from consciousness, and they accept the self-evident nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*) as being independent of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, regarding Brahman, one need only perform the removal of what has been superimposed by ignorance; there is no effort required for the knowledge of Brahman itself, because it is already extremely well-established.

To those whose intellects have been captivated by the specific forms of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) imagined through ignorance, [the Self], though extremely well-known, easy to understand, most proximate, and identical with their own self, appears unknown, difficult to comprehend, exceedingly remote, and as if something else entirely—this being the case for the undiscriminating. However, for those whose intellects have turned away from external forms and who have obtained the grace of the Guru and the Self, there is no happiness beyond this that is more well-established, easier to know, or more proximate.
Thus it has been said: "The dharma is directly perceivable" (*Gītā* 9.2), and so forth.

However, some who consider themselves wise say: "Because it is formless, the intellect does not reach the reality of the Self; therefore, steadfastness in right knowledge is difficult to achieve. This is true for those who lack the traditional lineage of teachers, who have not heard the Vedānta, whose intellects are excessively attached to external objects, and who have not exerted effort in the correct means of valid cognition. But for those who are the opposite of these, [it is not so].

The notion of reality regarding the worldly duality of the grasped and the grasper is extremely difficult to establish, because no other entity is perceived apart from the consciousness of the Self, as we have already stated: "This is exactly so, and not otherwise. And it has been said by the Blessed One: "That which is day for all beings is night for the sage who sees" (Gītā 2.69). Therefore, the cessation of the cognition of external forms and distinctions is itself the cause for taking refuge in the true nature of the Self.

For the so-called Self is never unestablished for anyone, nor is it something to be attained, abandoned, or acquired; for if that Self were unestablished, all activities directed toward one's own interest would result in being purposeless. Nor is it possible to imagine that the body and other such things exist for the sake of the insentient; nor is pleasure for the sake of pleasure, nor pain for the sake of pain. This is because all worldly transaction culminates in the realization of the Self.

Therefore, just as there is no dependence on other means of knowledge for the delimitation of one's own body, so too, because the Self is the innermost of all, there is no dependence on other means of knowledge for its realization; thus it is established that the steadfastness in the knowledge of the Self is well-known among the discerning.

Even for those who maintain that formless cognition (*jñāna*) is not itself perceptible, it must be admitted that the apprehension of the object of knowledge occurs solely by virtue of cognition; thus, cognition must be accepted as being extremely well-known, just like pleasure and other such states. Furthermore, because inquiry (*jijñāsā*) would otherwise be impossible: if cognition were unknown, it would be an object of inquiry just like the object of knowledge. Just as a knower desires to pervade the object of knowledge—such as a jar or similar things—by means of cognition, so too he would desire to know cognition itself through another cognition. But this is not the case. Therefore, cognition is extremely well-known, and for this very reason, the knower is also [well-known].

"It is well-known. Therefore, effort should not be made toward [theoretical] knowledge, but rather toward the cessation of the notion of self in that which is not-self. Consequently, steadfastness in knowledge is easily accomplished. This very supreme steadfastness in knowledge is now described: "How is it to be performed?
Being endowed with a purified intellect and having restrained the self with fortitude..."
Having abandoned the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, and having cast off attachment and aversion... 18.51.

Endowed with a pure intellect characterized by discernment and free from illusion, and having restrained—that is, brought under control—the self, which is the aggregate of the body and the senses, through fortitude; having abandoned sound and other objects—meaning those sense-objects beginning with sound, the implication being that he has set aside those necessary merely for the maintenance of the body and abandoned those in excess of them for the sake of pleasure; and having cast off and relinquished attachment and aversion toward those things obtained for the purpose of maintaining the body...
thereupon.
Frequenting solitary places, eating lightly, with speech, body, and mind restrained, he is constantly devoted to the yoga of meditation and has fully taken refuge in dispassion. 18.52.

One who frequents solitude (*viviktasevī*) is so called because it is his habit to resort to solitary places such as forests, riverbanks, mountain caves, and the like. One who eats lightly (*laghvāśī*) is one whose nature is to eat sparingly. These two—resorting to solitude and eating lightly—are mentioned here because they serve as causes for the clarity of the mind by warding off defects such as drowsiness. One whose speech, body, and mind are restrained (*yatavākkāyamānasaḥ*): he whose speech, body, and mind are controlled—that ascetic established in knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭha*) should be one whose speech, body, and mind are restrained.

Thus, having ceased all activities of the senses and being devoted to meditation (*dhyāna*) and yoga—where *dhyāna* is the contemplation of the nature of the Self and *yoga* is the one-pointed concentration upon the Self—he for whom these two are his primary duties is "devoted to meditation and yoga. The inclusion of the word "constantly" (*nityam*) is intended to demonstrate that there are no other duties to be performed, such as the recitation of mantras. Furthermore, he has fully resorted to dispassion (*vairāgya*), which is the state of being free from passion; that is, a total lack of craving for objects seen or unseen, having properly and constantly taken refuge in it.
Moreover, [he abandons] egoism, power, arrogance, desire, anger, and possessiveness.
Being liberated and free from the sense of "mine," peaceful, he is fit for becoming Brahman.

(18.53) "Ahaṃkāra" is the act of egoizing—that is, the conceit of "I" with respect to the body and so forth. "Bala" refers to power or capacity conjoined with desire and passion, and not merely the natural physical capacity of the body and such, because it is impossible to abandon that latter through mere renunciation. "Darpa" is pride, which arises immediately after joy and is the cause of transgressing dharma, according to the traditional teaching: "One who is joyful becomes proud; one who is proud transgresses dharma."

And having abandoned that—namely desire, longing, anger, hatred, and possessiveness—even though external possession may have been acquired through the necessity of maintaining the body or for the sake of performing dharma, provided one has renounced the defects of the senses and mind; having become a wandering mendicant of the highest order (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka*), free from the sense of "mine" even regarding the mere maintenance of the body and life, and therefore peaceful and tranquil, the ascetic who has withdrawn both joy and exertion becomes established in knowledge and is capable of attaining the state of Brahman (*brahmabhūya*).
By this sequence:
Having become Brahman, serene in self, he neither grieves nor desires;
equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion unto Me.

"Become Brahman" means having attained Brahman; "serene in self" means having acquired the nature of inner spiritual tranquility. He does not grieve—he does not sorrow or feel distress on account of any deficiency in his goals or any imperfection in himself. He does not desire—for desire for objects not yet attained is not possible for a knower of Brahman. Therefore, this is restated as the natural state of one who has become Brahman: "he does not grieve, he does not desire. Alternatively, there is another reading: "he does not rejoice."

"Equal toward all beings" means that, by comparison with oneself (*ātmaupamyena*), one views pleasure and pain in all beings as exactly the same. This does not refer here to the "vision of equality with the Self," because that will be described later in the verse: "By devotion he comes to know Me" (Gītā 18.55).

Being such a person, established in knowledge, he attains supreme, highest devotion—devotion characterized by knowledge—which is the fourth kind, as it has been said: "Four kinds of people worship Me" (Gītā 7.16).
Then, by means of that which is characterized by knowledge...
Through devotion he comes to know Me in truth, both who I am and what I am;
then, having known Me in truth, he enters into Me immediately thereafter. 18.55.

Through devotion, he recognizes Me in My true essence—Me who, though appearing with various distinctions created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), am in reality the Supreme Person (*uttama-puruṣa*) who has destroyed all distinctions of adjuncts, who is like space, non-dual pure consciousness whose sole flavor is unity, undecaying, fearless, and deathless. Then, having thus known Me in truth, he enters into Me immediately thereafter, following that very knowledge.

In this context, knowledge (*jñāna*) and the act of entering (*praveśakriyā*) are not intended to be distinct, as it is said: "Without knowing, one enters immediately thereafter. What then? It is knowledge alone, because there is no other result, and because it has been stated: "And know Me also as the Knower of the Field" (*Gītā* 13.2).

Now, is it not contradictory to say, "By that which is the supreme culmination of knowledge, one knows Me" (Gītā 18.50)? If you ask how it is contradictory, it is said in reply: at the very moment and regarding the very object that knowledge arises for the knower, the knower knows that object; thus, he does not require a culmination of knowledge characterized by the repetition of knowledge. And for this reason, one does not know through knowledge alone, but rather knows through the culmination of knowledge, which is the repetition of knowledge. This is not a fault.

The term "culmination" (*niṣṭhā*) is used to designate that state of knowledge—which is endowed with the causes for its own production and maturation, and which is free from opposing factors—that culminates in the certainty of self-experience. This refers to the knowledge of the identity between the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is produced by depending upon the cause for the arising of knowledge—namely, the teacher's instruction according to the scriptures—as well as the auxiliary causes such as the purity of the intellect and qualities like humility.

That state which consists of the firm certainty of experiencing one's own Self, accompanied by the renunciation of all actions based on the cognition of distinctions among the causal factors such as agency, is called the supreme steadfastness in knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*). This very steadfastness in knowledge is described as the fourth kind of devotion (*bhakti*), superior to the three types beginning with the distressed (*ārta*). Through that supreme devotion, one comes to know the Blessed Lord in His true essence; immediately thereafter, the cognition of a distinction between the Lord (*Īśvara*) and the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) ceases entirely.

Therefore, the statement that "one understands Me through devotion characterized by steadfastness in knowledge" is not contradictory. Furthermore, in this context, the entire body of scripture enjoining renunciation—consisting of the Vedāntas, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Smṛtis—is rendered meaningful, as established by reasoning, in such passages as: "Having known... they depart from here and lead the life of a mendicant" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1); "Therefore, they say that among these austerities, renunciation is superior" (Nārada Upaniṣad 2.79); and "Renunciation alone excelled" (Nārada Upaniṣad 2.78).

"Renunciation is the abandonment of actions" (BhG 5.13); "Having abandoned the Vedas, this world, and the next" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.23.13); "Abandon both dharma and adharma" (Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan 329.40), and so forth—these are the statements shown here. And it is not appropriate that these statements be purposeless; nor can they be mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), because they occur within their own specific context and because liberation consists in the nature of the inner self, which is immutable.

For it is not possible for one desiring to go to the eastern ocean and one desiring to go to the western ocean by way of the opposite direction to follow the same path. Furthermore, the steadfastness in knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*) consists in the devoted application to the cultivation of a continuous stream of cognitions directed toward the inner Self; and that is incompatible with coexistence with ritual action, just as going to the western ocean is incompatible [with going to the east]. Experts in the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are certain that there is a contradiction between these two as vast as the distance between a mountain and a mustard seed. Therefore, it is established that the steadfastness in knowledge must be accomplished only through the renunciation of all ritual actions.

The fruit of the yoga of devotion consisting in the worship of the Blessed One through one’s own action is the attainment of perfection—the fitness for steadfastness in knowledge; that yoga of devotion to the Blessed One, by means of which steadfastness in knowledge culminates in the fruit of liberation, is now being praised in this section on the conclusion of the meaning of the scripture, for the sake of strengthening the certainty regarding the meaning of the scripture: "Even while always performing all actions, taking refuge in Me, through My grace he attains the eternal, imperishable state" (18.56).

(18.56) Even while constantly performing all actions— even those that are prohibited— he who has me as his refuge— that is, Vāsudeva, the Lord, as his refuge— meaning one who has surrendered all states of being to me— even he, by my grace, that is, by the grace of me, the Lord, attains the eternal, perpetual, Vaiṣṇava state, which is imperishable. Since this is so:
Renouncing all actions with your mind in Me, regarding Me as the supreme goal, and taking refuge in the yoga of discernment, keep your mind constantly fixed on Me. 18.57.

With the mind—that is, with the intellect of discernment—having renounced all actions, whether their results are visible or invisible, in Me, the Lord, according to the principle stated in the verse, "Whatever you do, whatever you eat" (Gītā 9.27); being "intent on Me"—meaning one for whom I, Vāsudeva, am the supreme goal; and having taken refuge in "the yoga of the intellect"—that is, the state of a concentrated intellect—take that yoga of the intellect as your support.

"Be one whose mind is fixed on Me alone, having no other refuge; with your mind fixed on Me, always and at all times, you shall cross over all difficulties by My grace. But if, out of self-conceit, you do not listen, you shall perish. (18.58)

(18.58) With your mind focused on Me, by My grace you shall cross over—meaning you will transcend—all difficulties and all things hard to surmount that arise from the causes of saṃsāra. But if, out of egoism, thinking "I am wise," you do not listen to what I have said—that is, you do not accept it—then you will perish; you will go to destruction.
Furthermore, you should not think: "I am independent; why should I do what another says?"
If, relying on the ego-sense, you think "I will not fight," this resolve of yours is false; your own nature will compel you.
If, relying on egoism, you think—"I will not fight"—meaning you intend not to engage in battle—this resolve of yours is in vain; for your nature, the very character of a Kshatriya, will compel you.
And because, O Kaunteya, you are bound by your own action born of your nature.

"Out of delusion, you do not wish to do that which you will do even against your will. (18.60) O son of Kuntī, bound by your own nature-born qualities such as heroism and the like as previously described, and firmly fettered by your own individual karma, you shall perform— even though unwilling and under the sway of another— that very action which, out of delusion (*moha*), that is, through lack of discernment, you do not desire to do.
Because,
O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings,
causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion, as if they were mounted on a machine. 18.61.

(18.61) The Lord (*īśvara*), whose nature is to rule, Nārāyaṇa, dwells—attains his abode—in the region of the heart, the region of the heart of all beings, of all living creatures, O Arjuna; he is the pure inner self by nature, one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is purified, as seen from the Vedic revelation: "The day is black and the day is white" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 6.9.1). He stands there, maintaining his presence.

Regarding how He abides among them, it is said: "causing all beings to revolve," that is, making them perform their revolutions, as if they were mounted upon machines—here the word "as if" (iva) is to be understood as indicating that they are as if presided over by Him, just like wooden puppets and the like mounted on machines. The connection of the words is: "He abides causing them to revolve through His illusory power (māyā), by means of deception.
"Seek refuge in Him alone with your whole being, O Bhārata;
by His grace you shall attain supreme peace and the eternal abode. (18.62)

(18.62) Go for refuge, take shelter in that very Lord as a protection for the sake of removing the suffering of saṃsāra—take shelter with your whole being, with your entire self, O Bhārata. Then, by His grace, through the favor of the Lord, you shall attain supreme, most excellent peace, cessation, and My station, the highest abode of Viṣṇu, which is eternal and everlasting.
Thus has this knowledge, more secret than the secret, been declared to you by Me.
"Having reflected upon this in its entirety, do as you wish.

(18.63) Thus, this knowledge has been declared—that is, told—to you, which is more secret than the secret (*guhyāt guhyataram*), meaning an exceedingly hidden mystery, by me, the omniscient Lord. Having reflected—having performed deliberation and investigation—upon this entire teaching as it has been stated, and upon the collection of matters as they have been explained, do exactly as you desire.
Listen again as I speak; hear once more my supreme word, the most secret of all secrets.
Since you are dearly beloved to Me, I shall therefore speak what is for your benefit. 18.64.

(18.64) This is the most secret of all secrets—the most profoundly hidden and the ultimate mystery. Although it has been spoken more than once, listen again to my supreme, most excellent word. I shall not speak out of fear, nor for the sake of some material gain; rather, because you are my beloved and dear friend, being firm and unswerving in your devotion—on that account, I shall speak and declare to you what is for your highest good, the means for attaining knowledge, for that indeed is the most beneficial of all benefits.
"What is that? He says:
"Fix your mind on Me, be My devotee, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me.
You shall come to Me alone; I promise you this truly, for you are dear to Me. (18.65)

(18.65) Be intent on Me; let your mind be fixed on Me. Be My devotee; be engaged in My worship. Be a sacrificer to Me, having the habit of sacrificing to Me. Bow down to Me; perform even your salutation unto Me alone. Abiding thus, with the goal, the means, and the purpose all surrendered to Vāsudeva alone, you shall come to Me—you will attain Me. I promise this to you as the truth; I make a true pledge regarding this matter, because you are dear to Me.

The meaning of the passage is this: having thus understood the Blessed One’s truthfulness to His promise and having ascertained that the fruit of liberation necessarily follows from devotion to the Blessed One, one should become solely intent upon taking refuge in the Blessed One.

Having concluded the supreme secret of steadfastness in Karma-yoga—namely, taking refuge in the Lord—the author now states that the fruit of steadfastness in Karma-yoga, which is right vision (samyagdarśana) as prescribed in the essence of all Vedānta, must be explained: "Abandoning all duties, take refuge in Me alone."
"I shall liberate you from all evils; do not grieve.

(18.66) "All duties" (*sarvadharmān*): "all" and "those duties" constitute *sarvadharmāḥ*. Here, by the word *dharma*, even *adharma* (unrighteousness) is included, because what is intended to be expressed is *naiṣkarmya* (freedom from action). This is supported by such scriptural and traditional texts as: "Not one who has not desisted from evil conduct" (*Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 1.2.24), and "Abandon both dharma and adharma" (*Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan* 329.40). Thus, "having abandoned all duties" means having renounced all actions.

Take refuge in Me alone—the Self of all, equal, abiding in all beings, the Lord, the Infallible, free from birth in the womb, birth, old age, and death—thinking "I am indeed He"; the meaning is that you should resolve that there is nothing other than Me. I shall liberate you, whose intellect is thus determined, from all sins—which consist of the bonds of dharma and adharma—by manifesting My own essential nature.

And it has been said: "Abiding within their very being, I destroy [their ignorance] with the shining lamp of knowledge" (Gītā 10.11). Therefore, "do not grieve"—the meaning is that you should not give way to sorrow.

In this scripture of the Gītā, what is determined to be the means for attaining supreme liberation (*paramaniḥśreyasa*): is it knowledge, or action, or perhaps both? Whence arises this doubt? On one hand, statements such as "Having known which, one attains immortality" (Gītā 13.12) and "Then, having known Me in truth, after that he enters [Me]" (Gītā 18.55) show the attainment of supreme liberation through knowledge alone. On the other hand, there are statements such as "Your right is to action alone" (Gītā 2.47) and "Perform action alone" (Gītā 4.15).

They demonstrate the necessity of performing ritual actions (*karmāṇi*). Thus, because there is an instruction regarding the necessity of performing both knowledge (*jñāna*) and action, someone might have the doubt that even when combined, they constitute the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). What, then, is the fruit of this inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*) here? Is it not simply the determination that one or the other of these is the means for attaining the supreme good? Therefore, this must be investigated in greater detail.

Self-knowledge, however, is the cause of liberation (*kaivalya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), because it culminates in the fruit of liberation by means of subverting the cognition of duality. The notion of distinctions between action, agent, and fruit has been constantly active within the self due to ignorance (*avidyā*), such as: "This is my work, I am the doer, I shall perform this action for the sake of this result. This ignorance has been operative since beginningless time. Its subverter is [the realization]: "I am this very one, absolute, a non-doer, inactive, and devoid of fruit."

The knowledge concerning the Self, arising in the form "there is nothing other than Me," serves to negate the notion of duality which is the cause for the engagement in ritual action (*karma*). The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to exclude the two opposing positions: that the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results neither from rituals alone, nor from the combination of knowledge and ritual. Furthermore, because the supreme good is not something produced, its being accomplished by means of ritual action is untenable.

For an eternal entity is not produced by action or by knowledge. [Objection: In that case, even knowledge would be useless. [Reply: No, because when it serves to remove ignorance, it culminates in the visible fruit of liberation (*kaivalya*). It is observed that knowledge which removes the darkness of ignorance culminates in the fruit of liberation, just like the fruit of the light of a lamp which removes the darkness of the false cognition of a snake regarding an object such as a rope. For the fruit of the light is the culmination in the rope alone, once the conceptual construction of the snake and so forth has ceased; knowledge is likewise.

Furthermore, in the case of actions with visible purposes—such as the act of cutting or churning fire for which the agent and other factors are actively engaged—it is impossible for them to have any activity directed toward another result or another action once their fruit, such as the production of two pieces of wood or the manifestation of fire, has been attained. Just so, for the knower and other factors engaged in the practice of knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*) which has a visible purpose, it is impossible for there to be engagement in another action once the fruit of self-liberation (*ātmakaivalya*) has been attained; therefore, the practice of knowledge is not accompanied by ritual action.

If it is argued that [the desire for liberation] arises just like the performance of rituals such as the Agnihotra sacrifice, we say no; because when knowledge—which has isolation (*kaivalya*) as its fruit—is attained, the desire for the fruits of ritual action is logically untenable. For once knowledge whose fruit is isolation is reached, just as one who has obtained the result of water flooding everywhere has no further desire for the results of digging wells or constructing tanks, so too there is no possibility of desiring any other fruit or the ritual actions that serve as its means.

For it is not possible for one engaged in an action whose fruit is the attainment of a kingdom to be simultaneously engaged in an action whose fruit is the attainment of mere land, nor can there be a desire directed toward that [land]. Therefore, action does not possess the nature of being a means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Nor do knowledge and action possess this nature when combined. Furthermore, knowledge—which has liberation as its fruit—does not depend on the assistance of action, because they are contradictory, since knowledge functions by removing ignorance. Indeed, darkness is not the remover of darkness. Therefore, knowledge alone is the means to the supreme good.

No; for there would be the incurrence of sin (*pratyavāya*) from the non-performance of obligatory duties (*nitya-karma*), and because liberation (*kaivalya*) is eternal. As for the claim that the attainment of liberation occurs solely through knowledge, that is incorrect; because there would be sin—characterized by the attainment of hell and the like—from the non-performance of those obligatory rites prescribed in the Śruti. [Objection: If that is so, then since there is no liberation from actions, there is indeed no liberation at all. [Response: This is not a fault; because liberation is eternal.

From the performance of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*), there is the non-occurrence of transgression; from the non-performance of prohibited acts, there is the non-arising of an undesirable body; and from the avoidance of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*), there is the non-arising of a desirable body. Furthermore, when the body that initiated the present existence has fallen and the fruit of the karma that produced it has been exhausted, there is an absence of any cause for the production of another body. Since the self (*ātman*) no longer performs passion and other such afflictions, its abiding in its own essential nature is itself liberation (*kaivalya*); thus, liberation is achieved without effort.

If it is argued that there can be no destruction of the results of actions performed in many previous births—such as those resulting in the attainment of heaven or hell—which have not yet begun to bear fruit because their experience has not yet commenced, we say: no; for the experience of the suffering caused by the exertion of performing obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) is logically consistent with being the experience of those very results. Alternatively, obligatory duty may serve to destroy previously acquired demerit (*durita*), just like a rite of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

[Objection: Since commenced actions are exhausted solely through experience, and since no new actions are undertaken, liberation (*kaivalya*) is established without effort. [Reply: No; for the Śruti states, "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8), thus showing that no path other than knowledge exists for liberation. Furthermore, just as it is impossible to envelop space with a hide, the Śruti declares the impossibility of liberation for the ignorant. And the Purāṇic Smṛti says, "One attains liberation through knowledge."

Furthermore, because the destruction of meritorious actions whose fruits have not yet begun is impossible. Just as there is the possibility of previously acquired evil deeds whose fruits have not yet begun, so too there would be the possibility of meritorious deeds whose fruits have not yet begun. And since their destruction is impossible without producing another body, liberation would be impossible. Moreover, because the eradication of passion, hatred, and delusion—the causes of merit and demerit—is impossible except through the knowledge of the Self, the eradication of merit and demerit is impossible.

Furthermore, because it is heard in scripture that obligatory (*nitya*) rites have merit as their fruit, and because of Smṛti texts such as "The castes and stages of life are established in their own duties" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.2.2.3), the exhaustion of karma through these rites is untenable.

As for those who say: "Obligatory rites, being of the nature of suffering, are merely the fruit of previously committed evil deeds (*durita*); they have no other fruit apart from their own essential nature, since none is heard of in scripture, and they are enjoined on account of specific occasions such as living"; this is not so, because it is impossible for actions that have not been performed to yield a fruit, and it would result in the impossibility of accounting for the specific fruits of suffering.

As for the claim that the fruit of evil deeds committed in previous births is experienced as the suffering of exertion in the performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), that is incorrect. For it is not logically tenable that the fruit of a karma—which has not yet sprouted at the time of death to yield its result—should be experienced in a birth initiated by another karma.
