Otherwise, there would be no reason why the experience of the fruit of a karma leading to hell could not occur in a birth initiated by karmas such as the *agnihotra* for the sake of experiencing the fruit of heaven.

Furthermore, it is untenable for that evil (durita) to have specific sufferings as its fruit; for if one were to assume that when many evils exist—each having as its fruit the means to various distinct sufferings—the fruit of the performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) consists solely of the suffering from the exertion of such performance, then the affliction caused by pairs of opposites (*dvandva*), diseases, and so forth, could not possibly be postulated as being without a cause. One cannot reasonably maintain that only the suffering from the exertion of performing obligatory rites is the fruit of previously accumulated evil, while the suffering from carrying stones on the head and the like is not.

Moreover, this which is being stated—that the suffering resulting from the exertion of performing obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) is the fruit of previously committed evil deeds—is irrelevant. Why? Because it was the established premise that the destruction of previously committed evil deeds whose fruits have not yet ripened is not possible. In that context, you have asserted that the suffering from the exertion of performing obligatory duties is the fruit of action whose fruit has already ripened, and not of that whose fruit has not yet ripened.

Now, if you consider that all previously committed evil deeds (*durita*) have already begun to yield their fruit, then the qualification that "the fruit is merely the suffering of the exertion in performing obligatory rites" (*nityakarman*) is improper. Furthermore, it would follow that the injunctions for obligatory rites are purposeless, since the destruction of such evil deeds whose fruits have already begun is logically established through experience alone. Moreover, if the fruit of the enjoined obligatory rite were suffering, then that [suffering] would be seen as arising solely from the exertion of performing the obligatory rite, just like physical exercise and the like.
Therefore, the conceptualization that it belongs to another is untenable, because it is prescribed with the purpose of sustaining life and so forth.

In the case of obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*), just as with expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), it is untenable that they constitute the fruit of previously committed evil deeds. For when an expiation is prescribed for a particular sinful act as its occasion, that expiation is not the fruit of that sin. If, on the other hand, the suffering of the expiation were the fruit of that very sin which serves as the occasion, then the suffering resulting from the exertion of performing obligatory rites—occasioned by such things as the mere fact of living—would also have to be considered the fruit of those occasions (living, etc.), since there is no difference between obligatory rites and expiatory rites in their being occasional (*naimittika*) in nature.

Furthermore, since the suffering resulting from the exertion of performing both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites such as the *agnihotra* is equal, there would be no distinction between them; thus, the suffering from the exertion of performing obligatory rites alone would not be the fruit of previously committed evil deeds, whereas the suffering from the exertion of performing optional rites would be. Consequently, it would follow that even the latter is a fruit of previously committed evil deeds.

And this being so, the following are untenable: (1) the assumption based on presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that the suffering resulting from the exertion of performing obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) is the fruit of previously committed evil deeds—since no fruit is heard of for obligatory acts and their injunction would otherwise be inexplicable; (2) the inference that because the injunctions of obligatory acts would otherwise be inexplicable, they must have a fruit other than the suffering of the exertion of performance; and (3) [the claim of] contradiction.

Moreover, this is contradictory: it is asserted that while the obligatory rite (*nityakarman*) is being performed, the fruit of another action is experienced; yet, if it is admitted that this very experience is the fruit of the obligatory rite, then it is contradictory to say both that the obligatory rite has a fruit and that the obligatory rite has no fruit.

Furthermore, when the optional *agnihotra* and other such rites are being performed, the obligatory *agnihotra* and others are also performed by that very same ritual procedure (*tantra*). Thus, the fruit of the optional *agnihotra* and so forth would be exhausted by the very suffering of the exertion involved in it, because they share the same procedure. Alternatively, if the fruit of the optional *agnihotra* were something else entirely, such as heaven, then the suffering of the exertion for its performance would also have to be distinct [from that of the obligatory rite]. But this is not the case, as it contradicts what is observed.

For the suffering arising from the exertion of performing obligatory (*nitya*) rites is not seen to be distinct from the suffering arising from the exertion of performing optional (*kāmya*) rites. Furthermore, there is another point: an action that is neither enjoined nor prohibited bears fruit at its own time, but an action enjoined or prohibited by the scriptures would not bear fruit at that same time. Otherwise, there would be no effort toward the expectation of unseen fruits such as heaven, since the essential nature of actions like the *agnihotra* would be indistinguishable [from other acts], and the obligatory rites would be exhausted merely through the suffering of their performance.

The fact that optional rites (*kāmya-karman*) yield great fruits such as heaven is not something that can be attributed to the mere desire for those fruits, provided there is no excess in their constituent parts (*aṅga*), procedures (*itikartavyatā*), and so forth. Therefore, it is never logically tenable that obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*) lack an unseen fruit (*adṛṣṭa*). Consequently, knowledge alone—and not the performance of obligatory rites—is the cause for the complete destruction of action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, which is preceded by ignorance (*avidyā*). For all action whatsoever has ignorance and desire as its seed.

And thus it has been established that ritual action pertains to the ignorant, while the steadfastness in knowledge—preceded by the renunciation of all actions—pertains to the wise, as seen in such passages as: "Both of them do not know" (Gītā 2.19); "He who knows the indestructible, eternal" (Gītā 2.21); "By the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṃkhyas, and by the yoga of action for the Yogins" (Gītā 3.3); "For the ignorant, who are attached to action" (Gītā 3.26); and "But he who knows the truth, O mighty-armed one... (Gītā 4.34).

"Thinking that 'the qualities act upon the qualities,' one does not become attached" (Gītā 3.28); "having mentally renounced all actions, he remains" (Gītā 5.13); "the disciplined knower of reality should think, 'I do nothing at all'—that is to say, unlike the ignorant person who thinks, 'I am doing'; for one who desires to ascend, action is the means, but for one who has ascended and is established in yoga, tranquility alone is the means."

All three types of ignorant ones are base, for it is said: "But the wise one is My very Self—that is My view" (Gītā 7.18); and "The ignorant ritualists, desiring objects of desire, obtain the state of going and returning. On the other hand, those who are single-minded, meditating on Me, ever-disciplined, worship the Self as described—resembling space—and [it is said]: "I give that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me" (Gītā 10.10); that is to say, the ignorant ritualists do not come to Me.

Those who perform the work of the Blessed One, though they may be most disciplined among practitioners, are yet ignorant; their means culminate in the renunciation of fruits that become progressively inferior. However, those who worship the indefinable Imperishable possess the means described from "He who is not hateful toward any being" (Gītā 12.13) up to the end of the chapter, as well as the means of knowledge described in the three chapters beginning with the "Kṣetra" (Chapter 13). These are the knowers of the reality of the Blessed One, who have renounced all action based on the five causes such as the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and who abide in the supreme steadfastness in knowledge, possessing the realization of the oneness of the Self and its lack of agency.

The threefold fruit of actions—unpleasant results and so forth—does not accrue to those wandering mendicants who are supreme *paramahaṃsas* and have found refuge in the oneness of the Self with the nature of the Blessed Lord; however, it certainly does accrue to others who are ignorant, ritualistic performers, and non-renunciants. This is the division of the duties prescribed in the scripture of the *Gītā*.

If it is argued that the state of being preceded by ignorance (*avidyā*) for all action is unestablished, we say no; because it is like the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and so forth. Even though obligatory (*nitya*) action is understood through scripture, it nevertheless occurs only for one who possesses ignorance. Just as action characterized by the killing of a Brahmin and so forth—which, though understood through prohibitive scripture, becomes a cause of harm for one possessed of defects such as ignorance and desire, since otherwise its engagement would be impossible—so too it is with obligatory, occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) actions.

If it is argued that activity toward obligatory and other such rites is untenable as long as the Self is not known to be distinct from the body, we say no; for we observe activity in the form "I act" directed toward action—which consists of movement—by one who does not possess a [transcendent] Self. If it is argued that the notion of "I" with respect to the aggregate of the body and so forth is figurative (*gauṇa*) rather than false (*mithyā*), we say no; for it would follow that the notion is figurative even with respect to its effects. The notion of "I" with respect to the aggregate of the body and so forth, which belongs to the Self, is figurative.

Just as in the case of one's own son [it is said], "You indeed are my very self, O son" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.11), and as in common worldly usage, "This cow is my very life-breath," so it is here. This is certainly not a false cognition (*mithyā-pratyaya*). A false cognition occurs, however, in the case of a post and a person when their distinguishing features are not perceived. Nor does a figurative cognition (*gauṇa-pratyaya*) serve the purpose of the primary object, because its function is to praise the subject through the use of an elliptical simile (*luptopamā-śabda*).

Just as in the cases "Devadatta is a lion" and "The boy is fire," [the expressions] are intended solely for the purpose of praising Devadatta and the boy by virtue of their possessing common qualities such as cruelty and ferocity—being like a lion or like fire—and yet no actual effect of a lion or an actual effect of fire is accomplished on account of the secondary (gauna) verbal cognition; rather, one experiences misfortune through the effect of a false cognition.

One recognizes that the object of a figurative cognition is not the primary thing, as in "This is not a lion; it is Devadatta," or "This is not fire; it is a young brahmin boy. Likewise, action performed by the Self through the aggregate of the body and so forth—which is used figuratively—could not be said to have been performed by the primary Self, which is the true object of the notion of "I. For action performed by a figurative lion or fire could not be considered performed by the primary lion or fire.

Furthermore, no action is performed by the primary lion or fire through cruelty or ferocity, because they exist solely for the purpose of praise. And those being praised know, "I am not the lion," "I am not the fire"; for they do not think, "This is the work of the lion, and this is the work of me, the fire. Likewise, the realization, "This is not the work of the aggregate, but of me, the primary Self," would be more appropriate; it is not, however, "I am the agent, and this is my work."

And as for what they say—that "the Self performs action by means of its own memory, desire, and effort, which are caused by karma"—this is not so, because these are preceded by false cognition (*mithyā-pratyaya*). For memory, desire, effort, and the like are preceded by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of the results of actions that were themselves caused by false cognitions regarding the desirable and the undesirable.

Just as in this present life, merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) and the experience of their fruits are produced by attachment, aversion, and so forth, based on the conceit of identity with the aggregate of the body and other factors, so it was in past and even more distant lives; thus, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is beginningless and produced by ignorance (*avidyā*).

The past and the future are to be inferred. Consequently, it is established that through steadfastness in knowledge accompanied by the renunciation of all actions, there is the absolute cessation of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, because the identification with the body is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), when that [ignorance] ceases, the body cannot logically arise, and thus transmigratory existence is no longer possible. The identification of the self with the aggregate of the body and so forth is of the nature of ignorance; for in the world, no one who knows "I am distinct from cows and other things, and cows and other things are distinct from me" ever conceives of them as "I."

However, like the cognition of a person in what is actually a post, one who lacks discrimination might form the notion "I" with respect to the aggregate of the body and so forth; this does not occur for one who knows through discrimination. As for the notion of "I" directed toward a son, as in the text, "O son, you are indeed my self" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.11), that is based on the relationship between the born and the progenitor and is therefore figurative (*gauṇa*). And by means of a figurative self, a primary purpose cannot be accomplished—just as eating and other such acts cannot be performed by a figurative lion or fire—as is the case with the primary functions of a real lion or fire.

If it is argued that because the authority of the Vedic injunctions concerns objects not perceived by the senses, the duty of the Self is indeed performed by the secondary selves—the body, the senses, and so forth—this is not so; for their status as "Self" is produced by ignorance. Furthermore, the body, the senses, and the rest are not secondary selves; rather, being non-Selves, they are made out to be the Self solely through false cognition, since they exist when that [ignorance] exists and cease to exist when it is absent.

For among the undiscriminating—the ignorant children—it is observed that at the time of ignorance there arises the notion of "I" with respect to the aggregate of the body and so forth, such as "I am tall" or "I am fair. However, for the discriminating who know "I am other than the aggregate of the body and so forth," the notion of "I" does not arise with respect to that aggregate at that time. Therefore, because [the notion of "I"] is absent when the false notion is absent, it is produced by that [false notion] alone; it is not figurative.

For a figurative cognition or the employment of a word occurs only in the case of a lion and Devadatta, or a fire and a young brahmin, when their specific and general qualities are perceived as distinct; it does not occur when their specific and general qualities are not so perceived. As for what was stated—that [the identity of the Self with Brahman follows] "from the authority of scripture"—that is not correct, because the authority of that scripture pertains to matters beyond the reach of the senses (adṛṣṭa).

For the authority of the Śruti pertains to objects not apprehended by perception and other means of knowledge—namely, the relationship between the means and the end in the Agnihotra and other rites—and not to the domain of perception and the like, because its authority consists in revealing what has not been previously seen. Therefore, it is impossible to assume that the notion of "I," which is caused by perceived false knowledge, is merely figurative with respect to the aggregate of the body and so forth. Indeed, even a hundred Śrutis do not attain authority if they were to say, "Fire is cold or without light.
Even if they were to say, "Fire is cold or without light," there would still be some other intended meaning for the Śruti.

It is to be accepted because its validity cannot otherwise be accounted for; however, it is not [to be accepted] if it contradicts another means of valid knowledge or if it is self-contradictory. If it is argued that the scripture lacks authority due to the absence of an agent—since ritual action has an agent who possesses false cognition—the answer is no; for its purposefulness is established in the context of the knowledge of Brahman.

If it is argued that, like the scriptural injunctions regarding ritual action (*karmavidhi*), the scriptural injunctions regarding the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) would likewise result in a lack of authority, we say no; for there is no possibility of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*). Just as the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) with respect to the aggregate of the body and so forth is sublated once the Self is realized through the scriptural injunction for the knowledge of Brahman, so too the realization of the Self within the Self can never, by anyone, in any way whatsoever, be sublated. This is because such realization is inseparable from its fruit, just as fire is inseparably hot and luminous.

Nor does this render the scriptural injunctions regarding ritual action invalid, because their purpose is to produce an orientation toward the inner self by generating successive new impulses that suppress preceding ones. Even if the means is false, it possesses truth precisely through the truth of the end to be attained, just as in the case of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) that are supplementary to an injunction; and as in the world, when milk and such are to be made a child drink, one speaks of "cutting the top-knot" (*cūḍāvardhana*) and so forth to children or the insane.

Furthermore, the validity of those [means of knowledge] existing in other states is established directly, just as the validity of perception and so forth—caused by the identification with the body—is established prior to the knowledge of the Self. As for what you think—that although the Self is not itself active, it acts by its mere presence, and that alone constitutes the primary agency of the Self; [that is not so].

Just as it is well known that when soldiers are fighting, the king is said to be "fighting" even though he does not fight himself, yet is considered either victorious or defeated merely by his presence; and just as a commander-in-chief acts through speech alone, and the connection between the action and its fruit is seen to belong to both the king and the commander-in-chief; and just as the work of the officiating priests belongs to the sacrificer, so too the actions of the body and other instruments would be performed by the Self, because the fruit of the action accrues to the Self.

And just as a turner possesses primary agency even while inactive because he causes the iron to revolve, so too is it for the Self—this is incorrect; for it would entail that one who does not act is still an agent (*kāraka*). If you argue that an agent can be of many kinds, we say no; for even kings and others are seen to possess primary agency through their own activity. Indeed, a king himself engages in combat through his own action.

In the case of warriors, their primary agency lies in fighting and bestowing wealth, as well as in the enjoyment of the fruits of victory and defeat; likewise, for the sacrificer, his primary agency lies in the principal renunciation and the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Therefore, it is understood that any metaphorical attribution of agency to one who is not actively engaged is merely figurative (*gauṇa*).

If primary agency, characterized by one's own specific activity, is not perceived in the case of kings, sacrificers, and others, then agency would have to be figuratively attributed to them based on mere proximity—just as a magnet is said to cause the movement of iron—but such a primary activity is not observed in kings, sacrificers, and so forth. Therefore, agency based on mere proximity is merely figurative. And that being the case, the connection with the fruit of the action must likewise be merely figurative.

A primary effect is not brought about by a secondary means. Therefore, this which is sung—that "the Self, though inactive through the operations of the body and so forth, would be the agent and the enjoyer"—is indeed false. However, everything is possible when caused by delusion, as in a dream or in a magical illusion (māyā). Furthermore, during states such as deep sleep or meditative absorption, where the continuous stream of the delusive notion of the Self in the body and so forth is interrupted, no such misfortune as agency, enjoyment, and the like is perceived.

Therefore, it is established that this wandering in saṃsāra is caused solely by the cognition of error and is not the ultimate reality; thus, through right vision, there is absolute cessation. Having summarized the entire meaning of the Gītā scripture in this chapter, and especially at the end here, having made a concise conclusion for the sake of strengthening the meaning of the scripture, [the Lord] now states the rule for the tradition of the scripture:
"This [teaching] is never to be given to one who has not practiced austerity, nor to one who is not devoted."
"And it should not be spoken to one who does not wish to hear, nor to one who finds fault with Me.

(18.67) This scripture has been spoken by Me for your benefit, for the purpose of cutting off the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). It is connected with the distant term "should not be spoken" as follows: it must not be spoken to one who lacks austerity (*atapaska*), that is, to one devoid of penance. Even if a person possesses austerity, it must never—at no stage whatsoever—be spoken to one who is not devoted, meaning one who lacks devotion toward the Guru and the Divine. Furthermore, even if a person is devoted and possesses austerity, it must not be spoken to one who is unwilling to listen (*aśuśrūṣu*).

Furthermore, he who, regarding me, Vāsudeva, as an ordinary man, feels malice—attributing faults such as self-praise while failing to recognize my lordship—is also unfit; for him too, this should not be spoken. This scripture is to be taught to one who is free from malice toward the Blessed One, who is ascetic, devoted, and desirous of hearing.

This is understood by implication. In this context, because the option between "one who is wise" (*medhāvī*) and "one who is ascetic" (*tapasvī*) is presented, [it follows that] it should be taught either to an ascetic endowed with service and devotion, or to a wise person endowed with those same qualities. It should not be taught to one who lacks service and devotion, whether they be ascetic or wise. Nor should it be taught to one who harbors malice toward the Blessed One, even if they possess every other virtue. And it should be taught to one who possesses devotion and service toward the Guru. Such is the rule of the scriptural tradition (*śāstra-saṃpradāya-vidhi*). Now, he states the fruit for the author of the tradition:
He who shall declare this supreme secret among my devotees, having offered the highest devotion to me, will undoubtedly come to me alone. 18.68.

Whoever shall declare—meaning, shall speak and establish both in letter and in spirit—this supreme book, which is as described, consisting of the dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna for the sake of the highest beatitude, and which is a secret, most to be guarded, among those devoted to Me (madbhakteṣu)—just as it has been declared by Me to you; from the repeated mention of "devotion" (bhakti), it is understood that one becomes a fit recipient for the transmission of this scripture solely through devotion.

"How will he speak?"—it is said: "Having established supreme devotion toward Me, thinking, 'Service to the Blessed One, the Supreme Teacher, Acyuta, is being performed by me'—this is the meaning. This is his fruit: he shall come to Me alone; he is indeed liberated. There is no doubt here; one should not entertain any doubt. Furthermore:
"And among men, there is none who does what is more pleasing to Me than he."

And there shall be no one else on earth dearer to me than he. (18.69) Furthermore, among men, there is no one who performs a greater service for me—no one more exceptionally dear—than he who has established this tradition of the scriptures; the meaning is that there is simply no other such person among those currently living. Nor shall there ever be, even in future time, a second person on this earth who shall be dearer to me or perform a greater service than he.
And whoever shall study this sacred dialogue of ours, by him I am worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge; such is my conviction. (18.70)

(18.70) And whoever shall request [others] to recite or himself read this dharma-text—which is consistent with dharma (*dharmya*), meaning not departing from dharma, and which takes the form of a dialogue between us two—by him this [sacrifice] would have been performed. Among the sacrifices consisting of ritual recitation (*vidhi-japa*), whispered recitation (*upāṃśu*), and mental recitation (*mānasa*), the sacrifice of knowledge (*jñāna-yajña*) is the most distinguished because it is purely mental; therefore, the study of the Gītā scripture is praised by means of that sacrifice of knowledge.

Or rather, it is a rule regarding the fruit: the fruit of this [study] becomes equal to the fruit of the sacrifice of knowledge concerning the deities and so forth. "By that study, may I be desired—that is, worshipped—by Him"; such is my mind, my firm resolve.
Now, as for the listener: even a man who hears this with faith and without malice shall obtain this fruit.
Even he, being freed from sin, shall attain the auspicious worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds.

(18.71) Even that man who, being full of faith (*śraddhāvān*), being faithful (*śraddadhānaḥ*), and being free from malice (*anasūyaḥ*)—that is, devoid of envy—should merely listen to this book; by the use of the word "even" (*api*), it is implied how much more so one who possesses knowledge of its meaning—he too, liberated from evil, shall attain the auspicious and praiseworthy worlds of those whose actions are meritorious, such as the performance of the *agnihotra* sacrifice and other rites.

The Teacher asks out of a desire to discern whether the disciple has grasped the meaning of the teaching or not; the intention of the questioner is that, once it is known that he has not grasped it, he may cause him to grasp it even by means of another method. Furthermore, this demonstrates the duty of the Teacher: that one must apply further effort to bring the disciple to fulfillment.
"O Pārtha, has this been heard by you with a one-pointed mind?
O Dhanañjaya, has your delusion born of ignorance been destroyed? (18.72)

(18.72) "O Pārtha, have you heard what was spoken by me, and having heard it, has it been firmly grasped by you with a one-pointed mind and heart? Or [have you heard it] without negligence? Has that delusion born of ignorance—the confusion caused by ignorance, the state of non-discrimination, the natural lack of discernment—been utterly destroyed? For the sake of which this exertion of yours for hearing the scripture and my exertion as your teacher have been undertaken, O Dhanañjaya? Arjuna said:
Arjuna said:
"O Acyuta, my delusion is destroyed; through your grace, I have regained my memory.
I stand firm, my doubts dispelled; I shall do as you command. (18.73)

(18.73) Delusion born of ignorance—the cause of all the miseries of saṃsāra and as difficult to cross as the ocean—is destroyed. And the memory directed toward the reality of the Self has been attained, through the acquisition of which there is liberation from all the knots of the heart; this has come to me, O Acyuta, by your grace, by your favor, through my taking refuge in your grace.

By this response to the question regarding the destruction of delusion, it is shown with certainty that the fruit of knowing the meaning of all the scriptures is precisely this: for from knowledge comes the destruction of delusion and the attainment of the remembrance of the Self. And thus, in the Śruti, having introduced the statement "I grieve because I do not know the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3), the complete liberation from all knots [of the heart] through the knowledge of the Self is declared.

"The knot of the heart is severed" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8), and "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness? (Īśa Upaniṣad 7)—such is the wording of the Vedic mantra. Now, I am established in your teaching, with my doubts gone and my uncertainties dispelled. I shall carry out your word. My intention is that, through your grace, I have achieved my purpose and nothing further remains to be done by me. Thus the meaning of the scripture is concluded. Now, in order to demonstrate the connection of the narrative, Sañjaya said: Sañjaya said.
Sañjaya said:
Thus have I heard this wonderful conversation between Vāsudeva and the high-souled Pārtha, which causes the hair to stand on end. 18.74.

(18.74) Thus have I heard this wonderful dialogue, exactly as it was spoken, between Vāsudeva and the high-souled Pārtha— a conversation that causes extreme amazement, that makes the hair stand on end, and that produces horripilation; and this very [dialogue].
By the grace of Vyāsa, I have heard this supreme secret,
the Yoga, from Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga himself, as he spoke it directly. 18.75.

Then, by the grace of Vyāsa and through the attainment of divine vision, I heard this most secret and supreme discourse on Yoga—Yoga being so called because it is the subject matter of the book—or rather, this very Yoga as a dialogue between Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, and Arjuna, spoken by Him directly and not through tradition.
O King, remembering again and again this wonderful and meritorious dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna, I rejoice over and over again. (18.76)

(18.76) O King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, remembering again and again at every moment this wondrous dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna— this meritorious discourse which destroys sin even by being heard— I rejoice over and over again at every moment;
and remembering again and again that most wondrous form of Hari.
My wonder is great, O King, and I rejoice again and again.
(18.77) Recalling again and again that most wonderful universal form of Hari, my wonder is great, O King, and I rejoice again and again.
What more need be said?
Wherever there is Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, and wherever there is Pārtha, the wielder of the bow, there will surely be prosperity, victory, welfare, and sound policy; this is my conviction. 18.78.

(18.78) In whichever side (*pakṣa*) there is Kṛṣṇa—the Lord of Yoga (*yogeśvara*), for He is the master of all yogas because He is the source of the seed of all yoga—and in whichever side there is Pārtha, the wielder of the bow Gāṇḍīva, in that side of the Pāṇḍavas is *Śrī*—that is, victory; in that very side is *bhūti*, which is the specific expansion of *Śrī*; and in that side is *dhruvā nītiḥ*, meaning a constant and unfailing policy. Such is my conviction.
